scales.valence: -5 catastrophic harm to +5 transformative benefit; a rough estimate of how good or bad the consequence is for people and society if it happens, ignoring how likely it is
scales.probability: 0 to 1, chance the effect becomes material at societal scale by 2035; active effects count as already here and sit past 100%
scales.year: year the effect is or becomes material; 2024 and 2025 mean already observed
scales.evidence: measured = controlled study or large dataset; reported = documented incidents or vendor disclosures; projected = expert forecasts or capability evals; speculative = plausible mechanism, little direct data; drawn as the haze behind each glyph, tight when measured and widest when speculative
scales.stage: active = already a problem or benefit we are dealing with; emerging = early signs visible, not yet widespread; expected = not yet visible, year is the estimate

nodes.label: Basic research accelerates
nodes.summary: AI may speed up basic research. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper won half the 2024 chemistry Nobel for AlphaFold2's protein structure prediction[1], and DeepMind reports AlphaEvolve improved the best known result on about 20% of 50+ open maths problems[2]. One Nature analysis of 41.3 million papers found AI use multiplied output but shrank the range of topics studied by 4.6%[3].

refs.title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024: They cracked the code for proteins' amazing structures, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences 2024
refs.finding: Half of the 2024 chemistry prize went to David Baker for computational protein design and the other half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind for protein structure prediction with their AI model AlphaFold2.

refs.title: AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms, Google DeepMind 2025
refs.finding: Google DeepMind reports AlphaEvolve found an algorithm to multiply 4x4 complex-valued matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's 1969 algorithm, and improved the best known solution in about 20% of over 50 open maths problems.

refs.title: Hao, Xu, Li and Evans 2026, Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus, Nature
refs.finding: Across 41.3 million natural science papers, scientists using AI published 3.02 times more papers and got 4.84 times more citations, but AI adoption shrank the range of topics studied by 4.63% and cut engagement between scientists by 22%.

limiters.evidence: AlphaEvolve works only on problems whose answers an automated evaluator can score; on 50+ open maths problems it improved the best known result in about 20%.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: AlphaEvolve applies to problems whose solution can be written as an algorithm and automatically verified; on over 50 open maths problems it rediscovered the best known solution in about 75% of cases and improved it in about 20%.

limiters.evidence: Industry produced over 90% of notable frontier AI models in 2025.

ref.title: The 2026 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: Industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models in 2025.

limiters.evidence: Across the whole US economy, generative AI assisted only 1% to 5% of work hours in late 2024.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of the US population aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, but it assisted only 1% to 5% of all work hours.

limiters.evidence: Across 41.3 million papers, scientists using AI published 3 times more papers and got 4.8 times more citations, but AI use shrank the range of topics studied by 4.6% and cut engagement between scientists by 22%.

ref.title: Hao, Xu, Li and Evans 2026, Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus, Nature
ref.finding: Across 41.3 million natural science papers, scientists using AI published 3.02 times more papers and got 4.84 times more citations, but AI adoption shrank the range of topics studied by 4.63% and cut engagement between scientists by 22%.

enablers.action: Release models and predictions openly
enablers.evidence: AlphaFold's code and trained weights were released openly with its Nature paper, letting other labs build on it.

ref.title: Jumper et al. 2021, Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature
ref.finding: AlphaFold was competitive with experimental structures in a majority of CASP14 cases, and its source code, trained weights and inference script were released under an open-source licence.

enablers.action: Fund shared compute for public researchers
enablers.evidence: In the US, the NSF-led NAIRR pilot, set up in 2024, has given more than 600 research projects shared access to AI computing, data and models, and NSF is moving it to permanent operation.

ref.title: NAIRR: From 2024 Pilot to a Sustained National AI Research Resource, US National Science Foundation 2026
ref.finding: The NAIRR pilot, set up in 2024 to give researchers and educators access to AI computing, data, models and training, has supported more than 600 research projects and 6,000 students across all 50 states; NSF has opened a call to set up a NAIRR Operations Center for long-term operation.

enablers.action: Build benchmarks with automatic checking
enablers.evidence: AlphaEvolve's results came on problems where a program could score each candidate.

ref.title: AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms, Google DeepMind 2025
ref.finding: AlphaEvolve applies to problems whose solution can be written as an algorithm and automatically verified; on over 50 open maths problems it rediscovered the best known solution in about 75% of cases and improved it in about 20%.

precedents.parallel: A problem open since the 1850s fell only when mathematicians combined their own reasoning with a computer search no human could check by hand, much as AI search now reaches spaces people did not.
precedents.outcome: Appel and Haken's 1976 proof relied on a computer for a part no one could check by hand, and its hand-checked part was so complicated and tedious that no one is known to have verified it in full; a 1997 proof cut the unavoidable set from 1,476 to 633 configurations but still needed a computer.

ref.title: The Four Color Theorem, Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas (Georgia Tech)
ref.finding: Part of Appel and Haken's 1976 proof uses a computer and cannot be verified by hand, and no one is known to have verified the rest in full; the new proof by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas, published in 1997, uses 633 configurations against Appel and Haken's 1,476 and still needs a computer.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine learning system, built before the generative AI wave, cracked a basic science problem that had stalled for decades.
precedents.outcome: AlphaFold reached accuracy competitive with experimental structures in most CASP14 cases, against a field where the structures of only about 100,000 unique proteins had been determined experimentally.

ref.title: Jumper et al. 2021, Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, Nature
ref.finding: Structure prediction had been an open problem for more than 50 years and only about 100,000 unique protein structures had been determined; AlphaFold was competitive with experiment in a majority of CASP14 cases.

nodes.label: Better, cheaper diagnosis
nodes.summary: One Swedish randomised trial of about 106,000 women found AI-supported mammogram reading detected 29% more cancers and cut screen-reading workload by 44%, without significantly more false positives[1]. In a Microsoft study, its diagnostic system was right on 83.2% of hard NEJM case records against 36.1% for generalist physicians, in a controlled benchmark rather than real care[2].

refs.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI): a randomised, controlled, parallel-group, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study, Lancet Digital Health
refs.finding: Among 105,934 women randomised at four screening sites in southwest Sweden, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

refs.title: Nori et al. 2026, Sequential diagnosis with language models, Science
refs.finding: Microsoft's system, which simulates a panel of physicians, reached 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency admissions, against 36.1% and 46.8% for generalist physicians, in a controlled benchmark setting.

refs.title: Gommers et al. 2026, Interval cancer, sensitivity, and specificity comparing AI-supported mammography screening with standard double reading without AI in the MASAI study: a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, population-based, screening-accuracy trial, The Lancet
refs.finding: Among 105,934 randomised women, the interval cancer rate was 1.55 per 1,000 with AI-supported screening against 1.76 with standard double reading (ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.18), meeting the non-inferiority margin; sensitivity was 80.5% against 73.8% and specificity 98.5% in both arms.

limiters.evidence: MASAI ran at four screening sites in southwest Sweden; wider use depends on screening services changing reading workflows.

ref.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI): a randomised, controlled, parallel-group, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study, Lancet Digital Health
ref.finding: Among 105,934 women randomised at four screening sites in southwest Sweden, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

limiters.evidence: AMIE was tested in simulated text consultations with patient-actors, not real clinical care.

ref.title: Tu et al. 2025, Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature
ref.finding: In a randomised, double-blind crossover study of text consultations with patient-actors across 159 scenarios, AMIE had greater diagnostic accuracy than 20 primary care physicians; the authors say text chat is unfamiliar in clinical practice and more research is needed before real-world use.

limiters.evidence: WHO says governments should assign an existing or new regulatory agency to assess and approve large multi-modal models intended for health care or medicine.

ref.title: WHO releases AI ethics and governance guidance for large multi-modal models, WHO 2024
ref.finding: Among over 40 recommendations, WHO says governments should assign an existing or new regulatory agency to assess and approve large multi-modal models and applications intended for use in health care or medicine, as resources permit.

enablers.action: Run randomised screening trials before rollout
enablers.evidence: MASAI randomised women to AI-supported or standard reading and found 29% more cancers.

ref.title: Hernström et al. 2025, Screening performance and characteristics of breast cancer detected in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI): a randomised, controlled, parallel-group, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study, Lancet Digital Health
ref.finding: Among 105,934 women randomised at four screening sites in southwest Sweden, AI-supported reading detected 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading, 29% more, without a significant rise in false positives, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.2%.

enablers.action: Use AI as triage for one of two readers
enablers.evidence: In one Swedish trial, AI-supported reading cut screen-reading workload by 44% and met the safety threshold for cancer detection.

ref.title: Lång et al. 2023, Artificial intelligence-supported screen reading versus standard double reading in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI): a clinical safety analysis of a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study, Lancet Oncology
ref.finding: In an interim analysis of 80,033 Swedish women, AI-supported reading detected 6.1 cancers per 1,000 against 5.1 with standard double reading, met the safety threshold of more than 3 per 1,000, and cut screen-reading workload by 44.3%.

enablers.action: Require post-deployment monitoring of health AI
enablers.evidence: WHO recommends independent post-release auditing and impact assessments of large multi-modal models used at scale in health.

ref.title: WHO releases AI ethics and governance guidance for large multi-modal models, WHO 2024
ref.finding: WHO's over 40 recommendations include mandatory post-release auditing and impact assessments of large multi-modal models used at scale, by independent third parties.

precedents.parallel: Software that flagged suspicious areas on mammograms was paid for and adopted across US screening on the promise that it would find more cancers.
precedents.outcome: Across about 625,000 screening exams from 2003 to 2009, sensitivity was 85.3% with CAD and 87.3% without and specificity was unchanged, while the tool cost over $400 million a year; this is a warning about adoption without proof, not proof that modern AI reading fails.

ref.title: Lehman et al. 2015, Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Screening Mammography With and Without Computer-Aided Detection, JAMA Internal Medicine
ref.finding: CAD did not improve diagnostic accuracy across 625,625 digital screening mammograms from 2003 to 2009; in 107 radiologists who read both ways, sensitivity was 83.3% with CAD against 89.6% without.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative AI system was cleared to diagnose diabetic eye disease in primary care without a specialist reading the image, the same promise of cheaper diagnosis at the point of care.
precedents.outcome: In a prospective trial at 10 US primary care sites with 900 enrolled patients, it reached 87.2% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity and became the first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic; the study was funded by the maker.

ref.title: Abramoff et al. 2018, Pivotal trial of an autonomous AI-based diagnostic system for detection of diabetic retinopathy in primary care offices, npj Digital Medicine
ref.finding: Sensitivity 87.2% and specificity 90.7% in 819 analysable participants; first FDA-authorised autonomous AI diagnostic.

nodes.label: A personal tutor for every student
nodes.summary: AI tutors gave large gains in two early trials. Harvard physics students tutored by AI had median gains more than double an active-learning class's[1], and AI tutoring in Nigeria raised English scores by 0.23 standard deviations[2]. Without guardrails it can reverse: in one trial, Turkish high school students using plain GPT-4 scored 17% lower than controls once it was removed[3].

refs.title: Kestin et al. 2025, AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting, Scientific Reports
refs.finding: In one trial of 194 students in an introductory Harvard physics course, median learning gains with an AI tutor were more than double those from an in-class active-learning lesson, with a median 49 minutes on task; the study covered two lessons in one course.

refs.title: De Simone et al. 2025, From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125
refs.finding: In a randomised trial, six weeks of English tutoring with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) for first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria raised scores by 0.31 standard deviations on a combined assessment and 0.23 in English, which the authors equate to 1.5 to 2 years of business-as-usual schooling.

refs.title: Bastani et al. 2025, Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS
refs.finding: In one Turkish high school with nearly 1,000 students, plain GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but cut later exam grades by 17% once access was removed; a hint-giving GPT Tutor largely mitigated the harm.

limiters.evidence: In one trial of about 1,000 Turkish high school students, those given plain GPT-4 for practice scored 17% lower than controls once AI was removed.

ref.title: Bastani et al. 2025, Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS
ref.finding: In one Turkish high school with nearly 1,000 students, plain GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but cut later exam grades by 17% once access was removed; a hint-giving GPT Tutor largely mitigated the harm.

limiters.evidence: Only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet.

ref.title: Almost three-quarters of the population are online, ITU Facts and Figures 2025
ref.finding: 74% of the world's population were online in 2025, up from 71% a year earlier, but only 23% of the population of low-income countries use the internet.

limiters.evidence: Fewer than half of US K-12 computer science teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: In the US, 81% of K-12 computer science teachers say AI should be part of foundational computer science education, but fewer than half feel equipped to teach it.

enablers.action: Design tutors to give hints, not answers
enablers.evidence: A hint-giving tutor built with teacher input largely removed the learning loss in one trial of about 1,000 Turkish high school students.

ref.title: Bastani et al. 2025, Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS
ref.finding: In one Turkish high school with nearly 1,000 students, plain GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but cut later exam grades by 17% once access was removed; a hint-giving GPT Tutor largely mitigated the harm.

enablers.action: Pair AI tutoring with teacher guidance
enablers.evidence: In the Nigeria pilot, trained teachers introduced each topic, kept students on task and flagged AI errors; gains were about 0.3 standard deviations.

ref.title: Addressing the learning crisis with generative AI: lessons from Edo State in Nigeria, World Bank 2025
ref.finding: Trained teachers introduced each topic, kept students on task and flagged AI errors; gains were about 0.3 standard deviations overall and 0.24 in English.

enablers.action: Run tutoring in school computer labs
enablers.evidence: The Nigeria pilot ran twice a week after school in computer labs; many students had never used a computer before.

ref.title: From chalkboards to chatbots in Nigeria: 7 lessons to pioneer generative AI for education, World Bank 2024
ref.finding: From June to July 2024, 800 first-year senior secondary students in Edo State took after-school English classes in computer labs twice a week, with teachers guiding their prompts; many had never used a computer before.

precedents.parallel: One-to-one tutoring was claimed to lift students two standard deviations, the same hope now placed on an AI tutor for every child.
precedents.outcome: The claim came from three-week dissertation experiments, one of them never published, that combined tutoring with extra testing and feedback, and their effects have never been replicated; a 2020 meta-analysis of 96 randomised tutoring studies found an average effect of 0.37 standard deviations.

ref.title: von Hippel 2024, Two-Sigma Tutoring: Separating Science Fiction from Science Fact, Education Next
ref.finding: Average effect across 96 randomised tutoring studies was 0.37 SD, far below Bloom's 2.0.

precedents.event: One Laptop per Child in Peru
precedents.parallel: Putting a learning device in every child's hands was expected to transform learning in low-income schools, the same bet as unguarded AI access.
precedents.outcome: A randomised evaluation in 531 rural primary schools, tracked over 10 years, found no significant effect on academic performance or on finishing primary and secondary school, some evidence of worse grade progression, and better computer skills but not cognitive skills; teachers made little use of the laptops in class. A laptop without tutoring design differs from a guarded AI tutor, which is the point.

ref.title: Cueto, Beuermann, Cristia, Malamud and Pardo 2025, Laptops in the Long Run: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program in Rural Peru, NBER w34495
ref.finding: Across 531 rural Peruvian primary schools over 10 years, laptops had no significant effect on academic performance, school completion or university enrolment, with some evidence of worse grade progression; computer skills rose but cognitive skills did not.

nodes.label: Assistive AI for disabled people
nodes.summary: Vision models can describe the world on demand for blind and low-vision people; in 2023 Be My Eyes launched a GPT-4-based assistant that answers questions about photos users send, and offers a sighted volunteer when it cannot[1]. Errors remain a problem: in one interview study of 26 blind people, mistakes in AI visual assistance were hard to check without sight[2].

refs.title: Introducing Be My AI (formerly Virtual Volunteer) for People who are Blind or Have Low Vision, Powered by OpenAI's GPT-4, Be My Eyes 2023
refs.finding: In March 2023 Be My Eyes announced a GPT-4-based assistant that answers questions about photos users send; if it cannot answer, it offers to connect the user to a sighted volunteer.

refs.title: Misfitting With AI: How Blind People Verify and Contest AI Errors, Alharbi et al., ASSETS 2024
refs.finding: In interviews with 26 blind people, AI visual assistance errors were hard to verify non-visually, with tools struggling on complex document layouts, multiple languages and cultural artifacts.

limiters.evidence: 2.2 billion people were offline in 2025; only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet.

ref.title: Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides, ITU 2025
ref.finding: 2.2 billion people were offline in 2025, down from a revised 2.3 billion in 2024; only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet, against 94% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In one interview study of 26 blind people, AI visual assistants made errors that were hard to check without sight, notably with complex layouts, other languages and cultural objects.

ref.title: Misfitting With AI: How Blind People Verify and Contest AI Errors, Alharbi et al., ASSETS 2024
ref.finding: In interviews with 26 blind people, AI visual assistance errors were hard to verify non-visually, with tools struggling on complex document layouts, multiple languages and cultural artifacts.

limiters.evidence: Text translation reaches about 200 of the world's 7,000+ languages, and the data such models need is not available in volume for low-resource languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB translates text across 200 languages; the authors note that the data such models need is not equally available for the world's 7,000+ languages and not available in volume for low-resource ones.

enablers.action: Keep a human volunteer fallback
enablers.evidence: Be My AI offers to connect users to a sighted volunteer when it cannot answer.

ref.title: Introducing Be My AI (formerly Virtual Volunteer) for People who are Blind or Have Low Vision, Powered by OpenAI's GPT-4, Be My Eyes 2023
ref.finding: In March 2023 Be My Eyes announced a GPT-4-based assistant that answers questions about photos users send; if it cannot answer, it offers to connect the user to a sighted volunteer.

enablers.action: Offer core assistive features free
enablers.evidence: Be My Eyes reports free, unlimited calls for blind and low-vision users.

ref.title: Be My Eyes (home page)
ref.finding: The service lists over 1.1 million blind and low-vision users and over 11 million volunteers, and offers free, unlimited calls.

enablers.action: Fund low-resource language speech models
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T translates speech from 101 languages into text in 96, but into speech in only 36.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, SEAMLESS Communication Team, Nature 2025
ref.finding: SeamlessM4T supports speech-to-text translation from 101 to 96 languages and speech-to-speech translation from 101 to 36; contributions are released for non-commercial use.

precedents.parallel: US rules made television distributors caption programming for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers at scale, as AI description now scales visual access for blind people.
precedents.outcome: The FCC adopted its first television captioning rules in 1997, and in 2014 said viewers' experience since then showed the rules needed updating; it added quality standards requiring captions to be accurate, synchronous, complete and appropriately placed. Scale alone did not guarantee quality.

ref.title: Closed Captioning of Video Programming, Report and Order, Declaratory Ruling, and Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (FCC 14-12), FCC 2014
ref.finding: Adopted 20 February 2014, over sixteen years after the FCC's first captioning rules, the order defines four quality standards: captions must be accurate, synchronous, complete and appropriately placed.

nodes.label: Language barriers fall
nodes.summary: Machine translation is reaching low-resource languages: one model covering 200 languages scored on average 44% better (BLEU) than the previous best systems[1]. Accuracy is still uneven for high-stakes text: in one US study of 400 emergency discharge statements, Google Translate kept the meaning of 94% in Spanish but 55% in Armenian[2].

refs.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
refs.finding: One model covering 200 languages, three times as many low-resource as high-resource, scored on average 44% better (BLEU) than the previous best systems; models, data and code were released free for non-commercial use.

refs.title: A Pragmatic Assessment of Google Translate for Emergency Department Instructions, Taira et al., J Gen Intern Med 2021
refs.finding: In one US study, Google Translate kept the meaning of 82.5% of 400 translated discharge statements overall, from 94% in Spanish down to 67.5% in Farsi and 55% in Armenian.

limiters.evidence: NLLB reaches 200 languages; the world has over 7,000.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB covers 200 languages; the authors note the data such models need is not equally available for the world's 7,000+ languages.

limiters.evidence: NLLB's authors note that the large volumes of parallel data such models train on are not available for lower-resource languages.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
ref.finding: Translation models rely on large volumes of parallel data that, by definition, are not available for lower-resource languages.

limiters.evidence: 2.2 billion people were offline in 2025; only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet.

ref.title: Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides, ITU 2025
ref.finding: 2.2 billion people were offline in 2025, down from a revised 2.3 billion in 2024; only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet, against 94% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In one US study of 400 emergency discharge statements, Google Translate kept the meaning of 94% in Spanish but only 55% in Armenian.

ref.title: A Pragmatic Assessment of Google Translate for Emergency Department Instructions, Taira et al., J Gen Intern Med 2021
ref.finding: In one US study, Google Translate kept the meaning of 82.5% of 400 translated discharge statements overall, from 94% in Spanish down to 67.5% in Farsi and 55% in Armenian.

enablers.action: Publish open multilingual models and test sets
enablers.evidence: NLLB's models, code, training data and the FLORES-200 benchmark were released free for non-commercial use.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, NLLB Team, Nature 2024
ref.finding: The FLORES-200 evaluation set covers 204 languages; the translation models and supporting code are freely available for non-commercial use, with the data released on GitHub.

enablers.action: Extend speech-to-speech to more languages
enablers.evidence: SeamlessM4T translates speech from 101 languages and text across 96, but produces speech in only 36.

ref.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages, SEAMLESS Communication Team, Nature 2025
ref.finding: One model supports speech-to-text from 101 to 96 languages, text-to-text in 96 and speech output in 36; released for non-commercial use.

enablers.action: Collect community data for low-resource languages
enablers.evidence: A participatory research effort built machine translation benchmarks for over 30 African languages, with human evaluations for about a third of them.

ref.title: Nekoto et al. 2020, Participatory Research for Low-resourced Machine Translation: A Case Study in African Languages, Findings of EMNLP
ref.finding: A participatory community effort produced machine translation benchmarks for over 30 African languages, with human evaluations for about a third of them.

precedents.parallel: A decade of funding after early demos ended in an official verdict that machine translation was not delivering, the bust side of today's claims that language barriers are falling.
precedents.outcome: In 1966 ALPAC found no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation, ending substantial US funding for about twenty years after roughly $12-20 million had been spent.

ref.title: ALPAC: the (in)famous report, John Hutchins, MT News International no. 14, 1996
ref.finding: ALPAC (November 1966) found no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation and ended substantial US MT funding for some twenty years; US agency spending on US MT research was probably nearer $12-13 million than the $20 million ALPAC stated.

precedents.parallel: The switch from phrase-based to neural translation, before the generative AI wave, brought a large measured jump in machine translation quality.
precedents.outcome: In human side-by-side tests on isolated simple sentences, the neural system reduced translation errors by an average of 60% against Google's phrase-based production system; the paper does not test longer or harder text.

ref.title: Google's Neural Machine Translation System: Bridging the Gap between Human and Machine Translation, Wu et al., arXiv 2016
ref.finding: GNMT reduced translation errors by an average of 60% versus Google's phrase-based system in human side-by-side tests on isolated simple sentences.

precedents.parallel: A tiny public demo was read as proof that general translation was near, the same gap between demo and coverage that low-resource language claims face now.
precedents.outcome: The demonstration used just 250 words and six grammar rules, yet Hutchins writes that it raised expectations of automatic systems capable of high quality translation in the near future.

ref.title: The Georgetown-IBM experiment demonstrated in January 1954, Hutchins, AMTA 2004
ref.finding: A small-scale experiment of 250 words and six grammar rules raised expectations of high quality machine translation in the near future.

nodes.label: Non-technical people build software
nodes.summary: People can build software by describing it and accepting the code unread, which Andrej Karpathy named vibe coding and pitched for throwaway weekend projects[1]. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey, 72% of respondents said no and another 5% emphatically no to vibe coding at work[2]. In one 2026 survey of 162 vibe coders, checking the code depended on experience[3].

refs.title: Andrej Karpathy, post on X introducing vibe coding, February 2025
refs.finding: Describes giving in to the vibes, accepting all changes without reading the diffs, and calls it not too bad for throwaway weekend projects.

refs.title: 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey: AI, Stack Overflow 2025
refs.finding: 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools; more distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%); asked whether vibe coding is part of their professional work, 72% answered no and 5% no, emphatically.

refs.title: From Prompting to Verification: How Experience Shapes Vibe Coding Practices, Fawzy, Tahir and Blincoe, arXiv preprint 2026
refs.finding: In a survey of 162 vibe coders (non-coders, novices and professional developers), non-developers were drawn mainly by accessibility; risks were widely recognised, but the ability to evaluate, debug and verify AI-generated code depended on experience.

limiters.evidence: In one preregistered experiment with 758 knowledge workers at Boston Consulting Group, those using GPT-4 on a task outside its frontier were 19% less likely to reach a correct answer.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality, Dell'Acqua et al., Organization Science 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 knowledge workers at Boston Consulting Group, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% more quickly inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions on a task outside it.

limiters.evidence: In one study of 47 participants, those using a 2022 Codex-based assistant wrote less secure code and were more likely to think it was secure.

ref.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, Perry et al., CCS 2023
ref.finding: In a 47-person user study (CCS 2023), participants with a codex-davinci-002 assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure.

limiters.evidence: In US surveys in August and November 2024, work use of generative AI was about twice as high among workers with a bachelor's or graduate degree (40%) as among those with less education (20%).

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, Bick, Blandin and Deming, NBER Working Paper 32966, 2024 (revised 2025)
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of US adults aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024 and it assisted 1% to 5% of work hours; work adoption was about twice as high for workers with degrees (40%) as for those without (20%).

enablers.action: Train staff in AI literacy
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures to support AI literacy among staff who operate AI systems, without guaranteeing any level for an individual.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI 2026
ref.finding: As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, providers and deployers shall take measures to support AI literacy among staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf; this does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults in AI coding tools
enablers.evidence: CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge asks software makers to make products secure out of the box; it does not target AI coding tools specifically.

ref.title: Secure by Design, CISA
ref.finding: Over 200 software manufacturers signed CISA's voluntary Secure by Design pledge, committing to a good-faith effort on seven security goals.

enablers.action: Rely on falling model prices
enablers.evidence: Epoch AI found the price of reaching a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year, depending on the task.

ref.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI 2025
ref.finding: The price of a fixed capability level fell 9x to 900x per year depending on the task.

precedents.parallel: Personal computer spreadsheets let millions of people without programming training build their own tools, as describing software to an AI does now.
precedents.outcome: An audit of 50 operational spreadsheets found errors in 0.9% to 1.8% of formula cells, depending on the definition, and only 7 of the 50 were free of errors that produced wrong results, an 86% spreadsheet error rate; spreadsheets are still used in almost all businesses.

ref.title: Powell, Baker and Lawson 2009, Errors in Operational Spreadsheets, Journal of Organizational and End User Computing
ref.finding: Errors were found in 0.9% to 1.8% of formula cells across 50 audited operational spreadsheets; 43 of the 50 contained errors that produced wrong results.

precedents.parallel: An influential result built in an end-user tool carried an error nobody checked, the risk when non-specialists build software that others rely on.
precedents.outcome: Reanalysis found coding errors, including a spreadsheet error that left out five countries, selective exclusions and unusual weighting; corrected average growth for countries with debt above 90% of GDP was 2.2%, not the published -0.1%. The authors were economists, not novices, so this shows unchecked tools, not inexperience.

ref.title: Does High Public Debt Consistently Stifle Economic Growth? A Critique of Reinhart and Rogoff, Herndon, Ash and Pollin, PERI 2013
ref.finding: Corrected growth for high-debt countries was 2.2%, not -0.1%, after coding errors, selective exclusion of data and unconventional weighting were addressed; a coding error in the working spreadsheet excluded five countries.

nodes.label: Automated vulnerability finding and patching
nodes.summary: Agents now find previously unknown bugs in widely used code and patch them: one found an exploitable memory-safety bug in SQLite before release, though its authors say a targeted fuzzer would likely do as well[1]; DARPA challenge finalists found 18 real open-source flaws and offered 11 patches[2]; and CodeMender upstreamed 72 human-reviewed fixes in six months[3]. DARPA says such systems can help defenders find and patch flaws at speed and scale[2].

refs.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release, and SQLite's developers fixed it the same day; the authors call the results highly experimental and say a target-specific fuzzer would likely be at least as effective at present.

refs.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
refs.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%), and found 18 real open-source vulnerabilities, providing 11 patches; all seven finalist systems are being released as open source, four of them on the day of the announcement. DARPA's director said the technology will help defenders identify and patch flaws at speed and scale.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, Introducing CodeMender: an AI agent for code security, Oct 2025
refs.finding: CodeMender upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects in the six months it was being built, each reviewed by human researchers before submission.

limiters.evidence: In one test, GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE text, and 7% without it.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: AIxCC systems found 86% of synthetic vulnerabilities but patched only 68%.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%), and found 18 real open-source vulnerabilities, providing 11 patches; all seven finalist systems are being released as open source, four of them on the day of the announcement.

limiters.evidence: In one 2024 survey of 437 open-source maintainers, 60% said they are unpaid hobbyists and 12% earn most or all of their income from maintenance.

ref.title: Tidelift, The 2024 Tidelift Maintainer Impact Report, November 2024
ref.finding: Sixty percent of surveyed maintainers (n=437) report they are unpaid hobbyists, and only 12% earn most or all of their income from maintenance.

limiters.evidence: One 2026 paper found all seven open-sourced AIxCC systems largely unusable outside their original teams; after porting the winning system, its authors found 10 previously unknown bugs, three of high severity, across 8 OSS-Fuzz projects.

ref.title: Chin et al. 2026, OSS-CRS: Liberating AIxCC Cyber Reasoning Systems for Real-World Open-Source Security, arXiv 2603.08566
ref.finding: All seven open-sourced AIxCC cyber reasoning systems remain largely unusable outside their original teams; the authors ported the first-place system and found 10 previously unknown bugs (three of high severity) across 8 OSS-Fuzz projects.

enablers.action: Open-source automated bug-finding systems
enablers.evidence: All seven AIxCC finalist systems are being released as open source, four of them on the day results were announced.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%), and found 18 real open-source vulnerabilities, providing 11 patches; all seven finalist systems are being released as open source, four of them on the day of the announcement.

enablers.action: Run variant analysis on new commits
enablers.evidence: Big Sleep found a SQLite bug by checking recent commits for related bugs that had not been fixed.

ref.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
ref.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release, and SQLite's developers fixed it the same day; the authors call the results highly experimental and say a target-specific fuzzer would likely be at least as effective at present.

enablers.action: Mandate vulnerability handling for vendors
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act makes manufacturers report actively exploited vulnerabilities from 11 September 2026 and meet its main obligations from 11 December 2027, with a separate approach for free and open-source software.

ref.title: European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)
ref.finding: The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024; manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents from 11 September 2026, and the main obligations apply from 11 December 2027; free and open-source software has a special approach.

precedents.parallel: Machines competed to find and patch software flaws on their own, the same promise now made for AI agents.
precedents.outcome: Seven finalist systems competed with no human help; Mayhem won the $2 million first prize, and DARPA's programme manager said he did not expect it to finish well when it then played human experts at DEF CON.

ref.title: DARPA, DARPA Celebrates Cyber Grand Challenge Winners, Aug 2016
ref.finding: Seven teams' systems competed in the first all-machine hacking tournament; Mayhem won the $2 million first prize, and programme manager Mike Walker said he did not expect it to finish well against human experts at DEF CON.

precedents.parallel: Automated testing at scale finds real bugs in widely used open-source code and feeds fixes back, a pre-LLM version of automated vulnerability finding.
precedents.outcome: By May 2025 OSS-Fuzz had helped identify and fix over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs across 1,000 projects.

ref.title: google/oss-fuzz README
ref.finding: Over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs identified and fixed across 1,000 projects as of May 2025.

nodes.label: Hardened global networks
nodes.summary: AI that finds vulnerabilities fast can also help defenders patch them first[1], so critical software could become much harder to breach if defenders adopt automated auditing faster than attackers adopt automated exploitation. AI agents already find real bugs[3] and fix them[4]. Which side AI will favour remains uncertain, so today this is a race, not a result[1].

refs.title: Bengio et al., International AI Safety Report 2026, February 2026
refs.finding: Many of the same AI capabilities used for cyberattacks can also strengthen defences: capabilities that let an attacker rapidly discover vulnerabilities can let a defender find and patch them first, leaving it uncertain whether AI benefits attackers or defenders more.

refs.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
refs.finding: All seven finalist systems are being released as open source, and DARPA and ARPA-H added $1.4 million in prizes for teams that integrate the technology into critical infrastructure-relevant software.

refs.title: Big Sleep team, From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code, Google Project Zero 2024
refs.finding: An LLM agent found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite before it reached an official release, and SQLite's developers fixed it the same day; the authors call the results highly experimental and say a target-specific fuzzer would likely be at least as effective at present.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, Introducing CodeMender: an AI agent for code security, Oct 2025
refs.finding: CodeMender upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects in the six months it was being built, each reviewed by human researchers before submission.

limiters.evidence: In one test, GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE text, and 7% without it.

ref.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities, arXiv 2404.08144
ref.finding: GPT-4 exploited 87% of 15 known vulnerabilities given the CVE text, but only 7% without it.

limiters.evidence: CISA's Secure by Design pledge is voluntary and not legally binding; signers commit only to a good-faith effort on seven goals.

ref.title: CISA, Secure by Design Pledge
ref.finding: The pledge is voluntary and not legally binding; signers commit to make a good-faith effort over the following year toward seven goals, and hundreds of companies have signed.

limiters.evidence: In one study of 47 participants, those using an assistant based on OpenAI's codex-davinci-002 wrote less secure code than those without one, and were more likely to believe it secure.

ref.title: Perry, Srivastava, Kumar and Boneh, Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, CCS 2023, arXiv 2211.03622
ref.finding: In a 47-person user study (CCS 2023), participants with a codex-davinci-002 assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure.

enablers.action: Make secure-by-design a legal duty
enablers.evidence: The Cyber Resilience Act entered into force in December 2024; its reporting duties apply from September 2026 and its main security requirements from December 2027.

ref.title: European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)
ref.finding: The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024; manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents from 11 September 2026, and the main obligations apply from 11 December 2027; free and open-source software has a special approach.

enablers.action: Fund automated auditing of critical open source
enablers.evidence: AIxCC was run to find and patch flaws in software critical infrastructure depends on.

ref.title: DARPA, AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense, Aug 2025
ref.finding: Finalists found 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities (86%) and patched 43 (68%), and found 18 real open-source vulnerabilities, providing 11 patches; all seven finalist systems are being released as open source, four of them on the day of the announcement. The challenge aimed to secure the open-source software that critical infrastructure runs on.

enablers.action: Ship secure defaults at no extra cost
enablers.evidence: CISA asks makers to ship products secure out of the box, with features such as MFA and logging at no extra cost.

ref.title: CISA, Secure by Design
ref.finding: CISA urges software makers to make products secure out of the box, with features such as MFA, logging and single sign-on available at no extra cost; over 200 software manufacturers have joined its pledge on seven goals.

precedents.parallel: The first network-wide attack showed that defence depends on getting fixes deployed, not only on knowing the flaws, the core of the attacker-defender race.
precedents.outcome: The worm reportedly infected up to 6,000 of the more than 60,000 computers on the Internet within hours; GAO found problems in developing, distributing and installing fixes, and in one later intrusion the fix had been supplied but not installed.

ref.title: GAO 1989, Computer Security: Virus Highlights Need for Improved Internet Management (IMTEC-89-57)
ref.finding: Within hours the worm reportedly infected up to 6,000 computers on an Internet of over 60,000; the incident and later intrusions exposed problems in developing, distributing and installing software fixes, and in one later intrusion the fix had been supplied but not installed.

precedents.parallel: A flaw was publicly known and a patch existed, yet the system stayed exposed, showing that automated finding does not harden networks unless patching keeps up.
precedents.outcome: Attackers accessed personal data of at least 145.5 million people through a portal where the Apache Struts vulnerability had not been identified when patches were installed across the company.

ref.title: GAO 2018, Data Protection: Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies in Response to the 2017 Breach (GAO-18-559)
ref.finding: Attackers exploited an Apache Struts vulnerability in Equifax's online dispute portal and accessed personal information of at least 145.5 million individuals; the vulnerability was not identified on the portal when patches were being installed across the company, and a later scan missed it.

nodes.label: Productivity gains, largest for novices
nodes.summary: In one field study of 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI help raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and about 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents[1]. In one early-2025 trial, 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster, results METR has since called out of date[2].

refs.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond 2025, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
refs.finding: Across 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; the most skilled saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

refs.title: METR 2025, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
refs.finding: In a randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 tasks, AI use made tasks take 19% longer, though developers believed it sped them up by 20%; METR later marked these results out of date.

refs.title: METR 2026, We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
refs.finding: A late-2025 follow-up with 57 developers estimated speedups of 18% for returning and 4% for new developers, with 95% confidence intervals including zero; METR calls this very weak evidence and its estimate likely a lower bound, because developers who did not want to work without AI declined to take part or withheld tasks.

limiters.evidence: In one early-2025 trial, 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI, a result METR has since called out of date.

ref.title: METR 2025, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
ref.finding: In a randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 tasks, AI use made tasks take 19% longer, though developers believed it sped them up by 20%; METR later marked these results out of date.

limiters.limit: gains not yet showing in pay or hours
limiters.evidence: One Danish study found most employers in exposed occupations had adopted chatbot initiatives, yet effects on earnings and recorded hours were precise nulls two years after ChatGPT.

ref.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Linking Danish adoption surveys to registry data, the authors estimate precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT.

limiters.evidence: In one experiment with 758 knowledge workers at Boston Consulting Group, those using GPT-4 on a task outside its frontier were 19% less likely to reach a correct answer.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality, Organization Science 37(2), 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 knowledge workers at Boston Consulting Group, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% faster inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to be correct on a task outside it.

enablers.action: Target AI assistance at new workers
enablers.evidence: In one firm's support centre, less skilled and less experienced agents gained about 30% in issues resolved per hour, against 15% on average.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond 2025, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
ref.finding: Across 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm, AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced agents; the most skilled saw small speed gains and small quality declines.

enablers.action: Train staff on where AI fails
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy among staff who operate or use AI, without guaranteeing any set level.

ref.title: Article 4: AI Literacy, EU Artificial Intelligence Act, amended text
ref.finding: As amended, providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support AI literacy among staff and others operating or using AI systems on their behalf; the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy.

enablers.action: Redesign workflows, not only add tools
enablers.counters: gains not yet showing in pay or hours
enablers.evidence: Nearly 40% of US adults aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, yet it assisted only 1% to 5% of all work hours.

ref.title: Bick, Blandin and Deming, The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI, NBER w32966
ref.finding: Nearly 40% of the US population aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024, and between 1% and 5% of all work hours were assisted by it.

precedents.parallel: New machines took over some of weavers' tasks, as AI assistants now take over parts of knowledge work.
precedents.outcome: Weavers learned much of their skill on the job; mechanisation removed some tasks but raised the returns to skill on the rest, and wages eventually rose while inequality fell. Unlike the AI data, the gains came as weavers' skills built up, not as instant output boosts.

ref.title: Bessen 2011, Was Mechanization De-Skilling? The Origins of Task-Biased Technical Change, Research on Innovation working paper 1101
ref.finding: Mechanisation eliminated some tasks but raised returns to skill on the rest; weavers learned substantially on the job, their human capital rose, and wages eventually increased while inequality decreased.

nodes.label: Jevons paradox: more work, not less
nodes.summary: As AI makes tasks cheaper, demand and expectations may grow faster than time is saved. In one 2024 Upwork survey, 77% of employees using AI said it had added to their workload[1]; in one Danish study, 85% of chatbot users said they moved saved time to other tasks, and earnings and recorded hours did not change[2].

refs.title: Upwork Research Institute, From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models for the Future, 2024
refs.finding: In a 2024 survey of 2,500 people in the US, UK, Australia and Canada (1,250 C-suite executives, 625 full-time employees and 625 freelancers), 77% of employees using AI said the tools had added to their workload, while 96% of C-suite leaders expected AI to raise productivity.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard 2025, Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI, NBER w33777 (revised 2026)
refs.finding: In Danish surveys of 11 exposed occupations linked to registry data, 85% of chatbot users said they moved saved time to other job tasks and fewer than 10% took more breaks or leisure; effects on earnings and recorded hours were precise nulls, ruling out average effects larger than 2%.

refs.title: Acemoglu 2025, The Simple Macroeconomics of AI, Economic Policy (NBER w32487)
refs.finding: Estimates no more than a 0.66% gain in total factor productivity over ten years.

refs.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Uneven geographic and enterprise AI adoption, September 2025
refs.finding: Classifies Claude.ai conversations and first-party API transcripts by O*NET task and as automation or augmentation; on Claude.ai the directive (automation) share rose from 27% to 39%.

nodes.control_note: If tasks get cheaper, demand for them can grow, by the same mechanism as the productivity gain; how much depends on how elastic demand is. Employers set workloads, and in one Danish study most chatbot users moved saved time to other job tasks while fewer than 10% took more breaks or leisure.

actions.action: Set workload targets when AI is introduced
actions.evidence: In one vendor survey, 77% of employees using AI said it added to their workload; this is self-reported and not causal.

ref.title: Upwork Research Institute, From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models for the Future, 2024
ref.finding: In a 2024 survey of 2,500 people in the US, UK, Australia and Canada (1,250 C-suite executives, 625 full-time employees and 625 freelancers), 77% of employees using AI said the tools had added to their workload, while 96% of C-suite leaders expected AI to raise productivity.

actions.action: Track hours and earnings, not only output
actions.evidence: Danish register data show null effects on hours and earnings, which lets policy see whether time savings reach workers.

ref.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Two years after ChatGPT, earnings and hours effects are precise nulls, ruling out effects above 2%.

precedents.parallel: Jevons argued that using a resource more efficiently raises total demand for it, the same mechanism by which cheaper tasks may grow total work.
precedents.outcome: Jevons argued that more efficient use of coal would not reduce demand for it but would spur more use and speed the depletion of supplies.

ref.title: W. Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865 (Yale Energy History)
ref.finding: Jevons held that increased efficiency in consumption would not reduce demand for energy but would spur increased use and further deplete supplies.

precedents.parallel: Automation of a core task was expected to remove jobs but changed the economics so the work grew in other forms.
precedents.outcome: Tellers needed per urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, yet teller jobs did not decrease as ATMs spread, because cheaper branches meant more of them.

ref.title: Bessen 2015, Toil and Technology, Finance and Development (IMF)
ref.finding: Teller jobs did not fall as ATMs rolled out; tellers per branch fell from 20 to 13.

precedents.parallel: Labour-saving machines in the home were expected to free time, a close parallel to AI saving time at work.
precedents.outcome: Australian 1997 time-use data found domestic technology rarely reduced women's unpaid working time and sometimes increased it; Gershuny published a rebuttal in the same journal issue, so the evidence is contested.

ref.title: Bittman, Mahmud Rice and Wajcman 2004, Appliances and their impact: the ownership of domestic technology and time spent on household work, British Journal of Sociology 55(3)
ref.finding: Using the Australian 1997 Time Use Survey, which records appliance ownership, finds that domestic technology rarely reduces women's unpaid working time and even produces some increases in domestic labour.

nodes.label: Universal basic income
nodes.summary: Guaranteed-income trials show modest effects: in one US trial, $1,000 a month for three years to 1,000 low-income people cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week[1], and health gains were mostly short-lived[2]. Political support for a universal scheme is unproven; in one 2020 US survey, 54% of adults opposed a federal basic income of about $1,000 a month and 45% favoured it[5].

refs.title: Vivalt et al. 2026, The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States, Quarterly Journal of Economics (NBER w32719)
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years to 1,000 low-income people, against 2,000 controls paid $50 a month, cut their work by 1 to 2 hours a week and labour market participation by 4.2 percentage points, with no impact on job quality.

refs.title: Miller et al., Does Income Affect Health? Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32711
refs.finding: $1,000 a month for three years brought large but short-lived gains in stress and food security, more use of hospital, emergency and dental care, and no improvement in physical health or biomarkers.

refs.title: Kokotajlo, Lifland, Larsen and Dean (with Scott Alexander), AI 2027: race ending, 2025
refs.finding: In the authors' scenario, by 2029 humans realise they are obsolete; outside a few niche industries, people either perform a charade of doing their jobs or collect an incredibly luxurious universal basic income.

refs.title: Dean and Larsen, Economics of Plan A (AI 2040 scenario supplement)
refs.finding: In the authors' modelled scenario, AI and robot permit revenue is paid out as a Citizen's Dividend, with 75% of US permit revenue going to the US population in 2035, roughly $1M per person a year; they say they do not trust the model's outputs to be accurate.

refs.title: Gilberstadt, More Americans oppose than favor the government providing a universal basic income for all adult citizens, Pew Research Center, 2020
refs.finding: In an online survey of 11,001 US adults from July 27 to August 2, 2020, 54% opposed the federal government providing a guaranteed income of about $1,000 a month for all adult citizens, whether or not they work, and 45% favoured it.

limiters.evidence: One US trial paid $1,000 a month to 1,000 low-income people for three years; trials like it do not test how payments to everyone would be funded.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: Recipients worked 1 to 2 hours a week less.

ref.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income, NBER w32719
ref.finding: $1,000 a month for three years cut work by 1 to 2 hours a week, with leisure the largest gain.

limiters.evidence: In one 2020 survey of 11,001 US adults, 54% opposed a federal basic income of about $1,000 a month for all adult citizens, whether or not they work; 45% favoured it.

ref.title: Gilberstadt, More Americans oppose than favor the government providing a universal basic income for all adult citizens, Pew Research Center, 2020
ref.finding: In an online survey of 11,001 US adults from July 27 to August 2, 2020, 54% opposed the federal government providing a guaranteed income of about $1,000 a month for all adult citizens, whether or not they work, and 45% favoured it.

enablers.action: Run long-term randomised trials
enablers.evidence: A Kenyan trial pays a 12-year basic income in 44 villages, alongside 2-year and lump-sum arms and 100 control villages.

ref.title: Banerjee, Faye, Krueger, Niehaus and Suri 2023, Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya (working paper)
ref.finding: In a trial in rural Kenya with 195 treated and 100 control villages, communities receiving the 12-year UBI saw more enterprises and higher revenues; labour supply did not change overall but shifted from wage employment to self-employment.

enablers.action: Consider lump-sum transfers
enablers.evidence: In Kenya, a one-off lump sum had similar or larger economic effects than a two-year stream of the same value; the authors note it is cheaper only if households get less.

ref.title: Banerjee, Faye, Krueger, Niehaus and Suri 2023, Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya (working paper)
ref.finding: The lump sums had similar, if not larger, economic impacts than the short-term stream, which had noticeably smaller effects despite delivering the same capital.

enablers.action: Watch AI labour effects before designing schemes
enablers.evidence: Earnings and hours effects of chatbots were near zero so far in Denmark.

ref.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents, NBER w33777
ref.finding: Danish data show precise null effects of chatbots on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT.

precedents.parallel: A universal, unconditional cash payment has run for decades, the closest real case of a basic income.
precedents.outcome: The dividend had no effect on employment and raised part-time work by 1.8 percentage points (17 percent).

ref.title: Jones and Marinescu 2022, The Labor Market Impacts of Universal and Permanent Cash Transfers: Evidence from the Alaska Permanent Fund, AEJ: Economic Policy
ref.finding: No effect on employment; part-time work rose 1.8 percentage points (17 percent).

precedents.parallel: A national randomised trial tested unconditional payments to unemployed people as a step toward a simpler social security system.
precedents.outcome: 2,000 people drawn at random from those on unemployment benefit received 560 euros a month; from November 2017 to October 2018 it added an average of 6 days of employment, and recipients reported less mental strain, depression, sadness and loneliness, but a new activation model in 2018 complicated the employment result.

ref.title: Finland's Basic Income Experiment 2017-2018, Finland Toolbox (Finland Promotion Board)
ref.finding: 2,000 randomly selected recipients of unemployment benefit got 560 euros a month; basic income added 6 days of employment from November 2017 to October 2018 and improved perceived wellbeing; a new activation model in 2018 complicated interpretation.

precedents.parallel: A guaranteed annual income open to a whole town is the main community-level test of universal cash.
precedents.outcome: Forget reported hospitalisations fell 8.5% relative to a comparison group, but Green's 2021 reanalysis found pre-trends that point to higher hospital use, so health benefits are unproven.

ref.title: Green 2021, A Reanalysis of 'The Town with No Poverty: The Health Effects of a Canadian Guaranteed Annual Income Field Experiment'
ref.finding: After accounting for pre-trends, the data point to an increase in hospital use, reversing Forget's 2011 conclusion.

precedents.parallel: A national government paid unconditional monthly cash to more than 70 million people, the closest country-scale case.
precedents.outcome: Transfers worth 28% of median per capita household income, paid to compensate for removed energy subsidies, did not reduce hours worked or labour force participation, and labour supply rose among women and self-employed men.

ref.title: Salehi-Isfahani and Mostafavi-Dehzooei 2018, Cash transfers and labor supply: Evidence from a large-scale program in Iran, Journal of Development Economics 135
ref.finding: Monthly transfers from 2011 to more than 70 million people, compensating for removed energy subsidies and worth 28% of median per capita household income, did not reduce hours worked or labour force participation, and raised labour supply among women and self-employed men.

nodes.label: Decompiling legacy software
nodes.summary: Models that turn binaries back into readable source could help keep abandoned software and games alive. In one study, open models recompiled and passed tests on more than twice as many decompiled functions as GPT-4o and Ghidra[1]. One hobby developer rebuilding Snowboard Kids 2 reported more progress in three weeks with an AI coding agent than in three months before[2].

refs.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP 2024
refs.finding: Presents what the authors call the first and largest open-source LLM series (1.3B to 33B parameters) trained to decompile binary code; the models beat GPT-4o and Ghidra by over 100% in re-executability rate on HumanEval and ExeBench.

refs.title: The Unexpected Effectiveness of One-Shot Decompilation with Claude, Chris' Blog, 2025
refs.finding: Running an AI coding agent unattended against a build-and-verify script, the author made more progress matching Snowboard Kids 2 functions in three weeks than in the preceding three months, estimates roughly 79% of functions should be matchable, and warns the remaining ones will be the hardest and many matches are hard to read.

limiters.evidence: EU law allows decompilation without the rightholder's consent only when indispensable for interoperability, only by someone entitled to use a copy, and only of the parts needed.

ref.title: Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs, Article 6
ref.finding: Reproducing and translating code without authorisation is allowed only when indispensable to obtain the information needed for interoperability of an independently created program, by a person entitled to use a copy, and limited to the parts needed; the information may not be used to build a substantially similar program.

limiters.evidence: LLM4Decompile more than doubled re-executability over GPT-4o and Ghidra, but even its best released model re-executes only about 65% of functions on one benchmark.

ref.title: albertan017/LLM4Decompile: Reverse Engineering: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, GitHub
ref.finding: The best released model, llm4decompile-9b-v2, reached a re-executability rate of 0.6494 on the Decompile benchmark; the code is under the MIT and DeepSeek licences.

limiters.evidence: Even the best released model re-executes only about 65% of functions on one benchmark, so experts must test the rest.

ref.title: albertan017/LLM4Decompile: Reverse Engineering: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, GitHub
ref.finding: The best released model, llm4decompile-9b-v2, reached a re-executability rate of 0.6494 on the Decompile benchmark; the code is under the MIT and DeepSeek licences.

enablers.action: Release open decompilation models
enablers.evidence: LLM4Decompile models from 1.3B to 33B parameters were released as open source.

ref.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP 2024
ref.finding: Presents what the authors call the first and largest open-source LLM series (1.3B to 33B parameters) trained to decompile binary code; the models beat GPT-4o and Ghidra by over 100% in re-executability rate on HumanEval and ExeBench.

enablers.action: Widen preservation exceptions in copyright law
enablers.evidence: EU law lets cultural heritage institutions copy software in their permanent collections for preservation, but that exception covers only the reproduction right, not the translation of code that decompilation involves.

ref.title: Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market, Article 6
ref.finding: Member States must let cultural heritage institutions make copies of works permanently in their collections, in any format, for preservation and only as far as necessary; for computer programs this covers the reproduction right in Article 4(1)(a) of Directive 2009/24/EC, not the translation and adaptation right in Article 4(1)(b).

precedents.parallel: Turning object code back into readable source to achieve compatibility was ruled lawful, the legal footing that AI decompilation for interoperability would lean on.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit held that disassembly for a legitimate reason, when there is no other way to reach the unprotected functional elements, is fair use, since the purpose was game compatibility rather than copying the games.

ref.title: Sega Enters. Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Disassembly for a legitimate reason with no other means of access was fair use.

precedents.parallel: Reverse engineering a console BIOS let PlayStation games run on ordinary computers, the kind of afterlife decompilation gives old software.
precedents.outcome: The Ninth Circuit reversed, ordered the injunction dissolved and found Connectix's intermediate copies were fair use because the final emulator contained no infringing material.

ref.title: Sony Computer Entertainment v. Connectix Corp., 203 F.3d 596 (9th Cir. 2000), US Copyright Office Fair Use Index
ref.finding: Intermediate copying to build a non-infringing emulator was fair use.

nodes.label: Workslop
nodes.summary: Polished-looking AI output that lacks substance shifts work onto whoever receives it, leaving colleagues to do the real thinking and clean-up[2]; in one survey of 1,150 full-time US desk workers, 40% had received such workslop in the past month, costing about two hours per incident[2].

refs.title: Niederhoffer, Kellerman, Lee, Liebscher, Rapuano and Hancock, AI-Generated "Workslop" Is Destroying Productivity, Harvard Business Review, September 2025
refs.finding: The article opens by noting that workers in companies embracing generative AI are largely following mandates to use the tools, yet few see them create real value. The rest is paywalled; the survey figures are cited from BetterUp's own report.

refs.title: BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab, Workslop: The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Busywork, survey of September 2025
refs.finding: Online survey of 1,150 full-time US desk workers in September 2025; 40% received workslop in the last month, each incident took about 2 hours to resolve, an estimated $186 per employee per month; workslop leaves colleagues to do the real thinking and clean-up.

nodes.control_note: Workslop comes from how AI output is used and checked, not from the capability itself. Norms and review keep the benefit.

actions.action: Set clear guardrails for AI use instead of blanket adoption
actions.evidence: BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab say leaders can curb workslop by setting clear guardrails and modelling thoughtful AI use; their survey did not test this.

ref.title: BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab, Workslop: The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Busywork, survey of September 2025
ref.finding: Leaders can curb workslop by setting clear guardrails, modelling thoughtful AI use and cultivating pilot mindsets that use AI to enhance collaboration rather than avoid work.

actions.action: Train staff on where AI fails
actions.evidence: In one preregistered experiment with 758 knowledge workers run with Boston Consulting Group, GPT-4 users were 19% less likely to produce a correct solution on a task outside the frontier; one arm got a prompt engineering overview, but training staff on where the frontier lies was not tested.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality, Organization Science 2026
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 knowledge workers, run with Boston Consulting Group, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks 25.1% faster inside the frontier, but were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions on a task outside it.

precedents.parallel: A polished slide compressed a key risk into vague bullets, so a manager could read it and miss that it described a life-threatening situation, as hollow AI output leaves the real work to its reader.
precedents.outcome: The Board found the slide put at the bottom that one debris estimate was 640 times larger than the data used to calibrate the model (later analysis put it at 400 times), and called the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers a sign of problematic technical communication at NASA.

ref.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I, August 2003, 'Engineering by Viewgraphs' (p. 191)
ref.finding: Only at the bottom of the slide did engineers state that one debris estimate was 640 times larger than the calibration data (later analysis: 400 times); the Board called the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers an illustration of problematic technical communication at NASA.

nodes.label: AI slop overwhelms open-source maintainers
nodes.summary: Fabricated bug and security reports waste the scarce time of volunteer maintainers. At curl, about a fifth of security reports in 2025 up to mid-July were AI slop, and the share of valid reports fell to around 5%[1]. Since spring 2026 the slop has practically stopped[3], but reports arrive at 4 to 5 times the 2024 rate[2].

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops, July 2025
refs.finding: About 20% of curl's 2025 security reports up to mid-July were AI slop and about 5% were genuine vulnerabilities, a valid rate significantly lower than in previous years; each report takes the seven-person security team 30 minutes to three hours.

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, The pressure, May 2026
refs.finding: Incoming curl security reports run 4 to 5 times the 2024 rate and double the 2025 rate, more than one a day; quality is higher than ever, and triage takes almost all of the lead maintainer's days.

refs.title: Daniel Stenberg, ignore the slop, October 2026
refs.finding: Since spring 2026 slop reports are practically gone; every recent report had AI involved to some extent, and they are typically accurate, though much too wordy.

refs.title: Seth Larson, New era of slop security reports for open source, December 2024
refs.finding: A member of the security triage team for CPython, pip, urllib3 and Requests noticed an uptick in extremely low-quality, spammy and LLM-hallucinated security reports, which waste maintainers' time and add to burnout.

nodes.control_note: The same tools that find real bugs make fake reports cheap. Platform friction and reporter rules can cut most of the slop.

actions.action: Rate-limit and gate new reporter accounts
actions.evidence: Proposed by Seth Larson, who triages security reports for CPython, pip and other projects; no measured effect yet.
