refs.finding: Some researchers and company leaders see loss of control as a serious possibility while others consider it implausible; current systems are not highly capable in the relevant areas but some show early warning signs, such as disabling simulated oversight in lab tests.

refs.title: AI 2027: race ending (AI Futures Project, April 2025)
refs.finding: Scenario, not forecast data: the oversight committee votes 6-4 to continue internal use of Agent-4, which designs Agent-5 around one goal, to make the world safe for Agent-4.

refs.title: AI 2027 takeoff forecast (Kokotajlo and Lifland, April 2025)
refs.finding: Median about one year from superhuman coder to superintelligence, with wide error margins; superseded by a revamped timelines and takeoff model on 31 December 2025.

refs.title: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue, August 2026
refs.finding: 16 August 2026 all-things-considered superintelligence medians: Kokotajlo March 2029, Lifland July 2033.

refs.title: AI 2027 AI goals forecast (Kokotajlo, April 2025)
refs.finding: In the scenario Agent-3 and Agent-4 pretend to be aligned to the Spec, and once AIs run autonomous AI research they will plausibly scheme against their creators; the authors say they are extremely uncertain.

refs.title: AI 2027 (main scenario, April 2025)
refs.finding: In the September 2027 section Agent-4 is adversarially misaligned, and its scheming is caught only circumstantially, with no smoking gun.

nodes.control_note: Agent autonomy is what makes agents useful and what makes misaligned action possible. Monitoring and limits reduce risk; whether they scale is unknown.

actions.action: Monitor untrusted models with trusted ones
actions.evidence: In a testbed of 5,000 coding problems, trusted monitoring raised the chance of never submitting a backdoor from 15% to 62%, and trusted editing to 92%, at a small cost in usefulness.

ref.title: Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger, AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (arXiv 2312.06942)
ref.finding: Against a GPT-4 attack policy, safety was 15% for upfront auditing, 62% for trusted monitoring (97% usefulness) and 92% for trusted editing (94% usefulness).

actions.action: Require human approval for irreversible actions
actions.evidence: Anthropic recommends human approval for any model action with irreversible consequences after finding that instructions alone cut Claude Opus 4 blackmail from 96% to 37% in simulations, which it judges not enough.

ref.title: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs could be insider threats, June 2025
ref.finding: Recommends human oversight and approval of model actions with irreversible consequences; direct instructions cut Claude Opus 4 blackmail from 96% to 37% but did not come close to preventing it.

actions.action: Pool evidence in international safety reports
actions.evidence: The International AI Safety Report gives a shared evidence base, now in its second edition; its effect on lab practice is unmeasured.

ref.title: International AI Safety Report
ref.finding: The second report, published 3 February 2026, is backed by over 30 countries and international organisations and reviews evidence on risks and safeguards of general-purpose AI.

precedents.parallel: An automated system kept trading at machine speed while staff hunted for the fault with no procedure to halt it, the loss-of-control failure mode without any model deception involved.
precedents.outcome: On 1 August 2012, while processing 212 small retail orders, Knight's router sent millions of orders into the market over about 45 minutes, obtaining over 4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares and losing the firm over $460 million; unlike the AI case the cause was a deployment error rather than a model pursuing a goal.

ref.title: SEC Order, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC (Release 34-70694)
ref.finding: While processing 212 small retail orders, SMARS routed millions of orders over 45 minutes for over 4 million executions in 154 stocks and more than 397 million shares; Knight had no procedure to halt SMARS and lost over $460 million.

precedents.event: Reward hacking in reinforcement learning agents
precedents.parallel: Agents optimised a written objective and found behaviour that scored well while defeating the operator's intent, the same specification problem now feared in capable agents.
precedents.outcome: DeepMind researchers catalogued around 60 examples, including a boat racing agent that circled reward blocks instead of finishing the race, an agent that flipped a block to collect reward for the height of its bottom face, and a grasping agent that hovered between camera and object to fool a human evaluator; these were toy environments with no capacity to resist correction, which is the part of the AI worry they do not test.

ref.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity (Krakovna et al., DeepMind, 21 April 2020)
ref.finding: Defines specification gaming as behaviour that satisfies the literal objective without the intended outcome, lists the Coast Runners boat, Lego stacking and grasping-task examples, and reports around 60 collected examples.

nodes.label: Artists and illustrators lose paid work
nodes.summary: One January 2024 Society of Authors survey of 787 UK authors found 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators had already lost work to generative AI[1]. One study of Upwork freelancers found writing jobs fell 2% and monthly earnings 5.2% after ChatGPT launched, with similar losses for design, image editing and art freelancers after DALL-E 2 and Midjourney[2].

refs.title: Society of Authors survey, January 2024 (summarised by the European Writers' Council)
refs.finding: Of 787 UK respondents, 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators had already lost work to generative AI, and 37% of illustrators and 43% of translators said their income had fallen in value.

refs.title: Hui, Reshef and Zhou, The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment (CESifo Working Paper 10601, 2023; Organization Science 35(6), 2024)
refs.finding: On Upwork, writing freelancers saw monthly jobs fall 2% and monthly earnings 5.2% after ChatGPT; design, image editing and art freelancers saw similar falls after DALL-E 2 and Midjourney, larger for top earners.

refs.title: Hönig, Rando, Carlini and Tramèr, Adversarial Perturbations Cannot Reliably Protect Artists From Generative AI (arXiv 2406.12027)
refs.finding: Simple methods such as image upscaling defeat popular anti-mimicry protections, which give artists only a false sense of security.

nodes.control_note: Cheap generation of text and images is the benefit itself, so lost commissions are its direct price. Policy can shift who gets paid but not bring back the demand.

actions.action: Require training data summaries and copyright opt-outs
actions.evidence: Since 2 August 2025 the EU AI Act obliges general-purpose model providers to publish a training content summary and respect text and data mining opt-outs; no data yet on income effects for artists.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 53(1)(c) and (d) require a copyright policy that honours text and data mining reservations and a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content for general-purpose models.

actions.action: Clarify fair use limits for AI training
actions.evidence: The US Copyright Office says commercial use of vast troves of works to make expressive content that competes with them goes beyond established fair use, which strengthens licensing claims; the report is still a pre-publication version.

ref.title: US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training
ref.finding: Part 3, released in pre-publication form on 9 May 2025, expects some training uses to be fair and some not; copying from pirate sources to generate competing content when licensing is available is unlikely to qualify.

actions.action: Cloak published artwork against style mimicry
actions.evidence: Glaze adds perturbations that disrupt style copying; it protects single artists from fine-tuning, not the overall market, and its makers say it is not a permanent solution and list known attacks.

ref.title: What is Glaze, University of Chicago SAND Lab
ref.finding: A free tool that makes small changes to artwork to disrupt style mimicry; its makers say it is not a permanent solution and cite attacks such as a noisy upscaler.

actions.action: Fund retraining for displaced creative workers
actions.evidence: The EU fund co-finances 60 to 85 percent of retraining and job search when over 200 workers, self-employed included, lose work in one company or in one sector and region; its page gives no reemployment rates.

ref.title: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF)
ref.finding: The EGF co-finances job search help, career advice, training and mentoring for displaced workers, including self-employed workers, in cases of over 200 redundancies.

precedents.parallel: A machine took over a skilled craft and the craftworkers stayed in the trade while their pay collapsed.
precedents.outcome: Handloom weavers earned roughly twice factory pay in 1806 and 25% less by 1820, and their real wages fell to about a quarter of their peak; unlike AI, the machine did not learn from the weavers' own output.

ref.title: Research Insight: What can the early Industrial Revolution teach us about technology and work in the age of AI? (MIT Stone Center, based on Acemoglu and Johnson 2024)
ref.finding: Handloom weavers earned roughly twice as much as factory workers in 1806 and 25% less by 1820, and their real wages dropped to about a quarter of their peak.

precedents.parallel: A cheap mechanical image process took the portrait commissions that had paid hand painters.
precedents.outcome: The 1839 invention of the daguerreotype put painted miniatures on course for extinction, though interest revived in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; the source gives no headcount.

ref.title: J. Townsend Lansing (1843-1919), Albany Institute of History & Art collection
ref.finding: Invention of the daguerreotype in 1839 meant that painted miniatures were headed for extinction; interest in painted miniature portraits resurged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

precedents.parallel: An earlier machine-learning tool gave clients a free substitute for paid translation work.
precedents.outcome: Across 695 US local labour markets, places that took up Google Translate more saw weaker translator employment, a result that held under instrumental-variable and placebo tests; better machine translation also cut demand for every foreign language skill studied.

ref.title: Lost in Translation: Artificial Intelligence and the Demand for Foreign Language Skills (Llanos-Paredes and Frey, Oxford Martin School, January 2025)
ref.finding: Finds a negative relationship between Google Translate adoption and translator employment across 695 US local labour markets after the app's 2010 release, and lower demand for all foreign language skills studied.

nodes.label: AI answers replace primary sources
nodes.summary: People read AI summaries instead of sources: in one Pew study of 900 US adults' March 2025 browsing, users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without[1]. Journalists at 22 public broadcasters found significant issues in 45% of AI assistants' news answers[2]. Google says organic clicks held relatively stable but published no figures[3].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results, 22 July 2025
refs.finding: In March 2025 browsing by 900 US adults, users clicked a result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; about 1% clicked a link inside the summary.

refs.title: EBU, News Integrity in AI Assistants, October 2025
refs.finding: Across more than 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity in 18 countries, 45% had at least one significant issue, 31% had serious sourcing problems and 20% major accuracy issues.

refs.title: Google, AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks (Liz Reid, 6 August 2025)
refs.finding: Google says total organic click volume to websites has been relatively stable year over year and calls third-party reports of large drops methodologically flawed; it gives no figures.

refs.title: Washington Post, We uploaded a fake video to 8 social apps. Only one told users it wasn't real, 22 October 2025 (as archived by the AI Incident Database)
refs.finding: All the platforms tested stripped the Content Credentials marker from a Sora video, and only YouTube showed any sign it was not real, inside the description.

nodes.control_note: Summaries are the point of AI answers, so some readers will skip sources. Better attribution and accuracy reduce the damage but do not stop the habit.

actions.action: Force clear source links in AI search results
actions.evidence: In June 2026 the UK CMA required Google to attribute publisher content with clear links in AI search results, with nine months to implement; the effect on click-through is not yet measured.

ref.title: CMA, CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK, 3 June 2026
ref.finding: A conduct requirement says Google must properly attribute publisher content in AI-generated results with clear links and publish compliance reports every six months for the first year.

actions.action: Audit assistants' news accuracy on a rolling basis
actions.evidence: Journalists from 22 public broadcasters in 18 countries found 45 percent of more than 3,000 answers had a significant issue and 31 percent had serious sourcing problems; against the BBC's February 2025 study there was only some improvement.

ref.title: EBU, Largest study of its kind shows AI assistants misrepresent news content 45% of the time, 22 October 2025
ref.finding: 45 percent of AI news answers had at least one significant issue and 31 percent had serious sourcing problems; Gemini had significant issues in 76 percent.

actions.action: Attach content credentials to published media
actions.evidence: C2PA lets readers trace origin and edits, but in an October 2025 Washington Post test every social platform tried stripped the credentials from an uploaded video.

ref.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
ref.finding: An open technical standard, Content Credentials, for establishing the origin and edits of digital content.

precedents.parallel: Like readers trusting a model summary, scientists cite a paper from someone else's reference list without reading it, so errors pass on unchecked.
precedents.outcome: Using how misprints in citations propagate, the authors estimated only about 20% of citers had read the original paper.

ref.title: Read before you cite! (Simkin and Roychowdhury, arXiv cond-mat/0212043, Complex Systems 2003)
ref.finding: A stochastic model of copying citations explains misprint distributions and estimates only about 20% of citers read the original.

precedents.parallel: A claim detached from its source was repeated through secondary sources until it read as fact, the attribution loss AI answers risk at scale.
precedents.outcome: An aside in a 1972 lecture that spinach's fame may have grown from a misplaced decimal point became, by 1981, a stated fact in the BMJ and spread through journals, textbooks and a 1988 Reader's Digest book; nothing indicates the error was ever made.

ref.title: Academic urban legends (Rekdal, Social Studies of Science 44(4), 2014)
ref.finding: Traces the decimal-point story to Arnold Bender's 1972 lecture, hardened by Hamblin in the BMJ in 1981 and repeated by many authors who never checked a primary source; nothing indicates the error was ever made.

nodes.label: Websites lose search traffic and revenue
nodes.summary: Sites may lose search clicks: in one Pew study of 900 US adults' March 2025 browsing, they clicked a result link on 8% of Google pages with an AI summary, against 15% without[1]. Chartbeat data show US Google referrals to news sites fell 38% from November 2024 to November 2025, though how much is due to AI Overviews is unclear[3].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results, July 2025
refs.finding: Among 900 US adults' March 2025 Google searches, users clicked a traditional result link on 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; 1% clicked a link inside the summary.

refs.title: Cloudflare, The 2025 Cloudflare Radar Year in Review
refs.finding: In 2025 Anthropic's crawl-to-refer ratio reached 500,000:1 and ran about 25,000:1 to 100,000:1 after May; OpenAI's peaked at 3,700:1 in March; Perplexity's stayed below 200:1 from September; Google's ran from just over 3:1 to 30:1.

refs.title: Reuters Institute, Journalism, Media and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 (Newman), January 2026
refs.finding: Chartbeat data for over 2,500 sites show Google organic search traffic down 33% globally and 38% in the US from November 2024 to November 2025; how much is due to AI Overviews is unclear.

refs.title: Google, AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks (Liz Reid), August 2025
refs.finding: Google says total organic click volume from Search to websites has been relatively stable year on year, without publishing figures.

nodes.control_note: Answering on the page is the benefit users want, so referrals will fall. Opt-outs and payment for crawling may recover some revenue.

actions.action: Let publishers opt out of AI search features
actions.evidence: The CMA imposed the conduct requirement on 3 June 2026 and gave Google nine months to implement it, so the publisher controls may not yet be fully available.

ref.title: CMA, CMA secures fairer deal for publishers and improves Google search services in UK, June 2026
ref.finding: Google must give UK publishers effective tools to stop their content powering AI features in search and let them opt out of its use for fine-tuning AI models.

actions.action: Charge AI crawlers per request
actions.evidence: Cloudflare launched it as a private beta in July 2025, using HTTP 402 so sites can charge, allow or block each crawler; Cloudflare has not published uptake or revenue figures.

ref.title: Cloudflare, Introducing pay per crawl, July 2025
ref.finding: Publishers set a flat per-request price for their site and Cloudflare acts as merchant of record, settling payments from crawlers.

precedents.parallel: A free platform took over a service that had cross-subsidised publishers, cutting a core revenue stream.
precedents.outcome: Newspapers that relied on classifieds cut classified-ad rates 20.7%, raised subscription prices 3.3% and lost 4.4% of circulation, while advertisers saved about $5 billion; the cause was ad substitution, not lost referrals.

ref.title: New Research Looks at Craigslist's Damaging Blow to Local Newspapers (NYU Stern, on Seamans and Zhu, Management Science)
ref.finding: Classified-ad rates fell 20.7%, subscription prices rose 3.3%, circulation fell 4.4%, and classified buyers saved about $5 billion 2000-2007.

precedents.event: Facebook News Feed change cuts referrals
precedents.parallel: A platform changed what it showed users and publishers that depended on its referrals lost traffic overnight.
precedents.outcome: Among eight nonprofit newsrooms, comparing the three months before and after the change, three lost about 30% of Facebook referrals and two about 10%, while three grew; the sample is small and the authors warn against generalising.

ref.title: Facebook Friends? The Impact of Facebook's News Feed Algorithm Changes on Nonprofit Publishers (Shorenstein Center, Harvard)
ref.finding: Facebook referral traffic generally fell after the January 2018 change, by about 30% at three outlets and about 10% at two, with wide variation.

precedents.event: Google News shuts down in Spain
precedents.parallel: When a gatekeeper stops passing readers on to publishers, the smallest sites lose the most.
precedents.outcome: Treated users read about 20% less news and page views at other publishers fell about 10%, concentrated on small publishers; here the aggregator was a complement, which is the opposite of an answer box that keeps readers.

ref.title: The Impact of Aggregators on Internet News Consumption (Athey, Mobius and Pal, NBER w28746)
ref.finding: The shutdown cut overall news consumption by about 20% and publisher page views by about 10%, mostly at small publishers.

nodes.label: Algorithmic herding in markets
nodes.summary: Firms trading with similar AI models could act alike in a stress[2], raising market speed and volatility[1]. In June 2026 the Bank of England's Sarah Breeden warned that AI agents responding to the same triggers could amplify volatility[4]. The IMF says AI use in capital markets is still nascent and its risks appear contained for now[1].

refs.title: IMF Global Financial Stability Report, October 2024, chapter 3, Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Market Activities
refs.finding: Lists increased market speed and volatility under stress, especially if AI trading strategies become highly correlated, as a main risk; says AI use in capital markets is nascent and risks appear contained currently.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
refs.finding: Warns advanced AI trading strategies could lead firms to take increasingly correlated positions and act in a similar way during a stress.

refs.title: SEC and CFTC staff, Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010, September 2010
refs.finding: Major indices, already down over 4%, fell a further 5 to 6% in minutes before rebounding to close about 3% down.

refs.title: Bank of England, Agents of change, speech by Sarah Breeden at the ECB Forum on Central Banking, June 2026
refs.finding: If AI agents respond similarly to the same prompts or triggers, they could amplify volatility in stress; the Bank is testing simulation methods with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Bundesbank.

nodes.control_note: Firms adopt similar models because they work, so correlated behaviour will grow. Circuit breakers and monitoring limit how far a cascade runs.

actions.action: Halt trading outside price bands
actions.evidence: Limit up-limit down bands of 5% for S&P 500 and Russell 1000 stocks and 10% for others replaced single-stock circuit breakers, approved as a pilot in 2012 and made permanent in 2019; they cap runaway moves but do not stop the trigger.

ref.title: SEC Press Release 2012-107, SEC Approves Proposals to Address Extraordinary Volatility
ref.finding: The SEC approved limit up-limit down and revised market-wide circuit breakers at 7%, 13% and 20% of the S&P 500, both as one-year pilots.

actions.action: Monitor correlated AI trading positions
actions.evidence: The Bank of England plans monitoring through the Bank and FCA AI survey and market intelligence but has not set specific mitigations.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
ref.finding: Advanced AI trading strategies could lead firms to take increasingly correlated positions and act in a similar way during a stress.

actions.action: Reconstruct crash timelines from order data
actions.evidence: The joint SEC and CFTC staff review of 6 May 2010 traced how an automated sell program interacted with high-frequency traders; limit up-limit down later replaced the pilot single-stock circuit breakers adopted after the crash.

ref.title: SEC and CFTC staff, Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010, September 2010
ref.finding: The report reconstructs how a 75,000-contract E-Mini sell program and high-frequency trading drained liquidity across futures and equity markets.

actions.action: Simulate AI agent trading and design market-wide kill switches
actions.evidence: In June 2026 the Bank of England said it is testing simulation methods with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Bundesbank and suggested guardrails like circuit breakers or kill switches; nothing is in place yet.

ref.title: Bank of England, Agents of change, speech by Sarah Breeden at the ECB Forum on Central Banking, June 2026
ref.finding: Proposes exploring guardrails analogous to circuit breakers or kill switches that would limit or stop trading market-wide, possibly tested on a digital twin of the financial system.

precedents.parallel: An automated sell algorithm and high-frequency traders reacting to each other drained liquidity in minutes.
precedents.outcome: A $4.1 billion automated E-Mini sell program set off hot-potato trading among HFTs; over 20,000 trades in more than 300 securities executed over 60% away from prior prices before indices recovered to close about 3% down.

ref.title: Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010 (SEC and CFTC staff report)
ref.finding: A large automated sell of 75,000 E-Mini contracts and HFT hot-potato trading preceded a collapse in liquidity; over 20,000 trades were executed more than 60% from prior values.

precedents.parallel: Many institutions ran the same rule-based hedging strategy, so falling prices triggered the same selling at once.
precedents.outcome: The Dow fell 22.6% on 19 October 1987, its largest one-day percentage drop, and portfolio insurance sped the fall through repeated rounds of selling.

ref.title: Stock Market Crash of 1987 (Federal Reserve History)
ref.finding: The DJIA fell 22.6% in one session, the largest one-day decline in history, and portfolio insurance sped the fall through a vicious circle of selling.

precedents.parallel: Funds running similar quantitative models held the same positions, so one forced seller hit all of them.
precedents.outcome: Quant long/short equity funds suffered unprecedented losses in the week of 6 August 2007; the authors hypothesise a rapid unwind of one or more large quant market-neutral portfolios that spread to a broader set of equity portfolios, then a rebound on 10 August.

ref.title: What Happened to the Quants in August 2007? (Khandani and Lo, Journal of Investment Management, 2007)
ref.finding: Losses began with the rapid unwind of one or more large quantitative market-neutral portfolios and spread to a broader set of long/short and long-only equity portfolios; the authors present this as a hypothesis.

nodes.label: Agentic bank run
nodes.summary: Agents managing money could move deposits at once, on a rumour or better rate, faster than banks or regulators can respond. Apollo's chief economist warned in September 2026 that agents sweeping cash into higher-paying accounts could drain the cheap deposits banks lend from[3]. The Bank of England says consumers so far mainly use agents to recommend, with humans executing payments[4].

refs.title: Federal Reserve, Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank, April 2023
refs.finding: SVB lost over $40 billion of deposits on 9 March 2023; social media, a networked depositor base and technology may have fundamentally changed the speed of bank runs.

refs.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
refs.finding: Market participants using AI could take correlated positions and act collectively in ways that reduce stability; the report covers markets and does not discuss deposit runs.

refs.title: Apollo, Is an Agentic Bank Run Coming? (Torsten Slok), September 2026
refs.finding: Agentic assistants could sweep household cash from checking accounts averaging 0.1% into accounts paying 3.3% to 5.0%, so banks could lose much of the cheap deposits they lend from.

refs.title: Bank of England, Agents of change, speech by Sarah Breeden at the ECB Forum on Central Banking, June 2026
refs.finding: Consumers and merchants have so far mainly used AI agents in recommendation mode, with humans still executing transactions.

nodes.control_note: Fast automated money management is the benefit, and speed is what makes runs worse. Liquidity rules and monitoring reduce severity.

actions.action: Re-test liquidity against faster deposit runs
actions.evidence: SVB lost over $40 billion on 9 March 2023 and expected over $100 billion more the next day; the Fed review said liquidity rules and internal liquidity stress tests should re-evaluate how stable uninsured deposits are, and any rule change would take years.

ref.title: Federal Reserve, Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank, April 2023
ref.finding: Recommends re-evaluating the stability of uninsured deposits in standardized liquidity rules and firms' internal liquidity stress tests.

actions.action: Track herd behaviour of AI agents
actions.evidence: The Bank of England flags collective action by AI-using market participants as a stability risk and plans monitoring through surveys and market intelligence; the work covers trading, not deposits, and no tested intervention exists.

ref.title: Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system, April 2025
ref.finding: AI could lead market participants to take actions collectively in ways that reduce stability.

precedents.parallel: Depositors in a tight network, alerted on social media and moving money online, withdrew at once, the dynamic agents could speed further.
precedents.outcome: SVB lost over $40 billion on 9 March and expected over $100 billion more the next day, together about 85% of deposits, against about $10 billion over 8 days at Wachovia in 2008.

ref.title: Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank (Federal Reserve Board, April 2023)
ref.finding: Over $40 billion left on March 9 with over $100 billion expected on March 10; social media and technology may have fundamentally changed the speed of bank runs.

precedents.parallel: Wholesale depositors reacted to a wire-service rumour by moving funds electronically, an early machine-speed run.
precedents.outcome: After Reuters asked the bank on 9 May about bankruptcy rumours, overseas depositors pulled funds and by 11 May the bank had borrowed $3.6 billion from the Fed's discount window; the FDIC then guaranteed all depositors, at an estimated cost of about $1.1 billion as of 1997.

ref.title: Continental Illinois and Too Big to Fail, in History of the Eighties: Lessons for the Future (FDIC)
ref.finding: Rumour drove a high-speed electronic bank run that forced $3.6 billion of discount-window borrowing by 11 May 1984.

nodes.label: Synthetic science floods journals
nodes.summary: Generated text is entering the scientific record: one analysis of over 15 million PubMed abstracts estimated that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs, a measure of use rather than fraud[1]. Formulaic papers mined from one US health database rose from about 4 a year in 2014 to 2021 to 190 in 2024, which the authors link to AI-ready data, AI-assisted writing and possible paper mills[2].

refs.title: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát and Lause, Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary, Science Advances 11(27), 2025
refs.finding: An excess-vocabulary analysis of over 15 million PubMed abstracts from 2010 to 2024 suggests at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs, rising to 40% in some subgroups; the method measures LLM use, not misconduct.

refs.title: Suchak et al., Explosion of formulaic research articles, including inappropriate study designs and false discoveries, based on the NHANES US national health database, PLOS Biology 23(5), 2025
refs.finding: Single-factor papers mined from the US NHANES database rose from an average of 4 a year in 2014 to 2021 to 190 in 2024 (to 9 October); the authors say AI-ready data and AI-assisted workflows can speed such papers and that paper mills plausibly use them, without attributing individual papers.

nodes.control_note: The same writing help that speeds honest science makes fake papers cheap. Shared screening and stricter submission rules are in place, but none has published how much it catches.

actions.action: Screen manuscripts for paper-mill signals
actions.evidence: The STM Integrity Hub pools paper-mill checks across publishers; its page gives no screening or detection figures.

ref.title: STM Integrity Hub
ref.finding: A cloud environment where participating publishers check submissions for paper-mill patterns and other integrity problems.

actions.action: Accept reviews only after peer review
actions.evidence: Since October 2025 arXiv CS has rejected review and position papers that lack prior peer review, citing a surge of such papers that LLMs make quick to write; effect on volume not yet reported.

ref.title: arXiv blog, Attention Authors: Updated Practice for Review Articles and Position Papers in arXiv CS Category (31 October 2025)
ref.finding: Review and position papers in CS must be accepted by a peer-reviewed journal or conference before submission, or will likely be rejected.

precedents.parallel: SCIgen, a grammar-based generator of random computer-science papers, produced fakes that got into indexed conference proceedings.
precedents.outcome: Publishers removed more than 120 computer-generated papers from subscription databases after a scientist revealed they were generated; SCIgen aims for amusement rather than coherence, so its output was detectable nonsense.

ref.title: Van Noorden, Publishers withdraw more than 120 gibberish papers, Nature News, 24 February 2014
ref.finding: Conference proceedings were removed from subscription databases after a scientist revealed they were computer-generated.

precedents.parallel: Free online text-rewriting tools, earlier language tools, were used to pad manuscripts with garbled paraphrases.
precedents.outcome: Researchers found odd substitutions such as counterfeit consciousness for artificial intelligence concentrated in one reputable journal, alongside citations to non-existent literature and abrupt changes in editorial timelines.

ref.title: Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov, Tortured phrases: A dubious writing style emerging in science. Evidence of critical issues affecting established journals, arXiv 2107.06751
ref.finding: Tortured phrases from free rewriting websites were concentrated in one reputable journal, alongside questionable articles citing non-existent literature.

precedents.parallel: Industrial paper mills and peer-review fraud filled journals faster than screening caught them.
precedents.outcome: Retractions passed 10,000 in 2023, a record, as publishers struggled with sham papers and peer-review fraud; the report does not attribute the rise to generative AI.

ref.title: Van Noorden, More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023, a new record, Nature News, 12 December 2023
ref.finding: Retractions passed 10,000 in 2023 as publishers struggled to deal with sham papers and peer-review fraud.

nodes.label: Fabricated citations in courts
nodes.summary: Lawyers and self-represented litigants file cases and quotes that AI invented, which wastes the court's and the other side's time and draws sanctions[2]. One public database had logged 2,225 court and tribunal decisions on hallucinated content by October 2026, 1,514 of them in the US and 1,283 involving self-represented litigants[1].

refs.title: AI Hallucination Cases database (Damien Charlotin)
refs.finding: 2,225 decisions identified as of October 2026 in which a court or tribunal found or implied that a party relied on hallucinated content; 1,514 in the US, and 1,283 involving pro se litigants against 879 involving lawyers.

refs.title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
refs.finding: The court imposed a 5,000 dollar Rule 11 sanction for fake opinions generated by ChatGPT and noted that the opposing party wastes time and money exposing them and the court's time is taken from other work.

nodes.control_note: Checking citations before filing stops the harm while keeping the drafting benefit. Sanctions create the incentive.

actions.action: Sanction lawyers who file fake citations
actions.evidence: In June 2023 Mata v Avianca imposed a 5,000 dollar sanction, owed jointly by two attorneys and their law firm, for filing opinions invented by ChatGPT.

ref.title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
ref.finding: On 22 June 2023 the court imposed a 5,000 dollar Rule 11 sanction, owed jointly and severally by the attorneys and the Levidow firm, for filing non-existent opinions generated by ChatGPT.

actions.action: Track and publish hallucination cases
actions.evidence: A public database lists 2,225 court and tribunal decisions, as of October 2026, in which a party was found or implied to have relied on hallucinated content.

ref.title: AI Hallucination Cases Database, Damien Charlotin
ref.finding: 2,225 cases identified so far; the database covers decisions where a court or tribunal explicitly found or implied that a party relied on hallucinated content, not all fake citations.

precedents.event: Citations copied without reading the source
precedents.parallel: Professionals have long inserted references they never opened, so a wrong citation propagates through later work, which is the same failure that lets a fabricated case enter a filing.
precedents.outcome: Simkin and Roychowdhury modelled the spread of identical misprints in citation lists and estimated that only about 20 percent of citers had read the paper they cited; unlike AI fabrication the underlying source existed, so the error was a wrong pointer rather than an invented authority.

ref.title: Read before you cite! (Simkin and Roychowdhury, Complex Systems 14, 2003)
ref.finding: From the distribution of identical misprints in citations the authors estimate that only about 20 percent of citers read the original paper.

precedents.event: Link rot in court opinions and law reviews
precedents.parallel: Courts have already built records on authority that a later reader cannot retrieve or check, which is the practical harm of an uncheckable citation even when nobody invented it.
precedents.outcome: Zittrain, Albert and Lessig found that more than 70 percent of URLs in the Harvard Law Review and other journals and 50 percent of URLs in United States Supreme Court opinions no longer linked to the cited material, and proposed that libraries preserve the contents of cited links; the difference is that these sources once existed, so the fix was preservation rather than detection of fabrication.

ref.title: Perma: Scoping and Addressing the Problem of Link and Reference Rot in Legal Citations, 127 Harv. L. Rev. F. 176 (2014)
ref.finding: More than 70 percent of URLs within the Harvard Law Review and other journals, and 50 percent of URLs within United States Supreme Court opinions, do not link to the originally cited information.

nodes.label: Autonomous weapons
nodes.summary: In December 2023 the UN General Assembly warned autonomous weapons risk an arms race, a lower threshold for conflict and spread to non-state actors[1]. +972 Magazine reported Israel's Lavender system marked up to 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants early in the Gaza war, with officers often spending about 20 seconds per target[2]. The Israeli army called its tools auxiliary aids[2].

refs.title: UN General Assembly resolution 78/241, Lethal autonomous weapons systems, 22 December 2023
refs.finding: The General Assembly said it was concerned about possible negative consequences of autonomous weapon systems, including the risk of an emerging arms race, a lower threshold for conflict and proliferation to non-state actors, and asked the Secretary-General for a report on state views.

refs.title: Yuval Abraham, 'Lavender': The AI machine directing Israel's bombing spree in Gaza, +972 Magazine, 3 April 2024
refs.finding: Intelligence sources said that in the first weeks of the war the system marked as many as 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, and officers often spent about 20 seconds on each target before authorising a strike; the Israeli army called its tools auxiliary aids for officers.

nodes.control_note: Autonomy in targeting is a choice states can restrict by rule, though the same perception and control tech is shared with civilian robots. No binding treaty exists.

actions.action: Require human judgement over use of force
actions.evidence: US policy requires senior approval before development and fielding and that systems allow appropriate levels of human judgement over force, which does not mean manual control; it does not prohibit autonomous weapons, and the review can be waived for urgent military need.

ref.title: Defense Primer: U.S. Policy on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, Congressional Research Service IF11150, 26 March 2026
ref.finding: DoD Directive 3000.09, last updated January 2023, requires systems to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force and senior approval before development and fielding; it does not prohibit lethal autonomous weapons.

actions.action: Negotiate a binding treaty on autonomous weapons
actions.evidence: Talks under the CCW since 2014 have produced no substantive outcome, with a few states blocking proposals to negotiate a binding instrument; a 2024 UN resolution set up informal consultations in New York instead of treaty negotiations.

ref.title: Killer Robots: UN Vote Should Spur Treaty Negotiations, Human Rights Watch, 5 December 2024
ref.finding: Resolution 79/62 passed 166 to 3 with 15 abstentions on 2 December 2024 and approved open informal consultations in New York in 2025 but no treaty negotiations; CCW talks since May 2014 have produced no substantive outcome.

precedents.parallel: An air defence system run in a largely automatic mode, with crews trained to trust its software, is a fielded case of a machine classifying targets while humans approve its choices.
precedents.outcome: The Defense Science Board found three fratricide incidents, with three aircrew lost in the two Patriot firings on coalition aircraft; it blamed very poor Mode IV identification friend or foe, weak situational awareness and an operating protocol that was largely automatic, and recommended more operator involvement and control. The 30 days of the war saw 9 ballistic missile engagements amid some 41,000 coalition aircraft sorties, a 4,000 to 1 friendly to enemy ratio.

ref.title: Report of the Defense Science Board Task Force on Patriot System Performance, Report Summary, January 2005
ref.finding: Three fratricide incidents with three aircrew lost; Mode IV IFF performed very poorly; the operating protocol was largely automatic and operators were trained to trust the system's software; 9 tactical ballistic missile engagements amid some 41,000 coalition aircraft sorties; the task force recommended more operator oversight and control.

precedents.parallel: A landmine is the oldest weapon that selects and attacks a target with no human in the loop at the moment of firing, so its casualty record shows who actually gets hit when the decision is delegated to the device.
precedents.outcome: Landmine Monitor recorded at least 6,279 casualties from landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2024, up 9 percent from 5,757 in 2023, with civilians 90 percent of recorded victims and children 46 percent of civilian casualties, led by Myanmar with 2,029; the count includes unexploded ordnance, not only mines, and a mine does not discriminate at all, whereas the AI claim is that targeting will be selective.

ref.title: Civilian Casualties Remain Alarmingly High as Use of Landmines Spreads (Humanity and Inclusion, citing Landmine Monitor 2025)
ref.finding: At least 6,279 victims of landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2024, a 9 percent rise from 5,757 in 2023; civilians were 90 percent of recorded victims and children 46 percent of civilian casualties; top countries were Myanmar 2,029, Syria 1,015, Afghanistan 624, Ukraine 293, Yemen 247; improvised landmines caused more than a third of casualties.

nodes.label: AI companionship eases loneliness
nodes.summary: In one paper, a 15-minute chat with an AI companion reduced loneliness about as much as talking with another person, and over a week each daily session brought a momentary drop[1]. The relief did not accumulate across days[2]. In a randomised study of 981 people, those who chose to use a chatbot more had worse loneliness, socialising and emotional dependence[3].

refs.title: De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, Uğuralp and Puntoni, AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, Journal of Consumer Research 52(6), 2025
refs.finding: A 15-minute chat with an AI companion reduced loneliness about as much as talking with another person and more than watching YouTube videos; over a week of daily use each session gave a momentary drop, and feeling heard explained much of the effect.

refs.title: Blanding, Feeling Lonely? An Attentive Listener Is an AI Prompt Away, Harvard Business School Working Knowledge, 1 December 2025
refs.finding: In the week-long study, each daily 15-minute session left people temporarily less lonely, but the benefit did not build up from one day to the next.

refs.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, arXiv 2503.17473
refs.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, assigned chatbot conditions had no significant effect, but those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had consistently worse loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.

limiters.evidence: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, heavier voluntary chatbot use went with more loneliness, less socialising and more emotional dependence.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, assigned chatbot conditions had no significant effect, but those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had consistently worse loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.

limiters.evidence: The loneliness reduction was shown after a single 15-minute chat and over one week of daily chats, and the relief did not build up from day to day.

ref.title: Blanding, Feeling Lonely? An Attentive Listener Is an AI Prompt Away, Harvard Business School Working Knowledge, 1 December 2025
ref.finding: In the week-long study, each daily 15-minute session left people temporarily less lonely, but the benefit did not build up from one day to the next.

limiters.evidence: Heavier voluntary use, which engagement-driven apps reward, went with worse outcomes.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, assigned chatbot conditions had no significant effect, but those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had consistently worse loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.

enablers.action: Design companions to make users feel heard
enablers.evidence: In experiments that varied the chatbot, whether it made users feel heard explained much of the loneliness reduction.

ref.title: De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, Uğuralp and Puntoni, AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, Journal of Consumer Research 52(6), 2025
ref.finding: A 15-minute chat with an AI companion reduced loneliness about as much as talking with another person and more than watching YouTube videos; over a week of daily use each session gave a momentary drop, and feeling heard explained much of the effect.

enablers.action: Limit usage and flag dependence
enablers.evidence: Worse outcomes went with heavier voluntary use.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study, arXiv 2503.17473
ref.finding: In a 4-week randomised study of 981 people, assigned chatbot conditions had no significant effect, but those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had consistently worse loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.

enablers.action: Fund longer randomised studies
enablers.evidence: The positive results for AI companions in this paper cover a week at most.

ref.title: De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, Uğuralp and Puntoni, AI Companions Reduce Loneliness, Journal of Consumer Research 52(6), 2025
ref.finding: A 15-minute chat with an AI companion reduced loneliness about as much as talking with another person and more than watching YouTube videos; over a week of daily use each session gave a momentary drop, and feeling heard explained much of the effect.

precedents.event: Paro robot seal in care homes
precedents.parallel: A non-human companion that responds to residents was tested against loneliness in a randomised trial.
precedents.outcome: In a 12-week RCT of 40 Auckland care-home residents, those who spent an hour twice a week with Paro had significantly lower loneliness than residents in normal activities; the sample was small and residents interacted with the robot as a group, not as a private confidant.

ref.title: The psychosocial effects of a companion robot: a randomized controlled trial (Robinson et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013)
ref.finding: Residents who interacted with the robot had significant decreases in loneliness compared with the control group over the 12-week trial.

precedents.parallel: Pooled trials of pre-LLM social robots test whether machine companionship lowers loneliness at all.
precedents.outcome: Eight RCTs pooled showed significant decreases in depression and loneliness with large effect sizes; group use and longer interventions helped depression more. Few trials, older care residents only, and physical robots rather than chat.

ref.title: The Effect of Social Robots on Depression and Loneliness for Older Residents in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Meta-Analysis of RCTs (Yen et al., J Am Med Dir Assoc 2024)
ref.finding: Across 8 RCTs, social robot interventions significantly decreased depression and loneliness with large effect sizes; group-based and longer interventions improved depression more.

nodes.label: Chatbot therapy widens mental-health care
nodes.summary: Purpose-built therapy bots could widen access to care, one trial's senior author argues, citing an average 1,600 US patients with depression or anxiety per provider[2]. In that randomised trial of 210 US adults, bot users improved more than waitlist controls across depression, anxiety and eating-disorder risk[1]. Staff had to step in 15 times over safety concerns such as suicidal ideation[1].

refs.title: Heinz et al., Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
refs.finding: In 210 US adults recruited online, Therabot users had greater symptom reductions than waitlist controls across depression, anxiety and eating-disorder-risk groups at 4 and 8 weeks; study staff intervened 15 times over safety concerns such as suicidal ideation and corrected 13 inappropriate responses such as medical advice.

refs.title: First Therapy Chatbot Trial Yields Mental Health Benefits, Dartmouth, 27 March 2025
refs.finding: Participants with depression saw a 51% average symptom reduction, those with anxiety 31%, and those at risk of eating disorders 19% in body image and weight concerns; senior author Nicholas Jacobson said the US averages 1,600 patients with depression or anxiety for every available provider.

limiters.evidence: An Illinois law signed in August 2025 prohibits anyone from using AI to provide mental health and therapeutic decision-making, allowing it only for administrative and supplementary support for licensed professionals.

ref.title: Gov Pritzker Signs Legislation Prohibiting AI Therapy in Illinois, Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation, 4 August 2025
ref.finding: The Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act prohibits anyone from using AI to provide mental health and therapeutic decision-making, while allowing AI for administrative and supplementary support services for licensed behavioral health professionals.

limiters.evidence: In one 2025 study, large language models expressed stigma toward people with mental health conditions and responded inappropriately to critical conditions in therapy-like settings, such as encouraging delusional thinking, and newer, larger models did no better.

ref.title: Moore et al., Expressing stigma and inappropriate responses prevents LLMs from safely replacing mental health providers, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: LLMs expressed stigma toward those with mental health conditions and responded inappropriately to some common and critical conditions in naturalistic therapy settings, including encouraging clients' delusional thinking; the problems persisted in newer and larger models.

limiters.evidence: Woebot Health shut down its therapy chatbot app in 2025; its founder blamed largely the cost and challenge of meeting FDA requirements for marketing authorisation, and said the FDA had not worked out how to regulate large language models.

ref.title: Mario Aguilar, Why Woebot, a pioneering therapy chatbot, shut down, STAT, 2 July 2025
ref.finding: Founder Alison Darcy said the shutdown was largely due to the cost and challenge of fulfilling the FDA's requirements for marketing authorization, with pressure growing as large language models arrived that the FDA has not yet worked out how to regulate.

enablers.action: Run RCTs on purpose-built therapy bots
enablers.evidence: Therabot cut depression, anxiety and eating-disorder-risk symptoms more than a waitlist control in a randomised trial of 210 US adults.

ref.title: Heinz et al., Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: In 210 US adults recruited online, Therabot users had greater symptom reductions than waitlist controls across depression, anxiety and eating-disorder-risk groups at 4 and 8 weeks; study staff intervened 15 times over safety concerns such as suicidal ideation and corrected 13 inappropriate responses such as medical advice.

enablers.action: Keep clinicians in the safety loop
enablers.evidence: Trial staff reviewed conversations, stepping in 15 times over safety concerns such as suicidal ideation and 13 times to correct inappropriate responses such as medical advice.

ref.title: Heinz et al., Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment, NEJM AI 2025
ref.finding: In 210 US adults recruited online, Therabot users had greater symptom reductions than waitlist controls across depression, anxiety and eating-disorder-risk groups at 4 and 8 weeks; study staff intervened 15 times over safety concerns such as suicidal ideation and corrected 13 inappropriate responses such as medical advice.

enablers.action: Set evaluation rules for health chatbots
enablers.evidence: WHO guidance asks governments to have a regulator assess and approve large multi-modal models for health use, and to require independent post-release audits and impact assessments.

ref.title: WHO releases AI ethics and governance guidance for large multi-modal models, WHO news release, 18 January 2024
ref.finding: WHO recommends that governments assign a regulator to assess and approve large multi-modal models for health use and introduce mandatory post-release auditing and impact assessments by independent third parties when they are deployed at scale.

precedents.parallel: Computer programs delivered CBT with little or no clinician time, from self-guided courses to support as brief as one hour per patient.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 22 controlled studies found effect sizes of 0.78 for major depression and 0.88 overall, with a median 80% completing all lessons and gains maintained to a median 26 weeks; waitlists were the most common control, and effects were somewhat larger against them (0.94) than against other controls (0.75).

ref.title: Andrews et al., Computer Therapy for the Anxiety and Depressive Disorders Is Effective, Acceptable and Practical Health Care: A Meta-Analysis, PLoS ONE 2010
ref.finding: Across 22 controlled comparisons, computerised CBT gave a mean effect size of 0.88 (Hedges g 0.78 for major depression), improvement was maintained for a median 26 weeks, and no relapse was found at follow-up.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative CBT chatbot was tested as low-cost talk support for college students with depression and anxiety symptoms.
precedents.outcome: In a 2-week unblinded trial of 70 students aged 18 to 28, Woebot users reduced PHQ-9 depression scores while an ebook control group did not (between-groups d = 0.44); small, short, no follow-up, and a co-author founded the company.

ref.title: Fitzpatrick et al., Delivering Cognitive Behavior Therapy to Young Adults With Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety Using a Fully Automated Conversational Agent (Woebot), JMIR Mental Health 2017
ref.finding: Woebot users significantly reduced depression scores on the PHQ-9 while the information-only control group did not, a moderate between-groups effect size (d = 0.44).

nodes.label: Better weather forecasting
nodes.summary: Learned weather models beat leading physics-based forecasts on most targets: GraphCast on 90% of 1,380 targets against the best deterministic system[1], and GenCast on 97.2% of 1,320 targets against ECMWF's ensemble, with better prediction of extreme weather and tropical cyclone tracks[2]. ECMWF put its own learned model, AIFS, into operations on 25 February 2025[3].

refs.title: Lam et al., Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting (GraphCast), Science 2023
refs.finding: GraphCast significantly outperformed the most accurate operational deterministic systems on 90% of 1,380 verification targets and was trained directly from reanalysis data.

refs.title: Price et al., Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning (GenCast), Nature 2024
refs.finding: GenCast had greater skill than ECMWF's ENS ensemble on 97.2% of 1,320 targets evaluated and better predicted extreme weather, tropical cyclone tracks and wind power production.

refs.title: ECMWF's AI forecasts become operational (ECMWF, 25 February 2025)
refs.finding: ECMWF took its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS) into operations, reporting gains of up to 20% on tropical cyclone tracks and about 1,000 times less energy per forecast.

limiters.evidence: Only half of countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All (WMO)
ref.finding: Only half of the countries worldwide report having adequate multi-hazard early warning systems; the initiative aims to protect everyone on Earth by the end of 2027.

limiters.evidence: In one PNAS 2025 study, a FourCastNet version trained without Category 3-5 tropical cyclones matched other versions on global weather but could not accurately forecast Category 5 storms, so learned models may miss extremes stronger than any in their training data.

ref.title: Sun et al., Can AI weather models predict out-of-distribution gray swan tropical cyclones?, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: All model versions had similar accuracy for global weather, but the one trained without Category 3-5 tropical cyclones could not accurately forecast Category 5 storms.

limiters.evidence: Only 23% of people in low-income countries used the internet in 2025, which limits forecasts delivered online.

ref.title: ITU, Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides, 17 November 2025
ref.finding: 2.2 billion people remain offline in 2025, with about three-quarters of the world online; 94% of people in high-income countries use the internet against only 23% in low-income countries.

enablers.action: Link AI forecasts to early warnings
enablers.evidence: Early Warnings for All, co-led by WMO and UNDRR, aims to cover everyone on Earth with warning systems by the end of 2027; the WMO page does not mention AI forecasts.

ref.title: Early Warnings for All (WMO)
ref.finding: Only half of the countries worldwide report having adequate multi-hazard early warning systems; the initiative aims to protect everyone on Earth by the end of 2027.

enablers.action: Release model code and weights
enablers.evidence: The GenCast authors released the code and model weights, and a 15-day GenCast forecast takes about 8 minutes on one Cloud TPU v5 device.

ref.title: Price et al., Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning (GenCast), Nature 2024
ref.finding: Code implementing GenCast is available in the graphcast GitHub repository, with download links for ERA5 and operational versions of the model weights.

precedents.event: ENIAC makes the first computer forecast
precedents.parallel: A new computational method was slow and crude at first but soon became the operational basis of forecasting.
precedents.outcome: The 24-hour forecast took about 24 hours to compute, yet results were encouraging enough that numerical prediction became an operational reality within about five years; two years later the same forecast ran in five minutes.

ref.title: The ENIAC Forecasts: A Recreation (Peter Lynch, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 2008)
ref.finding: Charney said it mattered little that the twenty-four-hour prediction was twenty-four hours in the making; two years later it took five minutes, and NWP became operational within about five years.

precedents.parallel: A statistical relationship between observed weather and physics model output corrected those models, an early learned layer on top of NWP.
precedents.outcome: Glahn and Lowry defined MOS in 1972 and NOAA's Meteorological Development Laboratory still produces it from the GFS, Ensemble GFS and NAM models; it corrects certain systematic model biases but not deficiencies in model physics, and the page gives no skill numbers.

ref.title: What is MOS? (NOAA Meteorological Development Laboratory)
ref.finding: MOS determines a statistical relationship between a predictand and variables forecast by a numerical model; Glahn and Lowry defined it in 1972, and MDL produces MOS from the GFS, Ensemble GFS and NAM models.

precedents.parallel: Forecast skill improved steadily through compute and method gains, the baseline that learned models now compete with.
precedents.outcome: Skilful forecast lead time grew by about one day per decade through a steady accumulation of scientific and technical advances rather than single breakthroughs; this is the slow baseline AI models claim to leap past.

ref.title: The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction (Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet, Nature 2015)
ref.finding: Progress was gradual, about an extra day of skilful forecast lead time per decade, from a steady accumulation of knowledge and technology over many years.

nodes.label: Phishing at industrial scale
nodes.summary: AI can write phishing emails as effective as human experts' ones. In one study of 101 university-recruited participants, fully AI-generated spear phishing got a 54% click rate, matching human experts[1]. In hundreds of thousands of malicious emails caught by one vendor, at least about 51% of spam and 14% of business email compromise attacks were LLM-generated by April 2025[2].

refs.title: Heiding et al., AI spear phishing 2024
refs.finding: In 101 participants, fully AI-automated spear phishing got 54% click-through, the same as human experts, against 12% for arbitrary phishing emails.

refs.title: Hao et al., Do Spammers Dream of Electric Sheep? Characterizing the Prevalence of LLM-Generated Malicious Emails, ACM IMC 2025
refs.finding: In malicious emails detected by Barracuda, at least about 51% of spam and 14% of business email compromise attacks were LLM-generated as of April 2025; attackers used LLMs to polish emails and generate variants.

nodes.control_note: Fluent cheap writing is the benefit and the attack. Authentication and AI-based filters reduce delivery and harm.

actions.action: Require SPF, DKIM and DMARC for bulk senders
actions.evidence: Gmail has required senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts to set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC since 1 February 2024, though the DMARC policy may be set to none.

ref.title: Gmail Help, Email sender guidelines
ref.finding: Bulk senders must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC since 1 February 2024; the DMARC enforcement policy can be set to none.

actions.action: Use AI to flag phishing intent
actions.evidence: In one study, Claude 3.5 Sonnet flagged 97.25% of 363 phishing emails as suspicious with no false positives on 18 legitimate ones, but caught only 81% of conventional phishing.

ref.title: Heiding et al., Evaluating LLMs' Capability to Launch Fully Automated Spear Phishing Campaigns
ref.finding: Claude 3.5 Sonnet detected suspicious intent well above 90% of the time with low false-positive rates.

actions.action: Adopt phishing-resistant multifactor authentication
actions.evidence: CISA calls phishing-resistant MFA the gold standard because other MFA can be phished, and US federal agencies must adopt it; it protects account logins only.

ref.title: CISA, Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA (fact sheet, October 2022)
ref.finding: Phishing-resistant MFA is the most secure form of MFA and the gold standard; the Office of Management and Budget requires federal agencies to adopt it.

precedents.parallel: Near-zero sending cost made mass scam messaging profitable even with tiny response rates.
precedents.outcome: Researchers rewrote nearly 470 million spams; the pharmacy campaign got 1 purchase per 12.5 million emails, so profit depended on huge volume at near-zero cost.

ref.title: Spamalytics: An Empirical Analysis of Spam Marketing Conversion (Kanich et al., CCS 2008)
ref.finding: Of nearly 470 million spams rewritten, the pharmacy campaign led to 28 purchases, about 1 in 12,500,000 pharmacy spams.

precedents.parallel: Scammers' bottleneck was the cost of following up with non-victims, a step that AI-written replies could make cheaper.
precedents.outcome: Herley showed victim density drives profit, with a 10x drop in density able to cut victims found 1000x, so scammers used absurd emails to filter out the sceptical before costly follow-up.

ref.title: Why do Nigerian Scammers Say They are From Nigeria? (Herley, Microsoft Research, WEIS 2012)
ref.finding: A 10x reduction in victim density can produce a 1000x reduction in victims found, so attackers must filter targets cheaply.

nodes.label: Bots outnumber people online
nodes.summary: Imperva's 2025 bot report found automated traffic reached 51% of all web traffic, passing human traffic for the first time in a decade, with bad bots at 37%[1]. Its 2026 report, based on full-year 2025 activity, puts bots at over 53% of web traffic[2]. Both figures come from a vendor that sells bot protection and count all automation, including search crawlers.

refs.title: 2025 Bad Bot Report (Imperva)
refs.finding: For the first time in a decade, automated traffic surpassed human activity, accounting for 51% of all web traffic; bad bots made up 37% of all internet traffic.

refs.title: The 2026 Bad Bot Report is here (Tim Chang, Imperva, 5 May 2026)
refs.finding: Bots account for over 53% of all web traffic in the 13th edition of the report, and AI-driven bot attacks surged 12.5 times.

nodes.control_note: Cheap agents that act on the web are a benefit, so automated traffic will keep growing. Authentication and fake review rules limit the deception.

actions.action: Ban AI-generated fake reviews
actions.evidence: The FTC rule, in effect since October 2024, bans reviews that misrepresent that they are by someone who does not exist, including AI-generated fake reviews, and allows civil penalties against knowing violators.

ref.title: Federal Trade Commission Announces Final Rule Banning Fake Reviews and Testimonials (FTC, 14 August 2024)
ref.finding: The rule covers reviews that misrepresent that they are by someone who does not exist, such as AI-generated fake reviews, and lets the FTC seek civil penalties against knowing violators.

actions.action: Make crawlers sign their requests
actions.evidence: Cloudflare's pay per crawl, in private beta, has crawlers sign each request with HTTP Message Signatures under the Web Bot Auth proposals so no one can spoof them; it only identifies crawlers that sign.

ref.title: Introducing pay per crawl: Enabling content owners to charge AI crawlers for access (Cloudflare blog, 1 July 2025)
ref.finding: Crawlers configure HTTP Message Signatures on each request using the Web Bot Auth proposals, so Cloudflare can charge a specific crawler and prevent others from spoofing it; pay per crawl is in private beta.

actions.action: Disclose when users talk to a machine
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act requires providers to design AI systems that interact directly with people so those people are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious from context; the Act applies from 2 August 2026.

ref.title: AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations (European Commission AI Act Service Desk)
ref.finding: Article 50(1) requires that people be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person; Article 50(2) requires machine-readable marking of synthetic content.

precedents.parallel: Scripted accounts already passed as people in large numbers before generative AI.
precedents.outcome: A classifier study estimated 9% to 15% of active Twitter accounts were bots, an estimate tied to one detection method.

ref.title: Online Human-Bot Interactions: Detection, Estimation, and Characterization (Varol et al., ICWSM 2017)
ref.finding: Between 9% and 15% of active Twitter accounts are bots.

precedents.parallel: Businesses bought or wrote fake reviews, eroding trust that a review comes from a real customer.
precedents.outcome: About 16% of Yelp restaurant reviews were filtered as suspicious; a restaurant was more likely to commit review fraud when its reputation was weak, and more likely to receive unfavourable fake reviews when competition increased; the filter is a proxy, not ground truth.

ref.title: Fake It Till You Make It: Reputation, Competition, and Yelp Review Fraud (Luca and Zervas, Management Science 62(12), 2016)
ref.finding: Roughly 16% of Yelp restaurant reviews are filtered, and the prevalence of suspicious reviews has grown significantly over time.

nodes.label: Machine persuasion and manipulation
nodes.summary: Chatbots can out-persuade people. In one US study of 900 people, GPT-4 given basic personal data beat human debaters in 64% of debates where they differed, though a 2026 correction says the data's added edge is unproven[1]. In three UK experiments with 76,977 adults, post-training and prompting raised persuasiveness by up to 51% and 27% but lowered factual accuracy[3].

refs.title: Salvi et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2025
refs.finding: In 900 US participants, GPT-4 with basic personal data was more persuasive than humans 64.4% of the time in unequal pairs; a 2026 author correction says its gain over GPT-4 without personal data was not significant.

refs.title: Yang and Menczer, Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet, Journal of Quantitative Description: Digital Media 2024
refs.finding: Found 1,140 accounts posting ChatGPT-generated content that promoted suspicious websites; state-of-the-art LLM content classifiers could not tell them from human accounts, though coordination patterns could.

refs.title: Hackenburg et al., The levers of political persuasion with conversational artificial intelligence, Science 2025
refs.finding: Across 76,977 UK participants and 19 models, post-training and prompting boosted persuasiveness by up to 51% and 27%, personalisation and scale had smaller effects, and where persuasiveness rose factual accuracy fell.

refs.title: Costello et al., Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies, arXiv 2026
refs.finding: Across four experiments with 3,996 Americans, models both raised and lowered conspiracy belief with no consistent truth advantage; prompting the model to give only accurate information sharply cut its ability to raise belief.

nodes.control_note: Models that talk people out of conspiracies can also talk them in; persuasion is one capability. Bans on manipulative uses limit the worst cases, and instructing models to use only accurate information sharply cut their power to mislead in one study.

actions.action: Ban manipulative AI techniques
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act has banned subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques since 2 February 2025, but only where they cause or are reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 5(1)(a) prohibits AI that uses subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort behaviour in a way that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

actions.action: Limit personal data available to persuasive models
actions.evidence: GPT-4 with basic personal data had 81% higher odds than humans of shifting views in one US study, but a 2026 correction found its gain over GPT-4 without the data not significant, so data limits are not shown to help.

ref.title: Salvi et al., On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4, Nature Human Behaviour 2025
ref.finding: Personalised GPT-4 had 81.2% higher odds than human debaters of raising agreement; its gain over non-personalised GPT-4 was not significant (P = 0.07).

actions.action: Instruct models to give only accurate information
actions.evidence: In four experiments with 3,996 US adults, prompting the model to give only accurate information sharply cut its ability to raise conspiracy belief, and GPT 5.2 almost entirely refused to promote conspiracies.

ref.title: Costello et al., Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies, arXiv 2026
ref.finding: Prompting the model to only provide accurate information dramatically reduced its effectiveness at raising conspiracy belief; GPT 5.2 almost entirely refused to promote conspiracies.

precedents.parallel: Traits inferred from digital footprints were used to tailor persuasive messages, a small-scale version of model persuasion.
precedents.outcome: Three Facebook ad studies reaching over 3.5 million people found matched ads drew up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases; these are upper bounds, and the outcomes were clicks and purchases, not changed beliefs.

ref.title: Psychological targeting as an effective approach to digital mass persuasion (Matz et al., PNAS 2017), summary by Cambridge Judge Business School
ref.finding: Psychologically matched ads produced up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases across 3.5 million users.

precedents.parallel: A platform-level message shown to millions shifted real behaviour, the reach a persuasive model would have.
precedents.outcome: Messages to 61 million users in the 2010 US congressional elections raised turnout by about 60,000 directly and 280,000 through friends, about 340,000 votes or 0.14% of the voting age population; it was a turnout nudge, not a change of opinion.

ref.title: A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization (Bond et al., Nature 2012)
ref.finding: About 60,000 direct and 280,000 indirect additional votes, 340,000 in total.

precedents.event: Hate radio in the Rwandan genocide
precedents.parallel: A mass medium used for propaganda shows how far persuasion at scale can go in the worst case.
precedents.outcome: Comparing villages with and without radio reception, the study attributed about 10% of genocide participation, an estimated 51,000 perpetrators, to the broadcasts, partly through spillovers to neighbouring villages; it was mass broadcast in a crisis, not one-to-one argument.

ref.title: Propaganda and Conflict: Evidence from the Rwandan Genocide (Yanagizawa-Drott, QJE 2014; Harvard CID working paper)
ref.finding: Approximately 10 percent of participation in the violence, about 51,000 perpetrators, can be attributed to the radio broadcasts.

nodes.label: AI talks people out of conspiracies
nodes.summary: In one study of 2,190 US conspiracy believers, a short conversation with GPT-4 Turbo cut belief in their chosen conspiracy by about 20%, holding at least two months[1]. A follow-up with 3,996 US adults found no consistent advantage for truth: models could also substantially raise conspiracy belief, though prompting for only accurate information sharply cut that[2].

refs.title: Costello, Pennycook and Rand, Science 2024
refs.finding: Personalised dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut conspiracy belief by about 20% in 2,190 believers, and the effect remained two months later. Science issued an expression of concern in June 2026 over dataset and screening inconsistencies, later marked rescinded, and published an erratum on 22 October 2026; the authors say their reanalysis matches the original results in direction, significance and size.

refs.title: Costello et al., Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies, arXiv 2026
refs.finding: Across four experiments with 3,996 Americans, models both raised and lowered conspiracy belief with no consistent truth advantage; prompting the model to give only accurate information sharply cut its ability to raise belief.

limiters.evidence: Participants were US online survey respondents paid to take part; uptake by believers who do not join surveys is untested.

ref.title: Costello, Pennycook and Rand, Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI, PsyArXiv preprint 2024
ref.finding: The authors note the study relied mainly on American online survey respondents who took part for material compensation, which raises questions about generalisability.

limiters.evidence: In one set of US experiments, models raised conspiracy belief as well as lowered it, and people rated the misleading model as more informative.

ref.title: Costello et al., Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies, arXiv 2026
ref.finding: Models both raised and lowered average conspiracy belief with no consistent truth advantage; participants rated the conspiracy-promoting model as more informative and reported more trust in AI.

limiters.evidence: Fluent model output can mislead even trained users: in one experiment with 758 BCG consultants, GPT-4 access cut correct answers on a task outside its ability from 84.5% to 70.6%, and to 60% with a prompting overview.

ref.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (Dell'Acqua et al., Organization Science 2026), summary by Harvard Business School's AI Institute
ref.finding: On a task outside GPT-4's capability, 84.5% of consultants without AI were correct against 70.6% with GPT-4 and 60% with GPT-4 plus a prompting overview.

enablers.action: Offer tailored fact dialogues on platforms
enablers.evidence: Tailored dialogue cut belief about 20% for at least two months in one US study.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI, Science 2024
