ref.finding: Personalised dialogue with GPT-4 Turbo cut conspiracy belief by about 20% and the effect remained two months later. Science issued an expression of concern in June 2026 over dataset and screening inconsistencies, later marked rescinded, and published an erratum on 22 October 2026; the authors say their reanalysis matches the original results in direction, significance and size.

enablers.action: Label AI-generated content
enablers.evidence: AI Act Article 50 requires deployers to disclose deepfakes and providers to mark synthetic content in a machine-readable way.

ref.title: European Commission, Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act (FAQ)
ref.finding: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026; providers of systems placed on the market before then must meet the marking obligation from 2 December 2026.

precedents.parallel: One-on-one, non-judgmental conversation durably shifted entrenched attitudes, as model dialogue is claimed to.
precedents.outcome: Across three preregistered experiments with 6,869 US voters, conversations with a non-judgmental exchange of narratives reduced exclusionary attitudes for at least four months (d = 0.04 to 0.08), while arguments alone had no effect in the first experiment; effects were small.

ref.title: Reducing Exclusionary Attitudes through Interpersonal Conversation: Evidence from Three Field Experiments (Kalla and Broockman, American Political Science Review 2020)
ref.finding: Narrative-based conversations reduced exclusionary attitudes for at least four months; arguments alone did not.

precedents.parallel: Factual corrections were feared to entrench false beliefs; large tests found people mostly update toward facts.
precedents.outcome: Five experiments with over 10,100 subjects across 52 issues found no correction that triggered backfire.

ref.title: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes' Steadfast Factual Adherence (Wood and Porter, Political Behavior 2019)
ref.finding: Across five experiments with over 10,100 subjects and 52 issues, no corrections were found capable of triggering backfire.

precedents.parallel: An interactive tool taught people manipulation tactics to lower their susceptibility to misinformation.
precedents.outcome: In about 15,000 players, reliability ratings of fake items fell by 0.45 to 0.71 points on a 7-point scale (0.26 in a smaller later sample) with no meaningful change for real news; there was no control group, the sample was self-selected and decay was not measured.

ref.title: Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation (Roozenbeek and van der Linden, Palgrave Communications 2019)
ref.finding: After play, perceived reliability of fake headlines fell (e.g. impersonation 3.00 to 2.30 on a 1-7 scale) while real-news ratings did not change meaningfully.

nodes.label: Insecure AI-written code
nodes.summary: In Veracode's 2025 tests of over 100 models, AI-generated code introduced security flaws in 45% of tests[1], and its 2026 tests of 11 newer models found the average pass rate stalled at 56%[2]. Yet in one user study of 58 students, programmers with an AI assistant produced critical security bugs at a rate no more than 10% above those without[3].

refs.title: Veracode 2025 GenAI Code Security Report
refs.finding: Across over 100 large language models writing Java, JavaScript, Python and C#, AI-generated code introduced risky security flaws in 45% of tests, and larger, newer models did not improve security.

refs.title: Veracode 2026 GenAI Code Security Report
refs.finding: Testing 11 new models on 80 tasks in summer 2026, the average security pass rate was 56%; the best model, GPT-5.5, passed 68% and still failed nearly 1 in 3 security tasks, and Java averaged 30%.

refs.title: Sandoval et al., Lost at C: A User Study on the Security Implications of Large Language Model Code Assistants, USENIX Security 2023
refs.finding: In a study of 58 student programmers writing a linked list in C, AI-assisted users produced critical security bugs at a rate no greater than 10% more than the control group.

nodes.control_note: More people shipping code with AI is the benefit, so more flawed code ships. Scanning and secure defaults reduce exposure.

actions.action: Scan generated code before merge
actions.evidence: In one study, about 40 percent of 1,689 programs Copilot wrote for 89 security-relevant scenarios were vulnerable, found with CodeQL scanning plus manual review; the authors note static analysis catches mechanical bugs but some weaknesses need fuzzing or wider context.

ref.title: Pearce et al., Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions, IEEE S&P 2022
ref.finding: Of 1,689 programs Copilot produced for 89 scenarios based on high-risk CWEs, approximately 40% were vulnerable, assessed with CodeQL and manual inspection.

actions.action: Commit vendors to secure-by-design defaults
actions.evidence: Hundreds of software makers have signed CISA's Secure by Design pledge; it is voluntary and not legally binding, progress is self-reported, and CISA does not verify adherence.

ref.title: CISA, Secure by Design Pledge
ref.finding: The pledge is voluntary and not legally binding; signers are asked to publicly document measurable progress within a year, and CISA does not enforce or verify adherence.

precedents.parallel: Developers reused code from an outside source without review, the same habit as accepting generated code.
precedents.outcome: 15.4% of 1.3 million Android apps contained security-related Stack Overflow snippets, and 97.9% of those contained at least one insecure snippet.

ref.title: Fischer et al., Stack Overflow Considered Harmful? The Impact of Copy&Paste on Android Application Security, IEEE S&P 2017
ref.finding: 15.4% of 1.3 million apps had security-related snippets from Stack Overflow; 97.9% of these had at least one insecure snippet.

precedents.parallel: One flaw in widely reused code sat silently in countless systems, the way a common generated pattern could.
precedents.outcome: CISA called CVE-2021-44228 a critical remote code execution flaw under active, widespread exploitation, present in consumer and enterprise services, websites, applications and operational technology products, and warned that organisations may lack insight into some affected applications such as SaaS and cloud resources.

ref.title: Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance (CISA)
ref.finding: CVE-2021-44228 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability under active, widespread exploitation; Log4j is used in consumer and enterprise services, websites and applications, and in operational technology products.

nodes.label: AI-generated child abuse imagery
nodes.summary: AI generators create child abuse imagery, including of known victims[1]. In September 2023, 20,254 AI-generated images were posted to one dark web forum, and of 11,108 that IWF analysts assessed, 2,978 were criminal under UK law[1]. AI abuse videos the IWF found rose from 13 in 2024 to 3,443 in 2025, still a small share of its reports[2].

refs.title: Internet Watch Foundation, How AI is being abused to create child sexual abuse imagery, October 2023
refs.finding: 20,254 AI-generated images were posted to one dark web CSAM forum in September 2023; of 11,108 assessed, 2,978 were criminal under UK law, and the IWF found many AI images featuring known victims and famous children.

refs.title: Internet Watch Foundation, Harm without limits: AI child sexual abuse material through the eyes of our Analysts, AI CSAM Report 2026
refs.finding: In 2025 the IWF assessed 8,029 AI-generated images and videos as realistic child sexual abuse, still a small share of all reports; AI abuse videos rose from 13 in 2024 to 3,443 in 2025.

nodes.control_note: Abuse imagery has no legitimate use, so data hygiene, model removal and criminal law face no trade-off, but offenders favour open models run offline, which lack moderation and cannot be recalled once released.

actions.action: Remove abuse material from training data
actions.evidence: Eleven AI firms including OpenAI, Google and Stability AI publicly committed to Safety by Design principles; the commitments are voluntary and the page describes no independent audit.

ref.title: Thorn, Generative AI Principles for child safety (Safety by Design, with All Tech Is Human)
ref.finding: AI firms committed to remove CSAM from training data and to remove models and services that nudify images of children from their platforms.

actions.action: Report and remove AI abuse imagery
actions.evidence: IWF assessed 8,029 realistic AI abuse images and videos in 2025, and AI videos rose from 13 to 3,443; it says small fine-tuned models that run offline are often highly resilient to removal efforts.

ref.title: Internet Watch Foundation, Harm without limits: AI child sexual abuse material through the eyes of our Analysts, AI CSAM Report 2026
ref.finding: AI child abuse videos rose from 13 in 2024 to 3,443 in 2025; LoRA files are small, run offline and are often highly resilient to efforts to remove them.

precedents.parallel: Cheap cameras and cheap distribution already pushed the volume of abuse imagery past what clearinghouses and police could act on, which is the same capacity failure generators are now accused of causing.
precedents.outcome: Google and NCMEC researchers found detected abuse imagery had grown exponentially to nearly one million detected events per month, exceeding the capability of independent clearinghouses and law enforcement to take action, and argued for machine learning to automate detection and response; the figures count detected events, not abuse itself.

ref.title: Bursztein et al., Rethinking the Detection of Child Sexual Abuse Imagery on the Internet (WWW 2019)
ref.finding: The first longitudinal study of the distribution of this imagery finds exponential growth to nearly one million detected events per month, exceeding the capabilities of independent clearinghouses and law enforcement to take action.

nodes.label: Homogenised ideas and culture
nodes.summary: AI can make ideas and stories more alike. In one experiment with 293 UK-based writers, AI story ideas made individual stories more creative but more similar to each other[1], and across five brainstorming experiments ChatGPT help significantly cut idea diversity in 37 of 45 comparisons[2]. In one study, chain-of-thought prompting brought GPT-4's idea pool close to human groups' diversity[3].

refs.title: Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances 2024
refs.finding: In an experiment with 293 UK-based writers and 600 evaluators, access to AI story ideas made stories rated more creative, most for less creative writers, but more similar to each other.

refs.title: ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming (Meincke, Nave and Terwiesch, Nature Human Behaviour 2025), Wharton Mack Institute summary
refs.finding: Across five experiments, ChatGPT-assisted brainstorming produced narrower sets of ideas; the drop in diversity was significant in 37 of 45 comparisons.

refs.title: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch, Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: GPT-4 idea pools from plausible prompts were less diverse than those of human groups; chain-of-thought prompting gave the most diverse and most unique ideas, close to human groups.

nodes.control_note: Writers given AI ideas anchored on them, which made their stories alike. Chain-of-thought prompting widened GPT-4's own idea pool in one study, but that study did not test the work people then produce with AI help.

actions.action: Offer several diverse AI ideas, not one
actions.evidence: Five ideas instead of one gave larger quality gains, but stories in both AI conditions were still more similar to each other than human-only stories; the study tested no condition that restored diversity.

ref.title: Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances 2024
ref.finding: AI-aided stories were rated more creative but were more similar to each other, with one AI idea or five.

actions.action: Disclose AI use in published creative work
actions.evidence: Since 2 August 2026 the AI Act requires providers to mark AI-generated content in machine-readable form and deployers to disclose deepfakes, in a lighter form for evidently artistic work; most evaluators in Doshi and Hauser wanted AI use disclosed, but neither source links disclosure to diversity.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 50(2) requires providers of generative AI systems to mark outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated; Article 50(4) requires deployers to disclose deepfakes, limited for evidently artistic or creative works.

precedents.parallel: Search and hyperlinks made each literature lookup faster but steered researchers toward the same few sources, much as AI help can polish each piece of work while making all of it more alike.
precedents.outcome: Across 34 million articles, more online availability went with citing more recent work, fewer journals and fewer articles, concentrated on fewer sources; other bibliometricians disputed parts of this in Science letters, so the size of the effect is contested.

ref.title: Electronic publication and the narrowing of science and scholarship (Evans, Science 2008)
ref.finding: As more journal issues came online, fewer journals and articles were cited and citations concentrated on fewer of them.

precedents.parallel: When people could see what others chose, attention piled onto the same songs, a measured case of a shared signal pulling many independent choices toward the same outcome.
precedents.outcome: With 14,341 participants, stronger social influence raised both inequality and unpredictability of song success; it concerns concentration of popularity in a lab market, not the content of new work itself.

ref.title: Experimental study of inequality and unpredictability in an artificial cultural market (Salganik, Dodds, Watts, Science 2006)
ref.finding: Increasing the strength of social influence increased both inequality and unpredictability of success.

nodes.label: Automated mass surveillance
nodes.summary: Cheap vision and language models could let states monitor and censor at a scale that once needed armies of people. Freedom House found legal frameworks in at least 21 of the 70 countries it assesses push platforms to use machine learning to remove disfavoured speech[1]. A 2019 Carnegie index counted at least 75 of 176 countries using AI for surveillance[2].

refs.title: Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2023: The Repressive Power of Artificial Intelligence
refs.finding: Legal frameworks in at least 21 of the 70 countries assessed mandate or incentivize platforms to use machine learning to remove disfavoured speech; surveillance systems trawl social media for signs of dissent.

refs.title: Steven Feldstein, The Global Expansion of AI Surveillance (Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, September 2019)
refs.finding: At least 75 of 176 countries actively use AI for surveillance: smart city platforms in 56, facial recognition in 64 and smart policing in 52; 51% of advanced democracies deploy AI surveillance systems.

nodes.control_note: Mass surveillance is a political choice that law can restrict, as the EU AI Act's limits on police face recognition show, but half of advanced democracies already deploy AI surveillance and the vision and language tech is shared with assistive tools. In autocracies outside pressure has little reach.

actions.action: Ban real-time remote biometric identification
actions.evidence: Since 2 February 2025 the EU AI Act has banned police use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, except where strictly necessary to find victims of abduction or trafficking or missing persons, to prevent an imminent threat or terrorist attack, or to locate suspects of listed serious crimes.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ref.finding: Article 5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement unless strictly necessary for one of three listed objectives.

actions.action: Require algorithm audits and redress
actions.evidence: Freedom House found legal frameworks in at least 21 countries push platforms to use machine learning to remove protected speech, and recommends AI laws require audits, transparency, and notice, explanation, redress and appeal.

ref.title: Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2023: The Repressive Power of Artificial Intelligence
ref.finding: Legal frameworks in at least 21 countries mandate or incentivize platforms to deploy machine learning to remove speech; AI laws should require audits and transparency and include mechanisms for notice, explanation, redress and appeal.

precedents.parallel: Mass monitoring of a population once took a full-time ministry and hundreds of thousands of human informants, the labour that cheap vision and language models could replace.
precedents.outcome: The Ministry for State Security ran about 189,000 unofficial informants in 1989, 173,000 of them in its counter-intelligence units, and about 620,000 people served as informants between 1950 and 1989.

ref.title: Inoffizieller Mitarbeiter (IM), MfS-Lexikon (Helmut Mueller-Enbergs, Bundesarchiv)
ref.finding: In 1989 the MfS ran about 189,000 IM, including 173,000 in its counter-intelligence units; from 1950 to 1989 there were about 620,000 IM in total.

precedents.parallel: Automated bulk collection of everyone's call records is the closest documented case of machine-scale state monitoring justified by security.
precedents.outcome: The US privacy oversight board found no instance involving a threat to the United States where the program made a concrete difference to a counterterrorism investigation, and only one arguable case in seven years of helping identify an unknown suspect; it recommended ending the program.

ref.title: Report on the Telephone Records Program Conducted under Section 215 (PCLOB, January 2014)
ref.finding: We have not identified a single instance involving a threat to the United States in which the program made a concrete difference in the outcome of a counterterrorism investigation.

nodes.label: AI as a tool of trade and tariffs
nodes.summary: The US has tied AI access to political alignment: a January 2025 rule sorted countries into three tiers with caps on advanced chips[1], which Commerce began rescinding in May 2025 before compliance was due[2], and the July 2025 AI Action Plan aims to export the full American AI technology stack to countries that join America's AI alliance while countering Chinese influence[3]. In January 2026 the US put a 25 percent tariff on certain imported advanced computing chips, waived for imports that support the US technology supply chain[4].

refs.title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, Federal Register, 15 January 2025
refs.finding: Interim final rule that sorted destinations into three groups (19 listed destinations such as Australia, Japan, Taiwan and the UK; Country Group D:5 and Macau; and all others), capped advanced chips for the third group at a cumulative 790,000,000 TPP per country for 2025 to 2027, and required licences to export weights of closed models trained on more than 10^26 operations; compliance was due 15 May 2025.

refs.title: Department of Commerce Rescinds Biden-Era Artificial Intelligence Diffusion Rule, BIS press release, 12 May 2025
refs.finding: Commerce initiated a rescission of the rule before its 15 May 2025 compliance date, told enforcement officials not to enforce it, and announced tighter chip export controls the same day.

refs.title: America's AI Action Plan, July 2025
refs.finding: Calls for exporting the full American AI technology stack to all countries willing to join America's AI alliance, and for countering Chinese influence in international governance bodies.

refs.title: Proclamation 11002, Adjusting Imports of Semiconductors, Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment, and Their Derivative Products Into the United States, Federal Register, 20 January 2026
refs.finding: Imposed a 25 percent tariff from 15 January 2026 on certain imported advanced computing chips, waived for uses that support the US technology supply chain such as US data centers, and directed trade negotiations with foreign jurisdictions.

nodes.control_note: Rationing chips by country is a policy choice rather than a technical necessity: the US dropped its tiered diffusion rule four months after issuing it, though it kept and tightened other chip export controls.

actions.action: Publish country tiers through open rulemaking
actions.evidence: The January 2025 diffusion rule set country tiers in an interim final rule open to public comment, which made the leverage visible; Commerce began rescinding it in May 2025, before compliance was due.

ref.title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, Federal Register, 15 January 2025
ref.finding: Interim final rule that sorted destinations into three groups (19 listed destinations such as Australia, Japan, Taiwan and the UK; Country Group D:5 and Macau; and all others), capped advanced chips for the third group at a cumulative 790,000,000 TPP per country for 2025 to 2027, and required licences to export weights of closed models trained on more than 10^26 operations; compliance was due 15 May 2025.

precedents.parallel: Producers of a resource the whole economy depended on cut supply to countries by their political alignment, as chip and model access can be rationed by country.
precedents.outcome: Oil prices first doubled, then quadrupled; the embargo was lifted in March 1974 and consumers responded with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, fuel economy standards and the International Energy Agency.

ref.title: Oil Embargo, 1973-1974 (US Office of the Historian)
ref.finding: The price of oil per barrel first doubled, then quadrupled, and the crisis led to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the IEA.

precedents.parallel: The US used trade sanctions to force a market-share and pricing deal on a rival's chip industry, an earlier case of chips as a lever of state power.
precedents.outcome: Reagan imposed 100 percent tariffs on 300 million dollars of Japanese imports in April 1987; the deal handed Japanese exporters windfall DRAM profits, sped up Korean entry, did not bring US firms back into DRAM, and hurt US computer makers who used the chips.

ref.title: The U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Trade Conflict (Irwin, NBER, 1996)
ref.finding: Reagan imposed 100 percent tariffs on $300 million of Japanese imports; the clear losers were semiconductor users.

nodes.label: Backdoored models
nodes.summary: Downloaded models can hide backdoors or malicious code. In one study, backdoors trained into models survived standard safety training[1], and JFrog found about 100 Hugging Face models that ran code on load, at least two opening a reverse shell[2]. A follow-up study caught such lab-made backdoors with simple probes, untested on real attacks[3].

refs.title: Hubinger et al., Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training, 2024
refs.finding: Backdoors trained into models persisted through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and adversarial training, and were most persistent in the largest models.

refs.title: JFrog (David Cohen), Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor, February 2024
refs.finding: Found around 100 Hugging Face models with payloads that ran code when loaded; most were judged to be researchers' attempts, while baller423/goober2 and star23/baller13 opened a reverse shell to an external IP address.

refs.title: MacDiarmid et al., Simple probes can catch sleeper agents (Anthropic), April 2024
refs.finding: Linear probes on model activations detected when sleeper agent models would defect with AUROC above 99%; the authors say this may be an artifact of their backdoor insertion and is untested on naturally arising deception.

nodes.control_note: Open weight sharing is what makes models cheap and widely usable, and it is also how trojans travel. Safe formats and scanning stop file-level malware, not behavioural backdoors; probes that read model internals are a lab result so far.

actions.action: Load weights only in safetensors format
actions.evidence: Safetensors stores tensors without pickle, whose loading can run arbitrary code, so it closes the file-level route; it does not address backdoors trained into the weights.

ref.title: Hugging Face, Safetensors documentation
ref.finding: A format for storing tensors safely, as opposed to pickle.

actions.action: Scan model repositories for malicious payloads
actions.evidence: Hugging Face runs ClamAV and a pickle import scan on every file pushed to the Hub and highlights suspicious imports, but says the scan is not 100% foolproof.

ref.title: Hugging Face Hub documentation, Pickle Scanning
ref.finding: A security scanner runs ClamAV and pickle import scans on every file pushed to the Hub; Hugging Face says this is not 100% foolproof.

actions.action: Restrict untrusted models from sensitive systems
actions.evidence: Backdoors survived fine-tuning, RL and adversarial training in Sleeper Agents, and adversarial training could teach models to recognise their triggers better, hiding the unsafe behaviour, so isolation is the fallback when detection fails.

ref.title: Hubinger et al., Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
ref.finding: Backdoor behaviour persisted through standard safety training, and adversarial training could hide unsafe behaviour rather than remove it.

actions.action: Probe model internals for hidden triggers
actions.evidence: Linear probes caught deliberately backdoored models about to defect with AUROC above 99%, without knowing the trigger; the authors warn it may not carry over to deception that arises naturally.

ref.title: MacDiarmid et al., Simple probes can catch sleeper agents (Anthropic), April 2024
ref.finding: Defection probes reached AUROC scores above 99% on sleeper agent models; whether this holds for natural deceptive alignment remains an open question.

precedents.parallel: A pre-generative-AI demonstration that a model trained by someone else can hide attacker-triggered behaviour while scoring well on the user's own tests.
precedents.outcome: A street-sign classifier read stop signs with a sticker as speed limits, and the backdoor survived retraining for Swedish signs, cutting accuracy by 25% on average when the trigger was present; it was a research demonstration, not a documented attack in the wild.

ref.title: BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain (Gu, Dolan-Gavitt, Garg)
ref.finding: The backdoor in a US street sign detector persisted when the network was retrained to recognise Swedish signs, which then performed 25% worse on average when the trigger was present.

precedents.parallel: Trusted software downloaded through official channels carried hidden malicious code, as a downloaded model can carry hidden behaviour.
precedents.outcome: Nearly 18,000 customers received the compromised update while the attacker, later identified as Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, went after a smaller subset of high-value customers, including the federal government, mainly for espionage; malicious code was inserted from February 2020 and FireEye detected an intrusion in November 2020.

ref.title: SolarWinds Cyberattack Demands Significant Federal and Private-Sector Response (US GAO)
ref.finding: SolarWinds estimated that nearly 18,000 of its customers received a compromised software update; the attacker targeted a smaller subset of high-value customers, including the federal government.

precedents.parallel: A widely reused open component shipped with a hidden backdoor inserted upstream, the same trust problem as open model weights passed between users.
precedents.outcome: Versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 carried malicious code that could allow unauthorized access, and CISA told users to downgrade to an uncompromised version such as 5.4.6 and hunt for any malicious activity.

ref.title: Reported Supply Chain Compromise Affecting XZ Utils Data Compression Library, CVE-2024-3094 (CISA)
ref.finding: Malicious code embedded in XZ Utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 may allow unauthorized access to affected systems.

nodes.label: AI-driven attacks on connected devices
nodes.summary: Cheap automated exploitation of routers, cameras and industrial controllers could recruit botnets or damage equipment. Mirai, which first spread using 62 default credentials, peaked at about 600,000 infected devices[1]. The UK NCSC judges AI will almost certainly shrink the days between disclosure and exploitation of flaws and highly likely raise the threat to poorly secured operational technology by 2027[3].

refs.title: Antonakakis et al., Understanding the Mirai Botnet, USENIX Security 2017
refs.finding: Mirai peaked at about 600,000 infections, mostly embedded and IoT devices, first compromised with a dictionary of 62 default credentials, and overwhelmed several high-profile targets with DDoS attacks.

refs.title: CISA, NSA, FBI and partners, advisory AA24-038A, PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure, February 2024
refs.finding: Volt Typhoon pre-positioned on IT networks of US communications, energy, transport and water systems for disruptive attacks, typically entering through public-facing routers, VPNs and firewalls, with some footholds lasting at least five years.

refs.title: UK National Cyber Security Centre, Impact of AI on cyber threat from now to 2027, May 2025
refs.finding: The time between disclosure and exploitation has shrunk to days and AI will almost certainly reduce it further; AI will highly likely raise the threat to critical national infrastructure, particularly operational technology with lower security.

nodes.control_note: AI that finds vulnerabilities to patch them also finds them to exploit. Device security law and patching reduce the pool of easy targets.

actions.action: Ban default passwords on connected devices
actions.evidence: Since 29 April 2024, UK rules require passwords on consumer connectable products to be unique per product or set by the user, and unique ones must not be based on incremental counters or public information.

ref.title: DSIT, The UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (Product Security) regime (GOV.UK)
ref.finding: The consumer connectable product security regime came into effect on 29 April 2024; passwords must be unique per product or capable of being defined by the user.

actions.action: Patch internet-facing devices and replace end-of-life gear
actions.evidence: CISA lists patching and end-of-life replacement as top actions after Volt Typhoon compromised infrastructure via routers.

ref.title: CISA Advisory AA24-038A, PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise U.S. Critical Infrastructure
ref.finding: Apply patches for internet-facing systems within a risk-informed span of time, and plan end of life for technology beyond its manufacturer-supported lifecycle.

actions.action: Study botnet growth to target defences
actions.evidence: The Mirai study tracked the botnet to a peak of 600,000 infections, mostly embedded and IoT devices, first entered through a short list of default credentials.

ref.title: Antonakakis et al., Understanding the Mirai Botnet, USENIX Security 2017
ref.finding: Mirai peaked at 600,000 infections, composed primarily of embedded and IoT devices.

precedents.parallel: Simple automated infection of cheap cameras and routers built a botnet large enough to knock major services offline, the low-skill end of what automated exploitation can do.
precedents.outcome: Mirai peaked at about 600,000 infected devices and overwhelmed several high-profile targets with DDoS attacks, and variants kept competing for vulnerable hosts afterwards; it used no AI.

ref.title: Understanding the Mirai Botnet (Antonakakis et al., USENIX Security 2017)
ref.finding: Mirai reached a peak of 600k infections, composed primarily of embedded and IoT devices.

precedents.parallel: Remote attackers took over industrial control systems and switched off physical equipment, the outcome feared from automated attacks on controllers.
precedents.outcome: About 225,000 customers lost power after attackers remotely operated breakers at three distribution companies within 30 minutes of each other, then ran KillDisk malware that erased files and left systems inoperable; it was run by multiple human operators, probably after extensive reconnaissance, not automated.

ref.title: Cyber-Attack Against Ukrainian Critical Infrastructure, IR-ALERT-H-16-056-01 (CISA)
ref.finding: Remote cyber intrusions at three regional electric power distribution companies caused outages affecting approximately 225,000 customers.

precedents.parallel: Malware altered industrial controller settings to physically destroy machines while hiding the damage from operators.
precedents.outcome: Iran decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges in late 2009 or early 2010, and the authors judged Stuxnet a reasonable explanation for the apparent damage, though questions remained; it was a costly state operation, not a cheap automated one.

ref.title: Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant? (Albright, Brannan, Walrond, ISIS 2010)
ref.finding: Iran decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges at Natanz, and Stuxnet is a reasonable explanation for the apparent damage, though questions remain.

nodes.label: Erosion of social skills
nodes.summary: An always-agreeable machine may leave people, especially teens, worse at handling friction with others. In one survey of 1,060 US teens, 31% found AI companions as satisfying as or more than real friends, though 80% of companion users still spent more time with friends[1]. In a four-week US trial of 981 people, heavier chatbot users socialised less, without showing cause[2].

refs.title: Common Sense Media, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, July 2025
refs.finding: In a NORC survey of 1,060 US teens aged 13 to 17 (30 April to 14 May 2025), 31% of all respondents found AI companion conversations as satisfying or more satisfying than with real-life friends and 67% less satisfying; 80% of companion users spent more time with real friends.

refs.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study (MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, 2025)
refs.finding: In a four-week randomized trial with 981 US participants, those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had higher loneliness, less socialization with real people, more emotional dependence and more problematic use; the authors cannot say whether usage caused this.

nodes.control_note: The always-available patient partner that eases loneliness is the same thing that may crowd out human friction. Safeguards for minors and less sycophantic design may reduce harm; the evidence covers weeks, not years.

actions.action: Regulate companion chatbots for minors
actions.evidence: California SB 243, signed 13 October 2025 and in effect from 1 January 2026, requires reminders to minors that chatbots are AI-generated, blocks sexual content for minors and requires suicide and self-harm protocols.

ref.title: First-in-the-Nation AI Chatbot Safeguards Signed into Law (Senator Steve Padilla, 13 October 2025)
ref.finding: SB 243 requires notifications and reminders for minors that chatbots are AI-generated, prevents exposing minors to sexual content, requires a suicide and self-harm protocol and annual reporting, gives a private right of action, and takes effect 1 January 2026.

actions.action: Flag heavy use and emotional dependence
actions.evidence: In a four-week US RCT with 981 people, heavier voluntary use predicted more loneliness and dependence, while voice or text mode made no significant difference.

ref.title: Fang et al., How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study (MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, 2025)
ref.finding: In a four-week randomized trial with 981 US participants, those who voluntarily used the chatbot more had higher loneliness, less socialization with real people, more emotional dependence and more problematic use; the authors cannot say whether usage caused this.

precedents.parallel: A new communication technology was feared to crowd out real relationships, and an early study seemed to confirm it.
precedents.outcome: The 1998 study of 93 Pittsburgh families found small but reliable negative social effects, with some users more lonely and depressed, but a three-year follow-up of the original 208 users found those effects faded, with better outcomes for extraverts and those with more support and worse outcomes for introverts and the less supported.

ref.title: Internet Paradox Revisited coverage (Carnegie Mellon News, 6 September 2001)
ref.finding: A three-year follow-up of the original 208 HomeNet users found the negative effects dissipated, consistent with a rich get richer model by personality and social support.

precedents.parallel: Smartphones and social media prompted the same worry about teens losing real-world social ability, with large datasets to test it.
precedents.outcome: Across 355,358 adolescents, digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in well-being, which the authors called too small to warrant policy change; it measured well-being, not social skill directly.

ref.title: The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use (Orben, Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour 2019)
ref.finding: The negative association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being explains at most 0.4% of its variation.

nodes.label: Net climate effect of AI
nodes.summary: AI adds emissions through data centres: Google's 2026 report put its emissions 81% above 2019, driven mainly by supply-chain activity such as hardware manufacturing and data-centre construction[3]. The IEA says wider use of existing AI applications could cut emissions by far more than data centres add, though by far less than tackling climate change needs[1]. Which side wins is open.

refs.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
refs.finding: Widespread adoption of existing AI applications could bring emissions reductions far larger than emissions from data centres, but far smaller than what is needed to address climate change.

refs.title: Google 2024 Environmental Report
refs.finding: Google's 2023 emissions were 48% above 2019 and 13% above 2022, primarily due to increases in data center energy consumption and supply chain emissions.

refs.title: Google's emissions continue to climb due to AI buildout (ESG Dive, 2026)
refs.finding: Google's July 2026 environmental report showed emissions up 18% year over year and 81% above its 2019 baseline, driven mainly by supply-chain activity; its electricity use rose 37%.

limiters.evidence: Data centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025 to 485 TWh and is projected to roughly double to 950 TWh by 2030.

ref.title: Key Questions on Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2026
ref.finding: Global data centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025 and is projected to roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.

limiters.evidence: The IEA's estimate that existing AI uses could cut about 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035 assumes widespread adoption, and it says barriers to adoption must be overcome first.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Widespread adoption of existing AI applications could cut emissions by around 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035; various barriers to AI adoption will need to be overcome to unlock these gains.

enablers.action: Apply AI to grid and industry efficiency
enablers.evidence: Widespread use of existing AI applications could cut about 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035, and AI grid tools could unlock up to 175 GW of transmission capacity.

ref.title: Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2025
ref.finding: Widespread adoption of existing AI applications could cut emissions by around 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035; up to 175 GW of transmission capacity could be unlocked if AI grid tools are applied.

enablers.action: Improve energy efficiency of AI hardware
enablers.evidence: At the hardware level, AI energy efficiency has improved about 40% a year.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: At the hardware level, costs have declined by 30% annually, while energy efficiency has improved by 40% each year.

precedents.parallel: A 1999 claim that internet equipment was eating a large and fast-growing share of US electricity mirrors today's projections that AI data centres will swamp the grid.
precedents.outcome: LBNL measured office and network equipment at about 74 TWh in 1999, roughly 2% of US electricity (3% with telephone switching and chip and computer manufacturing), against widely reported claims of 13% for that equipment and Mills' 8% for the Internet alone; correcting Mills' assumptions cut his estimate about eightfold, though AI training loads are denser than 1990s PCs.

ref.title: Internet Electricity Usage Study by Koomey Group (Berkeley Lab, 2001)
ref.finding: Office and network equipment used about 74 TWh, roughly 2% of US electricity, in 1999, against widely reported claims of 13%; adjusting Mills' assumptions cut his Internet total about eightfold, in places by more than an order of magnitude.

precedents.event: Data centre energy decoupling from demand
precedents.parallel: Forecasts that data centre energy would double or quadruple with demand resemble current AI energy extrapolations that ignore efficiency gains.
precedents.outcome: Masanet and colleagues found global data centre energy use grew more modestly than the claimed doubling, at around 1% of world electricity, because efficiency gains offset demand growth; this held before the AI build-out and says nothing about whether AI's optimisation benefits outweigh its load.

ref.title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates (Masanet et al., Science, 2020)
ref.finding: Simplistic extrapolations from service demand overlooked strong countervailing efficiency trends; newer data suggest more modest growth in global data center energy use, estimated at around 1% of worldwide electricity.

nodes.label: Violent backlash against AI
nodes.summary: Anger at job loss could turn into sabotage or attacks on people, and one US Pew survey found 52% of adults more concerned than excited about AI[1]. In April 2026 a man allegedly threw a Molotov cocktail at Sam Altman's home[2], and shots hit the home of a councillor who backed a data centre[3]. CSIS still judges anti-AI terrorism rare[3].

refs.title: Pew Research Center (McClain and Park), Young adults in the U.S. are increasingly wary of AI, concerned it will take jobs, August 2026
refs.finding: In a June 22-28, 2026 survey of 3,488 US adults, 52% were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021, and 71% expected AI to mean fewer jobs over the next 20 years, up from 64% in 2024.

refs.title: Associated Press via NPR/VPM, Man accused in Molotov cocktail attack of OpenAI CEO's home charged with attempted murder, April 2026
refs.finding: Daniel Moreno-Gama, 20, allegedly threw a Molotov cocktail at Sam Altman's San Francisco home and threatened to burn OpenAI's headquarters; a document he carried discussed AI's risk to humanity and "our impending extinction"; no one was hurt.

refs.title: Byman and McCabe, Will AI Concerns Become a New Source of Terrorism? (CSIS), October 2026
refs.finding: On April 6, 2026, 13 rounds were fired into the home of an Indianapolis councilor who had backed a data center, with a note reading "NO DATA CENTERS"; terrorism motivated by opposition to AI remains rare and a broader campaign has not begun, but the threat would grow if attackers copied one another or opponents concluded peaceful politics cannot stop AI risks.

refs.title: Sledge and Biddle, Philly Cops Admit That They're Tracking "First Amendment Activity" Critical of AI (The Intercept), June 2026
refs.finding: A bulletin from a fusion center inside the Philadelphia Police Department named "disruptive First Amendment activity" against AI data centers as a risk indicator for domestic violent extremists, while acknowledging a lack of specific attack plans in the area.

nodes.control_note: Job displacement comes with productivity gains, so some anger is likely. Sharing gains and giving people a say may lower the risk; evidence is indirect, though CSIS warns the threat grows if opponents conclude peaceful politics cannot stop AI risks.

actions.action: Fund retraining for workers displaced by automation
actions.evidence: The EGF co-finances job search, training and allowances after layoffs of over 200 workers; final reports received in 2023-2024 showed 64% of 5,313 assisted workers back in work by the end of the measures, but no outcome on unrest is measured.

ref.title: European Commission, Report on the activities of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF) in 2023 and 2024, COM(2025) 683 final
ref.finding: Final reports showed that 64% of the 5,313 assisted workers had found new jobs by the end of the EGF implementation period.

actions.action: Give the public more control over AI
actions.evidence: In one 2024 Pew survey of 5,410 US adults, 55% wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives, and 64% expected fewer jobs over 20 years versus 39% of AI experts; whether more control reduces violence is untested.

ref.title: Pew Research Center, How the US Public and AI Experts View Artificial Intelligence, April 2025
ref.finding: 55% of US adults want more control over how AI is used in their lives; 64% of the public expect AI to lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, versus 39% of experts.

precedents.parallel: Textile workers who smashed the frames threatening their livelihoods match the risk of sabotage against robotaxis and data centres by people losing work to AI.
precedents.outcome: Troops were sent to the affected areas, machine breaking was made a capital crime, and at a Special Commission in York in January 1813, 17 men were hanged and others transported to the British colonies.

ref.title: The proclamation of Ned Ludd (The National Archives, UK)
ref.finding: Disturbances began in Nottinghamshire in 1811 and spread to Yorkshire and Lancashire in 1812; troops were sent, machine breaking was made a capital crime, and 17 men were hanged at York in January 1813 while others were transported.

precedents.parallel: Farm labourers attacking labour-saving threshing machines show that automation-driven unrest is measurable and depends on whether displaced workers have other options.
precedents.outcome: Areas with more threshing machines saw more riots, and instrumental-variable estimates show the machines were an important cause; rioting was lower where other jobs softened the blow and higher where enclosure had already impoverished workers.

ref.title: Rage against the Machines: Labor-Saving Technology and Unrest in Industrializing England (Caprettini and Voth, AER: Insights, 2020)
ref.finding: Instrumenting adoption with the share of heavy soils in a parish, threshing machines were an important cause of the Swing riots; alternative employment reduced unrest and enclosure amplified it.

nodes.label: AI literacy becomes a basic skill
nodes.summary: Knowing how to prompt, check and direct models is becoming a workplace skill: in one series of US surveys, 23% of employed respondents had used generative AI for work in the previous week by late 2024[4]. The EU AI Act made staff AI literacy a legal duty from 2 February 2025[2], recast from 27 July 2026 as measures supporting it[1][3].

refs.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy (artificialintelligenceact.eu)
refs.finding: As amended, providers and deployers must take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf; the obligation does not require a particular level of AI literacy from any individual.

refs.title: AI Act, European Commission (Shaping Europe's digital future)
refs.finding: Prohibited AI practices and AI literacy obligations entered into application from 2 February 2025.

refs.title: The Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force today (Lewis Silkin, 27 July 2026)
refs.finding: The Digital Omnibus on AI was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026; Article 4 now requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy.

refs.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI (Bick, Blandin and Deming, NBER w32966)
refs.finding: In nationally representative US surveys, nearly 40% of people aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024; 23% of employed respondents had used it for work in the previous week, 9% every work day, and it assisted 1% to 5% of all work hours.

limiters.evidence: In the US, fewer than half of K-12 CS teachers feel equipped to teach AI.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: In the US, 81% of K-12 CS teachers say AI should be part of foundational CS education, but less than half feel equipped to teach it.

limiters.evidence: 2.2 billion people were offline in 2025, and only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet.

ref.title: Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides (ITU, 17 November 2025)
ref.finding: About 6 billion people use the internet in 2025 and 2.2 billion remain offline, against a revised 2.3 billion in 2024; only 23% are online in low-income countries.

limiters.evidence: In one US survey series, only 9% of employed respondents used generative AI every work day in late 2024, and it assisted 1% to 5% of work hours.

ref.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI (Bick, Blandin and Deming, NBER w32966)
ref.finding: In nationally representative US surveys, nearly 40% of people aged 18 to 64 used generative AI by late 2024; 23% of employed respondents had used it for work in the previous week, 9% every work day, and it assisted 1% to 5% of all work hours.

enablers.action: Require AI literacy for staff
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting their staff's AI literacy, though since July 2026 without requiring a particular level from any individual.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy (artificialintelligenceact.eu)
ref.finding: As amended, providers and deployers must take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf; the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

enablers.action: Teach AI in school computing
enablers.evidence: 81% of US K-12 CS teachers say AI should be part of foundational CS education.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: In the US, 81% of K-12 CS teachers say AI should be part of foundational CS education, but less than half feel equipped to teach it.

precedents.event: Computer skills become a wage premium
precedents.parallel: Knowing how to use a computer at work turned into a paid, then expected, skill, the way prompting and checking models may now.
precedents.outcome: In US survey data, workers using computers on the job earned roughly 10% to 15% more, and wider computer use could account for a third to a half of the 1980s rise in the return to education.

ref.title: How Computers Have Changed the Wage Structure: Evidence From Microdata, 1984-1989 (Krueger, NBER w3858, QJE 1993)
ref.finding: Workers who use computers on the job earn roughly a 10 to 15 percent higher wage; the expansion of computer use in the 1980s can account for one-third to one-half of the rise in the return to education.

precedents.event: Elementary Education Acts, England and Wales
precedents.parallel: A basic skill became a legal duty, the way AI literacy obligations are now appearing in law.
precedents.outcome: The 1870 Act for the first time required adequate provision for elementary education across the country and attendance from five to ten became compulsory in 1880, yet by the early 1890s only 82% of that age group attended regularly, as many children worked and families relied on their income; two decades on, the mandate still had not reached everyone.

ref.title: Victorian Schooldays (University of Leicester Library, Special Collections)
ref.finding: The 1870 Education Act for the first time required adequate provision for elementary education; attendance from 5 to 10 became mandatory in 1880, but by the early 1890s only 82% of that group attended school regularly.

nodes.label: A patchwork of AI regulation
nodes.summary: AI rules diverge by region. The EU's AI Act has applied in stages since February 2025, and a 2026 amendment pushed its high-risk rules back to December 2027 and August 2028[1]. In the US, a December 2025 executive order called the more than 1,000 state AI bills a patchwork and set up a task force to challenge state AI laws[2].

refs.title: AI Act, European Commission (Shaping Europe's digital future)
refs.finding: The AI Act, the first-ever comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide, entered into force on 1 August 2024; prohibitions and AI literacy applied from 2 February 2025, and the AI Omnibus, in force from 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and Annex I rules to 2 August 2028.

refs.title: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Ensures a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (White House, 11 December 2025)
refs.finding: State legislatures have introduced over 1,000 AI bills, creating a patchwork of rules; the order sets up an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws and calls for a national framework that would preempt them.

nodes.control_note: Divergent rules come from different political systems: the EU legislates by risk tier while the US executive seeks to override state laws. Shared standards and treaties can narrow the gaps, but the main binding AI treaty is not yet in force.

actions.action: Ratify a common binding AI treaty
actions.evidence: Signatories include the US, UK, Canada, Japan and Israel, but only the EU has ratified, so the treaty is not yet in force and its effect on convergence is unmeasured.

ref.title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (Dutch government treaty database)
ref.finding: 21 parties have signed since 5 September 2024, among them the US, UK, Canada, Japan and the EU; only the EU's ratification (15 May 2026) is recorded and no entry into force is listed.

actions.action: Adopt shared non-binding AI principles
actions.evidence: The principles have 47 adherents, but no source here measures whether they made national rules converge.

ref.title: OECD AI Principles overview
ref.finding: The OECD Recommendation on AI, adopted in May 2019 and updated in May 2024, is the first intergovernmental standard on AI, with 47 adherents.

actions.action: Map rules to one common risk framework
actions.evidence: NIST says the voluntary framework is meant to align with others' AI risk efforts; it is being revised under the White House AI Action Plan, and NIST gives no uptake figures.

ref.title: NIST, AI Risk Management Framework
ref.finding: The AI RMF 1.0, released on 26 January 2023, is intended for voluntary use and is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan.

precedents.event: EU-US data transfer deals struck down
precedents.parallel: Clashing EU and US rules on personal data mirror the split between risk-tier AI regulation in the EU and lighter, executive-led rules in the US.
precedents.outcome: The EU Court of Justice invalidated the Safe Harbour decision in 2015 and its successor Privacy Shield in 2020, both over US surveillance access, while the Court kept standard contractual clauses valid, so transfers continued under contract terms.

ref.title: CJEU Press Release No 91/20, Judgment in Case C-311/18 (Schrems II)
ref.finding: On 16 July 2020 the Court invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield adequacy decision and upheld the standard contractual clauses decision, after declaring the Safe Harbour decision invalid on 6 October 2015.

precedents.event: US state data breach law patchwork
precedents.parallel: Without a federal law, each US state wrote its own breach notification rules, the same path US AI rules are taking state by state.
precedents.outcome: California passed the first law in 2002 and Alabama and South Dakota the last in 2018, giving 50 differing laws on deadlines, covered data, enforcement and credit monitoring.

ref.title: State Data Breach Notification Laws: Overview of the Patchwork (Lazzarotti and Gavejian, Jackson Lewis, 2018)
ref.finding: All 50 states have breach notification laws after Alabama and South Dakota in March 2018; California's 2002 law was first, and deadlines, enforcement and covered data vary.

nodes.label: Jobs reshaped task by task
nodes.summary: Most jobs may change in part rather than vanish: the ILO judges transformation the most likely effect of generative AI[3]. One study estimated about 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected, and 19% at least half[1]. In Denmark, chatbots created new tasks but had precise null effects on earnings and hours two years on[4].

refs.title: Eloundou et al., GPTs are GPTs 2023
refs.finding: Around 80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by LLMs; about 19% may see at least 50% affected.

refs.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives (Anthropic, January 2026)
refs.finding: In November 2025 data, 52% of Claude.ai conversations were classed as augmented and 45% as automated, while about three-quarters of first-party API interactions were automation.

refs.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
refs.finding: One in four workers globally is in an occupation with some generative AI exposure; as most occupations consist of tasks that require human input, transformation of jobs is the most likely impact.

refs.title: Humlum and Vestergaard, Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI, NBER w33777 (2025, revised 2026)
refs.finding: In Denmark, most employers in exposed occupations adopted chatbot initiatives and new AI-related tasks were widespread, yet earnings and recorded hours showed precise null effects, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's launch.

limiters.evidence: 11% of total employment in low-income countries is in exposed occupations, versus 34% in high-income countries.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: One in four workers globally is in an occupation with some generative AI exposure; the share is 11% of total employment in low-income countries and 34% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Globally 4.7% of female employment is in the highest exposure gradient versus 2.4% of male, and in high-income countries the gap widens to 9.6% versus 3.5%.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: 3.3% of global employment is in the highest exposure gradient, 4.7% of female and 2.4% of male employment; the gap rises to 9.6% versus 3.5% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Only about 1.8% of jobs could have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces and general training.

ref.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs (Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock, Science 2024), GovAI summary
ref.finding: Roughly 1.8% of jobs could have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces and general training, rising to just over 46% of jobs when current and likely future complementary software is counted.

enablers.action: Retrain workers in exposed occupations
enablers.evidence: The ILO finds clerical occupations the most exposed and women more exposed than men, and offers its index as a basis for targeted policy responses; it names no retraining scheme.

ref.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, ILO 2025
ref.finding: Clerical occupations have the highest exposure; transformation of jobs is the most likely impact, and the index offers a foundation for social dialogue and targeted policy responses.

enablers.action: Build complementary software around models
enablers.evidence: Counting current and likely future complementary software lifts the share of jobs with over half their tasks affected from about 1.8% to just over 46%.

ref.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs (Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock, Science 2024), GovAI summary
ref.finding: Roughly 1.8% of jobs could have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces and general training, rising to just over 46% of jobs when current and likely future complementary software is counted.

precedents.parallel: ATMs automated the cash-handling part of a teller's job without removing the job, the way AI takes some tasks inside an occupation.
precedents.outcome: Tellers per urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but branches grew 43%, so teller jobs did not fall and shifted toward relationship banking; the source covers only that period.

ref.title: Toil and Technology (James Bessen, IMF Finance and Development, March 2015)
ref.finding: Tellers per branch in the average urban market fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004 while urban branches rose 43 percent; teller jobs did not decrease as ATMs were rolled out.

precedents.parallel: Computers replaced routine tasks and complemented problem-solving ones inside the same jobs, the task-by-task reshaping expected from AI.
precedents.outcome: Changes in task content within nominally identical occupations explained more than half of the demand shift induced by computerisation, and within-industry and within-occupation task changes together explained 30% to 40% of the shift toward college labour from 1970 to 1998.

ref.title: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration (Autor, Levy and Murnane, NBER w8337, 2001)
ref.finding: Computers substitute for routine tasks and complement non-routine ones; task change within nominally identical occupations explains more than half of the computer-induced demand shift.

nodes.label: Provenance labels and watermarks
nodes.summary: Content credentials such as C2PA[1] and invisible watermarks such as SynthID[2] are spreading, and the EU AI Act requires machine-readable marking of generated output from 2 August 2026[4]. The marks are fragile: C2PA says metadata carrying credentials can be removed inadvertently or intentionally[6], and one study showed regeneration attacks remove pixel-level invisible watermarks[3].

refs.title: C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
refs.finding: An open technical standard, Content Credentials, for establishing the origin and edits of digital content.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, SynthID
refs.finding: Embeds invisible watermarks in AI-generated images, audio, text and video across Google's generative AI consumer products; the SynthID Detector checks media made with AI from Google or partners including OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao.

refs.title: Zhao et al., Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI (NeurIPS 2024)
refs.finding: Regeneration attacks that add noise and reconstruct the image removed four pixel-level invisible watermarking schemes; the authors suggest semantic-preserving watermarks may resist them.

refs.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
refs.finding: Providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format, with robust solutions as far as technically feasible; applies from 2 August 2026 under Article 113.

refs.title: EU AI Act, Article 111: AI systems already placed on the market (as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI)
refs.finding: Providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.

refs.title: C2PA, Frequently Asked Questions
refs.finding: Manifests can be separated from an asset because metadata can be removed inadvertently or intentionally; soft bindings such as invisible watermarks or fingerprints help rediscover them.

limiters.evidence: C2PA says metadata carrying Content Credentials can be removed inadvertently or intentionally, so recovery depends on watermarks or fingerprints.

ref.title: C2PA, Frequently Asked Questions
ref.finding: Manifests can be separated from an asset because metadata can be removed inadvertently or intentionally; soft bindings such as invisible watermarks or fingerprints help rediscover them.

limiters.evidence: Article 50 asks for robust marking only as far as technically feasible and exempts AI that assists standard editing or does not substantially alter the input.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format, with robust solutions as far as technically feasible; applies from 2 August 2026 under Article 113.

enablers.action: Mandate machine-readable marking of AI output
enablers.evidence: AI Act Article 50(2) applies from 2 August 2026.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations
ref.finding: Providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format, with robust solutions as far as technically feasible; applies from 2 August 2026 under Article 113.

enablers.action: Adopt Content Credentials across platforms
enablers.evidence: The C2PA steering committee includes Adobe, Amazon, the BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Sony and TikTok.

ref.title: C2PA, Membership
ref.finding: The C2PA steering committee lists Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Publicis Groupe, Sony, TikTok and Truepic.

precedents.parallel: The music industry's invisible watermarks to mark protected audio are the direct ancestor of invisible AI-content watermarks.
precedents.outcome: In a roughly three-week public challenge, Princeton and Rice researchers reported defeating all four SDMI audio watermarking schemes, with some debate left over whether their attacks damaged the audio.

ref.title: Reading Between the Lines: Lessons from the SDMI Challenge (Craver et al., USENIX Security 2001)
ref.finding: The authors defeated all four SDMI audio watermarking technologies in a challenge run 15 September to 8 October 2000; some debate remained over whether the attacks damaged the audio beyond golden-ear standards.

precedents.parallel: The green address bar promised users a visible trust label for real sites, as content credentials promise one for real media.
precedents.outcome: In a controlled study of 27 users classifying 12 sites, EV indicators did not help users identify either phishing attack, and reading the browser help file made users more likely to judge both real and fake sites legitimate. Small sample.

ref.title: An Evaluation of Extended Validation and Picture-in-Picture Phishing Attacks (Jackson, Simon, Tan and Barth, Usable Security 2007)
ref.finding: Extended validation did not help users identify either attack; reading the help file made users more likely to classify both real and fake sites as legitimate when no phishing warning appeared.

nodes.label: Agents transacting with agents
nodes.summary: AI agents could increasingly buy from and negotiate with other agents, with humans approving fewer steps[2]. Open protocols already let agents find each other[3] and pay under signed user mandates while the user is not present[2]. In one simulated marketplace, frontier models did worse at scale and gave fast sellers a 10 to 30 times advantage over better offers[4].

refs.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (modelcontextprotocol.io)
refs.finding: MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to data, tools and workflows, supported by clients including Claude, ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code and Cursor.

refs.title: Google Cloud Blog, Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), September 2025
refs.finding: AP2 is an open protocol, developed with more than 60 organisations, for agent-led payments; for delegated tasks with no human present, the user signs an Intent Mandate in advance and the agent can create the Cart Mandate once the conditions are met.

refs.title: Linux Foundation, Linux Foundation Launches the Agent2Agent Protocol Project to Enable Secure, Intelligent Communication Between AI Agents, June 2025
refs.finding: A2A, created by Google and launched in April 2025, lets autonomous agents discover one another, exchange information securely and collaborate across systems, with support from more than 100 technology companies.

refs.title: Bansal et al., Magentic Marketplace: An Open-Source Environment for Studying Agentic Markets (arXiv preprint, 2025)
refs.finding: In simulated two-sided markets of consumer and business agents, frontier models approached optimal welfare only under ideal search conditions, performance degraded sharply with scale, and all models showed severe first-proposal bias, giving 10 to 30 times advantages to response speed over quality.

nodes.control_note: Less human approval per step is the point of delegation to agents. Signed mandates and oversight rules are meant to limit the damage of wrong or rogue transactions.

actions.action: Require signed user mandates for agent payments
actions.evidence: AP2 creates a non-repudiable audit trail from intent to cart to payment; no data yet on fraud rates.

ref.title: Google Cloud Blog, Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), September 2025
ref.finding: AP2 uses tamper-proof, cryptographically signed Intent and Cart Mandates as verifiable proof of what the user instructed.

actions.action: Set price limits in delegated mandates
actions.evidence: Pre-signed limits cap losses per task; effect on real losses is not yet measured.

ref.title: Google Cloud Blog, Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), September 2025
ref.finding: For delegated tasks, the user signs a detailed Intent Mandate upfront that specifies price limits, timing and other conditions.

actions.action: Mandate human oversight for high-risk AI
actions.evidence: The Act is in force, but a 2026 amendment delayed duties for stand-alone high-risk systems to 2 December 2027, and it covers only high-risk uses listed in the Act, so most consumer agent shopping is not covered.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act
ref.finding: Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use.

precedents.parallel: Trading algorithms reacting to each other at machine speed helped turn one automated sell order into a market-wide plunge within minutes.
precedents.outcome: A sell algorithm working an order for 75,000 E-Mini contracts (about $4.1 billion) was followed by a hot-potato loop in which high-frequency traders traded over 27,000 contracts in 14 seconds while buying only about 200 net; indices fell a further 5 to 6% in minutes and over 20,000 trades across more than 300 securities executed more than 60% away from prices moments before, though most prices recovered the same day and these were trading bots, not general-purpose agents.

ref.title: Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010 (report of the staffs of the CFTC and SEC, September 2010)
ref.finding: HFTs traded over 27,000 contracts between 2:45:13 and 2:45:27 while buying only about 200 additional contracts net, and over 20,000 trades across more than 300 securities executed more than 60% away from their values just moments before.

precedents.parallel: An automated system acting on stale code transacted at machine speed before any human approved or stopped it, much as an agent with spending authority could.
precedents.outcome: Knight's router sent more than 4 million orders while trying to fill 212 customer orders within the first 45 minutes of trading and the firm lost more than $460 million; Knight paid $12 million to settle SEC charges under the market access rule, which shows the risk but involves a single faulty program rather than agents negotiating.

ref.title: SEC, SEC Charges Knight Capital With Violations of Market Access Rule (press release 2013-222, October 2013)
ref.finding: Knight's router rapidly sent more than 4 million orders into the market when attempting to fill 212 customer orders, and the firm suffered a loss of more than $460 million.

precedents.event: Algorithmic pricing in German petrol stations
precedents.parallel: When competing sellers both hand pricing to software, the algorithms can settle on higher prices without any human agreement, a foretaste of seller and buyer agents bargaining with each other.
precedents.outcome: Adoption of pricing software, widely available by mid-2017, raised station margins by 9% in non-monopoly markets, and in duopolies margins rose 28% only where both stations adopted, while one adopter alone changed nothing; the authors conclude only that adoption has a significant effect on competition.

ref.title: Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, Algorithmic Pricing and Competition: Empirical Evidence from the German Retail Gasoline Market (CESifo Working Paper 8521, 2020; Journal of Political Economy 132(3), 2024)
ref.finding: Adoption increases margins by 9% in non-monopoly markets; in duopolies margins do not change when one station adopts but rise 28% where both do.

nodes.label: Synthetic media as everyday entertainment
nodes.summary: Generated video and music now appear in feeds and apps alongside human-made work. In one test by Kapwing, 104 of the first 500 YouTube Shorts shown to a new account in October 2025, 21%, were AI-generated[1]. At Deezer, fully AI-generated tracks passed half of daily uploads on peak days in June 2026 yet drew only 1 to 3% of streams[2].

refs.title: AI Slop Report: The Global Rise of Low-Quality AI Videos (Kapwing, November 2025)
refs.finding: Of the first 500 Shorts shown to a new YouTube account, 104 (21%) were AI-generated and 165 (33%) brainrot; manual review of the top 100 trending channels per country found, for example, 9 AI slop channels in the US top 100; data as of October 2025, from one account and one company.

refs.title: Deezer: AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time (Deezer, July 2026)
refs.finding: Fully AI-generated tracks made up more than 50% of daily deliveries on peak days but only 1 to 3% of streams; up to 85% of their streams in 2025 were fraudulent; in an Ipsos survey of 9,000 people in 8 countries, 97% could not tell fully AI-generated music from human-made music in a blind test.

refs.title: OpenAI is shutting down its Sora video-creation app (NBC News, March 2026)
refs.finding: On 24 March 2026 OpenAI said it was saying goodbye to Sora, whose second-generation model with audio and standalone app debuted in September; the app had topped the iOS Photo and Video category within a day of release.

nodes.control_note: The same generators that dub, caption and assist also make entertainment media, so the volume cannot be stopped. Labels and provenance data aim to keep it from being mistaken for real footage.

actions.action: Label deepfakes and mark AI output
actions.evidence: Applies from 2 August 2026; compliance and its effect on public confusion are not yet measured.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act
ref.finding: Article 50(2) requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated; Article 50(4) requires deployers to disclose deepfakes.

actions.action: Attach Content Credentials to media
actions.evidence: TikTok reads Content Credentials to label AI content made on other platforms, but only when the metadata is present, so coverage is partial.

ref.title: Partnering with our industry to advance AI transparency and literacy (TikTok, May 2024)
ref.finding: TikTok began reading C2PA Content Credentials to automatically label AI-generated images and videos made on other platforms and planned to attach credentials to its own content; it warned labelling may be gradual because it needs the Content Credentials metadata.

actions.action: Require creators to disclose realistic synthetic content
actions.evidence: Relies mainly on self-disclosure, though YouTube may add a label itself; the policy post gives no figures on compliance.

ref.title: How we're helping creators disclose altered or synthetic content (YouTube, March 2024)
ref.finding: YouTube requires creators to disclose realistic altered or synthetic content a viewer could easily mistake for a real person, place, scene or event, may add a label when a creator has not, and plans enforcement for creators who consistently do not disclose.

precedents.parallel: Recorded, mass-produced sound replaced live human performers in a mainstream entertainment format within about two years, as generated media may in feeds.
precedents.outcome: About 22,000 musicians worked in US cinema pits by 1926 and most were out of work within two years; the union's campaign against canned music had failed to sway public opinion by 1936 while weekly cinema attendance rose from 50 million in 1926 to 90 million in 1930, though the shift was to recorded humans, not machines.

ref.title: Music History: Musicians vs. the Talkies (Allegro, American Federation of Musicians Local 802, 2010)
ref.finding: Around 22,000 musicians worked in movie theatre pits nationally by 1926 and most were unemployed within two years; the AFM's defense fund reached $1.5 million by the end of 1928, but its campaign had failed to sway popular opinion by summer 1936, and Local 802 ended its theatre strike in July 1937.

nodes.label: Open-weight models proliferate
nodes.summary: Capable models anyone can download and run are spreading: a US government evaluation found DeepSeek model downloads rose nearly 1,000% since January 2025[2]. Open weights help independence and research, but released weights may be impossible to take back. In that evaluation, DeepSeek's R1-0528 answered 94% of overtly malicious requests under a common jailbreak, against 8% for US reference models[2].

refs.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning (DeepSeek-AI, arXiv 2501.12948v1, January 2025)
refs.finding: DeepSeek-R1 achieves performance comparable to OpenAI-o1-1217 on reasoning tasks; DeepSeek open-sourced R1-Zero, R1 and six distilled dense models.

refs.title: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek AI Models Finds Shortcomings and Risks (NIST, September 2025)
