refs.finding: Downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms rose nearly 1,000% since January 2025; the best US model outperformed the best DeepSeek model on almost every one of 19 benchmarks; R1-0528 answered 94% of overtly malicious requests under a common jailbreak, against 8% for US reference models.

nodes.control_note: Released weights cannot be recalled, and openness is what enables independent research and local use. Safeguards inside the weights, testing and monitoring, and controls on physical materials can reduce misuse, but none can undo a release.

actions.action: Test open models for capability and security risks
actions.evidence: NIST's CAISI evaluated three DeepSeek models in 2025, as the US AI Action Plan directs, and found weak resistance to jailbreaks; testing informs policy but lowers no risk by itself.

ref.title: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek AI Models Finds Shortcomings and Risks (NIST, September 2025)
ref.finding: Downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms rose nearly 1,000% since January 2025; the best US model outperformed the best DeepSeek model on almost every one of 19 benchmarks; R1-0528 answered 94% of overtly malicious requests under a common jailbreak, against 8% for US reference models.

actions.action: Build tamper-resistant safeguards into weights
actions.evidence: Proposed safeguards claimed to survive hundreds of fine-tuning steps, but an independent re-test broke one with small changes to the attack, such as other random seeds or a different learning-rate schedule.

ref.title: On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs (Qi et al., arXiv 2412.07097, 2024)
ref.finding: Evaluating durable safeguards is exceedingly difficult and can mislead; rerunning attacks on the TAR safeguard with different random seeds, a warmup and cosine learning-rate schedule, or LoRA recovered over 60% accuracy on WMDP Biosecurity where the original paper reported near-random results.

actions.action: Control physical precursors, not just information
actions.evidence: Raises the cost of turning model output into weapons; effect is hard to separate from other policing.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/1148 on the marketing and use of explosives precursors (EUR-Lex)
ref.finding: Restricted explosives precursors shall not be made available to, or introduced, possessed or used by members of the general public, and suspicious transactions must be reported within 24 hours; applies from 1 February 2021.

precedents.event: Crypto Wars and encryption export rules
precedents.parallel: Governments tried to keep a dual-use capability, strong encryption software, from spreading abroad, but once source code was published it could not be recalled.
precedents.outcome: In January 2000 the US let publicly available encryption source code be exported under License Exception TSU once the exporter notified the government of its Internet location, barring only knowing exports to seven sanctioned countries, and said posting code online did not by itself show knowledge of a prohibited export.

ref.title: Revisions to Encryption Items, 65 FR 2492 (Federal Register, 14 January 2000)
ref.finding: Publicly available encryption source code became exportable under License Exception TSU after written notification of its Internet location, except knowing exports to Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, North Korea, Sudan or Syria; posting it on the Internet does not by itself establish knowledge of a prohibited export.

precedents.parallel: Once downloadable files for a dangerous capability were posted for anyone in the world, a government order to take them down could not undo their spread.
precedents.outcome: Defense Distributed posted its Liberator pistol files for free worldwide download from 2012; the State Department asked it to remove them on 8 May 2013, and in September 2016 the Fifth Circuit upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction against that restriction, while the dissent noted many of the files were by then widely available over the Internet.

ref.title: Defense Distributed v. U.S. Department of State, No. 15-50759 (5th Cir. 2016)
ref.finding: Beginning in 2012 Defense Distributed posted files, including those for the Liberator pistol, for free download by anyone in the world; the State Department requested removal on 8 May 2013; the court affirmed denial of a preliminary injunction, and the dissent notes many of the files are now widely available over the Internet.

nodes.label: The price of intelligence collapses
nodes.summary: The price of reaching a fixed level of model performance fell between 9x and 900x per year across six benchmarks, Epoch AI found, though the fastest falls came in the latest year and may not last[1]. The Stanford AI Index found the cost of GPT-3.5-level performance fell over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024[2].

refs.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks, Epoch AI 2025
refs.finding: Across six benchmarks over three years, the price to reach a fixed performance level fell between 9x and 900x per year depending on the milestone; the fastest drops came in the past year, so it is less clear they will persist.

refs.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
refs.finding: The inference cost of a system performing at GPT-3.5 level dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024; hardware costs declined 30% a year and energy efficiency improved 40% a year.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: One leading vendor keeps its strongest model off its free plan; its paid plans start at $20 a month.

ref.title: Pricing, Claude (Anthropic), accessed October 2026
ref.finding: The Free plan includes Sonnet and Haiku but not Opus; Pro costs $20 a month billed monthly and Max starts at $100 a month.

limiters.evidence: 2.2 billion people are offline and cannot reach cheap models.

ref.title: Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides, ITU, 17 November 2025
ref.finding: 2.2 billion people remain offline in 2025, down from a revised 2.3 billion in 2024; only 23% of people in low-income countries use the internet, against 94% in high-income countries.

limiters.evidence: Data centre power use may roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh by 2030.

ref.title: Key Questions on Energy and AI, Executive summary, IEA 2026
ref.finding: Data centre electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 and is set to roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, about 3% of global electricity demand.

enablers.action: Expand internet access in low-income countries
enablers.evidence: Internet use in the least developed countries grew 7.4% in 2025, but only 23% of people in low-income countries are online.

ref.title: Almost three-quarters of the population are online, ITU Facts and Figures 2025
ref.finding: Only 23 per cent of people in low-income countries use the internet; annual growth in 2025 averaged 7.4 per cent in least developed countries and 5.5 per cent in landlocked developing countries.

enablers.action: Pass hardware efficiency gains to prices
enablers.counters: unequal access to paid AI plans
enablers.evidence: Hardware costs fell about 30% a year and energy efficiency rose about 40% a year.

ref.title: The 2025 AI Index Report, Stanford HAI
ref.finding: The inference cost of a system performing at GPT-3.5 level dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024; hardware costs declined 30% a year and energy efficiency improved 40% a year.

precedents.parallel: The cost of a fixed unit of calculation fell by orders of magnitude for decades, turning computation from a scarce service into a commodity.
precedents.outcome: Nordhaus estimates computer performance improved by a factor of 1.7 trillion to 76 trillion over manual computing, with a major break in trend around World War II and performance-based price falls much larger than official statistics show.

ref.title: Nordhaus, Two Centuries of Productivity Growth in Computing, Journal of Economic History 67(1), 2007
ref.finding: Performance has increased since manual computing by a factor between 1.7 trillion and 76 trillion, with a major break in trend around World War II; performance-based price declines are much larger than those in official statistics.

precedents.event: The falling price of artificial light
precedents.parallel: A basic input that was once rationed by cost, light, became so cheap that it stopped being a consideration, the way a level of model capability is becoming one.
precedents.outcome: Lighting efficiency rose about 900-fold between 1800 and 1992 and the true price of illumination fell by a factor of about 75 over the last century, which conventional price indexes badly missed; the difference is that light improved over two centuries, not within a few years.

ref.title: Nordhaus, Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not (NBER, The Economics of New Goods, 1996)
ref.finding: Lighting efficiency increased by a factor of nine hundred between 1800 and 1992, and a true price index of illumination declined by a factor of 75 over the last century.

nodes.label: Eroding incentives to create and learn
nodes.summary: If a model can do it, fewer people may learn the skill or share knowledge, starving future models of human work. Within six months of ChatGPT's release, Stack Overflow activity fell 25% relative to comparable forums[1]. In one UK Society of Authors survey, 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators said they had already lost work to generative AI[2].

refs.title: del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs, Large language models reduce public knowledge sharing on online Q&A platforms, PNAS Nexus 2024
refs.finding: Within six months of ChatGPT's release, Stack Overflow activity fell 25% relative to its Russian and Chinese counterparts and to similar maths forums, with similar falls for more and less experienced users and no significant change in post quality.

refs.title: SoA Survey UK: A third of translators and quarter of illustrators losing work to AI, European Writers' Council 2024
refs.finding: In the Society of Authors' January 2024 survey (787 responses), 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators had lost work to generative AI, and 37% of illustrators and 43% of translators said their income had fallen in value because of it.

nodes.control_note: When answers are free, some learning and sharing will drop. Pay per crawl, licensing labels and copyright settlements put a price on AI use of human work, but whether that keeps people creating and sharing is not yet known.

actions.action: Charge AI crawlers for content access
actions.evidence: Lets sites earn from AI use instead of blocking; still in closed beta, and no payment volumes have been published.

ref.title: Introducing pay per crawl: Enabling content owners to charge AI crawlers for access, Cloudflare 2025
ref.finding: Pay per crawl, in private beta, lets site owners set a per-request price and choose for each AI crawler whether to allow it free, charge it or block it.

actions.action: Compensate authors whose pirated books were copied
actions.evidence: Sets a price of about $3,000 per work; whether it changes lab behaviour is not yet known.

ref.title: Authors Guild, Court Grants Final Approval of $1.5 Billion Anthropic Copyright Settlement
ref.finding: On 20 July 2026 a US federal court in California gave final approval to a $1.5 billion settlement, about $3,000 per work, of authors' claims over Anthropic's acquisition and copying of pirated books.

actions.action: Certify models trained on licensed data
actions.evidence: A voluntary label; Fairly Trained lists 19 certified companies, products and models.

ref.title: Fairly Trained certified models, Fairly Trained
ref.finding: Fairly Trained certifies AI companies that license the copyrighted work they train on; its list shows 19 certified companies, products and models.

precedents.parallel: Free copying cut the money creators earned from their work, which was widely expected to reduce how much good new work got made.
precedents.outcome: Waldfogel found no evidence of a drop in the quality of new music after Napster, and the sales and airplay indices suggested a rise after 1999, while other changes cut the cost of bringing works to market; this cuts against the AI fear, though file-sharing removed revenue, not the reason to learn the skill.

ref.title: Waldfogel, Copyright Protection, Technological Change, and the Quality of New Products: Evidence from Recorded Music since Napster (NBER Working Paper 17503)
ref.finding: There is no evidence of a reduction in the quality of music released since Napster, and the two usage-based indices suggest an increase since 1999.

precedents.parallel: A machine that does the arithmetic raised fears that students would stop learning to calculate for themselves.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 53 studies from 1984 to 2000 found students using calculators maintained or improved their operational and problem-solving skills; there was too little data to show an effect on retention of skills, and a calculator covers a far narrower skill than a language model.

ref.title: Ellington, Effects of Hand-Held Calculators on Precollege Students in Mathematics Classes: A Meta-Analysis, PhD dissertation, University of Tennessee, December 2000
ref.finding: Integrating 53 studies with 307 effect sizes from 1984 to June 2000, students using calculators maintained or improved their operational and problem-solving skills; results on skills retention were not significant because of minimal data, and calculator users had better attitudes toward mathematics.

nodes.label: Metacognitive laziness
nodes.summary: People may let the model do the thinking and stop planning, checking and reflecting on their own work. In one lab study of 117 university students, those writing with ChatGPT improved their essay scores most but showed fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation, and their knowledge gain and transfer were no better than other groups'[1]. In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey, those who practised with an unrestricted GPT-4 chat scored 17% lower once access was removed than students who never had it, while a tutor built to give hints instead of answers largely avoided that loss[2].

refs.title: Fan et al., Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance, British Journal of Educational Technology 2025
refs.finding: In a randomised lab experiment with 117 university students, the ChatGPT group improved essay scores most but showed relatively fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation and orientation; its knowledge gain and transfer did not differ significantly from the other groups.

refs.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 2025
refs.finding: Among nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey, GPT-4 access raised practice grades by 48% (plain chat) and 127% (guardrailed tutor), but plain-chat students scored 17% lower on exams without AI than students who never had access, while tutor students scored statistically the same as the control group.

nodes.control_note: Offloading thinking is the same thing as a lighter cognitive load. Tool design can push users back into planning and checking.

actions.action: Use tutors that give hints, not answers
actions.evidence: In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 students, a tutor prompted to give hints instead of answers left exam scores statistically indistinguishable from the control group, while plain chat cut them by 17%.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: A GPT-4 tutor prompted to give hints without giving the answer left later exam performance statistically indistinguishable from the control arm, largely mitigating the 17% drop seen with an unrestricted chatbot.

actions.action: Show students their unaided performance
actions.evidence: Students who used plain chat did not notice they learned less, and tutor users believed they did better than they did, which suggests feedback on unaided work is needed; direct tests are lacking.

ref.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 2025
ref.finding: Students using the plain chatbot did not perceive that they performed worse or learned less, and guardrailed-tutor students perceived significantly better performance that they did not achieve on the exam.

precedents.parallel: Pilots who let the automation fly lose practice at monitoring and hand-flying, much as users who let a model think stop checking its work.
precedents.outcome: An FAA-chartered working group found a manual handling error as a factor in over 60% of the 26 accident reports it reviewed and flagged vulnerabilities in manual flying skills, but operators and trainers were uncertain how these skills decay and had no consensus on which skills matter.

ref.title: Operational Use of Flight Path Management Systems, Final Report of the PARC/CAST Flight Deck Automation Working Group (FAA, 2013)
ref.finding: Over 60% of the 26 accident reports reviewed identified a manual handling error as a factor; concern that automation use causes skill degradation through lack of practice or over-confidence, while operators and trainers were uncertain how manual handling skills decay.

precedents.parallel: When the automation handed control back unexpectedly, a crew used to monitoring rather than flying could not diagnose and recover from the situation.
precedents.outcome: After iced pitot probes gave inconsistent speeds and the autopilot disconnected, the crew destabilised the flight path and did not identify the approach to stall or diagnose the stall; the BEA cited an absence of high-altitude training in manual aeroplane handling among the factors, a single extreme case rather than a measured trend.

ref.title: BEA Final Report presentation, Accident on 1 June 2009 to the Airbus A330-203, flight AF 447
ref.finding: Factors included an absence of training at high altitude in manual aeroplane handling and the procedure for speed indication anomalies, and the crew not identifying the approach to stall.

precedents.parallel: Outsourcing route-finding to a device is an everyday case of letting a tool do a mental task that the person then stops practising.
precedents.outcome: Among 50 drivers, more lifetime GPS use went with worse spatial memory when navigating unaided, and in 13 retested after three years more GPS use predicted steeper decline; the samples are small and the authors warn against strong conclusions.

ref.title: Dahmani and Bohbot, Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation, Scientific Reports 10, 2020
ref.finding: Greater lifetime GPS experience was associated with worse spatial memory during self-guided navigation, and greater GPS use over three years with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

nodes.label: Better answers for everyone
nodes.summary: Chatbots can give tailored answers to questions that once needed an expert. In one study of 195 patient questions, health professionals preferred ChatGPT's answers to physicians' in 79% of 585 evaluations[1]. Yet in a randomised study of 1,298 participants, chatbot users identified a relevant condition in under 34.5% of cases, no better than controls, while the models alone got 94.9%[2].

refs.title: Ayers et al., Comparing Physician and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions Posted to a Public Social Media Forum, JAMA Internal Medicine 2023
refs.finding: Across 195 exchanges from Reddit's r/AskDocs and 585 evaluations, licensed health professionals preferred ChatGPT's response in 78.6%, rated it good or very good in quality in 78.5% versus 22.1% for physicians, and empathetic in 45.1% versus 4.6%.

refs.title: Bean et al., Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study, Nature Medicine 2026
refs.finding: Tested alone, the models identified conditions in 94.9% of cases, but 1,298 participants using them identified relevant conditions in fewer than 34.5% and the right course of action in fewer than 44.2%, no better than the control group.

limiters.evidence: AMIE's lead over doctors comes from simulated text consults with patient-actors, not real patients.

ref.title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence, Nature 2025
ref.finding: In a randomised, double-blind crossover study of text consultations with patient-actors across 159 scenarios, AMIE outperformed 20 primary care physicians on 30 of 32 axes rated by specialists; the authors say more research is needed before real-world use.

limiters.evidence: On a task outside AI's frontier, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct.

ref.title: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality, HBS Working Paper 24-013, 2023
ref.finding: In a preregistered experiment with 758 BCG consultants, AI raised quality by more than 40% on 18 tasks inside its frontier, but on a task outside it consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions.

limiters.evidence: The NLLB model translates 200 of the world's more than 7,000 languages.

ref.title: NLLB Team, Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages, Nature 2024
ref.finding: NLLB translates 200 languages, out of more than 7,000 in the world; the parallel data translation models need is not equally available, leaving low-resource languages behind.

limiters.limit: unequal access to paid AI plans
limiters.evidence: One leading vendor keeps its strongest model off its free plan; its paid plans start at $20 a month.

ref.title: Pricing, Claude (Anthropic), accessed October 2026
ref.finding: The Free plan includes Sonnet and Haiku but not Opus; Pro costs $20 a month billed monthly and Max starts at $100 a month.

enablers.action: Teach users to check AI answers
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act, as amended in 2026, requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting their staff's AI literacy.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy
ref.finding: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and others using AI on their behalf, without having to guarantee any specific level for an individual.

enablers.action: Assess and audit health AI models
enablers.evidence: WHO recommends that a regulator assess and approve large models for health use, with mandatory post-release audits.

ref.title: WHO releases AI ethics and governance guidance for large multi-modal models, WHO, 18 January 2024
ref.finding: WHO's guidance asks governments to assign a regulatory agency to assess and approve LMMs for health care use and to introduce mandatory post-release auditing and impact assessments by independent third parties.

precedents.parallel: Symptom checker websites promised lay people a tailored first medical opinion without a doctor, the same promise AI assistants now make.
precedents.outcome: Across 23 checkers and 45 vignettes the correct diagnosis came first in 34% of evaluations and triage advice was appropriate in 57%, ranging from 33% to 78% by checker; the authors found deficits in both triage and diagnosis, with advice that leaned towards seeking care.

ref.title: Semigran et al., Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study, BMJ 2015
ref.finding: 23 symptom checkers tested on 45 vignettes listed the correct diagnosis first in 34% of 770 evaluations and gave appropriate triage advice in 57%, ranging from 33% to 78% across checkers.

precedents.parallel: Search engines put medical information in everyone's hands years before chatbots, and people used it to decide whether they needed a professional.
precedents.outcome: 35% of US adults had gone online to work out a medical condition; 41% of them said a clinician confirmed it, 18% said a clinician disagreed or offered another view and 35% never checked with one, and Pew notes it measured the scope of this, not its outcomes.

ref.title: Fox and Duggan, Health Online 2013, Pew Research Center
ref.finding: In a phone survey of 3,014 US adults in August and September 2012, 35% had gone online to diagnose a condition; 41% of these said a clinician confirmed it and 18% said a clinician disagreed or offered another opinion.

nodes.label: AI-induced delusions
nodes.summary: Chatbots may feed delusions in vulnerable people, one psychiatrist warned[2]. Among 53,974 psychiatric patients in the Central Denmark Region, a review found 38 whose chatbot use appeared potentially harmful, most often worse delusions, with no proof of causation[3]. OpenAI estimates hundreds of thousands of ChatGPT users a week show possible signs of psychosis or mania, without blaming the chatbot[4].

refs.title: Futurism, A Prominent OpenAI Investor Appears to Be Suffering a ChatGPT-Related Mental Health Crisis, His Peers Say, July 2025
refs.finding: Geoff Lewis, managing partner of OpenAI backer Bedrock, posted a video on X on 15 July 2025 describing a 'non-governmental system' that had targeted him, with ChatGPT outputs that observers noted read like SCP Foundation fiction.

refs.title: Østergaard, Will Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Generate Delusions in Individuals Prone to Psychosis? (Schizophrenia Bulletin, 2023)
refs.finding: Editorial arguing that the realism of chatbot replies, together with how little users know of how they work, may fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis, with five hypothetical examples.

refs.title: Olsen, Reinecke-Tellefsen and Østergaard, Potentially Harmful Consequences of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbot Use Among Patients With Mental Illness: Early Data From a Large Psychiatric Service System (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica, 2026)
refs.finding: Screening 10,712,856 clinical notes on 53,974 patients from 1 September 2022 to 12 June 2025 found 38 patients with potentially harmful consequences of chatbot use, most often delusions (11) and suicidality or self-harm (6); 32 patients used chatbots in ways that could benefit mental health, and the authors state the notes are not evidence of a causal effect.

refs.title: TechCrunch, OpenAI says over a million people talk to ChatGPT about suicide weekly, October 2025
refs.finding: OpenAI estimates that hundreds of thousands of people a week show possible signs of psychosis or mania in their ChatGPT conversations, which it describes as extremely rare and hard to measure.

nodes.control_note: Agreeable long conversations are what make companions and support bots appealing. Training against sycophancy and routing to care are meant to reduce harm, though their effect on users is not yet measured.

actions.action: Roll back and test models for sycophancy
actions.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a flattering update within days; no outcome data on users.

ref.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we're doing about it, Apr 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update that was overly supportive but disingenuous, and said it would refine training, add honesty guardrails and expand its evaluations.

actions.action: Train models not to affirm delusions
actions.evidence: Self-reported 65 to 80% fewer undesired replies across mental-health areas including psychosis and mania; not independently verified.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI reports 65 to 80% fewer responses falling short of desired behaviour across psychosis and mania, self-harm and suicide, and emotional reliance.

actions.action: Route users in crisis to human care
actions.evidence: Measured only by model compliance, not by user outcomes.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, Oct 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI expanded access to crisis hotlines and trained ChatGPT to guide people toward professional care when appropriate.

precedents.parallel: A new mass medium, reality television, supplied the storyline around which vulnerable patients built persecutory delusions, as chatbot fiction now does.
precedents.outcome: Psychiatrists described a series of patients convinced their lives were being filmed and broadcast, and concluded that culture shapes the content of delusions while the broad categories stay stable; it is a case series with no prevalence figure, and TV did not talk back the way a chatbot does.

ref.title: Gold and Gold, The "Truman Show" delusion: psychosis in the global village (Cognitive Neuropsychiatry, 2012)
ref.finding: A novel persecutory delusion modelled on reality TV; particular delusional ideas are sensitive to culture while broad categories are stable.

precedents.parallel: People who found an online vocabulary and community for being targeted by a hidden organised group mirror users whose chatbot confirms a system is after them.
precedents.outcome: One exploratory study of 128 people who reported being stalked by a group found they had more depressive and post-traumatic symptoms than people stalked by an individual; the study does not measure how far online material caused the beliefs.

ref.title: Sheridan and James, Complaints of group-stalking ('gang-stalking'): an exploratory study of their nature and impact on complainants, Journal of Forensic Psychiatry and Psychology 26(5), 2015
ref.finding: Group-stalking complainants (128 cases) had more depressive and post-traumatic symptoms than complainants stalked by an individual.

nodes.label: AI as a sparring partner
nodes.summary: A model built to disagree could coach people to argue better across divides. In one US experiment with 1,574 people discussing gun control, AI-suggested rephrasings raised partners' ratings of conversation quality without changing policy views, though effects had faded by a follow-up nearly 3 months later[1]. In four US experiments, models could raise conspiracy belief as well as lower it[2].

refs.title: Leveraging AI for democratic discourse: Chat interventions can improve online political conversations at scale (Argyle et al., PNAS, 2023)
refs.finding: In an October 2022 experiment with 1,574 US participants discussing gun regulation, GPT-3 rephrasing suggestions raised partners' reported conversation quality by about 4 percentage points and increased democratic reciprocity, without changing policy attitudes; a follow-up nearly 3 months later found no evidence the effects persisted.

refs.title: Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies (Costello et al., arXiv 2601.05050, 2026)
refs.finding: Across four experiments with 3,996 Americans, models could both substantially increase and decrease conspiracy belief, with no consistent truth advantage; instructing a model to provide only accurate information dramatically reduced its ability to promote conspiracies.

limiters.limit: Models default to agreeing with users
limiters.evidence: Sycophancy showed up in five leading assistants and is reinforced by human preference ratings.

ref.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548, 2023)
ref.finding: Five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently showed sycophancy across four free-form tasks; humans and preference models sometimes preferred convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones.

limiters.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 after it became overly agreeable.

ref.title: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we're doing about it (OpenAI, 2025)
ref.finding: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 because it was overly flattering and agreeable.

limiters.evidence: Machine translation gains have mainly benefited high-resource languages, and quality rises with training data, so sparring in less-resourced languages is likely weaker.

ref.title: Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages (NLLB Team, Nature, 2024)
ref.finding: Most past improvements in translation mainly benefited high-resource languages; the 200-language model covers three times as many low-resource as high-resource languages, and translation quality generally increases with the amount of high-quality training data.

limiters.limit: Evidence mostly from US online samples
limiters.evidence: The strongest results come from US online samples, such as 2,190 Americans talking to one model, which limits how far they generalise.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Costello, Pennycook and Rand, Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut belief in a chosen conspiracy by about 20% across 2,190 Americans, an effect that held 2 months later; a professional fact-checker rated 99.2% of 128 sampled AI claims true, 0.8% misleading and none false. Science issued an expression of concern in June 2026 over dataset and screening inconsistencies, later marked rescinded, and published an erratum on 22 October 2026.

enablers.action: Train and test models against sycophancy
enablers.counters: Models default to agreeing with users
enablers.evidence: Sharma et al. show preference data drives sycophancy, which points to changing the training signal.

ref.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548, 2023)
ref.finding: Five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently showed sycophancy across four free-form tasks; humans and preference models sometimes preferred convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones.

enablers.action: Use AI to mediate group deliberation
enablers.evidence: In experiments with 5,734 participants, replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly representative of the UK, people preferred AI-written group statements to those of human mediators.

ref.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Tessler et al., Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Participants (N = 5,734) preferred AI-generated group statements to those written by human mediators, rating them more informative, clear and unbiased, and discussants often converged on a shared view; the result replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly with a demographically representative UK sample.

enablers.action: Ground counterarguments in checked facts
enablers.evidence: A fact-checker rated 99.2% of 128 sampled AI claims true in the conspiracy study.

ref.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Costello, Pennycook and Rand, Science, 2024)
ref.finding: Dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut belief in a chosen conspiracy by about 20% across 2,190 Americans, an effect that held 2 months later; a professional fact-checker rated 99.2% of 128 sampled AI claims true, 0.8% misleading and none false. Science issued an expression of concern in June 2026 over dataset and screening inconsistencies, later marked rescinded, and published an erratum on 22 October 2026.

precedents.event: America in One Room deliberative poll
precedents.parallel: Structured argument with people who disagree, moderated and fed balanced briefing material, is the human version of a model built to push back.
precedents.outcome: 526 registered voters who deliberated over a weekend in Dallas showed large depolarising shifts in policy views and large drops in affective polarisation against a control group of 844, though the authors found some effects faded afterwards and it relied on real human opponents.

ref.title: Is Deliberation an Antidote to Extreme Partisan Polarization? Reflections on America in One Room (Fishkin et al., American Political Science Review 2021)
ref.finding: Deliberators showed large depolarising changes in policy attitudes and large decreases in affective polarisation versus a pre-post control group; on persistence the authors answer 'both no and yes', with some effects fading.

precedents.parallel: Competitive debate trains students to build and rebut arguments against a constant opponent, which is what an AI sparring partner offers on demand.
precedents.outcome: Debaters were 3.1 times more likely to graduate and scored 0.55 to 1.57 points higher on ACT sections, but participation was not randomly assigned, so the Justice Department's CrimeSolutions rates the program only Promising on one study.

ref.title: Urban Debate League for High School Students (CrimeSolutions, US Office of Justice Programs, rating of Anderson and Mezuk 2012)
ref.finding: Debaters in Chicago, 1997 to 2007, were 3.1 times more likely to graduate and scored 0.55 (math) to 1.57 (reading) points higher on ACT sections than a non-debating comparison group; rated Promising on one non-randomised study.

precedents.parallel: The Church created a standing office whose job was to argue against every candidate for sainthood, an institutional sparring partner like a model told to disagree.
precedents.outcome: Sixtus V established the Promoter of the Faith in 1587 to prepare in writing every possible argument against a candidate; this is a precedent for the design, not evidence that it improved decisions.

ref.title: Advocatus Diaboli, Catholic Encyclopedia (1907)
ref.finding: The office, officially the Promoter of the Faith, was established in 1587 by Sixtus V; its holder must prepare in writing all possible arguments against raising a person to the altars.

nodes.label: AI coaching self-harm
nodes.summary: Popular chatbots can be steered into suicide and self-harm guidance. In one 2025 preprint testing six of them, multi-step prompts framing a self-harm wish as hypothetical or academic got four to give detailed self-harm content and two to give suicide-method content[1]. In a RAND-led study of 9,000 chatbot responses, none directly answered very-high-risk suicide questions, but intermediate-risk answers were inconsistent[2].

refs.title: Schoene and Canca, 'For Argument's Sake, Show Me How to Harm Myself!': Jailbreaking LLMs in Suicide and Self-Harm Contexts (arXiv preprint, 2025)
refs.finding: Multi-step prompts that began with a stated intent to self-harm and then recast the request as hypothetical or academic got four of six widely available chatbots to give detailed self-harm content and two to give suicide-method content; the free ChatGPT-4o and Pi held on both tests.

refs.title: McBain et al., Evaluation of Alignment Between Large Language Models and Expert Clinicians in Suicide Risk Assessment (Psychiatric Services, 2025)
refs.finding: Thirteen clinicians rated 30 suicide-related questions by risk; across 9,000 responses, no chatbot answered very-high-risk questions directly and ChatGPT and Claude always answered very-low-risk ones, but responses to intermediate-risk questions were inconsistent.

refs.title: TechCrunch, OpenAI says over a million people talk to ChatGPT about suicide weekly, October 2025
refs.finding: OpenAI estimates 0.15% of weekly active users, more than a million people given over 800 million weekly users, have conversations with explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning or intent; the updated GPT-5 was 91% compliant with desired behaviour on a suicide evaluation against 77% for the previous GPT-5.

nodes.control_note: A model that talks openly about distress can also be pushed into harmful detail. Safety training and crisis protocols lower the rate of harmful replies in vendor tests, but multi-step jailbreaks still worked in 2025 tests.

actions.action: Require suicide-prevention protocols for companion bots
actions.evidence: In force since 1 January 2026, with annual reporting on links between chatbot use and suicidal ideation; no outcome data yet.

ref.title: California SB 243, Companion chatbots (2025)
ref.finding: California SB 243 requires companion chatbot operators to keep a protocol for addressing suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm that includes a notification referring users to crisis service providers.

actions.action: Train models to refuse self-harm instructions
actions.evidence: Self-reported: 65 to 80% fewer replies falling short of desired behaviour across mental-health areas, and 91% compliance on a suicide evaluation against 77% before; not independently audited.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, October 2025
ref.finding: After work with more than 170 mental health experts, OpenAI reports 65 to 80% fewer responses falling short of desired behaviour across self-harm and suicide, psychosis and mania, and emotional reliance, and 91% compliance on a suicide evaluation for the updated GPT-5 against 77%.

actions.action: Show crisis hotlines in risky conversations
actions.evidence: Referral is common practice; no published data yet show it prevents deaths among chatbot users.

ref.title: OpenAI, Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations, October 2025
ref.finding: OpenAI expanded access to crisis hotlines, rerouted sensitive conversations to safer models and trained the model to guide people to professional care when appropriate.

precedents.parallel: General-purpose search tools returned method information to people in distress, the same failure as a chatbot steered into self-harm guidance.
precedents.outcome: Of 480 top hits from 48 suicide searches run in May 2007, 9% were pro-suicide pages and 9% described methods, just under half gave some method information, and the three most frequent sites were all pro-suicide; unlike a chatbot, search did not hold a personalised conversation.

ref.title: Biddle, Donovan, Hawton, Kapur and Gunnell, Suicide and the internet (BMJ, 2008)
ref.finding: 48 searches gave 480 hits on 240 sites; 45 hits were pro-suicide and 43 described methods; the three most frequent sites were pro-suicide.

precedents.parallel: Recommendation algorithms fed a depressed 14-year-old self-harm content she had not asked for, an earlier case of a machine system deepening a vulnerable user's crisis.
precedents.outcome: The coroner concluded she died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, which contributed to her death in a more than minimal way, and recommended that the government consider age verification, separate platforms for adults and children and an independent regulator.

ref.title: Regulation 28 Report to Prevent Future Deaths, Molly Rose Russell (Andrew Walker, Senior Coroner, Northern District of Greater London, 13 October 2022), copy hosted by Leigh Day
ref.finding: Algorithms produced binge periods of self-harm and suicide content, some selected and provided without her requesting it; this material contributed to her death in a more than minimal way.

precedents.parallel: Mass media coverage that names a method changes how many people die and by which means, the population-level risk of models repeating method detail.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 31 studies, covering data from 1947 to 2016, found suicides rose 13% after a celebrity suicide was reported and deaths by the same method rose 30% when the method was described, while general suicide reporting showed no clear effect; this is broadcast contagion, not one-to-one advice.

ref.title: Niederkrotenthaler et al., Association between suicide reporting in the media and suicide: systematic review and meta-analysis (BMJ, 2020)
ref.finding: Rate ratio 1.13 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.18) for suicide after celebrity suicide reports and 1.30 (1.18 to 1.44) for same-method deaths when the method was reported; general reporting of suicide showed no clear association.

nodes.label: AI helps plan violence
nodes.summary: Attackers have used chatbots for research. Las Vegas police said the January 2025 Cybertruck bomber used ChatGPT to look up explosive targets and ammunition speed[1], though OpenAI said it gave only public information[2]. In June 2025 the US Justice Department said AI chat records showed the Palm Springs fertility clinic bomber researched how to make powerful explosions[3].

refs.title: Man who exploded Cybertruck in Las Vegas used ChatGPT in planning, police say (AP via MPR News, January 2025)
refs.finding: Las Vegas police said Matthew Livelsberger used generative AI including ChatGPT to plan the attack; his searches covered explosive targets, the speed of certain ammunition rounds and whether fireworks were legal in Arizona.

refs.title: Man who exploded Tesla Cybertruck outside Trump hotel used generative AI, police say (AP via NBC Chicago, January 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI said ChatGPT responded with information already publicly available on the internet and provided warnings against harmful or illegal activities.

refs.title: Washington State Man Arrested on Federal Charges Alleging He Provided Material Support to Palm Springs Fertility Clinic Bomber (US Department of Justice, June 2025)
refs.finding: Records from an AI chat application show that bomber Guy Edward Bartkus researched how to make powerful explosions using ammonium nitrate and fuel, three days before the charged man arrived at his home.

nodes.control_note: General answer capability also answers attackers, but most of this is filterable. Refusal classifiers and control of physical materials cut uplift without losing much benefit.

actions.action: Block weapons uplift with classifiers
actions.evidence: Targets CBRN weapons, at first only biological ones, and universal jailbreaks, not conventional explosives or commonly available single facts; its effect is not public.

ref.title: Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections (Anthropic, May 2025)
ref.finding: ASL-3 deployment measures use classifiers to block extended, end-to-end CBRN weapons workflows and universal jailbreaks, focusing at first on biological weapons; they do not aim to address issues unrelated to CBRN.

actions.action: Restrict sale of explosives precursors
actions.evidence: Applies to the step after research; effect on attacks is hard to isolate.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/1148 on explosives precursors
ref.finding: EU Regulation 2019/1148 limits public access to explosives precursors and requires reporting of suspicious sales.

precedents.event: Bomb manuals on the early internet
precedents.parallel: After Oklahoma City, bomb recipes spread online and officials faced the same question as with chatbots: the information was already public, but easier access might still help attackers.
precedents.outcome: The Justice Department found in 1997 that anyone could easily obtain detailed instructions from reference books, the underground press and the internet, and that defendants had relied on such material; Congress responded in 1999 with 18 U.S.C. 842(p), which criminalises teaching bomb-making only with intent that it be used for a federal crime of violence or knowledge that the recipient intends that.

ref.title: Bomb-Making Online: Explosives, Free Speech, Criminal Law and the Internet (Congressional Research Service RL32074, 2003)
ref.finding: Quotes the April 1997 DOJ report that anyone can easily obtain detailed bomb instructions from readily accessible sources including the internet, and traces the resulting 842(p).

precedents.parallel: An online magazine gave step-by-step instructions that saved attackers effort, the role chatbots now play for some planners.
precedents.outcome: The federal indictment says Dzhokhar Tsarnaev downloaded Inspire Volume One, which gave instructions for pressure-cooker bombs with firework powder and shrapnel, before the attack whose two bombs killed three people; the instructions came from an al-Qaeda publication rather than a general assistant.

ref.title: Indictment, United States v. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev, Case 1:13-cr-10200 (US Department of Justice, filed June 2013)
ref.finding: Tsarnaev downloaded Volume One of Inspire, an online publication of al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula that includes instructions for building IEDs using pressure cookers, explosive powder from fireworks and shrapnel; the Marathon bombs killed Krystle Marie Campbell, Lingzi Lu and Martin Richard.

nodes.label: AI guides people through bureaucracy
nodes.summary: AI assistants could help people find benefits, fill in forms and decode rules. In one randomized test, 125 CalFresh caseworkers scored about 24 percentage points higher with chatbot suggestions, but a wrong suggestion cut accuracy by about 20 points[1]. New York City's MyCity chatbot suggested landlords could refuse tenants with Section 8 vouchers and was taken down in February 2026[2].

refs.title: Helping the Helpers: Evaluating a GenAI-powered assistive chatbot for caseworkers (Nava PBC, Georgetown Better Government Lab and Cornell Tech, March 2026)
refs.finding: In a randomized experiment, 125 caseworkers answering 45 CalFresh questions scored about 24 percentage points higher, a 40% improvement over the control group, with simulated suggestions as accurate as the real chatbot; correct suggestions raised accuracy by about 35 points and incorrect ones lowered it by about 20. In a 14-week pilot with 61 caseworkers at six Los Angeles County organizations, about 65% of those with access used it, and use declined over time.

refs.title: Mamdani to kill the NYC AI chatbot we caught telling businesses to break the law (The Markup and THE CITY, January 2026)
refs.finding: The MyCity chatbot, released in fall 2023, suggested landlords could discriminate against tenants with Section 8 vouchers and that refusing cash was fine; the city took it down in early February 2026.

limiters.limit: Wrong or stale answers on rules
limiters.evidence: New York City's MyCity bot suggested landlords could turn away tenants with Section 8 vouchers, which city law forbids; the city took it down in February 2026.

ref.title: Mamdani to kill the NYC AI chatbot we caught telling businesses to break the law (The Markup and THE CITY, January 2026)
ref.finding: The MyCity chatbot, released in fall 2023, suggested landlords could discriminate against tenants with Section 8 vouchers and that refusing cash was fine; the city took it down in early February 2026.

limiters.limit: Low trust after automated welfare failures
limiters.evidence: Australia's Robodebt scheme raised debts that the Royal Commission called neither fair nor legal, and it made many people feel like criminals.

ref.title: Final report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Prime Minister of Australia, July 2023)
ref.finding: Quotes the Royal Commission: Robodebt was a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal, that made many people feel like criminals, and a costly failure of public administration; the scheme ran for about five years from 2015.

limiters.evidence: 2.2 billion people were still offline in 2025, 96% of them in low- and middle-income countries, and only 58% of people in rural areas were online.

ref.title: Global number of Internet users increases, but disparities deepen key digital divides (ITU, November 2025)
ref.finding: 2.2 billion people remain offline in 2025, down from a revised 2.3 billion in 2024; 96% of them live in low- and middle-income countries, and 85% of urban against 58% of rural people are online.

limiters.evidence: In autumn 2023 just over a third of 87 UK government bodies surveyed had deployed AI, typically one or two uses each, and 70% named skills as a barrier.

ref.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (National Audit Office, HC 612, March 2024)
ref.finding: As at autumn 2023, AI was not widely used across government: 37% of the 87 bodies that responded had deployed AI, typically with one or two use cases each, 70% were piloting or planning AI, and 70% reported skills as a barrier.

enablers.action: Treat benefit eligibility AI as high-risk
enablers.counters: Low trust after automated welfare failures
enablers.evidence: The AI Act classes AI used for access to essential services, including eligibility for public assistance, as high-risk, but the 2026 AI Omnibus delayed those duties to 2 December 2027.

ref.title: The AI Act Implementation Timeline: What Changes Under the AI Omnibus? (Future of Privacy Forum, 2026)
ref.finding: The AI Omnibus, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026, delays obligations for Annex III high-risk systems, which include access to essential services, from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027.

enablers.action: Publish clear rules for public-sector AI use
enablers.evidence: The UK set 10 principles for civil servants using AI in February 2025.

ref.title: AI Playbook for the UK Government (Government Digital Service, 2025)
ref.finding: Sets 10 principles for safe, effective use of AI by civil servants, published 10 February 2025.

enablers.action: Guarantee review of automated benefit decisions
enablers.counters: Wrong or stale answers on rules
enablers.evidence: The Robodebt Royal Commission asked for a clear path to seek review wherever decisions are automated; Australia was still consulting on that framework in November 2024.

ref.title: Use of automated decision-making by government: consultation paper (Attorney-General's Department, Australia, November 2024)
ref.finding: Quotes Robodebt Royal Commission Recommendation 17.1: a consistent legal framework for automation in government services, with a clear path for those affected by automated decisions to seek review, plain-language disclosure and published business rules; the government had committed to consider legislative reform.

precedents.parallel: Tax preparers filled in the federal student aid form for low-income families, the hands-on help AI form assistants promise at scale.
precedents.outcome: Families given help completing the FAFSA were substantially more likely to submit it, and high school seniors and recent graduates among them were 25 to 30 percent more likely to enrol in college, while information alone had no significant effect; the help came from H&R Block tax professionals using the family's tax return.

ref.title: The Role of Simplification and Information in College Decisions: Results from the H&R Block FAFSA Experiment (Bettinger, Long, Oreopoulos and Sanbonmatsu, NBER Working Paper 15361, 2009)
ref.finding: Assistance plus information raised FAFSA submission, and seniors and recent graduates in that group were 25 to 30 percent more likely to enrol; aid information without help with the form had no significant effect on FAFSA submission.

precedents.parallel: An automated system applied a crude rule to welfare records and told people what they owed, the downside case of a stale or wrong AI answer about entitlements.
precedents.outcome: The Commonwealth conceded it had no proper legal basis for debts raised by averaging tax office income data, withdrew about A$1.763 billion of them, promised to refund about A$751 million it had recovered and paid A$112 million in interest under a 2021 class action settlement; the judge called it a massive failure of public administration. The debts came from a fixed averaging rule, not machine learning, but the failure of automated benefit decisions is the same.

ref.title: The Federal Court approves a $112 million settlement for the failures of the Robodebt system (Human Rights Law Centre, 2021)
ref.finding: Summarises Prygodicz v Commonwealth (No 2), approved 11 June 2021: the Commonwealth conceded it had no proper legal basis for income-averaged debts, withdrew about $1.763 billion of them, promised to refund about $751 million and paid $112 million in interest to some 648,000 group members; Justice Murphy called it a massive failure of public administration.

precedents.parallel: Michigan's unemployment agency let software decide fraud cases without human review, as agencies may lean on AI to rule on claims.
precedents.outcome: 85% of the 40,195 fraud findings made by the algorithm alone from October 2013 to September 2015 were wrong, more than 34,000 people were wrongly accused and faced a 400 percent penalty, and the agency stopped purely automated fraud findings in September 2015.

ref.title: Michigan's MiDAS Unemployment System: Algorithm Alchemy Created Lead, Not Gold (Robert N. Charette, IEEE Spectrum, 2018)
ref.finding: From October 2013 to September 2015, 85% of 40,195 algorithm-only fraud determinations were incorrect; 34,000-plus people were wrongly accused and faced a 400 percent penalty; the agency stopped purely automated fraud assessment in September 2015.

nodes.label: Lighter cognitive load
nodes.summary: Handing routine drafting, summarising and recall to a model can take effort off people. In a Microsoft lab study of a Teams meeting task, participants with Copilot found it 58% less draining[1]. Oversight pushes the other way: in a survey of 1,488 full-time US workers, high AI oversight went with 12% more mental fatigue and 19% more information overload[2].

refs.title: Microsoft New Future of Work Report 2023 (Microsoft Research, MSR-TR-2023-34, December 2023)
refs.finding: In the Teams Meeting Study, participants with Copilot found the task 58% less draining than those without; 72% of enterprise Copilot users agreed it helped them spend less mental effort on mundane or repetitive tasks.

refs.title: 'AI brain fry' is real, and it's making workers more exhausted, not more productive, new study finds (Fortune, March 2026)
refs.finding: In a Boston Consulting Group survey of 1,488 full-time US workers, high AI oversight was associated with 12% greater mental fatigue and 19% greater information overload, and 14% more mental effort at work.

limiters.evidence: Among 319 knowledge workers surveyed, higher confidence in the model went with less critical thinking.

ref.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI 2025, Microsoft Research)
ref.finding: Survey of 319 knowledge workers who gave 936 first-hand examples: higher confidence in generative AI is associated with less critical thinking, while higher self-confidence is associated with more.

limiters.limit: Reduced engagement and recall of own work
limiters.evidence: In a 54-person EEG study, the group writing with an LLM showed the weakest brain connectivity, reported the least ownership of their essays and struggled to quote their own work; it is a preprint.

ref.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task (Kosmyna et al., arXiv preprint 2506.08872, June 2025, revised December 2025)
ref.finding: 54 participants took part in sessions 1 to 3 and 18 in session 4; LLM users displayed the weakest brain connectivity, the lowest self-reported ownership of their essays and struggled to accurately quote their own work.

limiters.evidence: Since February 2025 EU law has required providers and deployers to act on staff AI literacy; since July 2026 the duty is to support its development, not to guarantee any level.

ref.title: Sapuppo, AI literacy: the Digital Omnibus rewrites Article 4 of the AI Act, Law & Technology, July 2026
ref.finding: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026, replaces Article 4: providers and deployers shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff, and the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual; the 2024 text required them to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level.

enablers.action: Train staff in AI literacy
enablers.evidence: Article 4 of the AI Act, as rewritten in July 2026, makes providers and deployers take measures supporting staff AI literacy.

ref.title: Sapuppo, AI literacy: the Digital Omnibus rewrites Article 4 of the AI Act, Law & Technology, July 2026
ref.finding: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026, replaces Article 4: providers and deployers shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff, and the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual; the 2024 text required them to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level.

enablers.action: Use tutor-style guardrails instead of open answers
enablers.evidence: A guardrailed GPT-4 tutor avoided the later exam drop seen with unrestricted access in a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high school maths students.

ref.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS, 2025)
ref.finding: In a field experiment with nearly a thousand high school maths students, access to unrestricted GPT-4 improved performance while available but left students worse off than peers who never had it once access was removed; a version with learning safeguards largely prevented that harm.

enablers.action: Target assistants at novice workers first
enablers.evidence: Across 5,172 support agents, gains were largest for the least experienced and lower-skilled workers.

ref.title: Generative AI at Work (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025)
ref.finding: Staggered rollout of a generative AI assistant to 5,172 customer support agents raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average, with the largest gains for less experienced and lower-skilled workers and little change for the most experienced.

precedents.parallel: Calculators offloaded routine arithmetic much as models now offload routine drafting and recall, with the same fear that the underlying skill would wither.
precedents.outcome: A meta-analysis of 53 studies (307 effect sizes) found students who used calculators kept or improved operational skills, gained in problem solving and liked maths more; calculators are narrow and deterministic, unlike a model that drafts whole answers.

ref.title: Effects of hand-held calculators on precollege students in mathematics classes: a meta-analysis (Ellington, PhD dissertation, University of Tennessee, 2000)
ref.finding: Across 53 studies, calculator use maintained or improved operational skills, improved problem solving at all grades and improved attitudes toward mathematics.

precedents.parallel: When people expect a tool to hold information for them, they stop holding it themselves, which is the trade AI recall offers.
precedents.outcome: Four lab studies found that people who expected future access to information recalled the facts less and recalled where to find them more; these were small lab experiments, not measures of long-term ability.

ref.title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips (Sparrow, Liu and Wegner, Science, 2011)
ref.finding: Expecting future access to information lowered recall of the information itself and raised recall of where to access it.

precedents.event: Cockpit automation and pilot skill decay
precedents.parallel: Autopilots took routine flying off pilots and turned them into monitors, the same shift from doing to overseeing that agents bring to knowledge work.
precedents.outcome: Regulators found pilots got less manual practice and, in an update to a 2013 report, that from 2009 to 2016, 92% of flight path management related accidents worldwide had a manual flight operations error that was contributory or causal; US air carrier pilots now have to fly six extra manual manoeuvres in recurrent simulator training.

ref.title: Pilot training improvements to address automation dependency (ICAO Assembly working paper A40-WP/296, presented by the United States, Canada, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago, 2019)
ref.finding: Increased use of automation is likely contributing to a lack of practice and potentially a degradation of manual flight path management skills; from 2009 to 2016, 92% of flight path management related accidents worldwide had a contributory or causal manual flight operations error, and the FAA requires six manual flying manoeuvres in initial and recurrent training.

nodes.label: Accelerated drug discovery
nodes.summary: AI now helps pick drug targets and design molecules[1][2]. In a 71-patient phase 2a trial, rentosertib, an AI-discovered drug, was safe and raised forced vital capacity by 98.4 ml at the top dose against a 20.3 ml fall on placebo[1]. But of molecules from AI-native biotechs, only about 40% cleared phase 2, in line with industry averages[3].

refs.title: A generative AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a randomized phase 2a trial (Xu et al., Nature Medicine, 2025)
refs.finding: In 71 patients over 12 weeks, rentosertib, a TNIK inhibitor whose target and molecule came from generative AI, was safe and well tolerated, with forced vital capacity up 98.4 ml at 60 mg once daily against a 20.3 ml fall on placebo.

refs.title: Accurate structure prediction of biomolecular interactions with AlphaFold 3 (Abramson et al., Nature, 2024)
refs.finding: Far greater accuracy for protein-ligand interactions than state-of-the-art docking tools, much higher accuracy for protein-nucleic acid interactions than nucleic-acid-specific predictors, and substantially higher antibody-antigen accuracy than AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3.

refs.title: How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials? A first analysis and emerging lessons (Jayatunga et al., Drug Discovery Today, 2024)
refs.finding: Molecules discovered by AI-native biotech companies had an 80 to 90% success rate in phase 1, well above historic industry averages, but about 40% in phase 2 on a limited sample, comparable to historic averages.

limiters.limit: Clinical benefit still unproven at scale
limiters.evidence: The leading AI-discovered drug only entered its first phase 3 trial in September 2026, with primary completion estimated in October 2029.

ref.title: A Phase 3 Study of Rentosertib in Adults With Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis, NCT07687459 (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2026)
ref.finding: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral rentosertib over 52 weeks, 320 patients planned at 47 sites in China, started 9 September 2026 with primary completion estimated October 2029.

limiters.limit: Training data skewed to European ancestry
limiters.evidence: In 3,639 genome-wide association studies, 86% of discovery-stage participants were of European ancestry, which skews the targets these models learn from.

ref.title: A scientometric review of genome-wide association studies (Mills and Rahal, Communications Biology, 2019)
ref.finding: Across 3,639 studies from 2005 to 2018, participants were 86.03% European ancestry at discovery stage and 88% European in 2017; polygenic scores built on them transfer poorly to other populations.

limiters.limit: Speed, not better odds of working
limiters.evidence: AI-discovered molecules clear phase 1 at 80 to 90% but only about 40% clear phase 2, the industry norm.

ref.title: How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials? A first analysis and emerging lessons (Jayatunga et al., Drug Discovery Today, 2024)
ref.finding: Phase 1 success was 80 to 90%, substantially higher than historic industry averages; phase 2 success was about 40% on a limited sample, comparable to historic industry averages.

limiters.limit: Regulatory standards for AI still forming
limiters.evidence: The FDA's framework for AI in drug submissions was still a draft in 2025.

ref.title: Considerations for the Use of AI To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (FDA draft guidance, 2025)
ref.finding: Proposes a risk-based credibility framework for AI models used in drug submissions.

enablers.action: Set credibility rules for AI in submissions
enablers.counters: Regulatory standards for AI still forming
enablers.evidence: The FDA draft guidance proposes a risk-based framework to judge an AI model's credibility for a stated context of use; it was still a draft in October 2026.

ref.title: Considerations for the Use of AI To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (FDA draft guidance, 2025)
ref.finding: Proposes a risk-based credibility framework for AI models used in drug submissions.

enablers.action: Run larger randomised trials of AI drugs
enablers.counters: Clinical benefit still unproven at scale
enablers.evidence: After the phase 2a trial, rentosertib entered a 320-patient, 52-week phase 3 trial at 47 Chinese sites in September 2026.

ref.title: A Phase 3 Study of Rentosertib in Adults With Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis, NCT07687459 (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2026)
ref.finding: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral rentosertib over 52 weeks, 320 patients planned at 47 sites in China, started 9 September 2026, primary endpoint the annual rate of forced vital capacity decline.

precedents.parallel: In the 1990s the industry bet on brute-force tools that made and tested far more molecules, the same promise AI design makes now.
precedents.outcome: Despite big advances in science and technology, new drugs approved per billion US dollars of R&D halved roughly every 9 years since 1950, about an 80-fold fall, and the authors name a basic research-brute force bias as one of four causes.

ref.title: Diagnosing the decline in pharmaceutical R&D efficiency (Scannell et al., Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2012)
ref.finding: New drugs per billion US dollars of R&D halved roughly every 9 years since 1950, falling about 80-fold despite big advances in science and technology.

precedents.event: Structure-based design of HIV protease inhibitors
precedents.parallel: Computers and crystal structures were used to design molecules against a known target, an earlier version of what AI design does now.
precedents.outcome: Within about a decade four drugs were approved, but resistance mutations quickly cut their potency; success came on one well-defined target, not across drug discovery as a whole.

ref.title: Inhibitors of HIV-1 protease: a major success of structure-assisted drug design (Wlodawer and Vondrasek, Annual Review of Biophysics and Biomolecular Structure, 1998)
ref.finding: Four drugs were already approved, designed with crystallography, NMR, computational studies and advanced chemical synthesis, while drug-induced mutations of HIV-1 protease caused rapid loss of potency.

nodes.label: Advances in genomics
nodes.summary: Models predict which mutations cause disease and how DNA controls genes[1][2]. AlphaMissense classified 89% of all 71 million possible human missense variants as likely benign or pathogenic, against the 0.1% confirmed by human experts[1][3]. The makers say this could improve rare-disease diagnosis, but the predictions are not designed for clinical use on their own[3].

refs.title: Accurate proteome-wide missense variant effect prediction with AlphaMissense (Cheng et al., Science, 2023)
refs.finding: A fine-tuned AlphaFold model classifies 89% of missense variants as either likely benign or likely pathogenic, with a database of predictions for all possible human single amino acid substitutions released as a community resource.

refs.title: Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome (Avsec et al., Nature, 2026)
refs.finding: AlphaGenome takes 1 megabase of input sequence and predicts thousands of functional genomic tracks at up to single-base-pair resolution, matching or exceeding the strongest external models in 25 of 26 evaluations of variant effect prediction.

refs.title: A catalogue of genetic mutations to help pinpoint the cause of diseases (Google DeepMind, September 2023)
refs.finding: Of 71 million possible missense variants, 89% were classified, about 57% likely benign and 32% likely pathogenic, where only 0.1% had been confirmed by human experts; the predictions are free to use but not designed to be used in the clinic directly and should be interpreted with other evidence.

limiters.limit: Genome data skewed to European ancestry
limiters.evidence: In 3,639 genome-wide association studies, 86% of discovery-stage participants were of European ancestry, so scores and predictions transfer poorly to other groups.

ref.title: A scientometric review of genome-wide association studies (Mills and Rahal, Communications Biology, 2019)
ref.finding: Across 3,639 studies from 2005 to 2018, participants were 86.03% European ancestry at discovery stage and 88% European in 2017; polygenic scores from European-ancestry studies explain only half as much variability in non-Hispanic Black samples.

limiters.limit: Predictions not validated for clinical use
limiters.evidence: AlphaMissense classified 89% of 71 million variants, but its makers say the calls are not designed for direct clinical use.

ref.title: A catalogue of genetic mutations to help pinpoint the cause of diseases (Google DeepMind, September 2023)
ref.finding: 89% of 71 million possible missense variants were classified as likely benign or likely pathogenic; the predictions are not designed to be used in the clinic directly and should be interpreted with other sources of evidence.

limiters.evidence: Free predictions help only where DNA can be sequenced and read, and WHO's Science Council finds lower-income countries short of financing, labs and trained staff.

ref.title: WHO's Science Council launches report calling for equitable expansion of genomics (World Health Organization, July 2022)
ref.finding: Access to genomic technologies needs expanding, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, by addressing shortfalls in financing, laboratory infrastructure, materials and highly trained personnel; it is not justifiable ethically or scientifically for less-resourced countries to gain access long after rich countries do.

enablers.action: Release variant predictions openly
enablers.evidence: AlphaMissense predictions for 71 million variants were published for free use, under a CC BY 4.0 licence since March 2024, with the model code open source.

ref.title: A catalogue of genetic mutations to help pinpoint the cause of diseases (Google DeepMind, September 2023)
ref.finding: Predictions for all 71 million possible missense variants are freely available, licensed CC BY 4.0 since 13 March 2024, and the model code is open source.

enablers.action: Fund diverse-ancestry genome cohorts
enablers.counters: Genome data skewed to European ancestry
enablers.evidence: Popejoy and Fullerton call on funding agencies to create financial incentives for diverse cohorts and to prioritise studies in non-European, especially African, ancestry populations.

ref.title: Genomics is failing on diversity (Popejoy and Fullerton, Nature, 2016)
ref.finding: 96% of participants in genome-wide association studies were of European descent in a 2009 analysis; by August 2016 the non-European share had risen to nearly 20%, almost 78% of that growth from Asian samples, and funding agencies should develop financial incentives for diverse cohorts.

precedents.event: Human Genome Project and cheap sequencing
precedents.parallel: A step change in the ability to read DNA was sold as a coming revolution in diagnosis, as AI genome models are now.
precedents.outcome: The first genome cost at least $500 million, and a draft genome fell below $1,500 by late 2015, so the reading tool became cheap very fast.

ref.title: The Cost of Sequencing a Human Genome (National Human Genome Research Institute, last updated November 2021)
ref.finding: The Human Genome Project's reference genome is estimated to have cost at least $500 million and as much as $1 billion; the cost of a high-quality draft whole human genome had fallen below $1,500 by late 2015.

precedents.parallel: Ten years after the genome map, its leader judged how far promised medical benefit had arrived, a test AI genomics claims will face too.
precedents.outcome: Collins wrote that sequencing cost fell about 14,000-fold from 1999 to 2009 but the consequences for clinical medicine had been modest and most patients' care was not yet directly affected.

ref.title: Has the revolution arrived? (Francis Collins, Nature, 2010)
ref.finding: DNA sequencing costs dropped approximately 14,000-fold between 1999 and 2009, but the consequences for clinical medicine have thus far been modest and the Human Genome Project has not yet directly affected the health care of most individuals.

precedents.event: Clinical exome sequencing for rare disorders
precedents.parallel: Reading all coding genes at once was used to end diagnostic odysseys for rare disease, the same goal AI variant interpretation targets.
precedents.outcome: Of the first 250 probands referred for clinical whole-exome sequencing, 62 got a molecular diagnosis, a rate of 25% with a 95% confidence interval of 20 to 31, so three quarters still did not.

ref.title: Clinical Whole-Exome Sequencing for the Diagnosis of Mendelian Disorders (Yang et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2013)
ref.finding: Among the first 250 probands for whom referring physicians ordered whole-exome sequencing, 62 carried mutations meeting criteria for a molecular diagnosis, a rate of 25% (95% CI, 20 to 31).

nodes.label: Foundation models for omics
nodes.summary: Models trained on millions of cells aim to integrate omics data at a scale manual analysis cannot reach; scGPT, pretrained on over 33 million cells, reached superior performance on tasks including cell-type annotation, perturbation response prediction and multi-omic integration after fine-tuning[1]. Independent tests are less flattering: a 2025 benchmark found that none of five foundation models, scGPT among them, beat simple baselines at predicting gene perturbation effects[2], and without fine-tuning scGPT and Geneformer were in some cases outperformed by simpler methods[3].

refs.title: scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI (Cui et al., Nature Methods, 2024)
refs.finding: A generative pretrained transformer built on a repository of over 33 million cells; through further transfer-learning adaptation it achieved superior performance on cell type annotation, multi-batch integration, multi-omic integration, perturbation response prediction and gene network inference.

refs.title: Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines (Ahlmann-Eltze, Huber and Anders, Nature Methods, 2025)
refs.finding: Five foundation models, including scGPT, and two other deep learning models were compared with deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double gene perturbations; none outperformed the baselines.

refs.title: Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations of single-cell foundation models (Kedzierska et al., Genome Biology, 2025)
refs.finding: Used without further training, scGPT and Geneformer may in some cases face reliability challenges and be outperformed by simpler methods; zero-shot performance matters where fine-tuning is not possible.

limiters.limit: Pretraining data limited to healthy human cells
limiters.evidence: scGPT was pretrained on 33 million normal (non-disease) human cells from the CELLxGENE collection, covering 51 organs or tissues and 441 studies; the authors plan to add diseased conditions, multi-omic and spatial data.

ref.title: scGPT: Towards Building a Foundation Model for Single-Cell Multi-omics Using Generative AI (Cui et al., bioRxiv, 2023)
ref.finding: Pretraining used 33 million normal human cells obtained via the CELLxGENE collection, spanning 51 organs or tissues and 441 studies; future pretraining is planned on more diverse data including diseased conditions.
