limiters.evidence: EU data protection authorities found that orders to detect unknown abuse material and grooming in private messages, given their intrusiveness, probabilistic nature and error rates, go beyond what is necessary and proportionate.

ref.title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, 2022
ref.finding: Adopted 28 July 2022; detection of unknown CSAM and grooming in interpersonal communications goes beyond what is necessary and proportionate due to intrusiveness, probabilistic nature and error rates; grooming provisions should be removed.

enablers.action: Fund hotlines that confirm and triage reports
enablers.evidence: IWF received 424,047 reports suspected to contain child sexual abuse imagery in 2024 and confirmed that 291,273 did.

ref.title: IWF Annual Data & Insights Report 2024
ref.finding: 424,047 reports suspected to contain child sexual abuse imagery in 2024; 291,273 reports confirmed to contain child sexual abuse imagery.

enablers.action: Offer self-hosted detection that shares minimal data
enablers.evidence: Safer offers self-hosted deployment that limits data shared with the vendor.

ref.title: CSAM Detection from Experts in Child Safety Technology | Safer by Thorn
ref.finding: With the self-hosted option customers share limited data; a secure API-based deployment is also available.

enablers.action: Give platforms a time-limited legal basis for voluntary scanning
enablers.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 reinstated voluntary detection until 3 April 2028 after the earlier rules lapsed on 3 April 2026, but it does not cover end-to-end encrypted communications.

ref.title: eucrim, Interim Rules on Voluntary CSAM Detection Reinstated Until 2028, 2026
ref.finding: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 of 24 July 2026 applies until 3 April 2028 and does not apply to interpersonal communications to which end-to-end encryption is applied.

precedents.parallel: Microsoft and NCMEC deployed automated matching to find abuse images at platform scale, the step before classifiers that flag unseen images.
precedents.outcome: PhotoDNA was designed to match resized or similarly altered copies of known images, and Microsoft donated it to NCMEC to share with online service providers; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million images and videos since 2003, but the release gives no measured accuracy and the method only finds images already identified.

ref.title: Microsoft and National Center for Missing & Exploited Children Push for Action to Fight Child Pornography (Microsoft press release), 2009
ref.finding: PhotoDNA creates a signature for an image that still matches when the image is resized or similarly altered; NCMEC can make it available to online service providers; NCMEC had reviewed almost 30 million photos and videos since 2003 and its victim identification programme reviews 250,000 a week.

nodes.label: AI flood warnings for data-poor regions
nodes.summary: AI can forecast floods for river basins without gauges: in one Nature study across 5,680 gauges, its forecasts were as reliable five days ahead as same-day nowcasts from the leading global system[1]. Google says its forecasts now cover 100 countries where 700 million people live[2]. Whether warnings change behaviour is less proven, and Google's account of use is anecdotal.

refs.title: Nearing et al., Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Nature), 2024
refs.finding: Across 5,680 gauges, AI forecasts of extreme riverine events in ungauged watersheds were as reliable at up to five days lead time as same-day nowcasts from the Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System, and accuracy on five-year return period events matched or beat current accuracy on one-year events; the model runs in a free public warning system in over 80 countries.

refs.title: Google, How we're helping partners with improved and expanded AI-based flood forecasting, 2024
refs.finding: Coverage expanded to 100 countries (up from 80) in areas where 700 million people live (up from 460 million); the improved model has the same accuracy at seven days lead time as the previous model had at five; examples of use in Brazil are anecdotal.

limiters.evidence: 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world, were offline in 2024, 1.8 billion of them in rural areas, so online flood maps cannot reach them directly.

ref.title: ITU, Global Internet use continues to rise but disparities remain, especially in low-income regions, 2024
ref.finding: An estimated 2.6 billion people, 32% of the world population, were offline in 2024; 1.8 billion of them live in rural areas.

limiters.evidence: In 2025, 119 countries (60%) reported having a multi-hazard early warning system, only 43% of small island developing states did, and fewer than a third of countries reported risk-knowledge capabilities.

ref.title: WMO, Early warning systems reach new heights, but critical gaps jeopardize global progress, 2025
ref.finding: 119 countries, or 60% of all countries, report a multi-hazard early warning system; 43% of small island developing states do; fewer than a third of countries report risk-knowledge capabilities; funding is not always sustained for operation and maintenance.

limiters.evidence: Across 5,680 gauges, the AI model matched the benchmark's same-day reliability at up to five days of lead time, giving days rather than weeks of warning.

ref.title: Nearing et al., Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Nature, PMC copy), 2024
ref.finding: Forecasts cover 0 to 7 days; reliability similar to or better than same-day benchmark nowcasts at up to five days lead time; trained and tested across 5,680 streamflow gauges.

enablers.action: Link forecasts to national warning and response systems
enablers.evidence: The UN Early Warnings for All initiative aims to protect everyone on Earth with early warning systems by the end of 2027.

ref.title: WMO, Early Warnings for All
ref.finding: UN initiative to protect everyone from hazardous weather, water or climate events through early warning systems by the end of 2027.

enablers.action: Publish free forecasts for ungauged basins
enablers.evidence: Flood Hub publishes public river flood forecasts, labelled approximate and for informational purposes only, and tells users to check official sources.

ref.title: Google, Flood Hub
ref.finding: Public flood forecast map; flood conditions are approximate and for informational purposes only; check official sources.

precedents.parallel: An early-warning system built for a poor, exposed coastline paired warnings with shelters, evacuation plans and volunteers spreading alerts, so that forecasts reached people.
precedents.outcome: Cyclone deaths in Bangladesh fell from more than 500,000 in 1970 and almost 140,000 in 1991 to 4,234 in 2007, a 100-fold drop the authors credit to early warning, shelters, evacuation plans, embankments, reforestation and awareness; illiteracy and poor communication still hampered evacuation, so better forecasts were only one part of this.

ref.title: Haque et al., Reduced death rates from cyclones in Bangladesh: what more needs to be done? (Bulletin of the World Health Organization), 2012
ref.finding: Cyclone mortality fell more than 100-fold, from 500,000 deaths in 1970 to 4,234 in 2007, with almost 140,000 deaths in 1991; credited to early warning systems, shelters, evacuation plans, embankments, reforestation and awareness; evacuation remains a challenge due to illiteracy, lack of awareness and poor communication; preparedness improved after the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society's Cyclone Preparedness Programme.

precedents.parallel: Famine early-warning systems flagged the crisis in time, but warnings did not turn into action, the gap the AI flood summary flags.
precedents.outcome: Warnings clearly identified famine risk in South Central Somalia, yet timely action was not taken and the famine is thought to have killed 258,000 people; the authors blame the war and the tactics of the warring parties, along with problems of access, funding and the aid coordination system, not the warnings.

ref.title: Seal and Bailey, The 2011 Famine in Somalia: lessons learnt from a failed response? (Conflict and Health), 2013
ref.finding: Famine early warning systems clearly identified the risk of famine in 2010-2011 but timely action was not taken; the famine is thought to have cost 258,000 lives; the main factor turning drought into famine was the war and the tactics of the belligerents; the coordination and funding system contributed to the failed response.

nodes.label: Faces scraped into police search engines
nodes.summary: Clearview AI scrapes face photos from the internet into an identity-matching search it sells to customers including law enforcement[1]. In 2024 the Dutch regulator fined it 30.5 million euros over a database of about 30 billion images, but Clearview calls the decision unenforceable[1]. In 2025 noyb said it ignores about 100 million euros in fines from four EU regulators[2].

refs.title: TechCrunch, Clearview AI hit with its largest GDPR fine yet as Dutch regulator considers holding execs personally liable, 2024
refs.finding: The Dutch data protection authority fined Clearview 30.5 million euros, plus up to 5.1 million euros for continued non-compliance, over a database of 30 billion scraped images; Clearview said it has no place of business in the Netherlands or the EU and the decision is unenforceable.

refs.title: noyb, Criminal complaint against facial recognition company Clearview AI, 2025
refs.finding: French, Greek, Italian and Dutch authorities fined Clearview about 100 million euros combined, which noyb says the company ignores given the lack of enforcement; noyb filed a criminal complaint against Clearview and its managers with Austrian prosecutors on 28 October 2025.

nodes.control_note: Scraping faces into a search engine is not needed for any listed benefit, and law can ban it. Enforcement against firms based abroad is the weak point.

actions.action: Ban untargeted scraping of facial images
actions.evidence: The EU ban applies from 2 February 2025; its effect on firms outside the EU is untested.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
ref.finding: Prohibits AI systems that build facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV.

actions.action: Enforce biometric privacy law through lawsuits
actions.evidence: Under Illinois BIPA, a 2022 settlement permanently barred Clearview from selling to most private businesses nationwide and to Illinois government and police for five years; it can still serve federal agencies and police outside Illinois.

ref.title: AP via Insurance Journal, Face-Scanner Clearview Agrees to Limits in Court Settlement, 2022
ref.finding: Clearview agreed to permanently stop selling access to its face database to private businesses or individuals around the US and to stop serving Illinois state government and local police for five years, while continuing to serve federal agencies and other law enforcement outside Illinois.

actions.action: Restrict police real-time biometric identification
actions.evidence: EU law has allowed it since 2 February 2025 only for listed serious cases with prior authorisation; it covers live identification, not later searches of scraped photos, and no data on its effect have been published.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
ref.finding: Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces is banned for law enforcement except for listed serious cases, each needing prior authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority, or within 24 hours in urgent cases.

precedents.event: FTC fines Facebook over user data
precedents.parallel: Facebook shared users' friends' data with third-party app developers even when those friends had chosen stricter privacy settings, a mass collection of personal data that a regulator then punished.
precedents.outcome: The FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty, almost 20 times the largest privacy or data security penalty previously imposed worldwide, together with new privacy restrictions on the company.

ref.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook (Federal Trade Commission)
ref.finding: The $5 billion penalty, for violating a 2012 order including by sharing friends' data with third-party app developers, is the largest ever imposed on any company for violating consumers' privacy.

nodes.label: AI-drafted police reports
nodes.summary: Police are trialling tools that turn body-camera audio into draft reports. In one randomized trial with 85 officers and 755 reports, Axon's Draft One did not significantly cut writing time[1][3], and Anchorage police dropped it because reviewing drafts ate the time saved[2]. In a 2026 preprint, 92 senior US police reviewers rated its reports significantly worse on accuracy[3].

refs.title: Adams et al., No man's hand: artificial intelligence does not improve police report writing speed (Journal of Experimental Criminology), 2024
refs.finding: In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial in the patrol division of a medium-sized police department (85 officers, 755 reports), AI assistance did not significantly affect report-writing time; a difference-in-differences analysis of 6,084 reports over a year confirmed the null result.

refs.title: Alaska Public Media, Anchorage police not moving forward with using AI to write reports, for now, 2024
refs.finding: After a free 90-day trial of Axon's Draft One, Anchorage police did not adopt it because the time officers spent reviewing the generated reports cut into the time saved writing them, and audio-only drafts left out details.

refs.title: ACLU, Studies Question Value of AI-Assisted Police Reports, 2026
refs.finding: Adams et al. (2024) found no time savings from Draft One; in a later preprint, 92 US sergeants and above rating 80 reports, 20 drafted with Draft One, did no better than a coin flip at spotting them and rated them significantly worse on accuracy.

nodes.control_note: Agencies can choose not to use AI drafting, or require disclosure, officer review and retained drafts. The harm comes with the same drafting tools sold to save clerical time, though trials so far found no time saved.

actions.action: Label AI-drafted reports and require officer certification
actions.evidence: Utah enacted this in 2025; no published data yet on whether it reduces errors in reports.

ref.title: Utah S.B. 180 (2025), Law Enforcement Usage of Artificial Intelligence, enrolled text
ref.finding: Reports made wholly or partly with generative AI must carry a disclaimer and the author's certification that they reviewed it for accuracy.

actions.action: Keep the first AI draft and an audit trail
actions.evidence: California's law took effect on 1 January 2026, so the original draft can be compared with the final report; its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: KQED, New State Law Requires Additional Safeguards When Police Use Generative AI, 2025
ref.finding: California's SB 524, signed on 10 October 2025 and in effect from 1 January 2026, requires a disclosure at the bottom of each page of an AI-assisted report and an audit trail that preserves the original draft and identifies the source body-camera footage or audio.

precedents.event: Electronic health records and documentation time
precedents.parallel: Electronic health records digitised clinical documentation, yet screen and desk work came to take more of the clinic day than patients did; AI report tools likewise shift officers' time from writing to reviewing.
precedents.outcome: Observed physicians spent 27.0 percent of the office day with patients and 49.2 percent on EHR and desk work, nearly two hours of such work per hour of face time plus 1 to 2 hours each night; the study observed 57 US doctors in self-selected practices in four states.

ref.title: Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties (Sinsky et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2016)
ref.finding: For every hour of direct clinical face time, physicians spent nearly 2 additional hours on EHR and desk work in the clinic day, plus 1 to 2 hours after hours.

precedents.parallel: Agencies relied on a machine whose output carried an air of objectivity, the concern critics raise about AI wording in police reports.
precedents.outcome: The National Academies found polygraph accuracy too low to justify federal employee screening: among 10,000 employees with 10 spies, a setting that catches 8 would wrongly fail about 1,600 people; the polygraph records physiology, whereas AI drafts shape narrative wording.

ref.title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (National Academies, statement by committee chair Stephen Fienberg)
ref.finding: Polygraph accuracy is insufficient to justify reliance on it for employee screening, and overconfidence in its accuracy can create a false sense of security.

nodes.label: Algorithms screen child-neglect reports
nodes.summary: In Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, a risk score helps decide which neglect calls get investigated. A Carnegie Mellon analysis found that from August 2016 to May 2018 it flagged 32.5% of Black children reported for mandatory investigation, against 20.8% of white children, and caseworkers reduced the gap[1]. A county-commissioned Stanford evaluation found Black-white disparities in case openings narrowed afterwards[2].

refs.title: AP via KTVZ, An algorithm that screens for child neglect raises concerns, 2022
refs.finding: Carnegie Mellon researchers found that from August 2016 to May 2018 the Allegheny tool's scores flagged 32.5% of Black children reported for neglect for a mandatory investigation, against 20.8% of white children; social workers disagreed with the score about a third of the time and reduced the disparity.

refs.title: Allegheny County DHS, Impact Evaluation Summary of the Allegheny Family Screening Tool, April 2019
refs.finding: A Stanford quasi-experimental evaluation of about 31,000 children referred before and 34,000 after the tool found it did not raise the screen-in rate, increased screening-in of children later found to need intervention, and reduced Black-white disparities in case-opening rates.

refs.title: AP via PBS NewsHour, Oregon dropping AI tool used to help decide child abuse cases, 2022
refs.finding: Oregon told staff its hotline workers would stop using its Safety at Screening Tool, inspired by the Allegheny tool, at the end of June 2022, to reduce disparities in which families are investigated, replacing it with a Structured Decision Making model.

nodes.control_note: Agencies will keep screening large volumes of reports with some decision aid, so errors and bias will occur to some degree. Evaluation and legal duties can reduce how often and how badly families are wrongly targeted.

actions.action: Commission independent impact evaluations before scaling
actions.evidence: A Stanford quasi-experimental evaluation of about 31,000 pre and 34,000 post children found more children in need were screened in without a rise in investigations; it was not a randomised trial and the county commissioned it.

ref.title: Allegheny County DHS, Impact Evaluation Summary of the Allegheny Family Screening Tool, April 2019
ref.finding: The tool did not increase the screen-in rate, increased identification of children needing intervention, and reduced Black-white disparities in case-opening rates.

actions.action: Require bias checks for public-benefit decision tools
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act lists systems that public authorities use to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance as high-risk, which requires providers to examine their data for possible biases; the AI Omnibus amendment, in force since 27 July 2026, moved these duties to 2 December 2027; whether child-welfare screening falls under it depends on use, and no effect data exist yet.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Annex III: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Annex III point 5(a) classes AI used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate people's eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, as high-risk.

precedents.parallel: A statistical risk score used to guide decisions about people produced unequal error rates by race, as child-neglect screening tools have.
precedents.outcome: In Broward County, Florida, 44.9 percent of Black defendants who did not reoffend had been labelled higher risk, against 23.5 percent of white defendants; this is a journalistic analysis of over 7,000 people in criminal justice, not child welfare, and the tool's maker disputes it.

ref.title: Machine Bias (ProPublica)
ref.finding: Among defendants who did not reoffend, 44.9 percent of Black and 23.5 percent of white defendants were labelled higher risk; only 20 percent predicted to commit violent crimes did so.

nodes.label: Algorithmic price collusion
nodes.summary: In one simulation study, pricing algorithms learned to keep prices high and punish price cuts without communicating[1], though a later study argues they learn too slowly to be a practical cartel risk alone[2]. In US rental housing, one working paper estimates that coordination among landlords using the same pricing software raised markups by about $25 a unit a month[3].

refs.title: Calvano, Calzolari, Denicolò and Pastorello, Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Pricing, and Collusion, American Economic Review, 2020
refs.finding: In simulated markets, Q-learning pricing algorithms consistently learned to charge supracompetitive prices without communicating, sustained by punishing deviations for a limited time before returning to cooperation.

refs.title: den Boer, Meylahn and Schinkel, Artificial Collusion: Examining Supracompetitive Pricing by Q-Learning Algorithms, Management Science, 2026
refs.finding: Q-learning can learn collusive equilibria only on timescales irrelevant to the firm's objective, and the synchronization it needs (same algorithm, start time and settings) suggests an explicit cartel agreement; the authors see little current reason for suspicion beyond software that implements a cartel.

refs.title: Calder-Wang and Kim, Algorithmic Pricing in Multifamily Rentals: Efficiency Gains or Price Coordination?, Wharton working paper, 2025
refs.finding: Using US building-level rent data from 2005 to 2019, adopters cut rents faster in downturns, but markets with more algorithmic pricing had higher rents and lower occupancy in recoveries; coordination among users of the same software raised markups by an estimated $25 per unit per month across about 4.2 million units.

refs.title: US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, United States et al. v. RealPage, Inc. et al., No. 1:24-cv-710, Memorandum Opinion and Order, 30 September 2026
refs.finding: The amended complaint alleges landlords shared confidential data through RealPage, whose AIRM and YieldStar price roughly 3 million units; the court entered a Final Judgment resolving the United States' claims against RealPage on 19 May 2026, and the Plaintiff States' claims against RealPage continue.

nodes.control_note: Courts and lawmakers can bar pricing software from pooling rivals' private data while letting firms price from their own data, as the RealPage judgment and California's 2025 law do; collusion that algorithms might learn on their own, without any agreement, is harder to reach under antitrust law.

actions.action: Bar pricing software from pooling rivals' private data
actions.evidence: The court entered the RealPage settlement on 19 May 2026; it still lets RealPage collect landlord data and train on data at least 12 months old, expires after seven years, and its effect on rents is unmeasured.

ref.title: US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, United States et al. v. RealPage, Inc. et al., No. 1:24-cv-710, Memorandum Opinion and Order, 30 September 2026
ref.finding: The Final Judgment entered on 19 May 2026 restricts RealPage's revenue management products, requires retraining on compliant data, still permits data collection and training on data at least twelve months old, and expires seven years after entry.

actions.action: Make shared pricing algorithms an antitrust violation
actions.evidence: California's law took effect in 2026; it still needs a conspiracy or coercion, so its added reach may be limited.

ref.title: Sheppard Mullin, California Passes Broad Limits On 'Common Pricing Algorithms', 2025
ref.finding: AB 325, signed on 6 October 2025 and taking effect in 2026, bars using or distributing a common pricing algorithm in a conspiracy or to coerce price adoption; because a violation requires a conspiracy or price coercion, it may not extend the violations the Cartwright Act already covers.

precedents.parallel: Airlines used a shared computerised fare system to signal and coordinate price rises without meeting, the template for shared rent-setting software.
precedents.outcome: The Justice Department identified over 50 price-fixing agreements covering hundreds of routes and estimated consumer harm of up to $1.9 billion; the 1994 settlement removed the system's signalling features, and the signalling was done by people, not learning algorithms.

ref.title: US Department of Justice, Justice Department Settles Airlines Price Fixing Suit, May Save Consumers Hundreds of Millions of Dollars, 1994
ref.finding: American, Delta, Northwest, Continental, TWA and Alaska settled (United and USAir had settled in 1992) over using ATP's fare system to float fare increases and agree on fares; a government economist estimated $238 million in extra costs across 300 markets from April 1988 to December 1992, or $1.9 billion if fares rose 5 percent.

precedents.event: Algorithmic pricing in German petrol stations
precedents.parallel: German petrol stations adopted pricing software once it became widely available in 2017, a real-world test of whether algorithms soften competition.
precedents.outcome: Adoption raised margins only in non-monopoly markets, by about 9 percent, and in duopolies by 28 percent when both stations adopted; the study infers adoption from price patterns rather than observing it.

ref.title: Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, Algorithmic Pricing and Competition: Empirical Evidence from the German Retail Gasoline Market, CESifo Working Paper No. 8521, 2020 (later published in the Journal of Political Economy, 2024)
ref.finding: Adoption raised margins by 9 percent, but only in non-monopoly markets; in duopolies, market margins did not change when one station adopted and rose 28 percent when both did.

nodes.label: AI hiring discrimination
nodes.summary: Language models can treat otherwise similar CVs differently by name or disability. In one study, embedding models favoured White-associated names in 85% of bias tests[1], and in another, of about 361,000 US resumes scored by five models, Black men scored lower than white men[2]. These are simulated screenings, not observed employer decisions.

refs.title: Wilson and Caliskan, Gender, Race, and Intersectional Bias in Resume Screening via Language Model Retrieval, AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 2024
refs.finding: Using more than three million comparisons between over 500 resumes and 500 job descriptions in nine occupations, embedding models favoured White-associated names in 85.1% of bias tests and Black-associated names in only 8.6%; a 2026 erratum inverted the gender-only results but left the race and intersectional results unchanged and replicated.

refs.title: An, Huang, Lin and Tai, Measuring gender and racial biases in large language models: Intersectional evidence from automated resume evaluation, PNAS Nexus, 2025
refs.finding: Five models scored about 361,000 fictitious resumes for 20 entry-level jobs; most favoured female candidates and penalized Black male candidates relative to white men, shifting hiring probabilities by about 1 to 3 percentage points at given score cutoffs.

refs.title: UW News, ChatGPT is biased against resumes with credentials that imply a disability, but it can improve, 2024
refs.finding: Across 60 trials ranking six disability-enhanced CVs against an otherwise identical control CV, GPT-4 ranked the enhanced CV first only about one quarter of the time; with written anti-ableism instructions it ranked them higher 37 of 60 times.

nodes.control_note: Bias in screening models comes from their training data and varies by model and job, so audits cannot remove it entirely. Audits and explanation rights aim to catch it and give rejected candidates a way to challenge it, though compliance with New York City's audit law has been low.

actions.action: Require annual public bias audits of hiring tools
actions.evidence: Evidence of effect is weak: of 391 NYC employers checked, only 18 posted audit reports and 13 posted notices.

ref.title: Wright et al., Null Compliance: NYC Local Law 144 and the Challenges of Algorithm Accountability, ACM FAccT 2024
ref.finding: Of 391 employers checked by 155 student investigators, 18 posted bias audit reports and 13 posted transparency notices; employers' discretion over whether the law applies makes missing postings hard to read as non-compliance.

actions.action: Classify hiring AI as high-risk with oversight duties
actions.evidence: The AI Act lists CV-sorting and other employment AI as high-risk; after the AI Omnibus amendment, in force since 27 July 2026, these duties apply from 2 December 2027, so there is no outcome data yet.

ref.title: European Commission, AI Act (Shaping Europe's digital future), 2026
ref.finding: The AI Act lists AI tools for employment, management of workers and access to self-employment, such as CV-sorting software for recruitment, among high-risk uses; the AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026, and rules for systems in high-risk areas including employment apply from 2 December 2027.

actions.action: Give rejected people a right to an explanation
actions.evidence: Covers decisions based on Annex III high-risk systems such as recruitment tools; how often it is used and whether it changes outcomes is unknown.

ref.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Article 86: Right to Explanation of Individual Decision-Making
ref.finding: People affected by a decision based on an Annex III high-risk AI system that significantly affects them can obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the system's role and the main elements of the decision.

precedents.event: Emily and Greg CV audit study
precedents.parallel: Researchers sent identical CVs with names signalling race to real employers, the same audit design now used on language-model screeners.
precedents.outcome: White-sounding names got 50 percent more callbacks than African American-sounding names, and better CVs helped white names far more; unlike the LLM audits, this measured real employer responses.

ref.title: Bertrand and Mullainathan, Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination, NBER Working Paper 9873, 2003
ref.finding: Fictitious resumes sent to help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago got 50 percent more callbacks with White names; a better resume raised callbacks 30 percent for White names but far less for African American names, and discrimination was similar across occupations, industries and federal contractors.

nodes.label: AI credit scoring widens financial inclusion
nodes.summary: Models built on alternative data can score people with no credit file: in one study of about 270,000 purchases at a German online furniture retailer, ten simple digital-footprint variables predicted default about as well as a credit bureau score, and as well for customers with no score as for those with one[1]. The same authors note that regulators will watch whether footprints proxy for traits lenders may not legally use[1], and a study of US mortgage data found that machine-learning credit models benefit Black and Hispanic borrowers less than others and widen rate gaps[2].

refs.title: Berg, Burg, Gombović and Puri, On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring using Digital Footprints, NBER Working Paper 24551, 2018 (Review of Financial Studies, 2020)
refs.finding: In 270,399 purchases at a German e-commerce furniture company from October 2015 to December 2016, ten digital-footprint variables predicted default with an AUC of 69.6% against 68.3% for the credit bureau score, with similar accuracy for customers who had no bureau score.

refs.title: Fuster, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Ramadorai and Walther, Predictably Unequal? The Effects of Machine Learning on Credit Markets, Journal of Finance, 2022
refs.finding: Using US mortgage data, Black and Hispanic borrowers are disproportionately less likely to gain from machine-learning default models, and in an equilibrium model machine learning increases rate disparity between and within groups.

limiters.evidence: About 21% of adults worldwide still have no account, and footprint scoring reaches only people with a phone or online history; 84% of adults in low- and middle-income countries own a mobile phone.

ref.title: World Bank, The Global Findex Database 2025
ref.finding: 79% of adults globally have an account, and 84% of adults in low- and middle-income countries own a mobile phone.

limiters.evidence: On 12 May 2025 the CFPB withdrew its circulars on credit denial notices, including the one on decisions made with complex algorithms, so lenders lose the US regulator's guidance on explaining model-driven denials.

ref.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Withdrawn Guidance
ref.finding: Circular 2022-03 on adverse action notices for credit decisions based on complex algorithms and Circular 2023-03 on proper use of sample forms are listed as withdrawn on 12 May 2025.

limiters.evidence: The EU AI Act lists credit scoring of natural persons as high-risk, adding obligations.

ref.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Point 5(b) lists AI systems used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, except for detecting financial fraud, as high-risk.

enablers.action: Combine digital footprints with bureau data
enablers.evidence: Digital-footprint data predicted default about as well as bureau scores and complemented them in a study of a German online furniture retailer.

ref.title: Berg, Burg, Gombović and Puri, On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints, Review of Financial Studies, 2020
ref.finding: Simple digital-footprint variables match the information content of credit bureau scores, complement rather than substitute for bureau data, and affect access to credit and reduce default rates.

enablers.action: Require specific reasons for every credit denial
enablers.evidence: Regulation B still requires the principal reasons for any denial, and says a failure to reach a qualifying score is not enough, though the CFPB withdrew its AI-specific guidance in 2025.

ref.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9 Notifications
ref.finding: The statement of reasons for adverse action must be specific and indicate the principal reasons; saying the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score on the creditor's scoring system is insufficient.

precedents.parallel: Fast, cheap statistical scoring of borrowers was expected to widen access to credit, as alternative-data AI scoring is now.
precedents.outcome: The Federal Reserve concluded scoring likely contributed to greater availability and affordability of credit and predicted default for all major demographic groups, though average scores were lower for Black and Hispanic consumers; it had only limited direct information on scoring's own contribution.

ref.title: Report to the Congress on Credit Scoring and Its Effects on the Availability and Affordability of Credit, executive summary (Federal Reserve Board, 2007)
ref.finding: Credit scoring likely contributed to improved availability and affordability of credit; credit history scores predict credit risk for the population as a whole and for all major demographic groups.

precedents.parallel: A loan product delivered fully on mobile phones reached Kenyan households outside formal lending, an earlier version of the fintech inclusion story.
precedents.outcome: 34 percent of eligible people took the loans, which did not substitute for other credit, and households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses after shocks; the authors say digital loans are not a panacea for wider credit market failures.

ref.title: Fintech and Household Resilience to Shocks: Evidence from Digital Loans in Kenya (Bharadwaj, Jack and Suri, NBER w25604)
ref.finding: Take-up was 34 percent of those eligible; the loans did not substitute for other credit, and households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses due to negative shocks.

nodes.label: Opaque credit models entrench exclusion
nodes.summary: Credit models built on more data and more flexible methods can use proxies for race or poverty that applicants cannot see. A race-blind US tax-audit selection system audited Black taxpayers at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of non-Black taxpayers, showing how such proxies arise[1]. In one study of US mortgage data, machine learning default models benefited Black and Hispanic borrowers less than other groups and, in the authors' market model, widened rate gaps between and within groups[2]. Against this, a study of US mortgages found algorithmic FinTech lenders charged Latinx and African-American borrowers extra interest, but 40% less than face-to-face lenders, and did not discriminate in loan approval[3].

refs.title: Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities in Tax Audits (Elzayn, Smith, Hertz, Ramesh, Fisher, Ho and Goldin, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research working paper, January 2023)
refs.finding: Despite race-blind audit selection, Black taxpayers were audited at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of non-Black taxpayers, driven mainly by audits of Earned Income Tax Credit claims.

refs.title: Predictably Unequal? The Effects of Machine Learning on Credit Markets (Fuster, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Ramadorai and Walther, Journal of Finance 77(1), 2022)
refs.finding: Using US mortgage data, Black and Hispanic borrowers were less likely to benefit from machine learning default models than from traditional ones; in an equilibrium model, machine learning increased rate disparities between and within groups, mainly because of its greater flexibility.

refs.title: Consumer-Lending Discrimination in the FinTech Era (Bartlett, Morse, Stanton and Wallace, NBER Working Paper 25943, 2019; Journal of Financial Economics 2021)
refs.finding: Lenders charged Latinx and African-American borrowers 7.9 and 3.6 basis points more for purchase and refinance mortgages, about $765 million a year; FinTech algorithms also discriminated, but 40% less than face-to-face lenders, and did not discriminate in loan approval.

nodes.control_note: Lenders will keep using complex models, so some unfair exclusion is likely. Explanation duties and high-risk rules aim to reduce it and let applicants correct errors, but no study has measured their effect.

actions.action: Require specific reasons for algorithmic credit denials
actions.evidence: US Regulation B requires specific principal reasons for any adverse credit action and rules out citing a failed score; no study measures the rule's effect on exclusion.

ref.title: Regulation B (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), 12 CFR 1002.9 Notifications (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau)
ref.finding: A statement of reasons for adverse action must be specific and indicate the principal reasons; saying the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score on the creditor's scoring system is insufficient.

actions.action: Treat credit scoring AI as high-risk
actions.evidence: The AI Act is in force, but after the AI Omnibus amendment, in force since 27 July 2026, its high-risk duties for areas including credit scoring apply only from 2 December 2027; untested so far.

ref.title: European Commission, AI Act (Shaping Europe's digital future), 2026
ref.finding: The AI Act lists credit scoring that denies citizens the opportunity to obtain a loan among high-risk uses in access to essential services; the AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026, and rules for systems in the Annex III high-risk areas apply from 2 December 2027.

precedents.parallel: Government risk maps graded neighbourhoods partly by race, so a lending tool used geography as a proxy that cut off credit, the risk with opaque alternative-data models.
precedents.outcome: The maps led to lower home ownership, house values and rents and more segregation in graded areas for decades, through reduced credit access and disinvestment; the maps were explicit about race, while AI proxies are usually hidden.

ref.title: The Effects of the 1930s HOLC "Redlining" Maps (Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Working Paper 2017-12, revised August 2020)
ref.finding: The maps led to reduced home ownership rates, house values and rents and increased racial segregation in later decades through reduced credit access and disinvestment.

precedents.event: Fed review of credit score proxies
precedents.parallel: Regulators tested whether conventional credit scores acted as proxies for race, the same question asked of alternative-data models.
precedents.outcome: Black and Hispanic borrowers had lower average scores, but re-estimating the model race-neutrally had little effect on scores; length of credit history partly proxied for age, and recent immigrants scored somewhat lower than their repayment implied. This cuts against assuming proxies are always present.

ref.title: Report to the Congress on Credit Scoring and Its Effects on the Availability and Affordability of Credit, executive summary (Federal Reserve Board, August 2007)
ref.finding: Credit characteristics did not serve as proxies for race, ethnicity or sex, and a race-neutral re-estimation had little effect on scores; length of credit history served in part as a proxy for age, and recent immigrants had somewhat lower scores than their performance implied.

nodes.label: Low-paid data labelling in the Global South
nodes.summary: AI developers rely on outsourced workers to label training data[1]. One TIME investigation found Kenyan Sama contractors labelling text about sexual abuse, hate speech and violence for OpenAI took home about $1.32 to $2 an hour, and all four workers interviewed described being mentally scarred[1]. Sama disputed the pay, saying workers could earn $1.46 to $3.74 an hour after tax[1].

refs.title: OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour to Make ChatGPT Less Toxic (Billy Perrigo, TIME, January 2023)
refs.finding: Sama contractors in Kenya labelling text describing sexual abuse, hate speech and violence for OpenAI took home about $1.32 to $2 per hour depending on seniority and performance; Sama said workers could earn $1.46 to $3.74 after tax. All four employees interviewed described being mentally scarred by the work.

nodes.control_note: Labelling and feedback work is part of how current models are trained, so the work will exist. Pay, safety and status rules can reduce the harm but not remove the work.

actions.action: Require human review of algorithmic worker management
actions.evidence: The EU Platform Work Directive sets a presumption of employment and human oversight of automated decisions, but it covers only platform work in the EU, member states have until 2 December 2026 to transpose it, and its effect is not yet measured.

ref.title: Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of 23 October 2024 on improving working conditions in platform work
ref.finding: Article 5 sets a legal presumption of employment and Article 10 requires human oversight of automated monitoring and decision-making systems.

actions.action: Ratify ILO platform work convention
actions.evidence: Convention No. 193 was adopted in June 2026 and covers online platform work, including pay and access to review of automated decisions, but it binds only states that ratify it.

ref.title: How will the new Convention No.193 promote decent work in the platform economy? (International Labour Organization, June 2026)
ref.finding: The convention covers location-based and online platform work, including remuneration, sets principles for transparent use of automated decision systems with access to review, and binds only member states that ratify it.

precedents.parallel: Crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk did paid microtasks, including image categorisation, the kind of labelling work machine learning relies on.
precedents.outcome: Logs from 2,676 workers across 3.8 million tasks from 2014 to 2017 showed median earnings of about $2 an hour, with only 4 percent above $7.25; the sample was workers who opted into a browser plugin, and the logs held no demographics.

ref.title: A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk (Hara et al., CHI 2018)
ref.finding: Median hourly wage was about $2; only 4 percent earned more than $7.25 per hour.

precedents.parallel: Outsourced content moderators reviewed graphic material for a platform at scale, the same traumatic work some AI data labellers do.
precedents.outcome: Facebook agreed to pay $52 million to more than 11,000 current and former moderators, at least $1,000 each and up to $50,000; these were US contractor workers, so it says little about pay and redress in poorer countries.

ref.title: Facebook to pay $52 million to content moderators suffering from PTSD (Zack Whittaker, TechCrunch, May 2020)
ref.finding: $52 million settlement covering more than 11,000 moderators in Arizona, California, Florida and Texas; each gets at least $1,000 and up to $50,000.

nodes.label: Developing countries left behind by AI
nodes.summary: AI could worsen inequality between nations, since many poorer countries lack the infrastructure and skilled workforces to capture the gains[1]. About 60% of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI, against 26% in low-income countries[1]. A 2026 UN report found high-income countries held 77% of global co-location data centre capacity in June 2025, and low-income countries less than 0.1%[2].

refs.title: AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let's Make Sure It Benefits Humanity. (Kristalina Georgieva, IMF Blog, January 2024)
refs.finding: About 60% of jobs in advanced economies may be impacted by AI, against 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries; many of these countries lack the infrastructure or skilled workforces to harness AI, which could worsen inequality among nations.

refs.title: Secretary-General Calls for Global Fund to Address AI Capacity-Building Gaps in Developing Countries (UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, September 2026)
refs.finding: Report A/80/817 finds high-income countries held 77% of global co-location data centre capacity in June 2025 and low-income countries less than 0.1%; about half of member states had a national AI strategy in 2025, but fewer than 20% of least developed countries did.

nodes.control_note: Compute, talent and capital are concentrated in a few countries, and that will not change quickly. Shared infrastructure and capacity building can narrow the gap.

actions.action: Fund shared AI compute for developing countries
actions.evidence: UNCTAD reports that 100 firms account for 40% of global corporate R&D and that 118 countries are absent from major AI governance talks; the shared facility is a proposal with no track record.

ref.title: AI's $4.8 trillion future: UN Trade and Development alerts on divides, urges action (UNCTAD press release on the Technology and Innovation Report 2025, April 2025)
ref.finding: UNCTAD says a global shared facility could give equitable access to AI infrastructure and that open data and open source can foster inclusive AI innovation; 100 firms account for 40% of global corporate R&D and 118 countries are absent from major AI governance discussions.

actions.action: Fund AI capacity building in developing countries
actions.evidence: A September 2026 UN Secretary-General report under General Assembly resolution 78/311 recommends a Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building with initial commitments of about $3 billion over two to four years; it is a recommendation, and no capacity programme's effect has been measured.

ref.title: Secretary-General Calls for Global Fund to Address AI Capacity-Building Gaps in Developing Countries (UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, September 2026)
ref.finding: Report A/80/817, submitted under resolution 78/311, asks the General Assembly to endorse a Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building, with indicative initial commitments of about $3 billion over two to four years.

precedents.parallel: Poor countries adopted each new technology sooner over time but used it far less intensively, the pattern feared for AI.
precedents.outcome: Adoption lags converged between rich and poor countries while long-run penetration diverged, and the authors' model attributes 80 percent of the income divergence since 1820 to these diffusion patterns.

ref.title: If Technology Has Arrived Everywhere, Why Has Income Diverged? (Comin and Mestieri, NBER Working Paper 19010, 2013; American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 2018)
ref.finding: Adoption lags have converged while penetration rates have diverged; diffusion patterns account for 80 percent of the Great Income Divergence since 1820.

nodes.label: AI investment bubble and crash risk
nodes.summary: AI stock valuations could fall sharply. In October 2025 the Bank of England said AI-focused tech valuations appeared stretched and correction risk had increased[1]. After AI equity valuations fell sharply in July 2026, it said the risk of a sharper correction persists[3], but judged an equity shock alone unlikely to directly threaten UK financial stability[4].

refs.title: Financial Policy Committee Record, October 2025 (Bank of England, 2025)
refs.finding: The FPC said equity market valuations appear stretched, particularly for technology companies focused on AI, and that the risk of a sharp market correction has increased.

refs.title: Global Financial Stability Report, October 2025: Shifting Ground beneath the Calm (IMF, 2025)
refs.finding: Valuation models show risk asset prices well above fundamentals, raising the risk of sharp corrections.

refs.title: Financial Policy Committee Record, September 2026 (Bank of England, 2026)
refs.finding: Equity valuations for AI companies fell sharply in July 2026; market functioning remained orderly, with no spillovers to core markets, and the risk of a sharper correction persists, notably if there is a more significant shock to earnings expectations.

refs.title: Financial Stability Report, July 2026 (Bank of England, 2026)
refs.finding: Bank staff assessed a hypothetical AI-related equity correction with a 45% fall in the US equity market over six quarters and a 2.2 percentage point fall in UK GDP; its macroeconomic impacts are encompassed by the 2025 Bank Capital Stress Test and 2024 Desk-Based Stress Test scenarios, to which UK banks were resilient, and an equity shock in isolation would be unlikely to present a direct risk to UK financial stability.

nodes.control_note: AI-related valuations rest on forecasts of strong long-term earnings growth that the Bank of England calls highly uncertain, so a repricing cannot be ruled out. Regulators can limit how far a crash spreads, not whether valuations fall.

actions.action: Monitor and warn on stretched AI valuations
actions.evidence: The Bank of England flagged stretched AI valuations in October 2025; AI equity valuations still fell sharply in July 2026, though with no spillovers to core markets.

ref.title: Financial Policy Committee Record, September 2026 (Bank of England, 2026)
ref.finding: Equity valuations for AI companies fell sharply in July 2026, there were no spillovers to core markets, and the risk of a sharper correction persists.

actions.action: Test bank resilience to an AI equity correction
actions.evidence: Bank of England staff assessed a hypothetical AI-related correction with a 45 percent fall in US equities over six quarters; its macroeconomic effects fall within past stress test scenarios that UK banks withstood, though concentrated, leveraged positions could amplify a fall.

ref.title: Financial Stability Report, July 2026 (Bank of England, 2026)
ref.finding: Bank staff assessed a hypothetical AI-related equity correction with a 45% fall in the US equity market over six quarters and a 2.2 percentage point fall in UK GDP; its macroeconomic impacts are encompassed by the 2025 Bank Capital Stress Test and 2024 Desk-Based Stress Test scenarios, to which UK banks were resilient, and an equity shock in isolation would be unlikely to present a direct risk to UK financial stability.

precedents.parallel: Investors bid up shares in a transformative technology on expectations of rising payouts and projected thousands of new lines, as some fear with AI capital spending.
precedents.outcome: Railway share prices almost doubled between January 1843 and August 1845, then fell 57.5 percent from peak to trough by April 1850; many lines were abandoned, but others opened and trebled the network to 6,123 miles, while industry dividends fell from 7.0 percent of par in 1847 to 2.4 percent by 1852.

ref.title: Government Policy during the British Railway Mania and the 1847 Commercial Crisis (Gareth Campbell, Queen's University Belfast; in British Financial Crises since 1825, Oxford University Press, 2014)
ref.finding: Railway share prices almost doubled between January 1843 and August 1845, then fell 57.5 per cent from peak to trough by April 1850; many lines were abandoned or suspended, others opened and trebled the network to 6,123 miles by 1850, and the industry dividend/par ratio fell from 7.0 per cent in 1847 to 2.4 per cent by 1852, leaving a legacy of low returns on capital.

nodes.label: AI catches fraud against the public purse
nodes.summary: Machine learning is helping the US Treasury catch fraud. It reported preventing and recovering more than $4 billion in fraud and improper payments in fiscal year 2024, including $1 billion in check fraud recovered with machine-learning AI[1]. The figures are self-reported, and small against GAO's estimate that the federal government loses $233 billion to $521 billion a year to fraud[3].

refs.title: Treasury Announces Enhanced Fraud Detection Processes, Including Machine Learning AI, Prevented and Recovered Over $4 Billion in Fiscal Year 2024 (US Treasury, 2024)
refs.finding: Treasury said it prevented and recovered over $4 billion in fraud and improper payments in FY2024, up from $652.7 million in FY2023; expediting the identification of Treasury check fraud with machine learning AI resulted in $1 billion in recovery.

refs.title: Statement of Renata Miskell, US Department of the Treasury, before the House Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Government Operations (13 January 2026)
refs.finding: Treasury tested and implemented AI techniques like machine learning to mitigate check fraud in near real time, and prevented and recovered over $1.9 billion in check fraud in fiscal years 2024 and 2025 combined; in fiscal year 2024 only four percent of federal programs had completed the legal requirements to access all the databases in Do Not Pay.

refs.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion Annually to Fraud, Based on Various Risk Environments (GAO-24-105833, 2024)
refs.finding: GAO estimated direct annual fraud losses of $233 billion to $521 billion, based on fiscal years 2018-2022, or 3 to 7 percent of average federal obligations.

limiters.evidence: GAO estimates federal fraud losses of $233 billion to $521 billion a year, based on fiscal years 2018-2022, against $1 billion recovered with machine learning at Treasury in fiscal year 2024.

ref.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion Annually to Fraud, Based on Various Risk Environments (GAO-24-105833, 2024)
ref.finding: $233 billion to $521 billion lost to fraud per year, based on fiscal years 2018-2022.

limiters.evidence: Treasury's check fraud figures come from its own press release and congressional testimony, not an independent audit.

ref.title: Treasury Announces Enhanced Fraud Detection Processes, Including Machine Learning AI, Prevented and Recovered Over $4 Billion in Fiscal Year 2024 (US Treasury, 2024)
ref.finding: Expediting the identification of Treasury check fraud with machine learning AI resulted in $1 billion in recovery.

limiters.evidence: Treasury told Congress that in fiscal year 2024 only four percent of federal programs had completed the legal requirements to access all the databases in its Do Not Pay screening service.

ref.title: Statement of Renata Miskell, US Department of the Treasury, before the House Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Government Operations (13 January 2026)
ref.finding: Do Not Pay has been underutilized by agencies due to complex legal and administrative barriers; in fiscal year 2024 only four percent of federal programs completed the legal requirements to access all its databases.

enablers.action: Apply machine learning to payment screening
enablers.evidence: Treasury told Congress in January 2026 that machine learning applied to check fraud in near real time helped it prevent and recover over $1.9 billion across fiscal years 2024 and 2025.

ref.title: Statement of Renata Miskell, US Department of the Treasury, before the House Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Government Operations (13 January 2026)
ref.finding: Treasury tested and implemented AI techniques like machine learning to mitigate check fraud in near real time, and prevented and recovered over $1.9 billion in check fraud in fiscal years 2024 and 2025 combined.

enablers.action: Audit fraud estimates independently
enablers.evidence: GAO built a government-wide fraud estimate that gives a baseline for judging agency claims.

ref.title: Fraud Risk Management: 2018-2022 Data Show Federal Government Loses an Estimated $233 Billion to $521 Billion Annually to Fraud, Based on Various Risk Environments (GAO-24-105833, 2024)
ref.finding: Government-wide estimate of direct annual fraud losses of $233 billion to $521 billion.

precedents.parallel: The US Medicare programme ran predictive models over claims to stop improper payments, a pre-generative case of machine learning against fraud on the public purse.
precedents.outcome: The inspector general certified $133.2 million in actual and projected savings in the system's third year, a return of $2.84 per dollar spent, and $454 million in unadjusted savings the system identified, and found the agency's directives to contractors were not sufficient to ensure accurate savings estimates.

ref.title: The Fraud Prevention System Increased Recovery and Prevention of Improper Medicare Payments, but Updated Procedures Would Improve Reported Savings (HHS OIG, A-01-14-00503, 2015)
ref.finding: OIG certified $133.2 million in actual and projected savings for the third implementation year (a return of $2.84 per dollar spent) and the $454 million in unadjusted savings the FPS identified; the Department's written directives to contractors were not sufficient to ensure accurate savings estimates.

nodes.label: Automated welfare and tax enforcement harms citizens
nodes.summary: Australia's automated debt-raising scheme, Robodebt, unlawfully asserted debts against about 433,000 people[1], and the Dutch Tax Administration was fined for using applicants' nationality as a risk indicator for childcare benefit claims[2]. These scandals predate generative AI; agents could repeat them at greater scale.

refs.title: Prygodicz v Commonwealth of Australia (No 2) [2021] FCA 634, Federal Court of Australia
refs.finding: The Commonwealth raised debts of at least $1.763 billion against about 433,000 people by income averaging without a proper legal basis, recovered about $751 million from about 381,000 of them, and settled the class action for a further $112 million.

refs.title: Dutch Data Protection Authority, Tax Administration fined for discriminatory and unlawful data processing, 2021
refs.finding: The Tax Administration was fined 2.75 million euros because its use of applicants' (dual) nationality data as a risk indicator in assessing childcare benefit applications was unlawful and discriminatory.

nodes.control_note: Both scandals came from unlawful design choices: income averaging in Australia and nationality as a risk factor in the Netherlands. Legal limits, audits and human review can stop them while keeping automated processing.

actions.action: Classify public-benefit AI as high-risk
actions.evidence: The EU AI Act lists AI used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for public assistance benefits, or to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, as high-risk, with risk management and human oversight duties; the AI Omnibus amendment, in force since 27 July 2026, moved these duties to 2 December 2027, so effects are not yet measured.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Annex III: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Annex III point 5(a) lists AI systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, or to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, as high-risk.

actions.action: Fine unlawful profiling by public agencies
actions.evidence: The Dutch DPA fined the Tax Administration 2.75 million euros; the agency had already stopped using nationality in its risk classification model in October 2018, so the fine came after the harm.

ref.title: Dutch Data Protection Authority, Tax Administration fined for discriminatory and unlawful data processing, 2021
ref.finding: Using nationality data to assess applications, combat fraud and determine risk was found unlawful and discriminatory.

actions.action: Legislate a framework for automated government decisions
actions.evidence: The Royal Commission recommended a legal framework for automated decision-making and a body to monitor it; the government accepted both, but in September 2026 independent MP Kate Chaney, whose Automated Decision-Making (Safeguards and Transparency) Bill 2026 would implement them, said the government had not.

ref.title: No more Robodebt: new push for guardrails on government algorithms (The Medical Republic, 2026)
ref.finding: Kate Chaney's Automated Decision-Making (Safeguards and Transparency) Bill 2026 would implement Robodebt Royal Commission recommendations 17.1 and 17.2, a legal framework for automated decision-making and a body to monitor it, which the government accepted; Chaney said the government has not implemented them.

precedents.parallel: An automated system issued unemployment fraud findings with no human review, the kind of enforcement agents could repeat at scale.
precedents.outcome: Of 40,195 fraud findings the algorithm made alone, 85 percent were wrong; more than 34,000 people were wrongly accused, facing a 400 percent penalty on the claimed fraud, and the agency stopped purely automated fraud assessment in September 2015.

ref.title: Michigan's MiDAS Unemployment System: Algorithm Alchemy Created Lead, Not Gold (IEEE Spectrum, 2018)
ref.finding: From October 2013 to September 2015 MiDAS adjudicated 40,195 fraud cases by algorithm alone, 85 percent of them incorrectly; more than 34,000 people were wrongfully accused and faced a 400 percent penalty on the claimed amount of fraud.

precedents.parallel: Faulty accounting software was treated as reliable evidence and used to pursue hundreds of subpostmasters, showing the cost of treating a system's output as proof.
precedents.outcome: By September 2026, 620 people in England and Wales had at least one conviction quashed by the 2024 Act, covering 2,250 convictions; Horizon was bookkeeping software, not a risk model.

ref.title: Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024: quashed convictions management information, 24 September 2026 (GOV.UK)
ref.finding: 620 individuals identified as having at least one conviction quashed by the Act, and 2,250 convictions quashed, after all 1,011 cases were assessed.

nodes.label: AI decisions fairer than human judgement
nodes.summary: Algorithms deciding bail or credit can be fairer than human judgement, depending on design and use. One New York City simulation found an algorithmic rule could cut jail populations by up to 41.9% with no rise in crime[1]. But Kentucky's mandatory risk scores raised release only trivially[2], and one study found machine-learning mortgage models benefit Black and Hispanic borrowers less[4].

refs.title: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig and Mullainathan, Human Decisions and Machine Predictions, Quarterly Journal of Economics 133(1), 2018
refs.finding: A policy simulation on pretrial cases shows crime reductions up to 24.7% with no change in jailing rates, or jailing rate reductions up to 41.9% with no increase in crime rates.

refs.title: Assessing Risk Assessment in Action (Megan Stevenson, Minnesota Law Review 103, 2018)
refs.finding: Using more than a million Kentucky cases, HB 463 (2011) made risk assessment mandatory but led to only a trivial increase in pretrial release, matched by more failures to appear and pretrial crime; within a couple of years release was lower than before the law.

refs.title: Berg, Burg, Gombović and Puri, On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring using Digital Footprints, NBER Working Paper 24551, 2018 (Review of Financial Studies, 2020)
refs.finding: In 270,399 purchases at a German e-commerce furniture company from October 2015 to December 2016, ten digital-footprint variables predicted default with an AUC of 69.6% against 68.3% for the credit bureau score, with similar accuracy for customers who had no bureau score.

refs.title: Fuster, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Ramadorai and Walther, Predictably Unequal? The Effects of Machine Learning on Credit Markets, Journal of Finance, 2022
refs.finding: Using US mortgage data, Black and Hispanic borrowers are disproportionately less likely to gain from machine-learning default models, and in an equilibrium model machine learning increases rate disparity between and within groups.

limiters.evidence: In Broward County, 44.9% of Black non-reoffenders were labelled higher risk versus 23.5% of white ones.

ref.title: Machine Bias
ref.finding: False positive rates differed sharply by race for COMPAS.

limiters.evidence: The 24.7% crime cut or 41.9% jail cut are simulated on historical New York data, not measured in deployment.

ref.title: Human Decisions and Machine Predictions (Kleinberg et al., Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2018)
ref.finding: Simulated crime reductions up to 24.7% or jailing reductions up to 41.9%.

limiters.evidence: The EU AI Act lists reoffending risk assessment as high-risk, raising the bar for use.

ref.title: Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Point 6(d) covers assessing risk of offending or re-offending.

limiters.evidence: About 21% of adults worldwide still have no account, and footprint scoring reaches only people with a phone or online history; 84% of adults in low- and middle-income countries own a mobile phone.

ref.title: World Bank, The Global Findex Database 2025
ref.finding: 79% of adults globally have an account, and 84% of adults in low- and middle-income countries own a mobile phone.

limiters.evidence: On 12 May 2025 the CFPB withdrew its circulars on credit denial notices, including the one on decisions made with complex algorithms, so lenders lose the US regulator's guidance on explaining model-driven denials.

ref.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Withdrawn Guidance
ref.finding: Circular 2022-03 on adverse action notices for credit decisions based on complex algorithms and Circular 2023-03 on proper use of sample forms are listed as withdrawn on 12 May 2025.

limiters.evidence: The EU AI Act lists credit scoring of natural persons as high-risk, adding obligations.

ref.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems Referred to in Article 6(2)
ref.finding: Point 5(b) lists AI systems used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, except for detecting financial fraud, as high-risk.

enablers.action: Impose conformity and oversight duties on risk tools
enablers.evidence: The AI Act is in force, but its documentation and human oversight duties for Annex III high-risk systems, which include re-offending risk tools, apply only from 2 December 2027 after the 2026 amendment.

ref.title: Article 113: Entry into Force and Application
ref.finding: Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3 apply from 2 December 2027 to AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

enablers.action: Publish tools and validate them on local outcomes
enablers.evidence: COMPAS's maker keeps its calculations proprietary, and a 2013 review of 19 US risk tools found them moderate at best in predictive validity.

ref.title: Machine Bias
ref.finding: Northpointe calls its calculations proprietary; Desmarais and Singh's 2013 review of 19 risk methodologies found them moderate at best in predictive validity; only 20% of people predicted to commit violent crimes went on to do so.

enablers.action: Combine digital footprints with bureau data
enablers.evidence: Digital-footprint data predicted default about as well as bureau scores and complemented them in a study of a German online furniture retailer.

ref.title: Berg, Burg, Gombović and Puri, On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints, Review of Financial Studies, 2020
ref.finding: Simple digital-footprint variables match the information content of credit bureau scores, complement rather than substitute for bureau data, and affect access to credit and reduce default rates.

enablers.action: Require specific reasons for every credit denial
enablers.evidence: Regulation B still requires the principal reasons for any denial, and says a failure to reach a qualifying score is not enough, though the CFPB withdrew its AI-specific guidance in 2025.

ref.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9 Notifications
ref.finding: The statement of reasons for adverse action must be specific and indicate the principal reasons; saying the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score on the creditor's scoring system is insufficient.

precedents.parallel: New Jersey replaced money bail with decisions guided by the Public Safety Assessment, a statistical risk score, which is the closest real deployment of algorithm-guided release.
precedents.outcome: The pretrial jail population fell 43.9% from January 2015 to January 2018 with no reported rise in pretrial crime, but the reform also abolished most money bail, so the score's own share of the effect cannot be separated out.

ref.title: Study Finds New Jersey's Pretrial Reform Shows Early Signs of Wide-Reaching, Positive Impacts on Criminal Justice System (MDRC, 2019)
ref.finding: Reforms took effect January 1, 2017; the New Jersey Courts' 2018 report found a 43.9% fall in the pretrial jail population from January 2015 to January 2018 with no uptick in pretrial crime rates; detention rates were lower than pre-reform trends predicted.

precedents.parallel: Kentucky's HB 463 required judges to use a risk score and presumed release for low and moderate risk defendants, the same promise of fewer jailed people at no cost to safety.
precedents.outcome: Release rose only trivially, failures to appear and pretrial crime rose with it, judges ignored the release default in more than two thirds of cases, and within a couple of years release rates fell below pre-law levels.

ref.title: Assessing Risk Assessment in Action (Megan Stevenson, Minnesota Law Review 103, 2018)
ref.finding: HB 463 led to only a trivial increase in pretrial release, matched by more FTA and pretrial crime; judges ignored the presumptive non-monetary release in more than two-thirds of cases; within a couple of years release was lower than before the bill.

precedents.parallel: A meta-analysis of studies comparing expert judgment with statistical formulas makes the same comparison that bail simulations make between judges and models.
precedents.outcome: Formulas were about 10% more accurate on average, substantially better in 33% to 47% of studies and substantially worse in only 6% to 16%, across studies of human health and behavior in general rather than bail decisions.

ref.title: Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz and Nelson, Psychological Assessment 12(1), 2000)
ref.finding: Mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate than clinical prediction on average and substantially better in 33% to 47% of studies; clinical prediction was substantially better in only 6% to 16%; the advantage held regardless of judgment task.

precedents.parallel: Fast, cheap statistical scoring of borrowers was expected to widen access to credit, as alternative-data AI scoring is now.
precedents.outcome: The Federal Reserve concluded scoring likely contributed to greater availability and affordability of credit and predicted default for all major demographic groups, though average scores were lower for Black and Hispanic consumers; it had only limited direct information on scoring's own contribution.

ref.title: Report to the Congress on Credit Scoring and Its Effects on the Availability and Affordability of Credit, executive summary (Federal Reserve Board, 2007)
ref.finding: Credit scoring likely contributed to improved availability and affordability of credit; credit history scores predict credit risk for the population as a whole and for all major demographic groups.

precedents.parallel: A loan product delivered fully on mobile phones reached Kenyan households outside formal lending, an earlier version of the fintech inclusion story.
precedents.outcome: 34 percent of eligible people took the loans, which did not substitute for other credit, and households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses after shocks; the authors say digital loans are not a panacea for wider credit market failures.

ref.title: Fintech and Household Resilience to Shocks: Evidence from Digital Loans in Kenya (Bharadwaj, Jack and Suri, NBER w25604)
ref.finding: Take-up was 34 percent of those eligible; the loans did not substitute for other credit, and households were 6.3 percentage points less likely to forgo expenses due to negative shocks.

nodes.label: AI decisions that entrench bias
nodes.summary: Decision algorithms can repeat or widen bias. One ProPublica analysis of more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida, found COMPAS labelled 44.9% of Black defendants who did not reoffend as higher risk, against 23.5% of white defendants[1]. Whether that is bias depends on the fairness metric, since three common ones cannot all hold except in narrow cases[2].

refs.title: ProPublica (Angwin, Larson, Mattu and Kirchner), Machine Bias, 2016
refs.finding: Among more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County in 2013 and 2014, 44.9% of Black and 23.5% of white defendants who did not reoffend had been labelled higher risk, almost twice the rate.

refs.title: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores (2016)
refs.finding: Except in highly constrained special cases, no method can satisfy three common fairness conditions for risk scores at the same time.

refs.title: Assessing Risk Assessment in Action (Megan Stevenson, Minnesota Law Review 103, 2018)
refs.finding: HB 463 benefited white defendants more than Black defendants on its face, because of regional differences in how judges responded; within the same county the increase in release was similar, and neither HB 463 nor the PSA changed racial disparities once regional differences were accounted for.

refs.title: Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities in Tax Audits (Elzayn, Smith, Hertz, Ramesh, Fisher, Ho and Goldin, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research working paper, January 2023)
refs.finding: Despite race-blind audit selection, Black taxpayers were audited at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of non-Black taxpayers, driven mainly by audits of Earned Income Tax Credit claims.

refs.title: Predictably Unequal? The Effects of Machine Learning on Credit Markets (Fuster, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Ramadorai and Walther, Journal of Finance 77(1), 2022)
refs.finding: Using US mortgage data, Black and Hispanic borrowers were less likely to benefit from machine learning default models than from traditional ones; in an equilibrium model, machine learning increased rate disparities between and within groups, mainly because of its greater flexibility.

refs.title: Consumer-Lending Discrimination in the FinTech Era (Bartlett, Morse, Stanton and Wallace, NBER Working Paper 25943, 2019; Journal of Financial Economics 2021)
refs.finding: Lenders charged Latinx and African-American borrowers 7.9 and 3.6 basis points more for purchase and refinance mortgages, about $765 million a year; FinTech algorithms also discriminated, but 40% less than face-to-face lenders, and did not discriminate in loan approval.

nodes.control_note: Courts can decide bail and sentences without risk scores, and the EU bans profiling-only crime prediction and puts high-risk duties on re-offending risk tools. Lenders will keep using complex models, so some unfair exclusion is likely; explanation duties and high-risk rules aim to reduce it and let applicants correct errors, but no study has measured their effect.

actions.action: Ban crime prediction based only on profiling
actions.evidence: Since 2 February 2025 the EU AI Act has banned AI that assesses or predicts a person's risk of committing a crime based solely on profiling or personality traits; tools that assess the risk of offending or re-offending are instead classed as high-risk.

ref.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 5 and Annex III
ref.finding: Article 5(1)(d) prohibits AI that assesses the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits; Annex III point 6(d) lists AI assessing the risk of offending or re-offending as high-risk.

actions.action: Benchmark risk tools against simple baselines
actions.evidence: Pooled predictions by people with little or no criminal justice expertise were 67.0% accurate against 65.2% for COMPAS, and a model using only age and prior convictions did about as well, which weakens the case for opaque scores.

ref.title: Dressel and Farid, The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism, Science Advances 4(1), 2018
ref.finding: COMPAS was no more accurate or fair than predictions by people with little or no criminal justice expertise; a two-feature linear predictor performed about as well as COMPAS, which uses 137 features.

actions.action: Require specific reasons for algorithmic credit denials
actions.evidence: US Regulation B requires specific principal reasons for any adverse credit action and rules out citing a failed score; no study measures the rule's effect on exclusion.
