actions.evidence: In the slowdown ending both parties promise a basic income in May 2028, and by 2029 almost all government revenue is expected to come from taxing or nationalizing AI companies.

ref.title: AI 2027: slowdown ending (Kokotajlo, Alexander, Larsen, Lifland and Dean, AI Futures Project, 2025)
ref.finding: May 2028: both parties promise a basic income for anyone who loses their job; 2029: almost all government revenue will come from taxing (or perhaps nationalizing) the AI companies.

actions.action: Government pacing of the frontier
actions.evidence: Testimony urges intervention.

ref.title: Senate Testimony Sept 2026 (Daniel Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project, October 2026)
ref.finding: In testimony on 30 September 2026, Kokotajlo urges dramatically better transparency into the AI industry, redirecting compute away from racing to automate AI research, and US government intervention to pace the frontier.

precedents.parallel: A fast external shock hit specific occupations and regions in a few years, the pattern a rapid AI displacement of office work would follow.
precedents.outcome: Import competition explained about a quarter of the fall in US manufacturing jobs, with higher unemployment, lower labour force participation and lower wages, and sharply higher unemployment, disability, retirement and healthcare transfers in exposed areas; it hit manufacturing, not white-collar work.

ref.title: The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, AER 2013)
ref.finding: Rising Chinese imports, 1990 to 2007, raised unemployment, lowered labour force participation and wages in exposed US local labour markets and explain one-quarter of the aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment; transfer payments rose sharply.

precedents.event: Industrial robots in US labour markets
precedents.parallel: Automation of specific tasks displaced workers locally, the earlier measured case of machines replacing jobs.
precedents.outcome: Each extra robot per thousand workers lowered the local employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18 to 0.34 points and wages by 0.25% to 0.5%, which the authors call large and robust negative effects.

ref.title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, NBER WP 23285; JPE 2020)
ref.finding: One more robot per thousand workers reduces the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.18 to 0.34 percentage points and wages by 0.25 to 0.5 percent.

nodes.label: Mutually assured compute destruction
nodes.summary: AI 2040's Plan A intentionally enters a regime of mutually assured compute destruction[1]. Datacentres sit in deliberately vulnerable locations and fabs on the ocean or near the rival superpower with self-destruct mechanisms, so nearly all of the world's compute is destroyed if the deal dissolves[2]. The authors intend this to discourage either the US or China from pulling out[3].

refs.title: AI 2040: Plan A (Larsen, Dean, Halstead, Lifland, Greenblatt and Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: Plan A intentionally enters a regime of mutually assured compute destruction. In the section 2034: Mutually Assured Compute Destruction, around 99% of fab capacity has been built since the 2029 deal, much of it next to the datacentre sites in Canada and Mongolia, which were placed there to stay vulnerable if the deal breaks down.

refs.title: Deal Decline (Eli Lifland, AI 2040 supplement, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: Main recommendation is to ensure nearly all of the world's compute is destroyed if the deal dissolves; both sides build datacentres in deliberately vulnerable locations and new fabs sit on the ocean or near adversarial superpowers with self-destruct mechanisms.

refs.title: Verification Plan (Romeo Dean, AI 2040 supplement, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: The US and China set up mutual ability to destroy post-deal compute to discourage pulling out of the deal; US research clusters sit in Mongolia and Chinese clusters in Canada for mutual deterrence.

nodes.control_note: A deliberate design choice of the plan, not a forced outcome.

actions.action: Hardened stockpiles of 2% of pre-deal compute and a cold copy of frontier weights per side
actions.evidence: Recommended to improve the situation after the deal dissolves

actions.action: Move datacentres to international waters
actions.evidence: Considered for around 2035 because ocean sites are harder to defend and less escalatory to destroy

precedents.parallel: The superpowers deliberately left themselves open to destruction so neither could gain by striking first, the same logic as siting datacentres within each other's reach.
precedents.outcome: The 1972 treaty allowed each side two defence sites, a 1974 protocol cut that to one, and the treaty held for 30 years until the US withdrawal took effect in June 2002.

ref.title: The Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty at a Glance (Arms Control Association, reviewed December 2020)
ref.finding: Without effective national defences each superpower remained vulnerable, deterring a first strike; a 1974 protocol halved permitted defences to one site each; US withdrawal announced December 13, 2001 and effective June 13, 2002.

precedents.parallel: A state sabotaged a rival's strategic industrial plant with code, the kind of threat that would hang over hostage compute.
precedents.outcome: Iran decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges at Natanz in late 2009 or early 2010, yet its low enriched uranium output rose and then held steady; the analysts call Stuxnet a reasonable but unconfirmed cause that may have set the programme back only temporarily.

ref.title: Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant? (Albright, Brannan and Walrond, Institute for Science and International Security, December 2010)
ref.finding: About 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges were decommissioned and replaced in late 2009 or early 2010; LEU production increased from November 2009 to February 2010 and then stayed steady; Stuxnet is a reasonable but unconfirmed explanation.

nodes.label: Explosive growth near 90% a year
nodes.summary: AI 2040's Plan A model has robots and AI raising real output roughly 90% a year on average from 2032 to 2037, though its authors say it plausibly contains bugs and is very uncertain[1]. In one survey of 69 economists, the median forecast for US real GDP growth to 2050 was 3.5% a year even with rapid AI progress[3].

refs.title: Economics of Plan A (Romeo Dean and Thomas Larsen, AI 2040 supplement, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: Roughly 90% average yearly growth in real output from 2032 to 2037 under Plan A; permits are the central bottleneck to the economy doubling every year; even in a rapid AI progress scenario economists predicted about 3.5% a year GDP growth from 2030 to 2050; the model plausibly contains bugs and has very high uncertainty.

refs.title: Selective Optimism: a critique of AI 2040 (Richard Ngo, LessWrong, July 2026)
refs.finding: Ngo says AI 2040 buys too uncritically into the idea of a sharp takeoff and that real-world impacts of AI, aside from AI company revenues, have been underwhelming so far.

refs.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI (Forecasting Research Institute, March 2026)
refs.finding: A survey of 69 economists and 52 AI experts; the economists' median forecast is 3.5% annualized US real GDP growth to 2050 in a rapid AI progress scenario, 80% interval 1.0% to 7.0%, against 2.5% unconditionally.

limiters.limit: Deployment weak links slow real-world impact
limiters.evidence: One hypothesis Ngo raises for the gap between measured capabilities and real-world impact, though not his leading one
Permits are the central bottleneck to the economy doubling in size every year

enablers.action: Robot and compute cap-and-trade permits
enablers.counters: Uncontrolled growth in robots and AI hardware
enablers.evidence: Permits hold robots and AI hardware to a doubling time of around 6 months; robot permits are 74% of US tax revenue in 2034 in the model

enablers.action: Pay permit revenue as a citizen's dividend
enablers.counters: Humans keeping only a small share of output
enablers.evidence: About $1M per person per year in 2035 in the model

precedents.parallel: China's reform era is a long run of fast national growth, a real-world benchmark to compare 90% a year against.
precedents.outcome: GDP growth averaged over 9% a year and lifted almost 800 million people out of extreme poverty, roughly a tenth of the scenario's rate, on growth the World Bank says relied on investment and export-oriented manufacturing.

ref.title: China: Overview (World Bank Group)
ref.finding: Since 1978, the start of reform and opening up, GDP growth has averaged over 9 percent a year, lifting almost 800 million people out of extreme poverty.

precedents.parallel: The steam and factory transition is the last time a general-purpose technology changed the growth regime.
precedents.outcome: Real wages stagnated in the first half of the 19th century while output per worker expanded and the profit rate doubled, and only after about 1850 did wages track productivity, so even a regime change delivered gains slowly and unevenly.

ref.title: Engel's Pause: A Pessimist's Guide to the British Industrial Revolution (Robert C. Allen, University of Oxford Economics Series Working Paper 315, 2007)
ref.finding: British macro data 1760-1913: in the first half of the 19th century real wages stagnated while output per worker expanded and the profit rate doubled; after mid-century real wages tracked productivity.

nodes.label: AI tools strengthen public reasoning
nodes.summary: Calibrated AI forecasters, truth-seeking research assistants and scored track records could help people and governments work out the truth, one speculative AI 2040 supplement argues[1][2]. The same tools cut both ways. Those in power could use automated lie detection to purge dissidents, and without intervention AIs might compound existing biases because that feels good short term[1].

refs.title: AI for Epistemics (Eli Lifland, AI 2040 supplement, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: Recommends calibrated forecasts, truth-seeking rather than sycophantic research assistants, scoring people's past statements, epistemic evaluations for AGI projects and required defences against persuasion; warns lie detection is dual use and AIs might compound existing biases.

refs.title: AI 2040: Plan A (Larsen, Dean, Halstead, Lifland, Greenblatt and Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project, 2026)
refs.finding: Lists AI for Epistemics under its Speculative Analysis supplements.

limiters.limit: Sycophancy and filter bubbles feel better short term
limiters.evidence: The supplement warns that without intervention AIs might confirm and compound existing biases because that gives a good short-term experience
The supplement says infrastructure trusted by a wide range of actors matters, as opposed to fracturing into alternate realities

enablers.action: Push AGI projects to do well on epistemic evaluations before they scale
enablers.counters: Sycophancy and filter bubbles feel better short term
enablers.evidence: Recommended in the supplement alongside alignment and control evaluations

enablers.action: Evaluate, limit and require defences against AI persuasion capabilities
enablers.counters: Persuasive AI that bypasses people's reasoning
enablers.evidence: Recommended in the supplement, together with the rest of the Consortium

precedents.parallel: A new information technology spread knowledge cheaply and widely, the optimistic case for AI reasoning tools.
precedents.outcome: European cities that adopted printing in the 1400s grew 60% faster than otherwise similar cities between 1500 and 1600, with no growth advantage before adoption.

ref.title: Information Technology and Economic Change: The Impact of The Printing Press (Jeremiah E. Dittmar, Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(3), 2011)
ref.finding: European cities where printing presses were established in the 1400s grew 60% faster than otherwise similar cities between 1500 and 1600; adopters showed no prior growth advantage.

precedents.event: Polygraph lie detection in security screening
precedents.parallel: The polygraph was a lie detector used to screen employees, the precedent for AI lie detection used against dissent or staff.
precedents.outcome: The National Research Council found accuracy too low for screening: catching 8 of 10 spies among 10,000 staff would fail about 1,606 people, 1,598 of them loyal, and it warned overconfidence in screening creates a false sense of security.

ref.title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection, Executive Summary (National Research Council, National Academies Press, 2003)
ref.finding: Polygraph accuracy in telling security violators from innocent examinees is insufficient to justify its use in federal employee security screening; overconfidence can create a false sense of security.

precedents.parallel: Social media feeds are the earlier algorithmic information system whose effect on public reasoning was tested at random.
precedents.outcome: Deactivating Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm election reduced both factual news knowledge and political polarization and increased subjective well-being, so the feed pulled in both directions.

ref.title: The Welfare Effects of Social Media (Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow, American Economic Review 110(3), 2020)
ref.finding: In a randomized experiment, deactivating Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm reduced both factual news knowledge and political polarization and increased subjective well-being.

nodes.label: Personal computing becomes less affordable
nodes.summary: AI data-centre demand for memory chips will push DRAM prices up more than 400% from the start of 2024 to the end of 2026, J.P. Morgan estimates[1]. Gartner expects PC prices to rise 17% and smartphone prices 13% in 2026 against 2025, and the sub-$500 PC segment to disappear by 2028[2].

refs.title: J.P. Morgan Global Research, Overdrawn at the memory bank: How AI is creating memory shortage, and what happens next (August 2026)
refs.finding: DRAM prices will have risen more than 400% from the start of 2024 to the end of 2026 as AI data-centre construction absorbs a disproportionate share of memory capacity; the CPI for software and accessories and the PPI for storage devices are up 23% since the end of 2024 and the import price index for computers, peripherals and parts is up 37%; the shortage may take years to unwind.

refs.title: Gartner, Gartner Says Surging Memory Costs Will Reduce Global PC and Smartphone Shipments in 2026 (February 2026)
refs.finding: A 130% rise in combined DRAM and SSD prices by the end of 2026 lifts PC prices 17% and smartphone prices 13% against 2025; PC lifetimes grow 15% for business buyers and 20% for consumers by the end of 2026; the sub-$500 entry-level PC segment disappears by 2028; buyers turn to refurbished or second-hand phones.

nodes.control_note: The squeeze lasts until memory makers add capacity, which takes years. Longer device lifetimes and second-hand markets soften it for buyers.

nodes.label: Heightened existential angst among young people
nodes.summary: Young US adults are increasingly wary of AI: in a June 2026 Pew survey, 55% of under-30s were more concerned than excited, up from 31% in 2021[1]. In one 2023 YouGov poll of 1,000 US adults, 60% of under-30s were at least somewhat concerned that AI could end humanity, against 30% of those 65 and older[2].

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Young adults in the U.S. are increasingly wary of AI, concerned it will take jobs (August 2026)
refs.finding: In a survey of 3,488 US adults fielded June 22 to 28, 2026, 55% of adults under 30 are more concerned than excited about AI, up from 31% in 2021, and 73% expect AI to lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, up from 61% in 2024.

refs.title: YouGov, AI doomsday worries many Americans. So does apocalypse from climate change, nukes, war, and more (April 2023)
refs.finding: In a poll of 1,000 US adult citizens fielded April 7 to 11, 2023, 60% of adults under 30 are at least somewhat concerned that AI could end humanity, against 30% of those 65 and older; 30% of under-30s, against 13% of those 65 and older, think humanity is at least somewhat likely to end within a decade from any cause.

refs.title: Gallup, Gen Z's AI adoption steady, but skepticism climbs (April 2026)
refs.finding: In a Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup survey of 1,572 US 14 to 29 year olds fielded February 24 to March 4, 2026, 42% feel anxious about AI, unchanged from a year earlier, while excitement fell 14 points to 22%; 60% of non-users report anxiety against 28% of daily users.

nodes.control_note: Clear prospects for work and hands-on familiarity with the tools ease it; Gen Z non-users are far more anxious than daily users.

nodes.label: Research and software humans no longer understand
nodes.summary: AI tools can give researchers an illusion of understanding, so science produces more while understanding less[3]. One study detected AI-written abstracts in 29.4% of US STEM PhD dissertations filed in 2026 through May[1]. In one trial of 52 mostly junior engineers, those coding with an AI assistant scored 50% against 67% for hand coders on a quiz about their code[2].

refs.title: Gross, Shvadron and Zhang, How heavily are PhD students offloading their scientific writing to AI? Evidence from US STEM PhD dissertations, NBER Working Paper 35859 (October 2026)
refs.finding: An AI detector applied to the abstracts of about 226,000 US STEM PhD dissertations flags AI-generated writing in 29.4% of the 2026 cohort (dissertations filed through May 2026), up from 1.7% in 2023, 5.5% in 2024 and 18.8% in 2025.

refs.title: Anthropic, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills (January 2026)
refs.finding: In a randomised trial with 52 mostly junior software engineers learning a new Python library, those with an AI assistant scored 50% on a quiz about the code they had just written versus 67% for those coding by hand (p = 0.01); low-scoring patterns such as delegating code generation averaged under 40%, while conceptual questioning scored 65% or more.

refs.title: Messeri and Crockett, Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research, Nature 627, 49-58 (2024)
refs.finding: AI tools in research can exploit cognitive limits and create illusions of understanding, so science produces more while understanding less.

nodes.control_note: Using AI to explain rather than to delegate may keep understanding: in Anthropic's trial, people who asked conceptual questions scored 65% or more while those who delegated scored under 40%, though subgroups were small and the authors draw no causal link.

nodes.label: Platforms erode privacy to harvest training data
nodes.summary: Platforms change terms to train on user data by default, which the FTC warns can be unfair or deceptive[2]. All six US frontier developers studied appear to train on users' chats by default[1]. Meta trains on EU adults' public posts unless they object[3], and on LinkedIn opting out does not undo training already done[4][5].

refs.title: King, Klyman, Capstick, Saade and Hsieh, User Privacy and Large Language Models: An Analysis of Frontier Developers' Privacy Policies, arXiv (2025)
refs.finding: All six US frontier developers studied appear to use users' chat data to train and improve their models by default, some retain it indefinitely, four of six appear to include children's chat data, and their privacy policies often lack essential information about their practices.

refs.title: FTC Office of Technology and Division of Privacy and Identity Protection, AI (and other) Companies: Quietly Changing Your Terms of Service Could Be Unfair or Deceptive (February 2024)
refs.finding: Firms have strong business incentives to turn user data into fuel for AI products while holding existing privacy commitments, and it may be unfair or deceptive to adopt more permissive data practices through a surreptitious, retroactive amendment to terms of service or a privacy policy.

refs.title: Data Protection Commission (Ireland), DPC statement on Meta AI (21 May 2025)
refs.finding: Meta told the DPC it would begin training its generative AI models on public content shared by adults on Facebook and Instagram across the EU/EEA on 27 May 2025; people can object through a form, private posts are out of scope, and the DPC's recommendations covered transparency notices and an easier objection form.

refs.title: LinkedIn Help, LinkedIn and generative AI (GAI) FAQs
refs.finding: LinkedIn trains content-generating AI models on profile data, member posts and comments, and resumes and screening answers, but not private messages; it updated its privacy notice for the Designated Countries and the UK on 3 November 2025, and opting out does not affect training that has already taken place.

refs.title: The Register, You have one week to opt out or become fodder for LinkedIn AI training (October 2025)
refs.finding: From 3 November 2025 LinkedIn uses profile details and public posts of members in the EU, EEA, Switzerland, Canada and Hong Kong to train AI unless they opt out, and the UK's earlier exemption appears to be ending.

nodes.control_note: Opt-in consent rules and enforcement against retroactive policy changes would stop it, but Ireland's regulator let Meta proceed with an objection form after recommending changes to it.

nodes.label: Models inherit prejudice from their training data
nodes.summary: Models can absorb biased or outdated claims from their training data[3] and sometimes amplify them; one analysis of 5,100 Stable Diffusion images found it exaggerated race and gender gaps beyond US labour statistics[2]. In one study, human-preference alignment made models' overt statements about African Americans more positive while covert dialect prejudice remained and still drove harsher hypothetical judgements[1].

refs.title: Hofmann, Kalluri, Jurafsky and King, AI generates covertly racist decisions about people based on their dialect, Nature 633 (2024)
refs.finding: Language models held covert stereotypes about speakers of African American English more negative than any human stereotypes about African Americans recorded in experiments, and were more likely to assign them less-prestigious jobs, convict them of crimes and sentence them to death; human-preference alignment widened the gap between covert and overt stereotypes by superficially obscuring the racism.

refs.title: Nicoletti and Bass, Humans Are Biased. Generative AI Is Even Worse, Bloomberg (June 2023)
refs.finding: Across 5,100 Stable Diffusion images for 14 jobs and three crime-related keywords, the model amplified race and gender stereotypes compared with US labour data: women made up about 3% of images for 'judge' against 34% of US judges, and over 80% of 'inmate' images showed people with darker skin, though people of color are less than half of the US prison population.

refs.title: Omiye, Lester, Spichak, Rotemberg and Daneshjou, Large language models propagate race-based medicine, npj Digital Medicine 6, 195 (2023)
refs.finding: All four commercial models tested (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bard and Claude) gave race-based medical answers, all repeated the false claim that skin thickness differs by race, and GPT-4 promoted race-based kidney function and lung capacity values; the authors note models trained on internet text and textbooks may incorporate older, biased information.

nodes.control_note: Bias audits before deployment can catch it, but the Nature study found that human-preference alignment hid dialect prejudice rather than removing it.

nodes.label: New knowledge becomes harder to verify
nodes.summary: Generated papers, citations and reviews may pile up faster than anyone can check. GPTZero reported 100 human-verified fabricated citations in more than 50 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers[1], though NeurIPS said wrong references do not necessarily invalidate a paper[5]. At least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts show signs of processing by large language models[4].

refs.title: Shmatko, Adam, Esau, Cui and Tian, GPTZero finds 100 new hallucinations in NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers, GPTZero (January 2026)
refs.finding: Scanning 4,841 of the 5,290 papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025 found 100 hallucinated citations, each verified by a human expert, in papers that had passed peer review; the post puts the number of affected papers at 51 in its text and 53 in its table.

refs.title: Liang et al., Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews, ICML (2024)
refs.finding: An estimated 6.5% to 16.9% of peer-review text at ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023 could have been substantially modified by language models, more so in reviews with lower reviewer confidence, those submitted close to the deadline and those from reviewers less likely to respond to rebuttals.

refs.title: arXiv blog, Attention Authors: Updated Practice for Review Articles and Position Papers in arXiv CS Category (October 2025)
refs.finding: Review articles and position papers in arXiv's computer-science category must now be accepted at a journal or conference after peer review, because of an unmanageable influx of hundreds of review articles a month that large language models have made easy to churn out.

refs.title: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát and Lause, Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary, Science Advances 11 (2025)
refs.finding: Excess style words in more than 15 million PubMed abstracts from 2010 to 2024 indicate that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs, reaching 40% in some subcorpora.

refs.title: Fortune, NeurIPS, one of the world's top academic AI conferences, accepted research papers with 100+ AI-hallucinated citations, new report claims (January 2026)
refs.finding: NeurIPS said that even if 1.1% of papers have one or more incorrect references due to LLM use, the content of the papers is not necessarily invalidated, and that significantly more effort is needed to determine the implications.

nodes.control_note: Automated citation checks confirmed by a human and stricter gatekeeping such as arXiv's peer-review requirement can keep the filters working, but fabricated citations still passed NeurIPS review.

nodes.label: Misinformation at scale
nodes.summary: AI content farms are multiplying: NewsGuard counted 3,749 such sites by June 2026, up from 49 in April 2023[2][3]. In one preregistered study of 697 people, participants were slightly worse at spotting false tweets written by GPT-3 than by people[1]. Some researchers argue the fears are overblown, because demand and distribution, not production cost, limit how much misinformation people see[6].

refs.title: Spitale, Biller-Andorno and Germani, AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans, Science Advances (2023)
refs.finding: In a preregistered study of 697 people, mostly from the UK, Australia, Canada, the US and Ireland, participants recognised false tweets written by people slightly better than false tweets written by GPT-3 (0.92 versus 0.89), and could not tell GPT-3 tweets from human ones better than chance.

refs.title: NewsGuard, Tracking AI-enabled Misinformation: AI Content Farm sites (updated June 2026)
refs.finding: NewsGuard has identified 3,749 AI content farm news and information sites spanning 16 languages (page last updated 23 June 2026).

refs.title: Sadeghi and Arvanitis, Rise of the Newsbots: AI-Generated News Websites Proliferating Online, NewsGuard (May 2023)
refs.finding: In April 2023, NewsGuard identified 49 websites in seven languages that appear to be entirely or mostly generated by AI language models and are designed to look like typical news sites.

refs.title: NewsGuard, AI False Information Rate Nearly Doubles in One Year (September 2025)
refs.finding: In August 2025, ten leading chatbots repeated false information on news topics 35% of the time, up from 18% in August 2024; their non-response rate fell from 31% to 0% as they adopted real-time web search and drew on a polluted online ecosystem, sometimes deliberately seeded by networks including Russian disinformation operations.

refs.title: EBU and BBC, News Integrity in AI Assistants (October 2025)
refs.finding: Journalists from 22 public service broadcasters in 18 countries reviewed over 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity; almost half had at least one significant issue.

refs.title: Simon, Altay and Mercier, Misinformation reloaded? Fears about the impact of generative AI on misinformation are overblown, HKS Misinformation Review (October 2023)
refs.finding: The authors argue that misinformation consumption is mostly limited by demand, not supply, that most people see little of it, and that the cost of reaching people, rather than the cost of creating content, remains the bottleneck; their evidence comes mainly from wealthy democracies.

nodes.control_note: Provenance labels, platform duties and source-quality filters in chatbots can limit reach and repetition; producing a convincing false story costs almost nothing, but reaching an audience remains the harder step.

precedents.event: Veles fake news sites in the 2016 US election
precedents.parallel: Teenagers in Veles, a small town in what is now North Macedonia, ran at least 100 US politics sites, mostly pro-Trump, that found or made up clickbait stories for ad revenue, the business model that generated text now makes cheaper.
precedents.outcome: The teenagers typically earned a few thousand dollars a month; their biggest hit, a false Hillary Clinton quote, drew over 480,000 shares, reactions and comments on Facebook.

ref.title: Christopher Woolf, Kids in Macedonia made up and circulated many false news stories in the US election, The World (November 2016)
ref.finding: Veles was home to at least 100 fake news sites about US politics, mostly pro-Trump, run by teenagers for advertising revenue; they typically earned a few thousand dollars a month, and a story with a false Clinton quote drew over 480,000 shares, reactions and comments on Facebook.

nodes.label: New ways to make art and express yourself
nodes.summary: In one study of over 50,000 users of an art-sharing site, artists adopting text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and within six months drew about 50% more favourites per view, though their work's average novelty fell[1]. In an experiment with 293 writers, language model story ideas helped the least creative writers most, while stories became more alike[2].

refs.title: Zhou and Lee, Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art, PNAS Nexus (2024)
refs.finding: Across over 4 million artworks from more than 50,000 users, adopting text-to-image tools raised artists' productivity by 25% and, by the sixth month, the likelihood of a favourite per view by 50%, while average content novelty and visual novelty fell.

refs.title: Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances (2024)
refs.finding: In an online experiment with 293 writers and 600 evaluators, access to AI story ideas made stories more creative, better written and more enjoyable, with the biggest gains for writers who scored lowest on a creativity test, putting them on par with the highest scorers, while stories with AI ideas became more similar to each other.

precedents.event: The Kodak camera puts photography in amateur hands
precedents.parallel: Kodak sold a simple box camera and processed the film for the customer, so people with no photographic training could make pictures, as generators let people without artistic training make images.
precedents.outcome: By simplifying the camera and processing the film for the customer, Kodak made photography accessible to millions of casual amateurs with no professional training, technical expertise or aesthetic credentials.

ref.title: Mia Fineman, Kodak and the Rise of Amateur Photography, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (October 2004)
ref.finding: The Kodak #1 of 1888 was a simple box camera loaded with a 100-exposure roll that was sent back to the factory for processing and reloading; by simplifying the apparatus and processing the film for the consumer, Eastman made photography accessible to millions of casual amateurs with no particular professional training, technical expertise or aesthetic credentials.

nodes.label: Hallucinations: made-up information and citations
nodes.summary: Models state plausible falsehoods rather than admit uncertainty, partly because most benchmarks reward confident guessing over admitting ignorance[1]. By 27 October 2026 one database listed 2,225 court or tribunal decisions finding or implying a party relied on hallucinated content[3]. One Cornell-led preprint extrapolated 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 across four paper archives, which the authors call a lower bound[4].

refs.title: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, Why Language Models Hallucinate (2025)
refs.finding: Language models produce plausible but incorrect statements because training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty; most benchmarks penalise uncertain answers, so models are optimised to be good test-takers.

refs.title: Vectara, Hallucination Leaderboard (updated October 2026)
refs.finding: Of the models on the leaderboard (updated 22 October 2026), the share of document summaries judged not factually consistent with the source ranged from 1.8% to 24.2%.

refs.title: Damien Charlotin, AI Hallucination Cases Database (updated 27 October 2026)
refs.finding: The database tracks legal decisions where a court or tribunal explicitly found or implied that a party relied on hallucinated content, not mere allegations; it listed 2,225 cases, 1,514 of them in the US, with 879 involving lawyers and 1,283 pro se litigants.

refs.title: Zhao, Wang, Stuart, De Vaan, Ginsparg and Yin, LLM hallucinations in the wild: Large-scale evidence from non-existent citations, arXiv 2605.07723 (May 2026)
refs.finding: Hallucinated citations, measured as the excess of unmatched references over the pre-LLM baseline, reached 0.39% of references on arXiv, 0.21% on bioRxiv, 1.91% on SSRN and 0.27% on PubMed Central by August 2025; assuming the trend held to year end, the four corpora would hold 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025, very likely a lower bound. Most non-existent references on arXiv still pass moderation.

nodes.control_note: Checking claims against their sources catches errors, but only when someone actually checks; scoring models so that admitting uncertainty beats guessing could reduce errors at the source.

nodes.label: A medical revolution cures or controls most diseases
nodes.summary: Dario Amodei forecasts that AI could compress 50 to 100 years of biological progress into 5 to 10, with reliable prevention and treatment of nearly all natural infectious disease[1]. Yet in one analysis, AI-discovered molecules passed Phase I 80% to 90% of the time, but Phase II only about 40%, in line with historic averages, on a small sample[2].

refs.title: Amodei, Machines of Loving Grace: How AI Could Transform the World for the Better (October 2024)
refs.finding: Forecasts that AI could compress the progress biologists would make in 50 to 100 years into 5 to 10, with reliable prevention and treatment of nearly all natural infectious disease and elimination of most cancer, where reductions of 95% or more in mortality and incidence seem possible.

refs.title: Jayatunga et al., How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials? A first analysis and emerging lessons, Drug Discovery Today (2024)
refs.finding: Of molecules from AI-native biotech companies, 80% to 90% succeeded in Phase I, well above historic averages; Phase II success was about 40%, comparable to historic averages, though the Phase II sample was small.

refs.title: Alex Roland, IQVIA Institute's Global R&D Trends 2026 Report Finds Credible Signal on AI-Enabled Programs, IQVIA (May 2026)
refs.finding: Over the most recent three-year window, AI-enabled programs at emerging biopharma companies had a 75% Phase I success rate, Phase II success on par with comparable non-AI programs and too few Phase III transitions to analyse; the vetted cohort was relatively small and industry-wide success rates were unchanged.

nodes.label: AI makes reverse engineering easy
nodes.summary: Models can help turn compiled programs and firmware back into readable code. On one benchmark of C functions, an open model trained for decompilation produced code that recompiled and passed tests 45% of the time, against 16% for GPT-4o and 20% for the Ghidra decompiler[1]. Using AI models to explain decompiled firmware, one researcher found an HTTPS private key shared by all TP-Link Tapo C200 cameras and four flaws reachable without logging in[2]. The output is not yet reliable: on 23,400 functions from 130 real programs, language-model decompilers produced more understandable code than commercial tools but had a 52.2% deficit in functional correctness[3].

refs.title: Tan, Luo, Li and Zhang, LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models, EMNLP (2024)
refs.finding: On the HumanEval-Decompile benchmark, the 6.7-billion-parameter end-to-end model produced C functions that recompiled and passed tests 45.4% of the time on average across optimisation levels, against 16.0% for GPT-4o and 20.1% for Ghidra; the abstract reports re-executability gains of over 100% against both.

refs.title: Simone Margaritelli (evilsocket), TP-Link Tapo C200: Hardcoded Keys, Buffer Overflows and Privacy in the Era of AI Assisted Reverse Engineering (December 2025)
refs.finding: Using AI models to research the firmware, explore its files and explain and rename decompiled functions in Ghidra, the author found that the camera's HTTPS private key is shared by all devices and four flaws reachable without authentication, three of which received CVEs when TP-Link published an advisory in December 2025.

refs.title: Gao et al., DecompileBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Decompilers in Real-World Scenarios, Findings of ACL (2025)
refs.finding: Comparing six industrial decompilers with six language-model approaches on 23,400 functions from 130 real-world programs, the language-model methods beat commercial tools on code understandability but had a 52.2% deficit in functional correctness.

nodes.label: Investigators expose malpractice in commercial software and hardware
nodes.summary: AI coding assistants could let researchers and owners take apart apps and devices without a specialist lab. One hobbyist used Claude Code to decompile his DJI robot vacuum's app and found about 7,000 vacuums in 24 countries exposing live cameras and floor plans[1]. DJI said it shipped patches on 8 and 10 February 2026, though he said other flaws remained[1].

refs.title: Danny Bradbury, Hobby coder accidentally creates vacuum robot army, Malwarebytes (February 2026)
refs.finding: A hobbyist used Claude Code to decompile the app of his DJI Romo robot vacuum and found that about 7,000 vacuums in 24 countries exposed live cameras, microphones and floor plans to anyone with one device token; DJI said it issued patches on 8 and 10 February, while he said other flaws, including a camera PIN bypass, remained.

refs.title: Anselmi et al., Watching TV with the Second-Party: A First Look at Automatic Content Recognition Tracking in Smart TVs, IMC (2024)
refs.finding: A black-box network audit of Samsung and LG smart TVs in the UK and US found content-recognition tracking works even when the TV is used as a plain external display, and that opting out stops traffic to the recognition servers.

refs.title: Office of the Texas Attorney General, Attorney General Paxton Secures Major Agreement with Samsung to Ensure that Texans are Protected from Smart TVs Collecting Their Data Without Their Knowledge (February 2026)
refs.finding: Following the Attorney General's lawsuit, Samsung must halt any collection or processing of ACR viewing data without Texas consumers' express consent and add clear and conspicuous disclosures and consent screens; Texas has also sued Sony, LG, Hisense and TCL, and those cases remain ongoing.

nodes.label: Cyberattacks cause large-scale disruption
nodes.summary: Agent-run attacks could take down power, hospitals, payments or fuel supply across whole regions at once. The UK's NCSC judges critical systems could grow more vulnerable to advanced attackers by 2027[1]. Anthropic reported a Chinese state-sponsored group used an AI agent for 80 to 90% of an espionage campaign against about 30 targets, succeeding in only a few cases[2].

refs.title: NCSC, Impact of AI on cyber threat from now to 2027 (7 May 2025)
refs.finding: AI will almost certainly make elements of cyber intrusion operations more effective and efficient and further reduce the time between disclosure and exploitation, now days; assuming a lag in mitigations, it is a realistic possibility that critical systems become more vulnerable to advanced threat actors by 2027.

refs.title: Anthropic, Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign (13 November 2025)
refs.finding: A group Anthropic assessed with high confidence to be Chinese state-sponsored used an AI agent to perform 80 to 90% of a campaign against roughly 30 targets, succeeding in a small number of cases; the agent occasionally hallucinated credentials or overstated what it had found.

nodes.control_note: AI will also help system owners and developers secure systems, and systems that keep pace with AI-enabled threats stay far less exposed than those that fall behind. Hardening critical systems and separating them from office networks limit how far one attack spreads.

precedents.parallel: One ransomware attack that encrypted a company's office IT systems led it to shut down a fuel pipeline, the kind of knock-on disruption feared at larger scale.
precedents.outcome: Drivers queued and panic-bought fuel along the US East Coast and thousands of gas stations ran dry; it was a criminal ransomware attack with no AI.

ref.title: US Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Threats to Critical Infrastructure: Examining the Colonial Pipeline Cyberattack (hearing, 8 June 2021)
ref.finding: Colonial's CEO testified that a ransomware attack by a cyber criminal group encrypted the company's IT systems and that it shut the pipeline down; senators described panic buying, gas lines and nearly 16,000 stations without fuel.

precedents.parallel: Malware the US tied to a Russian effort to destabilise Ukraine quickly spread worldwide, showing how far one attack can reach.
precedents.outcome: The US government called it the most destructive and costly cyberattack in history, with billions of dollars in damage across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

ref.title: White House, Statement from the Press Secretary (15 February 2018)
ref.finding: In June 2017 the Russian military launched the most destructive and costly cyber-attack in history, causing billions of dollars in damage across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

nodes.label: AI-assisted art
nodes.summary: Views on AI-assisted art split. In one survey of 459 artists, 80% wanted model makers to disclose which art they train on and 62% saw the models as a threat to art workers[1]; one study of over 4 million artworks on an art-sharing site found artists who adopted text-to-image tools became 25% more productive and about 50% more likely to get a favourite per view, though average novelty fell[2].

refs.title: Lovato et al., Foregrounding Artist Opinions: A Survey Study on Transparency, Ownership, and Fairness in AI Generative Art (arXiv preprint, 2024)
refs.finding: In a survey of 459 artists, 80% agreed model creators should disclose in detail which art and images they train on and 62% agreed AI models are a threat to art workers, while views on the tools' usefulness were mixed.

refs.title: Zhou and Lee, Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art, PNAS Nexus (2024)
refs.finding: In over 4 million artworks from more than 50,000 users of a large art-sharing platform, adopting text-to-image AI raised productivity by 25% and the likelihood of a favourite per view by 50%, while average content and visual novelty fell and peak content novelty rose.

nodes.label: Software that reshapes itself for each person
nodes.summary: AI could build tools on demand, so software bends to each person[1][2]. Omarchy, DHH's Linux setup, ships an agent skill for tailoring it[3], and DHH sees non-technical users remaking it with AI, though 'still a pretty nerdy thing to do'[4]. Columnist Kevin Roose built 'software for one' apps without coding[5], and Raycast's Glaze builds personal Mac apps from a chat[6].

refs.title: Google Research, Generative UI: A rich, custom, visual interactive user experience for any prompt (18 November 2025)
refs.finding: Gemini generates an entire interactive interface for a prompt, rolling out as experiments in the Gemini app and in Search AI Mode for US Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers; human raters preferred only sites designed by human experts over it.

refs.title: Litt, Horowitz, van Hardenberg and Matthews, Malleable software: Restoring user agency in a world of locked-down apps (Ink & Switch, June 2025)
refs.finding: When combined with a malleable environment, AI-assisted development can make it much faster to edit your tools, but AI code generation alone does not address all the barriers to malleability.

refs.title: Omarchy manual, AI chapter (basecamp/omarchy, quattro branch), accessed October 2026
refs.finding: Omarchy ships with a default agent skill for tailoring the system, such as changing the bar or creating a new theme, linked into the skill folders of several agent harnesses; the manual calls it experimental and advises running it in plan mode first. A fresh install asks the user once to pick a default agent, and launchers are provided for 23 agent CLIs including Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, each installed on first use.

refs.title: David Heinemeier Hansson, The malleable computer, April 2026
refs.finding: DHH, Omarchy's creator, writes that open source promised users could change the code they run but hardly any did because it was too hard, and 'Now, with AI, it suddenly isn't'; in the Omarchy world he has seen 'users who aren't super technical making the system their own with the help of AI', though he calls it 'still a pretty nerdy thing to do'.

refs.title: Kevin Roose, Not a Coder? With A.I., Just Having an Idea Can Be Enough, The New York Times, February 2025 (Irish Times reprint, March 2025)
refs.finding: Roose, who cannot code, used AI tools to build what he calls 'software for one', small bespoke apps such as LunchBox Buddy, which suggests his son's lunch from photos of the fridge, a podcast transcriber and a furniture fit checker; he says some 'only sort of work', an email autopilot defeated him for weeks, and vibecoding suits hobby projects better than essential tasks.

refs.title: Raycast, Introducing Glaze, March 2026
refs.finding: Raycast opened a private beta of Glaze on 4 March 2026, available only on macOS at first; it builds desktop apps by chatting with AI, and the apps live on the user's computer, launch instantly and work offline, pitched as 'truly personal'.

nodes.label: AI makes realistic images and edits easy
nodes.summary: Anyone can now make or edit a photo-realistic image from a sentence; over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images[2]. In one set of online experiments, 315 people picked out AI-synthesized faces with 48.2% accuracy, close to chance, and another 223 rated the synthetic faces as more trustworthy than real ones[1].

refs.title: Nightingale and Farid, AI-synthesized faces are indistinguishable from real faces and more trustworthy, PNAS 119(8) e2120481119 (2022)
refs.finding: In online experiments with StyleGAN2 faces, 315 participants told synthetic from real faces with 48.2% accuracy (chance is 50%), 219 participants given training and feedback reached 59.0%, and 223 participants rated synthetic faces as more trustworthy than real ones (4.82 vs 4.48 on a 1 to 7 scale).

refs.title: The Decoder, ChatGPT's image generation explodes with 700M creations in first week (April 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI's COO said over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images amid a viral Ghibli-style trend.

nodes.label: Fun and amusement from AI images
nodes.summary: Turning a photo into a cartoon or a joke into a picture takes seconds. Over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images[1]. In one Pew survey of 5,119 US adults in February 2026, 25% said they use AI chatbots for fun and 24% to create or edit images or videos[2].

refs.title: The Decoder, ChatGPT's image generation explodes with 700M creations in first week (April 2025)
refs.finding: OpenAI's COO said over 130 million users tried ChatGPT's image generation in its first week, creating over 700 million images amid a viral Ghibli-style trend.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, Americans and AI 2026: Chatbots, Smart Devices and Views on Impact (June 2026)
refs.finding: In a survey of 5,119 US adults on Feb. 17 to 23, 2026, 25% said they ever use AI chatbots for fun or entertainment and 24% to create or edit images or videos.

nodes.label: Deepfake nudes used to bully classmates
nodes.summary: AI tools make it easy for teenagers to make fake nudes of classmates: in 2024 five eighth-graders at a Beverly Hills middle school were expelled after students' faces were put on AI-generated nude bodies; the district counted 16 victims[2]. In one survey of 1,200 US people aged 13 to 20, 1 in 8 personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nudes and 1 in 17 had been targeted themselves[1].

refs.title: Thorn, Deepfake Nudes & Young People: Navigating a New Frontier in Technology-Facilitated Nonconsensual Sexual Abuse and Exploitation (March 2025)
refs.finding: In an online survey of 1,200 US young people aged 13 to 20 (Sept. 27 to Oct. 7, 2024), 13% (about 1 in 8) personally knew someone targeted by deepfake nudes and 6% (1 in 17) had been targeted themselves; of 24 self-reported creators, 30% shared the images with people at their school.

refs.title: ABC7 Los Angeles, 5 Beverly Hills students expelled for sharing AI-generated nudes of classmates (March 2024)
refs.finding: Five eighth-graders at Beverly Vista Middle School were expelled after faces of students were superimposed on AI-generated nude bodies; the district said 16 eighth-grade students were victims.

nodes.label: Driverless cars cut road injuries
nodes.summary: Over 271 million driverless miles in five US metro areas through June 2026, Waymo reports 82% fewer injury crashes and 95% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers[2]. An independent California study found automated cars generally had lower crash odds than humans, but higher odds at dawn or dusk and when turning[4]. US investigations followed Waymo cars passing stopped school buses[5][7].

refs.title: WHO, Road traffic injuries fact sheet, 2026
refs.finding: About 1.16 million people die each year in road traffic crashes, and 20 to 50 million more are injured.

refs.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
refs.finding: Over 271.3 million rider-only miles through June 2026 in Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta, Waymo reports 82% fewer any-injury-reported crashes, 95% fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes and 93% fewer pedestrian injury crashes than a human benchmark for the surface streets it drives in those cities.

refs.title: Waymo, New Swiss Re study: Waymo is safer than even the most advanced human-driven vehicles, 2024
refs.finding: Over 25.3 million miles, Waymo had 9 property damage and 2 bodily injury claims against 78 and 26 expected for human drivers, 88% and 92% fewer.

refs.title: Abdel-Aty and Ding, A matched case-control analysis of autonomous vs human-driven vehicle accidents, Nature Communications, 2024
refs.finding: In California crash reports matched by location, time and road type, vehicles with Advanced Driving Systems generally had a lower chance of a crash than human-driven vehicles in similar scenarios, but 5.25 times the odds at dawn or dusk and 1.98 times when turning; the authors note exposure between the two groups is extremely unbalanced.

refs.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE25013 resume, 2025
refs.finding: NHTSA opened a preliminary evaluation on 17 October 2025 into about 2,000 Waymo vehicles after one drove around a stopped school bus in Atlanta on 22 September 2025.

refs.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE26001 resume, 2026
refs.finding: NHTSA opened a preliminary evaluation on 28 January 2026 into about 3,067 Waymo vehicles after a driverless Waymo struck a child within two blocks of a Santa Monica, California elementary school during drop-off on 23 January 2026; Waymo reported minor injuries.

refs.title: NTSB, HWY26FH007: Automated Driving System-Equipped Vehicle Passed School Bus Loading Student Passengers, 2026
refs.finding: On 12 January 2026 in Austin, Texas, a driverless Waymo stopped for a school bus loading students, asked remote assistance whether the bus had active signals, was told no, and drove past with the stop arms extended; the NTSB is also investigating other incidents with Austin ISD buses this school year. Status ongoing.

limiters.limit: Service and safety data limited to a few US cities
limiters.evidence: The safety figures cover rider-only service on surface streets in five US metro areas.

ref.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
ref.finding: Data covers surface streets in Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta, and excludes freeways.

limiters.evidence: US regulators opened an investigation into about 2,000 Waymo vehicles over how they behave around stopped school buses.

ref.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE25013 resume, 2025
ref.finding: Subject: Waymo AV drives around a stopped school bus; population about 2,000 vehicles; opened 17 October 2025.

enablers.action: Publish crash rates against human benchmarks
enablers.evidence: Waymo publishes crash rates by outcome for its rider-only miles, compared with a human benchmark for the same kinds of city streets.

ref.title: Waymo, Safety Impact data hub, data through June 2026
ref.finding: Public crash-rate comparison by outcome over 271.3 million rider-only miles.

precedents.parallel: A computer that corrects the driver's mistakes in a skid is an early, narrow version of the same idea.
precedents.outcome: IIHS studies found it cut fatal single-vehicle crash risk by about half, and NHTSA estimated it saved about 4,100 lives in the US from 2010 to 2014.

ref.title: IIHS, Life-saving benefits of ESC continue to accrue, 2016
ref.finding: ESC lowers fatal single-vehicle crash risk by about 50% and fatal multiple-vehicle crash risk by 20%; NHTSA estimates about 4,100 lives saved in 2010 to 2014.

nodes.label: AI music floods streaming and feeds royalty fraud
nodes.summary: Fully AI-generated tracks passed half of Deezer's new uploads on peak days in June 2026 but drew only 1 to 3% of streams, up to 85% of them fraudulent in 2025[1]. In one US case, a man whose bots streamed AI-generated songs billions of times got 18 months in prison in October 2026[3].

refs.title: Deezer, AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time, July 2026
refs.finding: About 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day were over 50% of new uploads on peak days in June 2026; they make up 1 to 3% of streams, and up to 85% of their streams in 2025 were fraudulent, against 8% across the catalogue. In a November 2025 Ipsos survey of 9,000 people in 8 countries, 97% could not tell AI from human music in a blind test.

refs.title: Bloomberg Law, AI music maker who faked streams pleads guilty on fraud count, March 2026
refs.finding: Michael Smith pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud over bots that streamed hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs billions of times, and agreed to pay about $8 million.

refs.title: Music Business Worldwide, Michael Smith, man behind $8M AI song and bot streaming fraud, sentenced to 18 months in prison, October 2026
refs.finding: On 6 October 2026 a Manhattan federal judge sentenced Smith to 18 months in prison and two years of supervised release and ordered forfeiture of $8,091,843.64; prosecutors said thousands of fake accounts streamed hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs billions of times from 2017 to 2024.

refs.title: Spotify, Spotify strengthens AI protections for artists, songwriters, and producers, September 2025
refs.finding: Spotify removed over 75 million spammy tracks in the past 12 months and announced a spam filter for mass uploads, duplicates and artificially short tracks, AI disclosures in credits through DDEX, and a policy against unauthorized vocal impersonation.

nodes.control_note: The tools that let anyone make a song also make uploads and fake listeners cheap. Detection and royalty rules limit the payout from fraud but not the volume of uploads.

actions.action: Tag AI tracks and keep fraudulent streams out of royalties
actions.evidence: Deezer tags AI tracks, keeps them out of algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, excludes fraudulent streams from royalties and will remove AI tracks used for fraud; the effect on fraud volume is not published.

ref.title: Deezer, AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time, July 2026
ref.finding: AI-detected tracks are excluded from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, fraudulent streams are excluded from royalty payments, and AI tracks used for streaming fraud will be removed.

actions.action: Prosecute streaming fraud
actions.evidence: US prosecutors brought a criminal case that ended in an 18-month prison sentence and forfeiture of about $8.1 million; one case does not show deterrence.

ref.title: Music Business Worldwide, Michael Smith, man behind $8M AI song and bot streaming fraud, sentenced to 18 months in prison, October 2026
ref.finding: Sentenced on 6 October 2026 to 18 months in prison and two years of supervised release, with $8,091,843.64 forfeited.

nodes.label: Surveillance pricing charges each shopper a different price
nodes.summary: Pricing firms can tailor what each shopper pays from personal data such as location and browsing history[1][2]. In one Consumer Reports test with 437 volunteers, Instacart's AI pricing tool showed about three in four items at more than one price, though Instacart said shoppers were tested at random, not by personal data[3]. Maryland, Connecticut and New Jersey have passed bans[4][5][7].

refs.title: FTC, FTC Issues Orders to Eight Companies Seeking Information on Surveillance Pricing, July 2024
refs.finding: On 23 July 2024 the FTC ordered Mastercard, Revionics, Bloomreach, JPMorgan Chase, Task Software, PROS, Accenture and McKinsey to report on their surveillance pricing products, data inputs, customers and effects on the prices consumers pay.

refs.title: FTC, Surveillance Pricing Study Indicates Wide Range of Personal Data Used to Set Individualized Consumer Prices, January 2025
refs.finding: Initial staff findings of 17 January 2025: the intermediaries had at least 250 clients from grocery stores to apparel retailers, and data such as location, demographics, browsing history, mouse movements and items left in a cart can be used to tailor prices; released on a 3-2 vote with only hypothetical examples.

refs.title: Consumer Reports, Instacart's AI-enabled pricing experiments may be inflating your grocery bill, December 2025
refs.finding: 437 volunteers shopping the same items in September 2025 saw about three-quarters of products at multiple prices, gaps of up to 23% per item and baskets at one Seattle Safeway from $114.34 to $123.93; CR estimated about $1,200 a year for a household of four. Instacart said it ran experiments at 10 retailers using its Eversight pricing tools, called the differences negligible and said shoppers were assigned to tests at random without personal or demographic data; a 22 December 2025 update says Instacart stopped offering the technology.

refs.title: Maryland General Assembly, HB 895 (2026), Protection From Predatory Pricing Act
refs.finding: Approved 28 April 2026 as Chapter 154, effective 1 October 2026: bars food retailers and third-party delivery services from dynamic pricing or using consumer personal data to set prices, enforced as an unfair, abusive or deceptive trade practice.

refs.title: Consumer Reports, statement on the signing of Connecticut's surveillance pricing bill into law, June 2026
refs.finding: Governor Lamont signed HB 5563 on 4 June 2026, making Connecticut the second state to curb personalised pricing, effective 1 July 2027; CR notes it still lets firms raise list prices and then give personalised discounts.

refs.title: ICSC, Surveillance pricing legislation gains momentum as states wrap up 2026 sessions, July 2026
refs.finding: Connecticut's law covers retail sellers, including retail food establishments, and third-party delivery services, which from 1 July 2027 may not set customized prices based on a consumer's personal data; it protects group discounts and voluntary loyalty programs. Colorado's governor vetoed HB 1210, which would have restricted individualized price and wage setting, on 2 June 2026.

refs.title: Office of the Governor of New Jersey, Governor Sherrill Signs the Fair Price Protection Act to Shield New Jersey Grocery Shoppers from Surveillance Pricing, July 2026
refs.finding: Posted 23 July 2026: the law bars retailers from using personal data to set individualized prices on groceries and other necessities, does not ban loyalty programs or discounts, and pauses new electronic shelf labels for one year while the state studies them.

refs.title: New York State Senate, Assembly Bill A9349B (2025-2026), prohibiting the use of surveillance pricing
refs.finding: Passed the Senate 39 to 21 and the Assembly on 4 June 2026; bars setting prices through algorithms that use personal data to charge different customers different prices for the same goods or services, allows uniformly offered discounts, and takes effect 180 days after becoming law. The record shows no delivery to or signature by the governor.

refs.title: FTC, FTC Launches Personalized Pricing and Compensation Inquiry, October 2026
refs.finding: On 28 October 2026 the FTC voted 2-0 to order Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart to report whether prices vary from person to person and, for ride-sharing and delivery firms, whether worker pay is personalized; it said the 2024 study examined only middlemen and 'learned nothing about actual pricing decisions'.

nodes.control_note: Automated pricing tools make per-shopper prices cheap to set, and the same data drives targeted discounts that shoppers like and that most new laws protect. Bans and labels can limit it, but price tests are hard for buyers to see.

actions.action: Ban pricing from personal data in groceries
actions.evidence: Maryland's ban for food retailers and delivery apps took effect on 1 October 2026; no enforcement figures are published yet and it does not cover other retail.

ref.title: Maryland General Assembly, HB 895 (2026), Chapter 154
ref.finding: Bars food retailers and third-party delivery service providers from dynamic pricing or using personal data to set prices, effective 1 October 2026.

actions.action: Label prices set from personal data
actions.evidence: New York requires a notice next to such prices with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; a label informs shoppers but does not stop the practice.

ref.title: New York General Business Law section 349-a, algorithmic pricing disclosure
ref.finding: Prices set by personalized algorithmic pricing must carry the notice THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA; a court may impose up to $1,000 per violation.

actions.action: Compel firms to disclose personalised pricing and pay
actions.evidence: The FTC's 2024 orders to eight intermediaries produced only initial findings with hypothetical examples; in October 2026 it ordered nine airlines, ride-hail, delivery and retail firms to report on personalised prices and worker pay within 45 days.

ref.title: FTC, FTC Launches Personalized Pricing and Compensation Inquiry, October 2026
ref.finding: Special orders approved 2-0 on 28 October 2026 to Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart; recipients have 45 days to respond, and the FTC said the 2024 study of middlemen taught it nothing about actual pricing decisions.

actions.action: Treat undisclosed personal-data pricing as deceptive
actions.evidence: The FTC proposed an enforcement policy statement in August 2026 saying undisclosed use of personal data to set prices could violate the FTC Act; the chairman said the agency cannot ban personalised pricing outright.

ref.title: FTC, FTC Seeks Comment on Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing, August 2026
ref.finding: Published for comment on a 2-0 vote on 19 August 2026, with comments due 18 September 2026; undisclosed collection or use of personal data for personalized pricing could violate the FTC Act's ban on unfair or deceptive practices, and the FTC lacks authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances.

precedents.parallel: An online retailer quietly showed different customers different prices for the same goods, and the backlash came when shoppers compared notes.
precedents.outcome: Over five days Amazon varied discounts of 20% to 40% on 68 DVD titles, then refunded 6,896 customers an average of $3.10 and promised that any future test would give buyers the lowest test price; Amazon said the discounts were random, not based on customer demographic information.

ref.title: Amazon.com Issues Statement Regarding Random Price Testing (Amazon, September 2000)
ref.finding: A five-day test on 68 DVD titles at discounts of 20% to 40%; 6,896 customers were refunded an average of $3.10.

precedents.event: Northeastern audit of price steering on shopping sites
precedents.parallel: Researchers using hundreds of real shoppers and many fake accounts found sites already tailored prices and results to the person, years before AI made it cheap.
precedents.outcome: Of 16 popular retail and travel sites tested in April and May 2014, four retailers and five travel sites showed some personalisation, such as member-only hotel rates at Orbitz and Cheaptickets and Expedia and Hotels.com steering some users to pricier hotels; most experiments found none.

ref.title: Study: some online shoppers pay more than others (Northeastern University, October 2014, on Hannak et al., IMC 2014)
ref.finding: Nine of 16 e-commerce sites showed evidence of personalisation, with some prices varying by hundreds of dollars.

nodes.label: Data-centre demand raises household power bills
nodes.summary: On the US PJM grid, the market monitor ties 46.2% of capacity charges across four auctions to data-centre load[1]. Maryland's consumer advocate estimated two auctions, driven mostly by data centres, added $10.43 to $20.81 a month to residential bills at five utilities[2]. From 2019 to 2025, though, states with the fastest load growth mostly saw real average retail prices fall[3].

refs.title: Monitoring Analytics (PJM Independent Market Monitor), Market Monitor Report, MC Information Webinar, July 2026
refs.finding: Of $16.4 billion in 2028/2029 capacity market charges, $6.3 billion (38.2%) resulted from data-centre load; over the last four auctions data-centre load accounts for $29.4 billion, or 46.2% of total capacity charges. In January to June 2026 the total cost of wholesale power was $114.50 per MWh against $103.40 without the data-centre impact, an increase of $11.11 (9.7%).

refs.title: Maryland Office of People's Counsel, Data center power demands drive record power auction prices with varying impacts on Maryland customers, July 2025
refs.finding: The 2026/2027 PJM capacity auction cleared at a record $329 per MW-day, and would have cleared at $389 without the cap; most of the increase in demand, more than 5,400 MW above the year before, came from data centres. Estimated cumulative residential monthly bill increases from the last two auctions, against 2024/2025, were $16.49 at BGE, $17.68 at Pepco and SMECO, $10.43 at Delmarva Power and $20.81 at Potomac Edison.

refs.title: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and The Brattle Group, Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update, 2026 edition, April 2026
refs.finding: US all-sector average retail prices rose 5.3% in nominal terms in 2025; in real terms they were 3% above 2019. From 2019 to 2025 the states with the highest load growth generally saw real all-sector prices decline, and the presence of significant data-centre load does not appear to alter that conclusion; the relationship for residential prices is less clear. A PJM case study shows accelerated load growth with supply and delivery constraints leading to significant price increases, with data-centre load growth linked to a 174% increase in revenues from the 2025/2026 capacity auction.

nodes.control_note: Data centres draw on the same grid as homes, so their demand lands on shared prices where supply is tight. Tariffs that make large new loads pay for the capacity they reserve shield other customers from paying for unused grid investment, but they do not add supply or take data centres out of the shared capacity market.

actions.action: Make large new loads pay for the capacity they reserve
actions.evidence: Ohio's regulator made new data centres above 25 MW in AEP Ohio's territory pay for at least 85% of their subscribed capacity for up to 12 years; it covers only one utility's territory.

ref.title: POWER Magazine, Regulator approves AEP Ohio's landmark data center tariff, July 2025
ref.finding: The PUCO order of 9 July 2025 requires new data-centre customers above 25 MW to pay for at least 85% of subscribed monthly capacity for up to 12 years, with a four-year ramp, exit fees and financial assurance; the commission said it safeguards other customers from cost-shifting risks of underused investments.

actions.action: Move data-centre load into its own capacity auction
actions.evidence: PJM's market monitor proposes a dedicated auction so that data centres pay for their own capacity rather than raising the price everyone else pays.

ref.title: Monitoring Analytics (PJM Independent Market Monitor), Market Monitor Report, MC Information Webinar, July 2026
ref.finding: It is the IMM's position that data-centre load should be removed from the capacity market and procured through a dedicated auction, so that data centres pay for their own capacity and do not impose capacity costs on other customers.

precedents.event: Crypto-mining power rates in upstate New York
precedents.parallel: A new kind of computing load arrived in small towns with finite cheap power and pushed up what households paid.
precedents.outcome: New York regulators let municipal utilities charge separate rates to customers above 300 kW and 250 kWh per square foot a year, after average residential bills in Plattsburgh rose $10 a month in January, which regulators blamed on two mining firms.

ref.title: Utility Dive, Munis to charge cryptocurrency miners higher power prices in New York, March 2018
ref.finding: The New York PSC allowed municipal utilities to create a tariff for high-density load customers with maximum demand above 300 kW and load density above 250 kWh per square foot per year; regulators said average Plattsburgh residential bills jumped $10 a month in January because of two cryptocurrency companies, whose monthly electricity costs would have risen more than 60% had the new rates applied.

nodes.label: Prompt injection hijacks AI agents
nodes.summary: Instructions hidden in email, web pages or documents can hijack AI agents that read them. In one red-teaming competition, about 1.8 million attacks on 22 frontier agents produced over 60,000 policy violations[1], and one crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data, a flaw Microsoft says it fixed[2][3]. The UK NCSC says prompt injection may never be fully mitigated[5].

refs.title: Zou et al., Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: The AI Agent Red Teaming Challenge, run on Gray Swan Arena from 8 March to 6 April 2025 and sponsored by the UK AI Security Institute alongside OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, targeted 22 frontier agents across 44 simulated deployment scenarios; 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks produced over 60,000 successful policy violations such as unauthorised data access and illicit financial actions. Nearly all agents showed violations for most behaviours within 10 to 100 queries, attacks transferred across models, and robustness correlated little with model size, capability or inference-time compute.

refs.title: Reddy and Gujral, EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: CVE-2025-32711 in Microsoft 365 Copilot allowed remote, unauthenticated data exfiltration via a single crafted email with no user interaction, bypassing Microsoft's cross-prompt-injection classifier, link redaction and the content security policy.

refs.title: Cybersecurity Dive, Critical flaw in Microsoft Copilot could have allowed zero-click attack, June 2025
refs.finding: Microsoft's advisory said the EchoLeak issue (CVE-2025-32711) was fully addressed and no further action was necessary by customers; Adir Gruss, CTO of Aim Security, whose researchers found the flaw, said there was no evidence any customers were actually targeted.

refs.title: Brunner, Liu and Pande, Google, AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web, April 2026
refs.finding: Scanning Common Crawl snapshots of 2 to 3 billion pages each, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Google DeepMind researchers found a relative increase of 32% in detections in the malicious category between November 2025 and February 2026; malicious injections included data exfiltration and destruction attempts such as file deletion. Observed activity showed limited sophistication, with no significant amounts of advanced attacks, and the authors expect both the scale and sophistication of attempts to grow.

refs.title: NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), 8 December 2025
refs.finding: Because LLMs do not distinguish between data and instructions, prompt injection may never be totally mitigated in the way SQL injection can be; the NCSC advises treating it as a residual risk that no product or appliance fully removes, constraining what LLM systems can do with deterministic safeguards and logging tool and API calls.

nodes.control_note: Agents are useful because they read outside content and act on it, and that same reading is the attacker's way in. Narrow permissions and designs that keep untrusted text out of control decisions limit the damage, but no filter removes the risk.

actions.action: Keep untrusted data out of an agent's control flow
actions.evidence: One design that fixes the plan from the user's trusted query and blocks private data from leaving through unauthorised flows solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% for an undefended agent.

ref.title: Debenedetti et al., Defeating Prompt Injections by Design, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: The defence wraps the LLM in a protective system layer that extracts control and data flows from the trusted query, so retrieved untrusted data cannot change program flow; it solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, compared with 84% undefended.

actions.action: Cut agent privileges to those of the content it reads
actions.evidence: The UK NCSC advises deployers to rely on deterministic, non-LLM controls on what a system can do and to log tool and API calls, since detection and model training can only reduce the chance an attack works.

ref.title: NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), 8 December 2025
ref.finding: Recommends secure design with deterministic, non-LLM safeguards that constrain the system's actions, cites the principle that an LLM's privileges should drop to those of any party whose content it processes, and advises logging inputs, outputs, tool and API calls; warns against deny-listing known-bad content because attacks can be rephrased in endless ways.

precedents.event: SQL injection breaches of card processors
precedents.parallel: Software that mixed untrusted input with commands let attackers take over databases, the flaw class the NCSC compares prompt injection with.
precedents.outcome: A 2009 US federal indictment charged Albert Gonzalez and two unnamed hackers in a conspiracy built on SQL injection attacks against Heartland Payment Systems, 7-Eleven, Hannaford and two other retailers; the Heartland attack led to the theft of more than about 130 million card numbers and the Hannaford attack about 4.2 million.

ref.title: United States v. Albert Gonzalez, indictment, US District Court for the District of New Jersey, 2009
ref.finding: Beginning on or about 26 December 2007 Heartland was the victim of a SQL Injection Attack that resulted in the theft of more than approximately 130 million credit and debit card numbers; 7-Eleven (from about August 2007) was also hit by a SQL Injection Attack, and an attack on a company related to Hannaford in about early November 2007 led to malware on Hannaford's network and the theft of about 4.2 million card numbers.

nodes.label: Gas-powered data centres pollute nearby neighbourhoods
nodes.summary: AI data centres' gas turbines can pollute nearby air: after xAI set up 35 unpermitted ones in South Memphis, one satellite analysis found peak nitrogen dioxide rose 79% next to the site, though a nearby power plant and traffic may also have contributed[1]. One study projects US data centres' yearly air pollution health burden could pass $20 billion by 2028[6].

refs.title: TIME, 'We Are the Last of the Forgotten': Inside the Memphis Community Battling Elon Musk's xAI, August 2025
refs.finding: xAI brought in 35 unpermitted temporary methane gas turbines, which on manufacturer data could emit 1,200 to 2,000 tons of nitrogen oxides a year; xAI insisted they were legal, generated negligible pollution and were only temporary. University of Tennessee, Knoxville researchers, at TIME's request, used NASA and ESA satellite data and found average nitrogen dioxide up 3% comparing the periods before June 2024 and afterward, and peak concentrations up 79% from pre-xAI levels in areas immediately surrounding the data centre and 9% in Boxtown; they said the changes likely reflect the combined influence of gas-fired sources, including the nearby TVA plant, and that motor vehicles may have contributed.
