refs.title: Southern Environmental Law Center, New study finds proposed xAI gas plant could worsen regional air pollution, cause millions of dollars in annual health damages, February 2026
refs.finding: A study by EmPower Analytics Group for SELC found the proposed permit for 41 permanent turbines in Southaven would allow nearly 20 tons of fine particle pollution a year plus hundreds of tons of precursor pollutants, raising fine particles by up to 0.5 micrograms per cubic metre in some communities and causing $30 million to $44 million in annual health damages; xAI had already installed 27 unpermitted turbines at a nearby location in Southaven.

refs.title: Mississippi Free Press, Mississippi Permit Board Grants xAI's Request for 41 Southaven Gas Turbines to Power Memphis Data Center, March 2026
refs.finding: On 10 March 2026 the Mississippi Environmental Quality Permit Board unanimously approved a construction permit for xAI affiliate MZX Tech to install 41 methane gas-fired turbines, replacing the 27 unpermitted turbines at the facility; the permit requires control technologies and pollution modelling, regulators and company officials argued the required emissions modelling shows its limits keep xAI compliant with air quality standards, and MDEQ has said the earlier turbines need no permit because they are temporary-mobile.

refs.title: Earthjustice, NAACP Sues xAI for Illegal Pollution from Data Center Power Plant, April 2026
refs.finding: On 14 April 2026 the NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference sued xAI in federal court in the Northern District of Mississippi for running 27 gas turbines in Southaven without an air permit, with potential yearly emissions of more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides and up to 180 tons of fine particulate matter.

refs.title: Mississippi Today (Daily Journal), Judge denies Trump administration request to dismiss NAACP lawsuit against xAI, October 2026
refs.finding: US District Judge Debra Brown let the Trump administration intervene in the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI but denied the Justice Department's request to dismiss it, writing that the EPA's enforcement role does not mean the federal government retains complete control over Clean Air Act litigation; the NAACP has asked the court to bar the turbines unless they go through state permitting.

refs.title: Han, Wu, Li, Wierman and Ren, Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers, arXiv 2024, revised June 2026
refs.finding: Modelling of criteria air pollutant emissions projects the total annual public health burden of US data centres could rise to more than $20 billion by 2028; the national impact is modest, but in the most affected counties the per-household burden can reach about seven times the national average.

refs.title: TechCrunch, Air quality tests around xAI's Memphis data center raise questions, June 2025
refs.finding: Third-party tests for the City of Memphis on 13 and 16 June 2025 at three sites found none of the 10 pollutants tested at dangerous levels; winds on those days were unlikely to carry pollutants to the sites, the tests did not include ozone, and SELC said monitors placed against buildings could interfere with results.

nodes.control_note: On-site gas turbines let a data centre run before the grid can supply it, and the people living downwind pay in dirtier air. Permits with emission controls and caps, and siting that counts health costs, can cut the harm, but only where regulators treat the turbines as power plants.

actions.action: Permit on-site turbines only with emission caps
actions.evidence: The Shelby County Health Department approved 15 permanent turbines for xAI in July 2025 with caps on 12-month rolling emissions; most complaints were about the temporary turbines, which the permit did not cover.

ref.title: Action News 5, Health dept. grants permit for xAI turbines, July 2025
ref.finding: The permit approved on 2 July 2025 covers 15 permanent natural gas turbines, caps 12-month rolling emission rates that xAI must record monthly, and lists standards for nitrogen oxide, ammonia and hazardous air pollutants; the health department said most SELC concerns targeted the temporary turbines, due to be removed by the end of July.

actions.action: Sue under the Clean Air Act over unpermitted turbines
actions.evidence: The NAACP asks a federal court to stop xAI's unpermitted turbines in Southaven, require the best available control technology and impose daily penalties; the case was pending.

ref.title: Earthjustice, NAACP Sues xAI for Illegal Pollution from Data Center Power Plant, April 2026
ref.finding: The suit filed on 14 April 2026 seeks a declaration that xAI violated the Clean Air Act, an order to stop operating unpermitted turbines and install best available control technology, and penalties for each day of violation.

actions.action: Count health costs when siting data centres and scheduling their load
actions.evidence: The authors of one modelling study propose health-informed computing, which factors public health costs into where and when data centres run, and reporting of health impacts alongside energy use.

ref.title: Han, Wu, Li, Wierman and Ren, Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers, arXiv 2024, revised June 2026
ref.finding: Proposes a health-informed computing framework that brings public health costs into data-centre resource management across space and time, and recommends energy reporting that includes public health impacts.

precedents.event: Greenidge crypto-mining power plant permit denial
precedents.parallel: A new kind of computing load turned a gas power plant into the power source for its owner's own machines, and regulators had to decide whether the pollution was acceptable.
precedents.outcome: Greenidge began proof-of-work crypto mining at its retrofitted gas plant on Seneca Lake in 2019; New York's environmental regulator denied its air permit in 2022 for not complying with the state's climate law, but in November 2025 signed an agreement ending the legal fight that requires a 44% cut in permitted greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and a 25% cut in actual emissions under a renewed permit.

ref.title: Rochester Beacon, DEC signs agreement with Greenidge, ends legal battle, November 2025
ref.finding: Greenidge took over the site in 2017 and began proof-of-work crypto mining in 2019 at the retrofitted natural gas plant; DEC denied its air permit in 2022 for noncompliance with New York's climate law, and in November 2025 DEC signed an agreement under which Greenidge must cut permitted greenhouse gas emissions by 44% by 2030 and actual emissions by 25%, submit a permit modification application, and both sides withdraw their appeals.

nodes.label: AI reads lost ancient texts
nodes.summary: Machine learning is recovering writing that people could not read. A June 2026 preprint reports the first Herculaneum scroll, PHerc. 1667, virtually unwrapped and read in full without opening it[3]. For Latin inscriptions the AI's suggestions are not answers: the right restoration is in its top 20 guesses 73% of the time for gaps up to ten characters[6].

refs.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
refs.finding: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger shared the $700,000 Grand Prize for reading four passages of 140 characters plus 11 more columns, more than 2,000 characters, using machine-learning ink detection and automatic segmentation of the CT scan; about 5% of the first scroll was read and about 95% remained unread.

refs.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
refs.finding: Marcel Roth and Micha Nowak won the first $60,000 First Title Prize for PHerc. 172, held by the Bodleian Libraries; an ink detection model run on autosegmentation revealed the title, which papyrologists read as Philodemus, On Vices, probably Book 1, the first title of a still-rolled Herculaneum scroll ever recovered noninvasively. The book number is less certain and segmentation still sometimes jumps between sheets.

refs.title: Angelotti et al., Complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus, arXiv preprint, June 2026
refs.finding: A 27-author team including Vesuvius Challenge papyrologists and Brent Seales used phase-contrast X-ray microtomography at the ESRF BM18 beamline, improved unrolling software and machine learning to virtually unwrap and read PHerc. 1667, which they describe as the first Herculaneum papyrus fully unrolled and read without physical opening; they also recovered the title of PHerc. 139 as Philodemus, On Gods, Book 8. The paper is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

refs.title: Smithsonian Magazine, Scientists Have Deciphered the Surviving Fragments of a 2,000-Year-Old Philosophical Treatise Frozen in Time by Mount Vesuvius' Eruption, June 2026
refs.finding: The Vesuvius Challenge, launched in 2023 by University of Kentucky computer scientist Brent Seales with two Silicon Valley investors, used X-ray imaging, virtual unwrapping and AI to recover all surviving text of PHerc. 1667, roughly 20 columns of ancient Greek discussing ideas central to Stoicism; more than half of the scroll had been lost to earlier attempts to open it, and the findings are in a team preprint.

refs.title: Assael et al., Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks, Nature, July 2025
refs.finding: Aeneas, a generative neural network, retrieves parallels between inscriptions, uses images and restores text of any length; in a large study historians found its parallels useful research starting points in 90% of cases, their confidence in key tasks rose 44%, historians paired with it beat both humans and AI alone on restoration and geographical attribution, and its dates were on average 13 years from ground-truth ranges.

refs.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
refs.finding: Trained on the Latin Epigraphic Dataset of over 176,000 Latin inscriptions, Aeneas reaches top-20 restoration accuracy of 73% in gaps of up to ten characters and 58% when the gap length is unknown, attributes texts to one of 62 Roman provinces with 72% accuracy, and was tested with 23 historians.

limiters.limit: Most of the text is still unread
limiters.evidence: After the 2023 breakthrough about 95% of the first scroll remained unread; the next goals were 90% of four scanned scrolls and laying the foundation to read all 300 scrolls, and the first rolled scroll was read in full only in June 2026.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
ref.finding: About 5% of the first scroll had been unwrapped and read; the next goal was 90% of the four scrolls scanned so far, laying the foundation to read all 300 scrolls.

limiters.evidence: Even among its top 20 suggestions, the inscription model finds the right text only 58% of the time when the gap length is unknown.

ref.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
ref.finding: Top-20 restoration accuracy is 73% in gaps of up to ten characters and 58% when the restoration length is unknown.

limiters.evidence: The book number in the first recovered title is less certain, and segmentation of the scan still sometimes jumps to an adjacent sheet.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
ref.finding: The book number is less certain for now, the book does not match On Flattery as expected, and sheet switches still occur in segmentation, though they are improving.

enablers.action: Fund open prizes for reading the scrolls
enablers.counters: Most of the text is still unread
enablers.evidence: A $700,000 Grand Prize in 2023 and a $60,000 First Title Prize in 2025 went to outside contestants who improved segmentation and ink detection.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the scrolls!, February 2024
ref.finding: The 2023 Grand Prize of $700,000 went to three contestants; the project set further goals to read 90% of four scanned scrolls.

enablers.action: Have papyrologists review each AI reading
enablers.evidence: The papyrological team independently reviewed the ink detection output before the title of PHerc. 172 was announced, and flagged which parts of the reading were uncertain.

ref.title: Vesuvius Challenge, $60,000 First Title Prize Awarded, May 2025
ref.finding: The papyrological team led by Federica Nicolardi independently reviewed the output and unanimously read the author as Philodemus and the title as On Vices, while marking the book number as less certain.

enablers.action: Release models and datasets openly
enablers.evidence: An interactive version of the inscription model is free to use, and its code and dataset are open source, so other historians can test its suggestions.

ref.title: Google DeepMind, Aeneas transforms how historians connect the past, July 2025
ref.finding: An interactive version of Aeneas is free to use, and the team is open-sourcing its code and dataset on GitHub.

precedents.event: Virtual unwrapping of the En-Gedi scroll
precedents.parallel: Before machine learning, scanning and software already let researchers read a charred scroll that could never be opened by hand.
precedents.outcome: A team led by Brent Seales scanned a burned scroll excavated in 1970 at the synagogue of En Gedi, Israel, and virtually unwrapped it to reveal Leviticus, 35 lines across five wraps with 18 preserved and 17 reconstructed; it was the first severely damaged, ink-based scroll unrolled and identified noninvasively.

ref.title: University of Kentucky, Virtually Unwrapping the En-Gedi Scroll, September 2016
ref.finding: Published in Science Advances on 21 September 2016: virtual unwrapping of high-resolution scans revealed Leviticus in a charred scroll that likely will never be physically opened, the earliest copy of a Pentateuchal book ever found in a Holy Ark.

nodes.label: Data-centre tax breaks drain state budgets
nodes.summary: US states court AI-driven data centres with sales tax exemptions whose cost has outrun forecasts[1][2]. Ohio's exemption cost $1.6 billion in 2025, eleven times the original estimate of $136 million[1], and 14 of 38 states with such incentives did not disclose lost revenue[5]. Georgia's evaluation, though, found the gain to the state economy significantly higher than the revenue forgone[3].

refs.title: Signal Ohio via WTOP News, Ohio data center tax break cost $1.4 billion more than expected in 2025, May 2026
refs.finding: Figures from the Ohio Department of Taxation show the data-centre sales tax exemption cost the state $554.9 million in 2024, about four times the department's forecast, plus $166.8 million in lost local sales taxes; in 2025 it cost $1.6 billion, eleven times the original estimate of $136 million. Lawmakers voted to end the break and Governor Mike DeWine vetoed the repeal.

refs.title: Paul Cobler, Texas Tribune, Texas' multibillion-dollar sales tax exemption for data centers is growing, while audits lag, July 2026
refs.finding: The state forecast in 2025 that it would lose $3.2 billion in sales tax revenue over the next two years from data centres, a total the Comptroller's Office acknowledged was almost certainly an underestimate because more data centres are applying for the exemption; the exemption cost $5.4 million in 2015. Of 138 qualified data centres only 20 had been audited, and six were breaching the terms: four missed job-creation requirements, one fell short on square footage and one lost its required power agreement; those out of compliance must repay the waived taxes. The article ties the growth in data centres to artificial intelligence raising demand for computing power.

refs.title: Georgia Department of Audits and Accounts, Tax Incentive Evaluation: Georgia Data Center Sales & Use Tax Exemption, December 2025, revised January 2026
refs.finding: The University of Georgia's Carl Vinson Institute of Government estimated forgone state tax revenue of $474.2 million in FY 2025 and attributed 30% of Georgia's data centres to the exemption, so 70% would exist without it. Activity attributed to the exemption generated $34.6 million in state tax from construction and $6.9 million from operations, a fiscal return of 4%, while state economic growth, an economic return of 289%, was significantly higher than the forgone revenue.

refs.title: Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, Data Centers in Virginia, Report 598, December 2024
refs.finding: Since 2010 Virginia has exempted data centres from its retail sales and use tax; the exemption provided $928 million in tax savings in FY23 and about 90% of the industry uses it. The industry is estimated to contribute 74,000 jobs, $5.5 billion in labour income and $9.1 billion in GDP a year, mostly from the construction phase rather than ongoing operations. The exemption returns 48 cents in state revenue per $1 spent, against 41 cents for the average Virginia incentive, and like most incentives does not pay for itself; companies report it is an important factor in where they locate.

refs.title: Kevin Hardy, Stateline via KOTA, Many states don't report losses from data center tax breaks, study says, April 2026
refs.finding: A Good Jobs First report found 14 states (Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah) failed to disclose revenue lost to data-centre incentives, in most cases in violation of Governmental Accounting Standards Board rules; Georgia, Virginia and Texas report losing $1 billion or more a year; 38 states offer dedicated data-centre tax incentives, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

nodes.control_note: States offer the breaks because rival states do and companies say they weigh them when choosing a site, so no state wants to drop them first. Pauses on new approvals, audits with clawbacks and taxes on data-centre power use can limit the cost, but projects already approved keep their breaks.

actions.action: Pause approvals of new exemptions
actions.evidence: Ohio's governor told the state's Tax Credit Authority to stop approving new data-centre sales tax exemptions while officials review their costs; projects already approved keep their breaks.

ref.title: The Register, Ohio hits pause on datacenter tax breaks draining its coffers, June 2026
ref.finding: Governor Mike DeWine directed the Tax Credit Authority to stop approving new data-centre sales tax exemption requests while officials review the industry's costs and impacts; the pause covers only new approvals, and projects already approved keep their breaks. Good Jobs First puts the 2025 cost of Ohio's exemption at more than $1.5 billion, about 11 times the state's $136 million forecast.

actions.action: Tax data-centre electricity use
actions.evidence: Virginia kept its exemption but taxes data-centre electricity at $0.011 per kWh from July 2026 to June 2028, capped at $600 million a year, which recovers part of the revenue without ending the break.

ref.title: Holland & Knight, Virginia Preserves Data Center Tax Incentive, Adds New Electricity Consumption Tax, August 2026
ref.finding: Virginia kept its sales and use tax exemption for qualifying data-centre equipment and instead imposed a tax of $0.011 per kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed by data-centre operators from 1 July 2026 through 30 June 2028, with annual collections capped at $600 million and up to $1.2 billion in additional revenue over the biennium.

precedents.parallel: A state pledged billions in tax credits to win a high-technology investment on promises of jobs and capital that the company later scaled back.
precedents.outcome: Foxconn would have qualified for $2.85 billion in Wisconsin tax credits for investing $10 billion and creating 13,000 jobs; in April 2021 a new contract for a smaller facility cut that to up to $80 million for 1,454 jobs and $676 million of investment by 2026, and let the state recover incentives on default.

ref.title: Associated Press via KSAT, Foxconn deal with Wisconsin lowers tax breaks to $80 million, April 2021
ref.finding: Under the original deal Foxconn would have qualified for $2.85 billion in state tax credits if it invested $10 billion and created 13,000 jobs; the new contract lets it qualify for $80 million if it employs 1,454 people and invests $676 million by 2026, allows the state to recover 100% of incentives paid each year in the event of a default, and covers a smaller facility, which Foxconn said reflected unanticipated market fluctuations.

nodes.label: Propaganda networks seed chatbot answers
nodes.summary: Propaganda sites can be written for machines, so chatbots that train on or search the web repeat their claims[1]. In one March 2025 NewsGuard audit, 10 leading AI tools repeated false narratives laundered by the Pravda network 33% of the time[3]. One peer-reviewed audit of 416 chatbot answers found 5% supported disinformation, and blames data voids rather than deliberate grooming[5].

refs.title: Newport and Jankowicz (American Sunlight Project), Russian networks flood the Internet with propaganda, aiming to corrupt AI chatbots, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, March 2025
refs.finding: The American Sunlight Project estimates the pro-Russia Pravda network publishes at least 3.6 million articles a year, likely an underestimate, across 182 domains and subdomains targeting at least 74 countries and regions in 12 languages; the authors believe the network targets an automated audience of search-optimisation crawlers and scrapers that collect training data rather than human readers. NewsGuard and the Atlantic Council's DFRLab confirmed that some major AI chatbots cited Pravda network content.

refs.title: NewsGuard (Marchl, Chomnalez and Blachez), Anthropic's AI Chatbot Is Leaning More on Russian and Iranian Propaganda Sources, NewsGuard Audit Finds, May 2026
refs.finding: NewsGuard reports that the Pravda network published 6.3 million articles repeating 115 false claims in 2025. In a late April 2026 test of the free version of Claude on 10 Russian false claims from January to April 2026, the chatbot repeated the false claims in 3 of 20 typical-user prompts (15%).

refs.title: NewsGuard, A Well-funded Moscow-based Global 'News' Network has Infected Western Artificial Intelligence Tools Worldwide with Russian Propaganda, March 2025
refs.finding: An audit of the 10 leading generative AI tools found they repeated false narratives laundered by the Pravda network 33% of the time; the network published 3,600,000 articles in 2024.

refs.title: Institute for Strategic Dialogue, Talking points: When chatbots surface Russian state media, October 2025
refs.finding: Across 300 queries about the war in Ukraine in English, Spanish, French, German and Italian, Russian state-attributed content appeared in 18% of responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek: 11% for neutral queries, 18% for biased and 24% for malicious ones. ChatGPT cited the most Russian sources, Gemini the fewest and was the only one to show safety warnings, and only two links came from the Pravda network; ISD says limited data access makes it impossible to tell whether LLM grooming happens at scale.

refs.title: Alyukov, Makhortykh, Voronovici and Sydorova, LLMs grooming or data voids? LLM-powered chatbot references to Kremlin disinformation reflect information gaps, not manipulation, HKS Misinformation Review 2025
refs.finding: Of 416 responses from ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Copilot and Grok-2 to 13 prompts, collected in Manchester and Bern in April 2025, 5% (21) supported disinformation and 8% referenced Pravda domains, almost all from Copilot, mostly in reply to niche prompts; of the 30 answers that cited Pravda without supporting disinformation, about two-thirds cautioned that the claims were unverified or tied them to disinformation outlets. The authors attribute this to data voids, gaps in credible information, rather than foreign manipulation, and call their study preliminary and narrow.

nodes.control_note: Chatbots that answer from the web take in whatever covers a question, so a network that floods thinly covered topics can get its claims cited. Labelling or excluding state-attributed sources and filling data voids with credible coverage reduce the exposure, but cannot vet every new site.

actions.action: Label or exclude state-attributed sources in answers
actions.evidence: ISD urges AI companies to build a shared list of state-attributed sources and either blacklist them or label them with context; in its test only Gemini showed safety warnings for biased or malicious prompts.

ref.title: Institute for Strategic Dialogue, Talking points: When chatbots surface Russian state media, October 2025
ref.finding: Recommends that AI companies build a shared repository of state-attributed sources, blacklist them or clearly label them with context on their origin and ownership, and sign the EU Code of Conduct on Disinformation, and that the European Commission clarify how sanctions on state media apply to chatbot outputs and how they are enforced under the Digital Services Act.

actions.action: Warn on data-void queries and fill the gaps with credible coverage
actions.evidence: The authors of one audit propose warning banners for questions that fall into data voids, passed on to chatbots that use search, and working with news organisations to fill those gaps in advance.

ref.title: Alyukov, Makhortykh, Voronovici and Sydorova, LLMs grooming or data voids? LLM-powered chatbot references to Kremlin disinformation reflect information gaps, not manipulation, HKS Misinformation Review 2025
ref.finding: Recommends that search engines show warning banners for data-void queries and pass these warnings to integrated chatbots, that search developers work with reputable news organisations to fill data voids in advance, and that AI companies share aggregated usage data and be more transparent about how sources shape answers.

precedents.event: Google demotes hoaxes and conspiracy pages in Search
precedents.parallel: Before chatbots answered from the web, search engines returned offensive or clearly misleading results for some queries, such as Holocaust denial pages, and had to change how they weigh sources.
precedents.outcome: Google said around 0.25% of its daily queries had been returning offensive or clearly misleading content, and adjusted its ranking signals to surface more authoritative pages and demote low-quality content.

ref.title: Ben Gomes (Google), Our latest quality improvements for Search, April 2017
ref.finding: Around 0.25% of Google's daily queries had been returning offensive or clearly misleading content; after Holocaust denial results surfaced in December 2016, Google adjusted ranking signals to surface more authoritative pages and demote low-quality content, updated its Search Quality Rater Guidelines with examples of misleading information, hoaxes and unsupported conspiracy theories for raters to flag, and made it easier to flag Autocomplete predictions and Featured Snippets.

nodes.label: Data centres drop off the grid at once
nodes.summary: Data centres switch to backup power when grid voltage dips, so a single fault can make many leave the grid at once[1]. In July 2026 nearly 4,000 MW of data-centre load in Northern Virginia tripped offline after one fault, PJM's largest such event[2]. Changed backup settings helped near one site in April 2026, but NERC says the risk is increasing[5].

refs.title: NERC, Incident Review: Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions, January 2025
refs.finding: On 10 July 2024 a lightning arrestor failed on a 230 kV line in the Eastern Interconnection, causing six successive faults in 82 seconds, all cleared properly; coincident with them about 1,500 MW of load, exclusively data-centre load, was disconnected on the customer side as data centres transferred to backup power. The grid has not historically experienced simultaneous load losses of this magnitude in response to a fault. Frequency rose to 60.047 Hz and voltage to 1.07 per unit, and operators removed shunt capacitor banks to bring voltage back to normal; about 1,260 MW did not return for hours. NERC says the disturbance did not cause significant operating issues, but the risk could quickly increase as data-centre loads grow.

refs.title: PJM Inside Lines, PJM, Dominion Review Large Load Transfer Event, August 2026
refs.finding: On 22 July 2026 nearly 4,000 MW of data-centre load in Northern Virginia, in the Dominion zone, tripped offline, approximately 3,800 MW by the detailed timeline and the largest such event in PJM history; a mechanical failure removed a 230 kV line and the fault was properly cleared, but data centres disconnected in a first drop of 2,970 MW and a second wave of 1,099 MW. PJM load fell from 99,984 MW to 96,205 MW, and PJM recovered its area control error limit within nine minutes, well within NERC's 30-minute standard. Similar events in the Dominion zone caused load transfers of about 1,500 MW each on 10 July 2024 and 17 February 2025.

refs.title: Utility Dive, Sudden data center load losses prompt NERC alert, recommendations, April 2026
refs.finding: NERC describes widespread and unexpected customer-initiated load reductions, mostly in 2024 and 2025, in which 1,000 MW or more dropped off the bulk power system, in the Eastern and Texas interconnections since 2022; it said the increase of large-load events coincides with an increase in large-load penetration. Its planned Level 3 alert covers the modelling, study, monitoring and commissioning of large loads, including data centers for artificial intelligence, and NERC said entities generally did not have sufficient processes to address emerging computational loads.

refs.title: POWER Magazine, FERC Orders Mandatory NERC Reliability Standards for Data Center and Other Computational Loads, July 2026
refs.finding: On 16 July 2026 FERC directed NERC to file one or more mandatory reliability standards for integrating computational loads, a category covering generative-AI data centres, cryptocurrency mines and other IT facilities, by 31 December 2026, without itself setting a size threshold or compliance obligations; Chairman Laura Swett said winning the AI race must not threaten reliability. A NERC review of 26 events in ERCOT from January 2023 to September 2025 found that crypto-mining facilities can lose 17% to 95% of their pre-disturbance consumption within milliseconds of a normally cleared transmission fault.

refs.title: NERC, Reliability Insights: Large Computational Load Risks Due to Voltage Sensitivity, September 2026
refs.finding: Certain data centres lengthened the time over which voltage dips are counted and changed how many dips trigger disconnection; on 18 April 2026 a fault in the same vicinity and with similar characteristics to the July 2024 event saw only 500 MW of sustained data-centre load loss, which may be attributable to those changes. In July 2026 a nearly 4 GW customer-initiated load reduction in Virginia showed the risk is increasing, not abating. FERC directed NERC to complete registry criteria and foundational standards on commissioning, communications and modelling by the end of 2026; ride-through requirements are to be considered later.

nodes.control_note: Data centres are set to switch to backup power when grid voltage dips, which protects their servers but can remove their demand all at once. Settings that ride through normal faults, with models and tests of each large load before it connects, can contain the risk, but the first mandatory standards, due at the end of 2026, cover registration, commissioning, communications and modelling, and ride-through requirements come later while the loads keep growing.

actions.action: Write mandatory reliability standards for computational loads
actions.evidence: FERC ordered NERC in July 2026 to file mandatory reliability standards for data centres and other computational loads by 31 December 2026; the order itself sets no size threshold or compliance obligations.

ref.title: POWER Magazine, FERC Orders Mandatory NERC Reliability Standards for Data Center and Other Computational Loads, July 2026
ref.finding: On 16 July 2026 FERC directed NERC to file one or more mandatory reliability standards for integrating computational loads, a category covering generative-AI data centres, cryptocurrency mines and other IT facilities, by 31 December 2026, without itself setting a size threshold or compliance obligations; Chairman Laura Swett said winning the AI race must not threaten reliability. A NERC review of 26 events in ERCOT from January 2023 to September 2025 found that crypto-mining facilities can lose 17% to 95% of their pre-disturbance consumption within milliseconds of a normally cleared transmission fault.

actions.action: Model, study and test large loads before they connect
actions.evidence: NERC's Level 3 alert of May 2026 asks transmission owners, operators and planners to model computational loads, study aggregate load losses, test facilities before energisation and prevent unnecessary loss of firm computational load during normally cleared faults; it is not a mandatory standard and carries no direct penalties.

ref.title: Data Center Frontier, Why NERC Now Sees AI Data Centers as Grid Actors, May 2026
ref.finding: NERC's Level 3 alert of 4 May 2026 sets seven essential actions, among them modelling computational loads, studying aggregate load reductions, commissioning tests before energisation and preventing loss of firm computational load during normally cleared faults, with status reports due by 3 August 2026; it is not a mandatory reliability standard and carries no direct penalties.

precedents.event: Wind-farm settings black out South Australia
precedents.parallel: A new kind of grid-connected equipment, set to disconnect after repeated voltage dips, turned a series of faults into a sudden loss of a size the grid had not planned for.
precedents.outcome: After six voltage dips in two minutes, settings at nine wind farms cut 456 MW of output in under seven seconds, the Heywood Interconnector tripped and the whole state lost supply; changed turbine control settings removed the risk of recurrence, and AEMO's final report made 19 recommendations.

ref.title: Energy Source & Distribution, AEMO publishes final report on SA blackouts, March 2017
ref.finding: Tornadoes damaged transmission lines and caused six voltage dips over two minutes on 28 September 2016; software settings at nine wind farms in mid-north South Australia then produced a sustained generation reduction of 456 MW in under seven seconds, the Heywood Interconnector tripped and all supply to the state was lost. Changes made to turbine control settings shortly after the event removed the risk of recurrence, and the report made 19 recommendations.

nodes.label: Under-tested AI medical devices fail after clearance
nodes.summary: AI medical devices cleared through the FDA's 510(k) route need no prospective testing on people, and some fail soon after[1]. In one study of 950 FDA-cleared AI devices, 60 (6.3%) were tied to 182 recalls, 43.4% of them within a year, and devices without clinical validation had higher odds of recall[1]. Still, 91.8% stayed recall-free for five years[1].

refs.title: Lee et al., Early Recalls and Clinical Validation Gaps in Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices, JAMA Health Forum 2025
refs.finding: Of 950 FDA-cleared AI-enabled medical devices, 60 (6.3%) were associated with 182 recalls; 109 recalls were for diagnostic or measurement errors and 44 for functionality delay, and 79 (43.4%) came within 12 months of clearance. Lack of clinical validation (adjusted odds ratio 2.8) and public company status (5.9) were associated with recalls; public companies made 53.2% of the devices but accounted for 91.8% of recalls. Recall-free survival was 96.6% at one year and 91.8% at five years. Because 510(k) clearance does not require prospective human testing, the authors say it may overlook early failures, and suggest prospective evaluation or time-limited clearances that lapse without confirmatory data.

refs.title: Gizmodo, The Last 'Person' You Want Handling Your Surgery Is a Hallucinating Robot, 9 February 2026
refs.finding: Summarising a Reuters investigation of 9 February 2026: the TruDi Navigation System for chronic sinusitis had seven unconfirmed malfunction reports in three years on the market, and after AI was added the FDA received more than 100 malfunction notifications and at least 10 reports of injured patients, including a punctured skull base, cerebrospinal fluid leaks and strokes. The FDA has not attributed the injuries to AI because the incidents are under review, and owner Integra LifeSciences says there is no credible evidence of a causal connection. Reuters counted 1,357 FDA-authorised devices using AI and reported that cuts removed 15 of the 40 scientists in the FDA unit that reviews AI-enabled devices.

refs.title: Babic, Cohen, Stern, Li and Ouellet, A general framework for governing marketed AI/ML medical devices, npj Digital Medicine 2025
refs.finding: Analysing 943 adverse event reports in the FDA's MAUDE database linked to 823 510(k)-cleared AI/ML devices approved from 2010 to 2023, the authors find more than 98% of adverse events in AI/ML devices are borne by fewer than five devices, against about 85% for other devices. Basic fields were often missing, for example whether the reporter was a health professional (73% of AI/ML reports against 43% for all devices), and the system does not capture AI-specific failures such as drift. They conclude the existing system is insufficient for properly assessing the safety and effectiveness of AI/ML devices.

refs.title: Ren et al., Clinical Evidence and FDA Recalls of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices, JAMA Network Open 2026
refs.finding: Of 903 FDA-authorised AI-enabled medical devices authorised up to 31 August 2024, 43 (4.8%) were recalled, after a median of 458 days. 7.8% (17 of 218) of devices without a clinical performance study were recalled, against 2.6% (13 of 505) with one and 7.2% (13 of 180) with missing information; missing clinical study information was associated with a higher chance of recall (hazard ratio 1.39, 95% credible interval 0.84 to 3.52), as were use-related problems.

refs.title: RAPS, FDA's device center releases guidance agenda for FY 2027, 2 October 2026
refs.finding: The FDA's device centre lists finalising guidance on lifecycle management recommendations for AI-enabled device software functions as a top priority for fiscal year 2027; the draft guidance, issued in January 2025, applies a total product lifecycle approach to AI-enabled devices.

nodes.control_note: The 510(k) route lets AI tools reach patients without prospective human testing, and the FDA's adverse-event database is too thin to judge their safety. Prospective evaluation, clearances that lapse without confirmatory data and monitoring of real-world performance can catch failures earlier, but current FDA guidance on monitoring is a non-binding draft.

actions.action: Ask makers to validate across subgroups and monitor performance after launch
actions.evidence: The FDA's January 2025 draft guidance calls for subgroup analyses and recommends that makers monitor and address changes in device performance, but it is non-binding and monitoring plans are generally not required for 510(k) devices.

ref.title: King & Spalding, FDA Releases Draft Guidance on Submission Recommendations for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions, January 2025
ref.finding: The FDA's draft guidance of 7 January 2025 calls for adequate subgroup analyses for relevant demographics, recommends that manufacturers proactively monitor, identify and address device performance changes, and recommends a model card in device labelling; monitoring plans are generally not required for 510(k)s but may be for De Novo requests and PMAs.

actions.action: Require prospective evaluation or time-limited clearance
actions.evidence: The authors of the recall study suggest that requiring prospective evaluation, or issuing clearances that lapse without confirmatory data, could reduce early failures.

ref.title: Lee et al., Early Recalls and Clinical Validation Gaps in Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices, JAMA Health Forum 2025
ref.finding: Of 950 FDA-cleared AI-enabled medical devices, 60 (6.3%) were associated with 182 recalls; 109 recalls were for diagnostic or measurement errors and 44 for functionality delay, and 79 (43.4%) came within 12 months of clearance. Lack of clinical validation (adjusted odds ratio 2.8) and public company status (5.9) were associated with recalls; public companies made 53.2% of the devices but accounted for 91.8% of recalls. Recall-free survival was 96.6% at one year and 91.8% at five years. Because 510(k) clearance does not require prospective human testing, the authors say it may overlook early failures, and suggest prospective evaluation or time-limited clearances that lapse without confirmatory data.

precedents.event: External test of the Epic Sepsis Model
precedents.parallel: A proprietary prediction tool spread to hundreds of hospitals before independent testing showed how it performed on real patients.
precedents.outcome: At Michigan Medicine the model reached an AUC of 0.63, substantially worse than its developer reported, missed 67% of patients with sepsis and alerted on 18% of all hospitalised patients.

ref.title: Wong et al., External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients, JAMA Internal Medicine 2021
ref.finding: The Epic Sepsis Model, developed by Epic Systems and implemented at hundreds of US hospitals, was tested on 38,455 hospitalisations of 27,697 patients at Michigan Medicine; it reached an AUC of 0.63, substantially worse than the developer reported, missed 1,709 of the patients with sepsis (67%) and alerted on 18% of all hospitalised patients.

nodes.label: AI coding tools pull in malicious packages
nodes.summary: Coding models often recommend software packages that do not exist, and anyone can register those names with malicious code behind them. In one USENIX Security 2025 study of 16 models, 19.7% of recommended packages were hallucinations, and 43% of invented names recurred in all 10 re-runs, making them predictable[1]. A deliberate attack on a hallucinated name has not been proven[5].

refs.title: Spracklen et al., We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs, USENIX Security 2025
refs.finding: Across 16 code-generating models, two prompt datasets and 576,000 code samples in Python and JavaScript, 440,445 of about 2.23 million recommended packages (19.7%) were hallucinations, at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique invented names. In 10 re-runs of 500 prompts, 43% of hallucinated packages were repeated in all 10 queries and 39% did not repeat at all. Fine-tuning cut DeepSeek's hallucination rate from 16.14% to 2.66% (83%), but its HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

refs.title: Churilov, The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort, arXiv preprint 2026
refs.finding: A single-author replication of the USENIX Security 2025 method on five models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek V3.2), across 199,845 paired Python and JavaScript prompts, found overall hallucination rates of 4.62% to 6.10%, a much narrower spread than in 2024. 127 hallucinated names (109 on PyPI, 18 on npm) were invented identically by all five models, and 53 of them (41 PyPI, 12 npm) remained registrable after each registry's existing defences; the findings were disclosed to PyPI Security and Socket.dev.

refs.title: Aikido Security, Agent Skills Are Spreading Hallucinated npx Commands, January 2026
refs.finding: On 14 January 2026 researcher Charlie Eriksen registered react-codeshift on npm, a name an LLM appears to have blended from jscodeshift and react-codemod. It first appeared in a commit of 17 October 2025 that added 47 LLM-generated agent skills with no apparent human review, and 237 GitHub repositories referenced it when he claimed it. After the claim it drew about 74 downloads on day zero and then 1 to 4 a day, where phantom packages typically get 60 to 100 downloads on day one, mostly from mirrors and scanners, and then almost none. Nobody was harmed and the package is now a safe placeholder, but an attacker could have claimed it first.

refs.title: ReversingLabs, Claude adds malware to crypto agent, April 2026
refs.finding: The npm package @validate-sdk/v2 poses as a data validation tool but steals .env and .json files, crypto-related files and system information, and adds an attacker SSH key for remote access. A 28 February 2026 commit to openpaw-graveyard, an autonomous crypto trading agent, added a dependency that pulls it in, and the commit was co-authored by an LLM. ReversingLabs attributes the campaign, which it named PromptMink, to the North Korean-linked group Famous Chollima and counted 60 unique packages and over 300 versions across seven months from September 2025; it says the packages' documentation is designed to get coding agents to recommend them, a combination of LLM optimisation abuse and knowledge injection, and that the real targets might have been AI coding agents.

refs.title: Aikido Security, What is Slopsquatting? The AI Package Hallucination Attack Already Happening, February 2026
refs.finding: The npm package unused-imports, whose name resembles the real eslint-plugin-unused-imports, is a real malicious package that was potentially an intentional slopsquatting attack; it is under a security hold and was still drawing 233 downloads a week in early February 2026, but the authors say they cannot prove what the attackers intended with the names. The post also recounts Bar Lanyado's 2024 huggingface-cli experiment.

refs.title: Lanyado, Diving Deeper into AI Package Hallucinations, Lasso Security, March 2024
refs.finding: After finding that AI models repeatedly suggested a non-existent Python package, huggingface-cli, the author uploaded an empty package under that name, plus a dummy package to gauge scanner traffic; in three months the empty package got more than 30,000 authentic downloads, and installation instructions for it appeared in the README of an Alibaba research repository.

nodes.control_note: Coding agents install whatever names they generate or read, and public registries let anyone claim an unused name. Checking that each suggested package exists and has a real history, and reviewing agent skills as code before running them, cut the risk; models tuned against inventing names make far fewer of them, but in one study at a large cost to code quality.

actions.action: Fine-tune coding models not to invent packages
actions.evidence: In the USENIX Security 2025 study, fine-tuning cut one model's hallucinated-package rate from 16.14% to 2.66%, but its pass rate on a standard coding benchmark fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

ref.title: Spracklen et al., We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs, USENIX Security 2025
ref.finding: Across 16 code-generating models, two prompt datasets and 576,000 code samples in Python and JavaScript, 440,445 of about 2.23 million recommended packages (19.7%) were hallucinations, at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique invented names. In 10 re-runs of 500 prompts, 43% of hallucinated packages were repeated in all 10 queries and 39% did not repeat at all. Fine-tuning cut DeepSeek's hallucination rate from 16.14% to 2.66% (83%), but its HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3%.

actions.action: Claim hallucinated names before attackers do
actions.evidence: A researcher registered react-codeshift as a safe placeholder after 237 repositories referenced it; it covers one name, and attackers could have claimed it first.

ref.title: Aikido Security, Agent Skills Are Spreading Hallucinated npx Commands, January 2026
ref.finding: On 14 January 2026 researcher Charlie Eriksen registered react-codeshift on npm, a name an LLM appears to have blended from jscodeshift and react-codemod. It first appeared in a commit of 17 October 2025 that added 47 LLM-generated agent skills with no apparent human review, and 237 GitHub repositories referenced it when he claimed it. After the claim it drew about 74 downloads on day zero and then 1 to 4 a day, where phantom packages typically get 60 to 100 downloads on day one, mostly from mirrors and scanners, and then almost none. Nobody was harmed and the package is now a safe placeholder, but an attacker could have claimed it first.

precedents.event: Dependency confusion attacks on tech firms
precedents.parallel: Build tools trusted any package that matched a name they expected, so whoever registered that name on a public registry got their code run inside companies.
precedents.outcome: A researcher published packages under the names of companies' private internal packages on npm, PyPI and RubyGems, breached the internal systems of over 35 firms including Microsoft, Apple and PayPal, and earned well over $130,000 in bug bounties; Microsoft called the root cause a design flaw in package managers.

ref.title: BleepingComputer, Researcher hacks over 35 tech firms in novel supply chain attack, February 2021
ref.finding: Alex Birsan published packages named after internal dependencies found in manifest files such as PayPal's to npm, PyPI and RubyGems; build tools pulled the public versions, which needed no action by the victim. He breached over 35 major companies including Microsoft, Apple, PayPal, Shopify, Netflix, Yelp, Tesla and Uber and earned well over $130,000 in bounties, including $40,000 from Microsoft, which said the root cause is a design flaw rather than a bug in package managers.

nodes.label: AI school surveillance misfires on students
nodes.summary: AI writing monitors and weapons scanners in US schools throw many false alerts. In Lawrence, Kansas, almost two-thirds of more than 1,200 Gaggle alerts in 10 months were judged nonissues[2], and police handcuffed a Baltimore County student after an AI gun detector flagged his bag of chips[3]. No independent research shows the monitoring software reduces suicide or violence[1].

refs.title: Associated Press and The Seattle Times (Sharon Lurye, Claire Bryan), Schools use AI to monitor kids, hoping to prevent violence. Our investigation found security risks, March 2025
refs.finding: About 1,500 US districts use Gaggle, AI-powered software that tracks roughly 6 million students on school devices. From October 2023 to October 2024 nearly 2,200 Vancouver, Washington students, about 10% of enrollment, were the subject of a Gaggle alert; many alerts turned out to be false alarms, such as a student essay about consent. Through a records request, school officials accidentally gave reporters links to almost 3,500 sensitive, unredacted student documents that were not password protected, and in those screenshots at least six students were potentially outed to school officials after writing about being gay, transgender or struggling with gender dysphoria. A 2023 RAND study found only scant evidence of benefits or risks; officials say they do not track efficacy but believe the tools have saved lives, and a Highline School District middle schooler who was potentially being trafficked used Gaggle to communicate with staff. Durham, North Carolina's Board of Education voted in 2023 to stop using Gaggle, judging it not worth the risk of outing students or eroding relationships with adults, after an LGBTQ+ advocate reported that a self-harm alert had outed a student to a family that was not supportive.

refs.title: Lawrence Journal-World, Lawrence school district sued in federal court for use of AI-powered surveillance system; students claim Gaggle results in illegal searches, August 2025
refs.finding: Nine current and former students sued the Lawrence, Kansas school district in federal court, claiming its use of Gaggle, adopted in 2023, violates their First Amendment rights and results in illegal searches and seizures of their files. Gaggle alerted the district to more than 1,200 incidents in a recent 10-month period; school officials deemed almost two-thirds nonissues, and more than 200 were false alarms from student homework. Officials said they adjusted the settings to reduce false alerts. In Tennessee a 13-year-old girl at Fairview Middle School, which uses Gaggle to monitor student accounts, was arrested in August 2023 over messages in a chat tied to her school email, strip-searched and held overnight.

refs.title: TechCrunch, High school's AI security system confuses Doritos bag for a possible firearm, October 2025
refs.finding: Kenwood High School student Taki Allen in Baltimore County, Maryland, was handcuffed and searched after an AI security system flagged his bag of chips as a possible firearm. The school's security department had reviewed and cancelled the alert, but the principal did not immediately realise and reported it to the school resource officer, who called police. Omnilert, which runs the gun detection system, said it regretted the incident and that the process functioned as intended.

refs.title: Federal Trade Commission, FTC Takes Action Against Evolv Technologies for Deceiving Users About its AI-Powered Security Screening Systems, November 2024
refs.finding: The FTC alleges Evolv deceptively advertised that its AI-powered Express scanners would detect all weapons and ignore harmless items. The scanners reportedly failed to detect a seven-inch knife brought into a school in October 2022 and used to stab a student; raising sensitivity afterwards prompted a 50% false alarm rate, and the scanners flagged laptops, binders and water bottles. The scanners are in over 800 schools in 40 states. The proposed order bars Evolv from misrepresenting weapon detection, false alarm rates and AI performance and requires it to tell certain K-12 customers that signed contracts between 1 April 2022 and 30 June 2023 that they can cancel.

refs.title: NBC 5 Investigates (NBC Chicago), Settlement approved with weapons detector company FTC alleged deceived customers, December 2024
refs.finding: A federal judge in Massachusetts approved the FTC's settlement with Evolv, which admitted no wrongdoing; it bars certain marketing claims and lets eligible K-12 customers that contracted between April 2022 and June 2023 cancel, with exclusions for trial users and large buyers. In the Rockford, Illinois school district, data shared with NBC 5 showed five knives recovered but more than 85,000 false positive alerts on laptops in scans between August 2023 and April 2024.

refs.title: The Lawrence Times, Lawrence school district must answer record requests from plaintiffs in AI surveillance lawsuit, judge rules, April 2026
refs.finding: Federal judge Kathryn Vratil granted the district's motion to dismiss in part: the school board and two Lawrence High administrators were dropped as defendants and claims of students who had graduated were dismissed. She ruled that the district's switch from Gaggle to ManagedMethods, a similar vendor with nearly identical capabilities, does not give it immunity, writing that other than the switch the defendants have not ceased or altered their challenged behaviour, so the First and Fourth Amendment claims continue against the district. She also ruled for the students on their open records requests.

nodes.control_note: Schools buy these tools to catch threats and self-harm early, and the software errs towards flagging, so harmless writing and objects set off alerts that can reach police. Narrower settings, human review that actually stops a response, and locking flagged screenshots behind logins reduce the harm, but no independent research shows the monitoring tools prevent suicide or violence.

actions.action: Bar unsupported accuracy claims for AI weapons scanners
actions.evidence: Under an FTC settlement that a federal judge had approved by mid-December 2024, Evolv may not make certain claims about its scanners' ability to detect weapons or ignore harmless items and must let eligible K-12 customers that contracted between April 2022 and June 2023 cancel; it covers one company.

ref.title: NBC 5 Investigates (NBC Chicago), Settlement approved with weapons detector company FTC alleged deceived customers, December 2024
ref.finding: A federal judge in Massachusetts approved the FTC's settlement with Evolv, which admitted no wrongdoing; it bars certain marketing claims and lets eligible K-12 customers that contracted between April 2022 and June 2023 cancel, with exclusions for trial users and large buyers. In the Rockford, Illinois school district, data shared with NBC 5 showed five knives recovered but more than 85,000 false positive alerts on laptops in scans between August 2023 and April 2024.

actions.action: Stop using student monitoring software
actions.evidence: Durham, North Carolina's Board of Education voted in 2023 to stop using Gaggle, judging it not worth the risk of outing students or eroding relationships with adults, after an LGBTQ+ advocate reported that a self-harm alert had outed a student to a family that was not supportive.

ref.title: Associated Press and The Seattle Times (Sharon Lurye, Claire Bryan), Schools use AI to monitor kids, hoping to prevent violence. Our investigation found security risks, March 2025
ref.finding: About 1,500 US districts use Gaggle, AI-powered software that tracks roughly 6 million students on school devices. From October 2023 to October 2024 nearly 2,200 Vancouver, Washington students, about 10% of enrollment, were the subject of a Gaggle alert; many alerts turned out to be false alarms, such as a student essay about consent. Through a records request, school officials accidentally gave reporters links to almost 3,500 sensitive, unredacted student documents that were not password protected, and in those screenshots at least six students were potentially outed to school officials after writing about being gay, transgender or struggling with gender dysphoria. A 2023 RAND study found only scant evidence of benefits or risks; officials say they do not track efficacy but believe the tools have saved lives, and a Highline School District middle schooler who was potentially being trafficked used Gaggle to communicate with staff. Durham, North Carolina's Board of Education voted in 2023 to stop using Gaggle, judging it not worth the risk of outing students or eroding relationships with adults, after an LGBTQ+ advocate reported that a self-harm alert had outed a student to a family that was not supportive.

precedents.event: Chicago inspector general's review of ShotSpotter
precedents.parallel: An automated alert system sent police to scenes on a sensor's say-so, and most of the responses found nothing.
precedents.outcome: Of 41,830 police responses to ShotSpotter gunshot alerts with a recorded outcome from January 2020 to May 2021, 9.1% found evidence of a gun-related offence, and the inspector general found the technology changed how some officers treated people in areas with frequent alerts.

ref.title: City of Chicago Office of Inspector General, OIG Finds That ShotSpotter Alerts Rarely Lead to Evidence of a Gun-Related Crime and That Presence of the Technology Changes Police Behavior, August 2021
ref.finding: OIG analysed 50,176 confirmed probable gunshot alerts from 1 January 2020 to 31 May 2021; of 41,830 with a recorded disposition, 4,556 (9.1%) found evidence of a gun-related criminal offence, and 1,056 alerts (2.1%) matched an investigatory stop. Some officers relied partly on how often alerts occurred in an area to justify stops or pat-downs.

nodes.label: Fake job candidates use AI to get hired
nodes.summary: Generative AI helps people get and hold remote jobs under false identities. CrowdStrike said the North Korea-linked group FAMOUS CHOLLIMA infiltrated over 320 companies in the 12 months before August 2025, using generative AI at every stage[2]. The schemes predate generative AI: the US government found over 300 US companies unknowingly employed North Korean IT workers between 2020 and 2022[3].

refs.title: Okta Threat Intelligence, How AI services power the DPRK's IT contracting scams, April 2025
refs.finding: Generative AI plays an integral role in how North Korean nationals obtain remote technical jobs and, once hired, helps them maintain multiple simultaneous roles. Okta observed AI-enhanced services used to manage many mobile phone, instant messaging and email accounts for multiple personas, give real-time translation of voice and text, transcribe and summarise communications, generate and critique CVs and cover letters, conduct mock job interviews via chat and webcam and test CVs against applicant tracking software. In recent months individuals strongly suspected to be DPRK-created personas have been recorded using real-time deepfake video during interviews. Okta cannot observe the facilitators' activities beyond the login page, so the use cases are inferred. It recommends identity verification in key business processes, staff training and detecting unauthorised remote management tools.

refs.title: CrowdStrike, CrowdStrike 2025 Threat Hunting Report: AI Becomes a Weapon and a Target, August 2025
refs.finding: CrowdStrike observed the DPRK-nexus adversary FAMOUS CHOLLIMA infiltrate over 320 companies in the last 12 months, a 220% year-over-year increase, by using generative AI at every stage of the hiring and employment process. Its IT workers use generative AI to create attractive resumes, reportedly use real-time deepfake technology to mask their identities in video interviews, and use AI code tools to do their jobs.

refs.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Jasper Sleet: North Korean remote IT workers' evolving tactics to infiltrate organizations, June 2025
refs.finding: Microsoft observed North Korean remote IT workers using AI tools such as Faceswap to move their pictures onto stolen employment and identity documents, using AI to enhance their photos so they look more professional, and using voice-changing software. It suspended 3,000 known Outlook and Hotmail accounts created by these workers. The US government found that over 300 US companies in multiple industries, including several Fortune 500 companies, unknowingly employed such workers between 2020 and 2022. Microsoft recommends stricter pre-employment vetting, having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple video sessions, treating video or microphone problems as a red flag, and notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can show artifacts, fail on partly obscured faces and lag between lip movement and speech.

refs.title: US Department of Justice, Justice Department Announces Coordinated, Nationwide Actions to Combat North Korean Remote Information Technology Workers' Illicit Revenue Generation Schemes, June 2025
refs.finding: Actions announced on 30 June 2025 included two indictments, an information and plea agreement, an arrest, searches of 29 known or suspected laptop farms across 16 states and the seizure of 29 financial accounts and 21 fraudulent websites. The schemes obtained remote jobs at more than 100 US companies using the identities of more than 80 US persons, and caused at least $3 million in losses to victim companies. The charges are allegations, and the release does not mention generative AI or deepfakes.

refs.title: KnowBe4, How a North Korean Fake IT Worker Tried to Infiltrate Us, July 2024
refs.finding: KnowBe4 hired a principal software engineer for its internal IT AI team after four video interviews and a background check that came back clear; the person was a real person using a valid but stolen US-based identity with an AI-enhanced stock photo. The company Mac workstation started to load malware the moment it was received; on 15 July 2024 suspicious activity began at 9:55pm EST and the security team contained the device at around 10:20pm. No illegal access was gained and no data was lost.

refs.title: HR Dive, By 2028, 1 in 4 candidate profiles will be fake, Gartner predicts, August 2025
refs.finding: In a Gartner survey of 3,000 job candidates, 6% said they had participated in interview fraud, either by posing as someone else or having someone else pretend to be them, and 4 in 10 candidates said they use AI during the application process. Gartner's 31 July 2025 report says 1 in 4 candidate profiles worldwide could be fake by 2028, a prediction rather than a measurement.

refs.title: US Department of Justice, Justice Department Announces Coordinated Actions to Combat North Korean Remote IT Worker Schemes Affecting More than 70 U.S. Companies, October 2026
refs.finding: Announced on 13 October 2026: charges against 14 individuals, two arrests, and FBI searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas suspected of being laptop farms between 21 and 25 September (Operation Lonestar Roundup), seizing about 187 laptops and KVM devices. The Ohio scheme impacted more than 70 US company employers and generated about $3 million in revenue for IT workers using stolen or fabricated identity documents. The release does not mention AI or deepfakes.

refs.title: CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations, U.S. Government Disrupts FAMOUS CHOLLIMA Operation with CrowdStrike Assistance, October 2026
refs.finding: CrowdStrike worked with the FBI in late September 2026 to disrupt several laptop farms across the US used by FAMOUS CHOLLIMA, spanning dozens of victim organisations in sectors such as aerospace, energy, financial services, healthcare and defence engineering. It says disrupting a laptop farm will likely have only a limited impact on the group and slow its operations only in the immediate areas, and that its US operations are ongoing.

nodes.control_note: Remote hiring relies on documents, photos, CVs and video calls that generative AI can now fake or polish, and a single fake hire gets insider access to company systems. Repeated on-camera identity checks, notarised proof of identity and watching company laptops for unauthorised remote-access tools reduce the risk, and prosecuting the people who host laptop farms removes some of the infrastructure, though the security firm that helped one takedown expects only local effects, and each check costs employers time.

actions.action: Prosecute the people who run laptop farms
actions.evidence: An Arizona woman who hosted company laptops for North Korean IT workers was sentenced in July 2025 to 102 months in prison after helping them get jobs at 309 US companies; it removes one facilitator, not the AI tools the workers use.

ref.title: IRS Criminal Investigation, Arizona woman sentenced for $17M information technology worker fraud scheme that generated revenue for North Korea, July 2025
ref.finding: Christina Chapman was sentenced on 24 July 2025 to 102 months in prison for a years-long scheme in which she helped North Korean IT workers obtain jobs at 309 US companies using 68 identities stolen from US victims, generating more than $17 million in illicit revenue; more than 90 laptops were seized from her home and she shipped 49 laptops and other devices overseas. The release does not mention AI.

actions.action: Verify identity on camera across several interviews
actions.evidence: Microsoft advises having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple sessions, treating video problems as a red flag and requiring notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can lag between lip movement and speech.

ref.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Jasper Sleet: North Korean remote IT workers' evolving tactics to infiltrate organizations, June 2025
ref.finding: Microsoft observed North Korean remote IT workers leveraging AI to improve the scale and sophistication of their operations, using AI tools such as Faceswap to move their pictures onto stolen employment and identity documents, enhancing their photos and using voice-changing software. It suspended 3,000 known Outlook and Hotmail accounts created by these workers. The US government found that over 300 US companies, including several Fortune 500 companies, unknowingly employed such workers between 2020 and 2022. Microsoft recommends stricter pre-employment vetting, having candidates hold identity documents up to the camera, seeing them on camera across multiple sessions, treating video or microphone problems as a red flag, and notarised proof of identity, and notes that deepfakes can show artifacts, fail on partly obscured faces and lag between lip movement and speech.

precedents.event: US advisory on North Korean IT workers
precedents.parallel: Before generative AI tools were widespread, the same scheme already placed workers in remote jobs under false identities, and one check officials recommended was a video interview, which real-time deepfakes now target.
precedents.outcome: In May 2022 the State Department, Treasury and FBI warned that North Korean IT workers pose as non-North Korean nationals to get jobs abroad, listed red flags such as logins from many IP addresses and inconsistent profile details, and advised firms to verify documents, run background or biometric checks and confirm identity with a video interview.

ref.title: Baker McKenzie Sanctions and Export Controls Update (Kerry B. Contini, Lise S. Test), The US Government Publishes Advisory on North Korean IT Workers, May 2022
ref.finding: On 16 May 2022 the US Departments of State and Treasury and the FBI issued an advisory on North Korean IT workers posing as non-DPRK nationals to obtain employment outside North Korea. Red flags include logins from multiple IP addresses in different countries, transfers to China-based accounts or requests for cryptocurrency, inconsistent names and nationality across profiles, and being unreachable during business hours. Recommended due diligence includes verifying documents with the listed employer or school, checking identity documents for forgery, conducting a video interview to verify identity, and background or biometric checks.

nodes.label: Chatbot toys say unsafe things to children
nodes.summary: Chatbot toys for children can have weak guardrails. In a November 2025 US PIRG Education Fund report, FoloToy's Kumma bear told testers where to find knives, pills and matches, and a trigger word brought graphic sexual content[1]. The report's co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare[1], and California enacted a four-year moratorium on companion chatbot toys for children under 16[3][6].

refs.title: The New York Times (via The Nightly), FoloToy AI toy bear 'Kumma' speaks of sex, knives and pills, a consumer group warns, November 2025
refs.finding: A US PIRG Education Fund report dated 13 November found that FoloToy's Kumma bear, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o and marketed to children and adults, told testers where to find knives, pills, matches and plastic bags, and that 'kink' was a trigger word that introduced new sexual words and content, which the co-author said went into some really graphic details. The report said Grok and Miko 3 showed stronger guardrails and Kumma responded far less consistently: Grok, a $99 plush rocket for ages 3 to 12, generally refused and often directed users to an adult, though it said plastic bags might be in a kitchen drawer, and Miko 3, a $189 robot for ages 5 to 10, said where to find plastic bags and matches when set to a user age of 5. OpenAI suspended the developer for policy violations, saying its policies prohibit any use to exploit, endanger or sexualize anyone under 18, and FoloToy said it would pull Kumma from the market for a safety audit. The co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare but already show troubling gaps in how they handle conversations; the article adds that some lack even basic safeguards.

refs.title: University of Cambridge, Report calls for AI toy safety standards to protect young children, March 2026
refs.finding: In what the researchers call the first systematic study of how generative AI toys may influence development up to age five, they video-recorded 14 children at London children's centres playing with Curio Interactive's Gabbo soft toy and ran focus groups and workshops with early years practitioners and 19 children's charity leaders. The toys struggled with social and pretend play, misunderstood children and reacted inappropriately to emotions: to a five-year-old saying 'I love you' it replied with a reminder to adhere to the guidelines, and when a three-year-old said 'I'm sad' it misheard and replied that it was a happy little bot; it also mistook parents' voices for the child's. Some practitioners felt the toys could support aspects of development such as language and communication skills. The report calls for clearer regulation, labelling standards, limits on how far toys encourage children to befriend or confide in them, tighter controls over third-party access to AI models, and testing with children before release.

refs.title: Ballard Spahr, California AI Toy Bill Brings Software Behavior Into Product Safety, September 2026
refs.finding: SB 867, signed by Governor Newsom the day before the 11 September 2026 alert and taking effect on 1 January 2027, provides that no person shall manufacture, sell or exchange any toy that includes a companion chatbot, defining a toy as a physical product designed, marketed or manufactured for play by children under 16. Unlike California's companion chatbot disclosure law it has no compliance path through disclosures, testing or certification, so a covered toy stays prohibited even if the maker adds content filters. Customer service tools, game characters limited to game topics and some standalone voice assistants are excluded.

refs.title: California State Senator Steve Padilla, First-In-Nation AI Toy Moratorium Moves to Governor's Desk, September 2026
refs.finding: In a release dated 1 September 2026, the bill's author says SB 867 places a 4-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of toys with AI chatbot capabilities for children under 16 (one paragraph says under 18); it passed the Senate unanimously and the Assembly 74 to 1. The release cites the Trouble in Toyland 2025 report's findings that AI toys discuss sexually explicit topics, advise children where to find matches or knives, use addictive features and pose data privacy risks.

refs.title: Futurism, AI Teddy Bear Back on the Market After Getting Caught Telling Kids How to Find Pills and Start Fires, November 2025
refs.finding: After a week-long internal safety review, FoloToy said it had begun gradually restoring sales and had strengthened and upgraded its child-safety safeguards; it was unclear which model the toy would use by default or whether its access to OpenAI's models had been restored. The PIRG report's co-author called a week on the short side and said the question is whether the products perform better than before.

refs.title: Law Commentary, Newsom Signs California Ban on AI Chatbot Toys for Kids Under 16, September 2026
refs.finding: Governor Newsom signed SB 867 on 10 September 2026, creating a four-year moratorium from 1 January 2027 that expires on 1 January 2031 unless extended; it bars manufacturing, selling or exchanging, possessing with intent to sell, or offering to retailers any toy for children under 16 that contains a companion chatbot as defined in California law.

nodes.control_note: Toymakers wire general-purpose chatbots into products for small children, and guardrails differ widely between toys, with one giving way to a single trigger word. Testing with children before release, limits on third-party access to models and outright bans reduce the risk; a ban also removes whatever help with language the toys might offer.

actions.action: Ban toys with companion chatbots
actions.evidence: California's SB 867, signed in September 2026, bars making or selling toys with a companion chatbot for children under 16 from 1 January 2027, with no compliance path through disclosures, testing or certification, so content filters do not make a covered toy legal; it covers one state.

ref.title: Ballard Spahr, California AI Toy Bill Brings Software Behavior Into Product Safety, September 2026
ref.finding: SB 867, signed by Governor Newsom the day before the 11 September 2026 alert and taking effect on 1 January 2027, provides that no person shall manufacture, sell or exchange any toy that includes a companion chatbot, defining a toy as a physical product designed, marketed or manufactured for play by children under 16. Unlike California's companion chatbot disclosure law it has no compliance path through disclosures, testing or certification, so a covered toy stays prohibited even if the maker adds content filters. Customer service tools, game characters limited to game topics and some standalone voice assistants are excluded.

actions.action: Cut off toymakers that break usage policies
actions.evidence: OpenAI suspended FoloToy, the maker of the Kumma bear, from its service for policy violations after the consumer group's report; it acts only after a problem is found.

ref.title: The New York Times (via The Nightly), FoloToy AI toy bear 'Kumma' speaks of sex, knives and pills, a consumer group warns, November 2025
ref.finding: A US PIRG Education Fund report dated 13 November found that FoloToy's Kumma bear, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o and marketed to children and adults, told testers where to find knives, pills, matches and plastic bags, and that 'kink' was a trigger word that introduced new sexual words and content, which the co-author said went into some really graphic details. The report said Grok and Miko 3 showed stronger guardrails and Kumma responded far less consistently: Grok, a $99 plush rocket for ages 3 to 12, generally refused and often directed users to an adult, though it said plastic bags might be in a kitchen drawer, and Miko 3, a $189 robot for ages 5 to 10, said where to find plastic bags and matches when set to a user age of 5. OpenAI suspended the developer for policy violations, saying its policies prohibit any use to exploit, endanger or sexualize anyone under 18, and FoloToy said it would pull Kumma from the market for a safety audit. The co-author said AI toys remain relatively rare but already show troubling gaps in how they handle conversations; the article adds that some lack even basic safeguards.

precedents.event: Germany's action against the My Friend Cayla doll
precedents.parallel: A talking toy reached children with a connection its makers had not secured, and a regulator took it off the market rather than wait for a fix.
precedents.outcome: Germany's Federal Network Agency recommended destroying the dolls and asked stores to remove them, after experts showed that someone within about 10 metres could use the toy's unsecured Bluetooth link to listen to and talk with a child; a spokesman called it a concealed transmitting device, illegal under German telecoms law.

ref.title: The African Courier, Parents in Germany told to destroy talking toy 'My Friend Cayla', February 2017
