ref.finding: Germany's Federal Network Agency recommended destroying My Friend Cayla dolls or disposing of them professionally and asked stores to remove them after experts showed hackers could use an unsecured Bluetooth device in the toy to listen to and talk with a child; a student researcher said a Bluetooth device could connect to the doll within a radius of 10m. A spokesman said the doll amounted to a concealed transmitting device, illegal under German telecoms law. The vulnerability was first revealed in January 2015, and the marketer Vivid said the hacking examples were isolated and carried out by specialists.

nodes.label: Private chatbot conversations exposed
nodes.summary: Chatbot conversations, which can touch sensitive topics[1], have leaked through public links and browser extensions. Forbes found more than 370,000 Grok conversations indexed by Google because shared chats got public links with no warning[2], and extensions with more than 8 million users captured AI chats[5]. ChatGPT and Meta AI chats surfaced only after users chose to share and publish them[3][4][7].

refs.title: Mireshghallah, Antoniak, More, Choi and Farnadi, Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild, arXiv 2024
refs.finding: The authors analyse a random sample of 5,000 English conversations from WildChat, a corpus of one million conversations with commercial GPT models collected with user consent; personally identifiable information appears in unexpected contexts such as translation (48% of the time) and code editing (16%), over 70% of queries contain some detected PII, and almost 15% mention a non-PII sensitive topic such as sexual preferences or drug use. They conclude PII detection alone is insufficient and call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate their interactions.

refs.title: Forbes Australia, Elon Musk's xAI published hundreds of thousands of Grok chatbot conversations, August 2025
refs.finding: Clicking share on a Grok chat creates a unique URL that is made available to search engines such as Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo, with no warning or disclaimer to users; a Google search showed more than 370,000 indexed Grok conversations, some with intimate medical and psychology questions, names, personal details and at least one password, plus uploaded images, spreadsheets and documents. xAI did not respond to a request for comment.

refs.title: Search Engine Journal, OpenAI Is Pulling Shared ChatGPT Chats From Google Search, July 2025
refs.finding: Shared ChatGPT links were visible only to people with the URL by default, but users could tick a checkbox to make a shared chat discoverable by search engines; Fast Company found over 4,500 shared links indexed by Google, some with names, resumes and confidential work content. OpenAI disabled the option, which it called a short-lived experiment that introduced too many chances for accidental sharing, and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed content, though cached copies may appear for a while and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

refs.title: TechCrunch, The Meta AI app is a privacy disaster, June 2025
refs.finding: A share button in the Meta AI app lets users preview and publish an exchange to a public feed, and some users seemed unaware they were making text chats, audio and images public; posts included requests for help with tax evasion, questions about relatives' links to white-collar crime, a reference letter naming an employee facing legal trouble, and home addresses and court details. The app had about 6.5 million downloads since its April 2025 launch, per Appfigures.

refs.title: The Register, Browser 'privacy' extensions have eye on your AI, log all your chats, December 2025
refs.finding: Koi Security found that Urban VPN Proxy, 1ClickVPN Proxy, Urban Browser Guard and Urban Ad Blocker, with more than 8 million users on Chrome and Edge, capture chatbot conversations on platforms including ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Grok and Meta AI. Harvesting is set by a hardcoded flag with no user toggle; the consent prompt came in a silent update that users who installed before July 2025 never saw, and the researcher advises assuming conversations since July 2025 were captured. Urban VPN's privacy policy discloses AI data collection, which Koi calls misleading framing.

refs.title: Decrypt, OpenAI Ordered to Hand Over 20M ChatGPT Logs in NYT Copyright Case, December 2025
refs.finding: US Magistrate Judge Ona T. Wang ordered OpenAI to produce roughly 20 million de-identified ChatGPT user logs under a protective framework in The New York Times' copyright suit, finding the sample proportional to the needs of the case and writing that user privacy is only one factor; OpenAI had objected that the order was disproportionate and would force disclosure of millions of private conversations.

refs.title: Engadget, Meta warns users to 'avoid sharing personal or sensitive information' in its AI app, June 2025
refs.finding: Meta AI does not share chat histories by default, but many users shared chats to the public discover feed without realising they would become public. Meta added a disclaimer, shown only on the first share, that prompts posted are public and visible to everyone and that users should avoid sharing personal or sensitive information; a spokesperson said posting is a multi-step process designed to add friction.

refs.title: ABA Journal, ChatGPT creator must turn over 20M chat logs in copyright litigation, federal judge says, January 2026
refs.finding: US District Judge Sidney Stein affirmed Magistrate Judge Ona Wang's orders requiring OpenAI to produce a sample of 20 million chat logs to The New York Times and its co-plaintiffs, finding they were neither clearly erroneous nor contrary to law and that Wang adequately balanced users' privacy against relevance, relying on the 20 million limit, de-identification and an existing protective order. The plaintiffs had sought 120 million logs.

refs.title: Malwarebytes, AI chat app leak exposes 300 million messages tied to 25 million users, February 2026
refs.finding: Citing 404 Media, a researcher found that Chat & Ask AI, a wrapper app by Codeway that connects to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, had Firebase security rules left public so anyone with the project URL could read users' full chat histories, models and settings; he claims to have accessed 300 million messages from over 25 million users, including requests for suicide assistance. His scan found the same flaw in 103 of 200 iOS apps, and Codeway reportedly fixed it across its apps within hours of disclosure.

nodes.control_note: Chatbots give better help the more people tell them, so chat logs hold health, legal and money worries in one place. Private-by-default sharing, clear warnings, keeping share pages out of search and locking down app databases limit the leaks, but every stored copy, whether held by a vendor, an app, an extension or a court, is another place they can surface.

actions.action: Keep shared chats out of search engines
actions.evidence: OpenAI removed the option that let shared ChatGPT chats be found by search engines and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed links; cached copies may linger, and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

ref.title: Search Engine Journal, OpenAI Is Pulling Shared ChatGPT Chats From Google Search, July 2025
ref.finding: Shared ChatGPT links were visible only to people with the URL by default, but users could tick a checkbox to make a shared chat discoverable by search engines; Fast Company found over 4,500 shared links indexed by Google, some with names, resumes and confidential work content. OpenAI disabled the option, which it called a short-lived experiment that introduced too many chances for accidental sharing, and said it was working with search engines to remove indexed content, though cached copies may appear for a while and deleting a chat does not delete its share link.

actions.action: Warn users before a chat goes public
actions.evidence: Meta added a notice that prompts posted to its AI app's feed are public and visible to everyone, but it appears only on the first share.

ref.title: Engadget, Meta warns users to 'avoid sharing personal or sensitive information' in its AI app, June 2025
ref.finding: Meta AI does not share chat histories by default, but many users shared chats to the public discover feed without realising they would become public. Meta added a disclaimer, shown only on the first share, that prompts posted are public and visible to everyone and that users should avoid sharing personal or sensitive information; a spokesperson said posting is a multi-step process designed to add friction.

actions.action: Nudge users to share less with chatbots
actions.evidence: The authors of one study of real chatbot conversations call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate what they share, since detecting identifying details alone misses sensitive topics.

ref.title: Mireshghallah, Antoniak, More, Choi and Farnadi, Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild, arXiv 2024
ref.finding: The authors analyse a random sample of 5,000 English conversations from WildChat, a corpus of one million conversations with commercial GPT models collected with user consent; personally identifiable information appears in unexpected contexts such as translation (48% of the time) and code editing (16%), over 70% of queries contain some detected PII, and almost 15% mention a non-PII sensitive topic such as sexual preferences or drug use. They conclude PII detection alone is insufficient and call for nudging mechanisms that help users moderate their interactions.

precedents.parallel: Records of what people typed into a service, released with usernames swapped for numbers, still revealed who they were and what worried them.
precedents.outcome: AOL released about 19 million searches from more than 650,000 subscribers; The New York Times traced one user to a 62-year-old woman in Georgia, two employees were fired, the chief technology officer resigned and subscribers filed a class action under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act.

ref.title: Associated Press via NBC News, Subscribers sue AOL over data release, September 2006
ref.finding: AOL released about 19 million search requests from more than 650,000 subscribers over three months, replacing usernames with numbers; The New York Times traced user 4417749 to Thelma Arnold, 62, of Lilburn, Georgia. The researcher and another employee were fired, the chief technology officer resigned, and three subscribers filed a class action alleging violations of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act.

nodes.label: AI-written job applications stop signalling skill
nodes.summary: AI makes tailored job applications almost free to write, so they no longer signal skill. One working paper on 2.7 million Freelancer.com applications found employers stopped paying a premium for customised ones after LLMs[1], and in one study of an AI cover-letter tool the link between letter fit and callbacks fell by 51%[2]. Both studies cover single online platforms[4].

refs.title: Galdin and Silbert, Making Talk Cheap: Generative AI and Labor Market Signaling, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: Using Freelancer.com data on about 61,000 job postings and 2.7 million applications from 212,000 workers, and an LLM-based measure of how tailored an application is to the job, the authors find employers paid a premium for more customised applications before LLMs but not after; 14.03% of post-LLM applications used the platform's AI tool. In a simulated equilibrium where written applications carry no signal, top-quintile workers are hired 19% less often and bottom-quintile workers 14% more often, average wages fall about 5%, hiring per posted job about 1.5% and worker surplus about 4%.

refs.title: Cui, Dias and Ye, Signaling in the Age of AI: Evidence from Cover Letters, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: On a large online labour platform that introduced an AI cover-letter tool, access to the tool made cover letters more aligned with job posts and raised callback rates, and time spent editing AI drafts correlated with hiring success; after the tool arrived, the correlation between cover-letter alignment and callbacks fell by 51%, and employers relied more on other signals such as workers' prior work histories.

refs.title: eWeek, Job Seekers - Some Using AI - Flood LinkedIn With 11,000 Applications a Minute, June 2025
refs.finding: LinkedIn reports an average of 11,000 applications per minute, up 45% in a year, according to The New York Times; job seekers use tools such as ChatGPT to tailor resumes and apply to more roles, and recruiters told the Times this produces nearly identical resumes that make top candidates harder to distinguish. LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role reduces applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

refs.title: Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, What Happens to Hiring When AI Writes Job Applications?, January 2026
refs.finding: Freelancer.com added a one-click AI application tool in April 2023 and employers could not see which proposals were AI-generated; after AI, employers relied more on price and prior ratings, which hurt higher-ability workers. The 19% and 14% hiring effects come from a structural model. The article says high-value jobs may need fuller screening through live talking and maybe live tests, and co-author Anais Galdin suggests trial contracts that cover the first 10% of a job before a full-term contract.

refs.title: Wiles, Munyikwa and Horton, Algorithmic Writing Assistance on Jobseekers' Resumes Increases Hires, Management Science 2025 (NBER Working Paper 30886)
refs.finding: In a field experiment on an online labour market with nearly half a million jobseekers, those given algorithmic writing assistance on their resumes were hired 8% more often, with no evidence that employers were less satisfied; the authors' model suggests better writing does not signal ability but helps employers assess it.

nodes.control_note: Writing help is a real gain for applicants, and it is the same help that stops a written application showing effort or skill. Employers can shift to signals that are harder to fake, such as track records, live interviews and work tests, but those take more time to run.

actions.action: Weigh track records over written applications
actions.evidence: After an AI cover-letter tool arrived on one large online labour platform, employers relied more on workers' prior work histories as cover letters told them less.

ref.title: Cui, Dias and Ye, Signaling in the Age of AI: Evidence from Cover Letters, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: On a large online labour platform that introduced an AI cover-letter tool, access to the tool made cover letters more aligned with job posts and raised callback rates, and time spent editing AI drafts correlated with hiring success; after the tool arrived, the correlation between cover-letter alignment and callbacks fell by 51%, and employers relied more on other signals such as workers' prior work histories.

actions.action: Screen candidates with live interviews and tests
actions.evidence: A Tuck School article on the Freelancer.com study says high-value jobs may need fuller screening through live talking and maybe live tests, since employers on the platform could not see which proposals were written by AI.

ref.title: Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, What Happens to Hiring When AI Writes Job Applications?, January 2026
ref.finding: Freelancer.com added a one-click AI application tool in April 2023 and employers could not see which proposals were AI-generated; after AI, employers relied more on price and prior ratings, which hurt higher-ability workers. The 19% and 14% hiring effects come from a structural model. The article says high-value jobs may need fuller screening through live talking and maybe live tests, and co-author Anais Galdin suggests trial contracts that cover the first 10% of a job before a full-term contract.

actions.action: Show applicants how well they fit before they apply
actions.evidence: LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role cuts applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

ref.title: eWeek, Job Seekers - Some Using AI - Flood LinkedIn With 11,000 Applications a Minute, June 2025
ref.finding: LinkedIn reports an average of 11,000 applications per minute, up 45% in a year, according to The New York Times; job seekers use tools such as ChatGPT to tailor resumes and apply to more roles, and recruiters told the Times this produces nearly identical resumes that make top candidates harder to distinguish. LinkedIn says showing Premium subscribers how well they fit a role reduces applications from underqualified candidates by 10%.

precedents.parallel: When almost everyone can get the top mark, the mark stops telling apart the strongest candidates.
precedents.outcome: About 60% of Harvard College grades had become A's, up from about 40% a decade earlier and under a quarter 20 years earlier; the dean's report said grading was failing at its key functions, and a committee began weighing a limited number of A+ grades to distinguish the very best students.

ref.title: Bloomberg via Fortune, Harvard says it's been giving too many A grades to students, October 2025
ref.finding: About 60% of grades in Harvard College undergraduate classes are A's, up from about 40% a decade ago and less than a quarter 20 years ago; Dean Amanda Claybaugh's report says grading practices are failing at the key functions of grading, and a committee is considering a limited number of A+ grades that would distinguish the very best students.

nodes.label: AI-written peer reviews
nodes.summary: Some reviewers hand peer review to chatbots: the detection company Pangram classed 21% of about 70,000 ICLR 2026 reviews as fully AI-generated[1]. At ICML 2026, hidden PDF instructions caught 795 reviews breaking a no-LLM policy the reviewers had accepted[4]. AI can also help: in one randomised study at ICLR 2025, blinded researchers found reviews updated after AI feedback more informative[7].

refs.title: Pangram Labs, Pangram Predicts 21% of ICLR Reviews are AI-Generated, November 2025
refs.finding: Running its detector on about 19,000 papers and 70,000 reviews submitted to ICLR 2026, Pangram found 21%, or 15,899 reviews, fully AI-generated and over half with some form of AI involvement; the more AI present in a review, the higher its score, and AI-generated reviews were longer with a lot of filler. On 2022 reviews used as a negative control it found no confusions between fully AI-generated and fully human text.

refs.title: Liang et al., Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews, ICML 2024
refs.finding: Between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023 could have been substantially modified by LLMs; the estimated share was higher in reviews submitted close to the deadline, by reviewers less likely to respond to rebuttals and in reviews reporting lower confidence.

refs.title: ICLR Blog, A Retrospective on the ICLR 2026 Review Process, March 2026
refs.finding: ICLR 2026 received 19,525 valid submissions and 76,139 reviews from 18,054 reviewers. The chairs ran two LLM content detectors on all reviews and told area chairs about reviews both flagged as entirely LLM-generated, while noting the detectors' accuracy is far from perfect; all papers with confirmed hallucinated references were desk rejected, and reviewers repeatedly flagged for low-quality reviews will be removed from the pool.

refs.title: ICML Blog, On Violations of LLM Review Policies, March 2026
refs.finding: Hidden instructions watermarked into submission PDFs, asking an LLM to include two phrases drawn from a dictionary of 170,000, flagged 795 reviews (about 1% of all reviews) by 506 reviewers who had chosen, or said they were fine with, the policy allowing no LLM use; 497 submissions (about 2%) belonging to 398 reciprocal reviewers were desk rejected and 51 reviewers were removed from the pool. Each flagged review was checked by a human, and the chairs say the watermark is not difficult to circumvent and may catch only the most careless uses.

refs.title: Lin, Hidden Prompts in Manuscripts Exploit AI-Assisted Peer Review, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: 18 manuscripts on arXiv in July 2025 hid instructions aimed at AI-assisted peer review in white text or microscopic fonts, such as GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY; the author finds the prompts consistently serve the authors' interests, calls the practice a new questionable research practice, and notes publisher policies are inconsistent.

refs.title: Frontiers, Most peer reviewers now use AI, and publishing policy must keep pace, December 2025
refs.finding: A global survey of 1,645 active researchers in May and June 2025 found 53% of reviewers now use AI tools, many of them for drafting reports or summarising findings.

refs.title: Thakkar et al., Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025, arXiv 2025
refs.finding: A Review Feedback Agent gave optional feedback on vague comments, misunderstandings and unprofessional remarks to more than 20,000 randomly selected ICLR 2025 reviews; 27% of reviewers who received feedback updated their reviews, incorporating over 12,000 suggestions, and blinded researchers found the updated reviews more informative.

nodes.control_note: Writing a careful review takes hours of expert time, and a chatbot produces a plausible one in seconds. Clear rules, checks that catch undisclosed use and tools that help reviewers rather than replace them can limit the harm, but the organisers' own detectors and watermarks make mistakes or can be evaded.

actions.action: Plant hidden canary instructions in submissions to catch LLM reviews
actions.evidence: ICML 2026 watermarked submission PDFs with instructions only an LLM would see, flagged 795 reviews, desk rejected 497 submissions belonging to reciprocal reviewers and removed 51 reviewers; the chairs say the method is not difficult to circumvent.

ref.title: ICML Blog, On Violations of LLM Review Policies, March 2026
ref.finding: Hidden instructions watermarked into submission PDFs, asking an LLM to include two phrases drawn from a dictionary of 170,000, flagged 795 reviews (about 1% of all reviews) by 506 reviewers who had chosen, or said they were fine with, the policy allowing no LLM use; 497 submissions (about 2%) belonging to 398 reciprocal reviewers were desk rejected and 51 reviewers were removed from the pool. Each flagged review was checked by a human, and the chairs say the watermark is not difficult to circumvent and may catch only the most careless uses.

actions.action: Give reviewers AI feedback instead of AI-written reviews
actions.evidence: In one randomised study at ICLR 2025, feedback on more than 20,000 reviews led 27% of reviewers who received it to update their reviews, which blinded researchers found more informative.

ref.title: Thakkar et al., Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025, arXiv 2025
ref.finding: A Review Feedback Agent gave optional feedback on vague comments, misunderstandings and unprofessional remarks to more than 20,000 randomly selected ICLR 2025 reviews; 27% of reviewers who received feedback updated their reviews, incorporating over 12,000 suggestions, and blinded researchers found the updated reviews more informative.

precedents.event: Fake peer reviews at Tumor Biology
precedents.parallel: Peer review was faked before AI, letting papers through on reviews that did not come from genuine reviewers.
precedents.outcome: Springer retracted a record 107 papers from Tumor Biology in April 2017 over evidence of fake peer reviews and tied 12 retractions in Molecular Neurobiology to the same investigation; retractions over fake reviews passed 500.

ref.title: Retraction Watch, Springer purge of fake reviews takes down 10+ more neuroscience papers, June 2017
ref.finding: Springer retracted a record 107 papers from Tumor Biology in April 2017 after finding evidence they had been subject to fake peer reviews, then found the peer review process compromised in 12 brain cancer papers in Molecular Neurobiology; the number of papers retracted over fake reviews now exceeds 500.

nodes.label: AI crawlers strain sites that host free knowledge
nodes.summary: AI scrapers and fetchers put heavy load on sites that serve free content. Bots made up at least 65% of Wikimedia's most expensive traffic but about 35% of pageviews[1], and one buggy AI crawler downloaded 73 TB from Read the Docs in May 2024[4]. Across Cloudflare's network, AI bots averaged 4.2% of HTML requests in 2025, slightly less than Googlebot[5].

refs.title: Mueller, Danis and Lavagetto, Wikimedia Foundation, How crawlers impact the operations of the Wikimedia projects, April 2025
refs.finding: Bandwidth used for downloading multimedia content grew 50% since January 2024, not from human readers but largely from scraping bots collecting training data for large language models and other uses; bots account for at least 65% of the most expensive traffic reaching the core datacentres though they make up about 35% of pageviews. When a 1.5-hour video of the 1980 Carter-Reagan debate was streamed after Jimmy Carter's death in December 2024, network traffic doubled and a small number of connections filled up entirely for about an hour; the Foundation says bot-driven growth leaves less room for such events. Scrapers also hit the code review platform and bug tracker.

refs.title: Mueller, Danis and Lavagetto, Wikimedia Foundation, Quo Vadis, Crawlers? Progress and what's next on safeguarding our infrastructure, March 2026
refs.finding: A year on, the Foundation is blocking or throttling about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that do not follow its policies (revised on 15 April 2026 from 25% to include blocked media requests), which send up to billions of requests per day, after updating its robot policy, improving bot detection and starting to roll out global API rate limits in March 2026; crawler operators have turned to residential proxy networks that can span hundreds of millions of IP addresses, which makes blocking hard, and high-volume users are pointed to Wikimedia Enterprise. It also says LLM-powered search summaries and chatbots make users less likely to know the source or follow links, and that publishers across the web see more bot traffic and fewer human users.

refs.title: Fastly, New Fastly Threat Research Reveals AI crawlers make up almost 80% of AI bot traffic, Meta Leads AI Crawling As ChatGPT Dominates Real-Time Web Traffic, 19 August 2025
refs.finding: From mid-April to mid-July 2025, AI crawlers made up almost 80% of AI bot traffic seen on Fastly's network, with Meta at 52% of AI crawler traffic, Google 23% and OpenAI 20%. In some cases fetcher request volume exceeded 39,000 requests per minute, putting pressure on unprotected origin infrastructure and mimicking the effects of DDoS attacks even without malicious intent.

refs.title: Eric Holscher, Read the Docs, AI crawlers need to be more respectful, July 2024
refs.finding: One AI crawler downloaded 73 TB of zipped HTML files in May 2024, almost 10 TB in a single day, because of a bug that made it fetch the same files repeatedly, costing over $5,000 in bandwidth charges; after blocking AI crawlers, bandwidth for downloaded files fell 75%, from about 800 GB to about 200 GB a day.

refs.title: David Belson, Cloudflare, The 2025 Cloudflare Radar Year in Review: the rise of AI, post-quantum, and record-breaking DDoS attacks, December 2025
refs.finding: For data from 1 January to 2 December 2025, traffic from AI bots accounted for an average of 4.2% of HTML requests, ranging from 2.4% in early April to 6.4% in late June, while Googlebot alone made up 4.5%; the user agents with the most fully disallowed directives in robots.txt files were those of AI crawlers.

nodes.control_note: Models and chatbot answers need fresh pages from the web, and the cost of serving those pages falls on whoever hosts them. Rate limits, bot challenges and paid bulk access cut the load, but crawlers that hide behind residential proxies keep the fight going and the blocks can also catch real readers.

actions.action: Rate-limit and block crawlers that break the robot policy
actions.evidence: The Wikimedia Foundation began rolling out global API rate limits in March 2026 and blocks or throttles about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that break its policies, but crawlers using residential proxy networks that can span hundreds of millions of IP addresses are hard to block.

ref.title: Mueller, Danis and Lavagetto, Wikimedia Foundation, Quo Vadis, Crawlers? Progress and what's next on safeguarding our infrastructure, March 2026
ref.finding: A year on, the Foundation is blocking or throttling about 30% of automated requests from crawlers that do not follow its policies (revised on 15 April 2026 from 25% to include blocked media requests), which send up to billions of requests per day, after updating its robot policy, improving bot detection and starting to roll out global API rate limits in March 2026; crawler operators have turned to residential proxy networks that can span hundreds of millions of IP addresses, which makes blocking hard, and high-volume users are pointed to Wikimedia Enterprise. It also says LLM-powered search summaries and chatbots make users less likely to know the source or follow links, and that publishers across the web see more bot traffic and fewer human users.

actions.action: Make suspicious clients solve a proof-of-work challenge
actions.evidence: GNOME, the Linux Kernel Mailing List archive, sourcehut and FFmpeg adopted the Anubis challenge, and a Duke University pilot blocked more than 4 million unwanted requests a day; it relies on scrapers not running JavaScript, which bot makers may work around.

ref.title: Joe Brockmeier, LWN.net, Anubis sends AI scraperbots to a well-deserved fate, July 2025
ref.finding: Anubis, an MIT-licensed tool first built to keep scrapers from taking down its author's Git server, makes suspicious clients solve a proof-of-work challenge before reaching a site and has been adopted by GNOME, the Linux Kernel Mailing List archive, sourcehut and FFmpeg; a Duke University pilot blocked more than 4 million unwanted HTTP requests a day, with twelve people reporting problems in one week, usually because cookies were disabled. It works because most scraper bots do not run client-side JavaScript, and the article expects bot makers to find ways around it.

precedents.parallel: Site owners have long needed a way to tell crawlers which parts of a site to leave alone, because crawlers that visit a whole site can be a burden.
precedents.outcome: Martijn Koster defined the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 1994 and it was published as a standards-track IETF RFC only in September 2022; compliance is voluntary, and the standard says its rules are not a form of access authorization.

ref.title: Koster, Illyes, Zeller and Sassman, RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol, IETF 2022
ref.finding: The protocol, originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994, lets service owners tell crawlers which parts of a site they may access, since it may be inconvenient for service owners if crawlers visit the entirety of their URI space; it was published as a standards-track IETF RFC in September 2022, and its rules are not a form of access authorization.

nodes.label: Inflated AI claims mislead investors and customers
nodes.summary: Companies overstate what their AI can do to win money and customers. The US SEC fined two investment advisers $400,000 in total in March 2024 for claiming AI they did not use, and they settled without admitting or denying the findings[1]. US investors filed 15 AI-related securities class actions, still allegations, in the first half of 2026[5][6].

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence, March 2024
refs.finding: Delphia (USA) Inc. claimed from 2019 to 2023 to use AI and machine learning that incorporated client data in its investment process, capabilities the SEC found it lacked; Global Predictions Inc. called itself the 'first regulated AI financial advisor' in 2023. Without admitting or denying the findings, they agreed to pay $225,000 and $175,000 in civil penalties, $400,000 in total. Chair Gary Gensler said: 'Such AI washing hurts investors.'

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, Litigation Release No. 26282, Alberto Saniger Mantinan, a/k/a Albert Saniger, April 2025
refs.finding: The SEC charged the founder and former CEO of Nate, Inc. with raising over $42 million by telling Seed and Series A investors that the app used automated technology that relied on AI to complete purchases without human involvement; it alleges Nate relied largely on contract employees who entered orders by hand and that the app could not use AI to complete purchases. The SEC seeks injunctions, an officer-and-director bar, disgorgement and civil penalties.

refs.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Restaurant-Technology Company Presto Automation for Misleading Statements About AI Product, January 2025
refs.finding: From November 2021 to May 2023 Presto made false and misleading statements about Presto Voice, its AI drive-thru ordering product, including that it eliminated the need for human order-taking: for a period the speech recognition in all deployed units was owned and operated by a third party, and in the version using its own technology the vast majority of orders required human intervention. Presto settled without admitting or denying the findings and paid no civil penalty, citing its cooperation and remediation.

refs.title: US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Order Requires Workado to Back Up Artificial Intelligence Detection Claims, April 2025
refs.finding: In a proposed consent order, the FTC alleges Workado advertised its AI Content Detector as '98 percent' accurate at telling AI-written from human-written text, but independent testing found 53 percent accuracy on general-purpose content, and that the model was trained or fine-tuned only to classify academic content. Bureau of Consumer Protection director Chris Mufarrige said the product did no better than a coin toss.

refs.title: Cornerstone Research, Securities Class Action Filings Surge in the First Half of 2026 (press release for Securities Class Action Filings: 2026 Midyear Assessment, with the Stanford Law School Securities Class Action Clearinghouse), July 2026
refs.finding: Investors filed 15 AI-related securities class action lawsuits in the first half of 2026, on pace to nearly double the 2025 total; they were 13% of core filings, but their disclosure dollar loss ($385 billion) was 73% of the DDL Index for 2026 H1 ($529 billion), and five of the 17 Mega MDL filings were AI-related.

refs.title: Risk & Insurance, AI-Related Lawsuits Drive Sharp Rise In Securities Class Action Filings, August 2026
refs.finding: Reporting the Cornerstone Research midyear assessment: 15 AI-related filings in the first half of 2026 against a full-year 2025 total of 16; seven concerned AI development, five involved data centers and four involved AI infrastructure or hardware; AI-related filings made up 13% of core filings.

refs.title: Pranav, Hartmann and Lauscher, Auditing AI-Washing in German Startups: A Mixed-Methods Study of Marketing Claims and Perceptions, AIES 2026 (Proceedings vol. 9)
refs.finding: A University of Hamburg audit of 100 German startups with a seven-dimension codebook, plus 63 expert interviews, found three forms of exaggerated AI capability: claims without inspectable evidence, performance numbers without methodology and claims without acknowledged limits; claimed capabilities rarely matched the underlying systems, consumers who had met exaggerated claims withdrew trust from later AI marketing, and 38% of the sample were flagged for moderate or serious ethical concern. The authors recommend bringing startup AI claims under disclosure requirements and offering the codebook to regulators, investors and consumer-protection bodies.

nodes.control_note: Hype rewards any company that can claim the AI label, and investors and buyers rarely see what sits behind it. Regulators can demand evidence for AI claims and punish false ones, but the SEC and FTC cases described here carried modest penalties or none.

actions.action: Charge firms that claim AI they do not have
actions.evidence: The SEC has brought AI washing cases against investment advisers, a restaurant-technology company and a startup founder, with civil penalties of $400,000 in total in the 2024 adviser cases.

ref.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence, March 2024
ref.finding: Delphia (USA) Inc. claimed from 2019 to 2023 to use AI and machine learning that incorporated client data in its investment process, capabilities the SEC found it lacked; Global Predictions Inc. called itself the 'first regulated AI financial advisor' in 2023. Without admitting or denying the findings, they agreed to pay $225,000 and $175,000 in civil penalties, $400,000 in total. Chair Gary Gensler said: 'Such AI washing hurts investors.'

actions.action: Require evidence behind AI accuracy claims
actions.evidence: A final FTC order bars one AI detector maker from claiming accuracy unless competent and reliable evidence backs the claim; it binds only that company.

ref.title: US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Approves Final Order against Workado, LLC, Which Misrepresented the Accuracy of its Artificial Intelligence Content Detection Product, August 2025
ref.finding: The final order, approved 3-0 on 28 August 2025, bars Workado from claims about the effectiveness of any AI content detection product unless they are not misleading and backed by competent and reliable evidence, and requires it to keep that evidence, notify eligible customers and file compliance reports one year after the order and annually for three more years.

actions.action: Bring startup AI claims under disclosure rules
actions.evidence: The authors of one audit of German startups propose disclosure requirements for startup AI claims and offer their codebook to regulators, investors and consumer-protection bodies for routine audits.

ref.title: Pranav, Hartmann and Lauscher, Auditing AI-Washing in German Startups: A Mixed-Methods Study of Marketing Claims and Perceptions, AIES 2026 (Proceedings vol. 9)
ref.finding: A University of Hamburg audit of 100 German startups with a seven-dimension codebook, plus 63 expert interviews, found three forms of exaggerated AI capability: claims without inspectable evidence, performance numbers without methodology and claims without acknowledged limits; claimed capabilities rarely matched the underlying systems, consumers who had met exaggerated claims withdrew trust from later AI marketing, and 38% of the sample were flagged for moderate or serious ethical concern. The authors recommend bringing startup AI claims under disclosure requirements and offering the codebook to regulators, investors and consumer-protection bodies.

precedents.parallel: A startup raised money on a technology it said it had built, while most of the work ran on other companies' machines, much as the SEC later found that one AI drive-thru product ran for a time on a third party's speech recognition.
precedents.outcome: The SEC charged Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes and Ramesh Balwani with fraud after the company raised more than $700 million while the vast majority of patient tests ran on modified or commercial analyzers made by others; Holmes settled, without admitting or denying the allegations, with a $500,000 penalty and a 10-year bar from serving as an officer or director of a public company.

ref.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission, Theranos, CEO Holmes, and Former President Balwani Charged With Massive Fraud, March 2018
ref.finding: Theranos raised more than $700 million from investors while claiming its portable analyzer ran comprehensive blood tests from finger-drop samples; according to the complaint its analyzer could complete only a small number of tests and the vast majority of patient tests ran on modified and commercial analyzers made by others. It projected over $100 million in 2014 revenue and made a little more than $100,000. Holmes and Theranos neither admitted nor denied the allegations; Holmes agreed to a $500,000 penalty, a 10-year officer-and-director bar and the return of 18.9 million shares, and the SEC said it would litigate its claims against Balwani.

nodes.label: AI satellite monitoring exposes hidden fishing fleets
nodes.summary: Machine learning on satellite images can find ships that do not broadcast positions. One Nature study found about 75 percent of industrial fishing vessels worldwide are not publicly tracked[1]. In one Science study, 78.5% of 1,380 protected areas banning industrial fishing recorded no commercial fishing[2], but it cannot tell whether they keep boats out or sit where little fishing happens[3].

refs.title: Global Fishing Watch, New research harnesses AI and satellite imagery to reveal the expanding footprint of human activity at sea, January 2024
refs.finding: A study in Nature by researchers at Global Fishing Watch, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Duke, UC Santa Barbara and SkyTruth combined vessel GPS data with five years (2017 to 2021) of radar and optical satellite imagery, 2 million gigabytes, and used machine learning to judge which vessels were likely fishing. About 75 percent of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked, with much of that fishing around Africa and South Asia, and more than 25 percent of transport and energy vessel activity is missing from public tracking. Not all boats are legally required to broadcast their position; satellite monitoring of this kind is freely available to all nations, and the study's data is published on Global Fishing Watch's datasets and code page.

refs.title: National Geographic Pristine Seas (EurekAlert), New research: Satellite imagery detects illegal fishing activity, shows strict protections work, July 2025
refs.finding: Raynor et al., 'Little-to-no industrial fishing occurs in fully and highly protected marine areas', Science: of 1,380 marine protected areas studied, 78.5% recorded no commercial fishing; among those where satellites detected illegal fishing, 82% averaged under 24 hours of it a year; strongly protected areas had nine times fewer fishing vessels per square kilometre than unprotected coastal areas. About five billion AIS positions were paired with radar images, and AI models developed by Global Fishing Watch detected most fishing vessels over 15 metres, including those not broadcasting their location.

refs.title: UC Santa Barbara, The Current, Satellites show that strictly protected marine areas exclude industrial fishing, July 2025
refs.finding: Radar imagery analysed with AI found dark vessels absent from AIS, which missed almost 90% of the vessels detected by radar. The study does not establish why fishing is absent: further research is needed to tell whether protected areas exclude vessels or were designated where fishing demand is low. Lead author Jennifer Raynor suggests satellite tracking can help countries predict illegal activity and target patrols, and that resource-limited nations could partner with nonprofits such as Global Fishing Watch.

refs.title: Seguin, Le Manach, Devillers, Velez and Mouillot, Global patterns and drivers of untracked industrial fishing in coastal marine protected areas, Science 389(6758), July 2025
refs.finding: Combining vessel GPS data with satellite imagery, the authors detected industrial fishing in 47% of coastal marine protected areas worldwide from 2022 to 2024; about two-thirds of detected vessels did not appear in public monitoring systems, and untracked vessels were most common (80%) in the strictest management category, which aims to prohibit all extraction. Counting untracked vessels raised estimated fishing effort inside the areas by 28%, to about 4 hours per square kilometre per year, and vessel presence depended mainly on an area's size and remoteness, not its management category.

refs.title: NPR (Alabama Public Radio), New technology shows how illegal fishing has impacted oceans across the world, July 2025
refs.finding: Raynor's team found almost 80% of protected areas had no industrial fishing; Raphael Seguin's study looked at a larger group of protected areas that still allow some fishing and found industrial fishing in about half of them, two-thirds of it untracked. Seguin said the satellite technology could help enforcement by tracking illegal fishing in real time.

limiters.evidence: The AI models used in one 2025 study detect most fishing vessels over 15 metres, not every vessel.

ref.title: National Geographic Pristine Seas (EurekAlert), New research: Satellite imagery detects illegal fishing activity, shows strict protections work, July 2025
ref.finding: Raynor et al., 'Little-to-no industrial fishing occurs in fully and highly protected marine areas', Science: of 1,380 marine protected areas studied, 78.5% recorded no commercial fishing; among those where satellites detected illegal fishing, 82% averaged under 24 hours of it a year; strongly protected areas had nine times fewer fishing vessels per square kilometre than unprotected coastal areas. About five billion AIS positions were paired with radar images, and AI models developed by Global Fishing Watch detected most fishing vessels over 15 metres, including those not broadcasting their location.

limiters.limit: A hidden vessel is not proof of a crime
limiters.evidence: Not all boats are legally required to broadcast their position, so a vessel missing from public tracking is not by itself fishing illegally.

ref.title: Global Fishing Watch, New research harnesses AI and satellite imagery to reveal the expanding footprint of human activity at sea, January 2024
ref.finding: A study in Nature by researchers at Global Fishing Watch, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Duke, UC Santa Barbara and SkyTruth combined vessel GPS data with five years (2017 to 2021) of radar and optical satellite imagery, 2 million gigabytes, and used machine learning to judge which vessels were likely fishing. About 75 percent of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked, with much of that fishing around Africa and South Asia, and more than 25 percent of transport and energy vessel activity is missing from public tracking. Not all boats are legally required to broadcast their position; satellite monitoring of this kind is freely available to all nations, and the study's data is published on Global Fishing Watch's datasets and code page.

limiters.limit: Seeing boats does not remove them
limiters.evidence: Satellites detected industrial fishing in 47% of coastal protected areas from 2022 to 2024, and untracked vessels were most common, at 80%, in the strictest category, which aims to ban all extraction.

ref.title: Seguin, Le Manach, Devillers, Velez and Mouillot, Global patterns and drivers of untracked industrial fishing in coastal marine protected areas, Science 389(6758), July 2025
ref.finding: Combining vessel GPS data with satellite imagery, the authors detected industrial fishing in 47% of coastal marine protected areas worldwide from 2022 to 2024; about two-thirds of detected vessels did not appear in public monitoring systems, and untracked vessels were most common (80%) in the strictest management category, which aims to prohibit all extraction. Counting untracked vessels raised estimated fishing effort inside the areas by 28%, to about 4 hours per square kilometre per year, and vessel presence depended mainly on an area's size and remoteness, not its management category.

enablers.action: Make vessel detections free to every nation
enablers.evidence: Satellite monitoring of the kind behind the 2024 study is freely available to all nations, and the study's data is published openly.

ref.title: Global Fishing Watch, New research harnesses AI and satellite imagery to reveal the expanding footprint of human activity at sea, January 2024
ref.finding: A study in Nature by researchers at Global Fishing Watch, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Duke, UC Santa Barbara and SkyTruth combined vessel GPS data with five years (2017 to 2021) of radar and optical satellite imagery, 2 million gigabytes, and used machine learning to judge which vessels were likely fishing. About 75 percent of the world's industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked, with much of that fishing around Africa and South Asia, and more than 25 percent of transport and energy vessel activity is missing from public tracking. Not all boats are legally required to broadcast their position; satellite monitoring of this kind is freely available to all nations, and the study's data is published on Global Fishing Watch's datasets and code page.

enablers.action: Send real-time fishing alerts to patrols
enablers.counters: Seeing boats does not remove them
enablers.evidence: In one case reported by the platform that issued the alerts, Argentina's Coast Guard redirected a nearby vessel after speed and fishing alerts on a foreign fishing vessel inside its exclusive economic zone, and the vessel paid the fine and operational costs.

ref.title: Skylight (Allen Institute for AI), Real-Time Intelligence Powers Argentina's Fight Against Illegal Fishing, 2025
ref.finding: A speed alert flagged the Vanuatu-flagged XINRUN 579 sailing under 6 knots inside Argentina's exclusive economic zone, a speed local rules associate with trawling, and a fishing alert followed about 40 minutes later; analysts redirected a nearby Coast Guard vessel, the vessel was intercepted, and it paid the fine and the authorities' operational costs. The account comes from the platform that issued the alerts.

enablers.action: Target patrols where satellites predict poaching
enablers.counters: Seeing boats does not remove them
enablers.evidence: The lead author of one 2025 study suggests countries use satellite tracking to predict illegal activity and target patrols, with resource-limited nations partnering with nonprofits such as Global Fishing Watch.

ref.title: UC Santa Barbara, The Current, Satellites show that strictly protected marine areas exclude industrial fishing, July 2025
ref.finding: Radar imagery analysed with AI found dark vessels absent from AIS, which missed almost 90% of the vessels detected by radar. The study does not establish why fishing is absent: further research is needed to tell whether protected areas exclude vessels or were designated where fishing demand is low. Lead author Jennifer Raynor suggests satellite tracking can help countries predict illegal activity and target patrols, and that resource-limited nations could partner with nonprofits such as Global Fishing Watch.

precedents.parallel: Near-real-time alerts from satellite imagery let a government with weak enforcement aim its inspectors at illegal activity across a vast area.
precedents.outcome: Using clouds that blocked detection as a natural experiment, one study found that monitoring and enforcement curbed Amazon deforestation, and that the result was not driven by illegal clearing moving into neighbouring areas; a version was later published in a peer-reviewed economics journal.

ref.title: Assunção, Gandour and Rocha, DETERring Deforestation in the Amazon: Environmental Monitoring and Law Enforcement, Climate Policy Initiative Working Paper 003, November 2019
ref.finding: DETER processes satellite imagery and issues near-real-time deforestation alerts to target environmental enforcement in the Amazon. Using clouds that limit its detection as an instrument for the presence of environmental authorities, the authors find that monitoring and enforcement effectively curbed deforestation, with results holding across several robustness checks and not driven by illegal activity being displaced into neighbouring areas. A version appeared as DETER-ing Deforestation in the Amazon in American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 15(2), 2023.

nodes.label: Performers' voices cloned and sold without consent
nodes.summary: Voice cloning lets companies sell synthetic copies of a performer's voice. In a 2026 National Association of Voice Actors survey, 21% of respondents said they had knowingly lost a job to a synthetic voice[6], though it was not a random sample[2]. ElevenLabs says its voice creators had earned over $22 million by May 2026, a figure it reports itself[5].

refs.title: National Association of Voice Actors, Voice Actors Head to Washington to Address AI's Impact on Creative Economy, GlobeNewswire release via AOL, May 2026
refs.finding: About 21 percent of voice actors surveyed by NAVA this year reported losing work directly to AI, up from 14 percent one year earlier; NAVA leaders took the findings to panels in Washington, D.C. on 12 and 13 May 2026.

refs.title: National Association of Voice Actors, 2026 State of Voiceover Survey by NAVA, 2026
refs.finding: The survey was published on 22 January 2026 and closed on 22 February 2026 with 1,379 responses; NAVA's contact list of about 4,000 voice actors and voiceover professionals was one of three sources used to recruit participants.

refs.title: The Fashion Law, A Case Over AI Voice Clones Poses First-of-Its-Kind Questions, July 2025
refs.finding: In Lehrman et al. v. Lovo, Inc. (SDNY), voice actors Paul Lehrman and Linnea Sage allege Lovo obtained recordings of their voices through Fiverr in 2019 and 2020, saying they were for internal research only, then used them to create millions of voice-over productions without permission. On 10 July 2025 Judge Paul Oetken let right of publicity, breach of contract and state consumer protection claims proceed and dismissed false endorsement claims, finding the voices were the product being sold rather than source identifiers, and dismissed copyright claims because the voices were not independently copyrightable; misappropriating a voice could be actionable under New York's Civil Rights Law.

refs.title: AWN, SAG-AFTRA Ratifies New Deal with Video Game Companies, July 2025
refs.finding: The union struck after 18 months of negotiations, which broke down over concerns regarding consent and compensation for the use of AI replicas; the union called it an 11-month strike, and over 95% of voting members backed the new deal.

refs.title: ElevenLabs, $22 million earned by voice creators on ElevenLabs, May 2026
refs.finding: More than 10,400 voice creators have earned over $22 million from Professional Voice Clones shared in the ElevenLabs Voice Library, up from $11 million in November 2025; creators set use cases, price tier and a notice period, and can restrict use or remove their voice.

refs.title: National Association of Voice Actors, Voiceover Survey 2026, Part 3: AI, 2026
refs.finding: Asked 'Have you ever knowingly lost a job to a synthetic voice?', 21% of respondents answered yes and 79% no. 9% said a synthetic version of their voice or of a character they voiced had been created without their permission to their knowledge, 11% said a synthetic version of their voice had been used in a professional project, and 53% said they would be open to having a synthetic version of their voice ethically created in the future. Results are shown in charts on the page.

nodes.control_note: A clone can be built from recordings a performer made for some other purpose, as the Lovo case alleges. Contracts that require consent and disclosure, and laws that protect a person's voice and likeness, can limit commercial use. In the Lovo case a US court found the voices not independently copyrightable, so protection there rests on publicity and likeness rules that differ by state, while Denmark's 2026 bill would add protection for faces and voices to its copyright law.

actions.action: Require consent and disclosure before making digital replicas
actions.evidence: SAG-AFTRA's 2025 Interactive Media Agreement, approved by 95.04% of voting members, requires consent and disclosure for AI digital replica use and lets performers withdraw consent for new material during a strike; it covers only video game work under that union contract.

ref.title: GamesBeat, SAG-AFTRA union members approve end of strike with game firms over AI, July 2025
ref.finding: Members approved the 2025 SAG-AFTRA Interactive Media Agreement by 95.04% to 4.96% on 9 July 2025, ending an 11-month strike; the deal includes consent and disclosure requirements for AI digital replica use, the ability to suspend consent for generating new material during a strike, and a 15.17% compounded pay rise on ratification.

actions.action: Ban sharing realistic imitations of a person's face or voice without consent
actions.evidence: Denmark's government introduced a bill on 8 October 2026 that would amend copyright law to ban sharing realistic AI imitations of a person's face or voice made without permission, covering artists' performances too, with exceptions for satire and parody; the minister hopes it takes effect at the start of 2027.

ref.title: Euronews, Denmark introduces bill to protect people's faces and voices from deepfakes, October 2026
ref.finding: The bill amends Denmark's copyright law to prohibit sharing realistic AI-generated or manipulated imitations of a person's face or voice made without their permission, covers ordinary people and artists including imitations of their performances, aims to make platforms take down manipulated content quickly, and keeps exceptions for satire, parody, caricature and criticism; the culture minister hopes it takes effect at the start of 2027.

precedents.parallel: An advertiser that could not hire a famous singer copied her voice instead, the same use of a voice without consent that cloning now automates.
precedents.outcome: After Bette Midler declined to sing in a Ford commercial, its agency hired a former backup singer to sound as much like her recording as possible; the Ninth Circuit held that deliberately imitating a widely known, distinctive professional voice to sell a product is a tort in California, and sent the case to trial.

ref.title: Midler v. Ford Motor Co., 849 F.2d 460, US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, June 1988 (Caselaw Access Project)
ref.finding: Young & Rubicam hired Ula Hedwig to imitate Midler's recording of Do You Want To Dance after Midler declined; many people believed Midler was singing. The court reversed summary judgment, holding that when a distinctive voice of a professional singer is widely known and is deliberately imitated in order to sell a product, the sellers have appropriated what is not theirs and committed a tort in California.

nodes.label: AI-forged receipts and claim photos
nodes.summary: People now use image generators to fake expense receipts and insurance damage photos[1][4]. AppZen found AI-generated receipts made up about 14% of fraudulent receipts in September 2025, against none a year earlier[1], and 70.8% of receipts it flagged as fake by mid-May 2026[2]. AppZen says fakes are now almost always AI-made, not that expense fraud grew that much[2].

refs.title: Computerworld, The latest genAI scam: fake expense receipts, October 2025
refs.finding: Receipts made with generative AI accounted for about 14% of all fraudulent receipts AppZen saw in September 2025, against none a year earlier, and the Financial Times reported a worldwide surge in fake receipts made with image generators; Ramp's software found more than $1 million of fake invoices in three months. Companies check metadata and file name patterns, but these controls are far from secure because metadata can be deleted.

refs.title: Accounting Today, Use of AI receipts in expense fraud soars, June 2026
refs.finding: AI-generated receipts rose from 0% of receipts flagged as fake on AppZen's platform in March 2025 to 70.8% by mid-May 2026, based on 1,471 AI-generated fake receipts from 745 employees at 174 companies claiming $148,143; template fakes fell from 95% to 100% of flags to 29%, with the crossover in April 2026. AI fakes averaged about $100 with a median of about $32, against $182 for template fakes. AppZen says this does not mean expense fraud grew by that proportion, but that a receipt identified as fraudulent is now almost always AI-generated.

refs.title: Emburse, Four in Ten U.S. Employees Have Used AI to Generate Fake Expense Receipts, June 2026
refs.finding: In an online survey by Atomik Research of 1,000 professionally employed adults in the US and 1,000 in the UK, fielded 5 to 8 May 2026, 40% of US employees said they had used AI to generate a fake receipt for a business expense: 19% to fabricate a purchase, 15% to inflate a real one and 6% to replace a lost receipt; 40% of those used company-funded AI tools.

refs.title: Insurance Business, Aviva detects record £233 million in fraud as AI tools and ghost broking accelerate, June 2026
refs.finding: Aviva identified more than 18,400 suspect claims worth £233 million across its brands in 2025, a record level of claims fraud and the first figures combining Aviva and Direct Line; it is detecting a growing number of claims supported by AI-generated images and manipulated documents, particularly in motor insurance, where fraudsters fabricate accident scenes and damage imagery. Motor makes up more than seven in 10 detected fraud cases and its detected value rose 39%.

refs.title: CTMfile, Fake Receipts Taken over by Generative AI, July 2026
refs.finding: Reporting AppZen's data that AI-generated fakes went from none of the fake receipts it detected in March 2025 to 70.8% by mid-May 2026, the article quotes AppZen co-founder and CTO Kunal Verma saying fake receipts still represent an extremely small percentage of all receipts submitted by employees.

nodes.control_note: The same generators that make realistic pictures for art and fun make realistic receipts and damage photos, and the fakes lack the editing flaws that checks used to catch. Checking a claim against an independent record, such as the card transaction behind a receipt, cuts the payoff, but image checks alone are easy to beat.

actions.action: Match receipts to card transactions
actions.evidence: Because AI receipts lack the font, logo and pixel flaws that gave forgeries away, one trade report says matching each receipt against card transaction data, merchant category codes and payment times can confirm whether a purchase happened whatever the receipt looks like, and that virtual cards tie each payment to a single transaction.

ref.title: PYMNTS, AI-Generated Fake Receipts Now Make Up 71% of Expense Fraud, June 2026
ref.finding: AI receipt generators have made image-based fraud checks obsolete because their receipts lack the editing artefacts, such as inconsistent fonts, mismatched logos and pixelation, that flag forgeries; matching a receipt against card transaction data, merchant category codes and payment timestamps can confirm whether the purchase occurred, virtual cards link a specific payment to a specific transaction, and Emburse's chief revenue officer names virtual cards among the most effective controls.

actions.action: Screen submitted receipts with automated fake checks
actions.evidence: Expense platforms already scan receipts for signs of generation, such as metadata and file name patterns, but metadata can be deleted, so these checks are far from secure.

ref.title: Computerworld, The latest genAI scam: fake expense receipts, October 2025
ref.finding: Companies use AI to analyse metadata, patterns in file names and other details to spot fake receipts, but the control systems are far from secure since metadata can be deleted.

precedents.parallel: Cheap home computers and printers let ordinary people forge documents that once needed skill and special equipment, as image generators now do for receipts.
precedents.outcome: The US Secret Service told Congress that inkjet-made counterfeits rose from $174,924, about 0.5% of counterfeit currency passed in fiscal 1995, to $6,121,292, or 19%, in fiscal 1997; the Bureau of Engraving and Printing said its redesigned Series 1996 notes are difficult to reproduce with copiers or scanners, and the subcommittee chairman warned such features only work if people know about them and check.

ref.title: US House of Representatives, Subcommittee on Domestic and International Monetary Policy of the Committee on Banking and Financial Services, Counterfeiting Using Personal Computers, hearing, 31 March 1998
ref.finding: Secret Service Special Agent in Charge Dennis F. Lynch testified that inkjet-produced notes were $174,924, about 0.5% of counterfeit currency passed in the US, in fiscal 1995 and $6,121,292, or 19%, in fiscal 1997, an 805% increase; Acting Director Thomas Ferguson of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing said the Series 1996 features are difficult to reproduce with copiers or scanners, though no currency is counterfeit-proof; subcommittee chairman Michael Castle said anti-counterfeiting features only work if people are aware of them.

nodes.label: Labs claim discoveries built on experts' work
nodes.summary: AI labs claim discoveries before peer review, while experts whose unpublished work sits in their tools can lose credit. NYU's Tristan Buckmaster, who put drafts into OpenAI's Codex, says he does not know whether his data fed OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof[3], which experts say resembles his work only superficially[5]. A University of Copenhagen team says it found Anthropic's enzyme discovery first[6].

refs.title: Frank Landymore, OpenAI's Supposed Mathematical Breakthrough Devolves Into Explosive Drama as Mathematician Accuses It of Stealing His Work, Futurism, 10 September 2026
refs.finding: OpenAI says a swarm of AI agents, 10,000 according to its head of research Mark Chen, ran for 88 hours to solve the problem. OpenAI denied that its researchers or agents saw Buckmaster's work before publication but said it cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from his and Alpöge's usage of its products helped improve its models; Sébastien Bubeck called Buckmaster's claims false and inflammatory.

refs.title: Russell Brandom, OpenAI fought dirty on career-making math problem, says NYU mathematician, TechCrunch, 8 September 2026
refs.finding: OpenAI's post says its latest effort began on 1 September, inspired by rumours that two Millennium Prize problems had been solved, and that no specific user data was accessed to solve the problem, though, while unlikely, it cannot rule out that de-identified data from the pair's usage of its products helped. The article notes OpenAI reserves the right to train models on Codex interactions and that users can opt out.

refs.title: Tristan Buckmaster, statement, September 2026
refs.finding: Buckmaster and Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, put all drafts of their project into Codex. Buckmaster was told OpenAI's internal model had simply been given the problem statement, and Alpöge that very little human input was used; it then emerged a team had worked on it, and OpenAI eventually agreed its first prompt was sent after information about their work reached OpenAI. The smooth-force route was opened by Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa. When he asked about training on their Codex sessions he got no answer. He says he does not know whether their data was used and is not accusing anyone.

refs.title: OpenAI, Finite time blowup for Navier-Stokes, September 2026
refs.finding: The 166-page paper, credited to OpenAI, cites Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa's forced-singularity constructions for the 3D Euler equations and their extension with Zheng to hypodissipative Navier-Stokes.

refs.title: Joseph Howlett, OpenAI's blockbuster math proof isn't what you think it is, Scientific American, 13 October 2026
refs.finding: All the expert groups interviewed agree the proof does not follow Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa's program, and its similarities to Buckmaster and Alpöge's progress are superficial; some experts say a smaller initial team of OpenAI agents did follow the program for an intermediate result before the 10,000-agent swarm took a different path. OpenAI maintains its model could not have seen Buckmaster's data, and one expert says he sees no factual resolution of the dispute.

refs.title: Akanksha Mishra, Did Claude discover a new enzyme or 'stole' a biologist's work? Anthropic responds, ThePrint, 29 September 2026
refs.finding: Anthropic said on 23 September 2026 that Claude, running 950 agents for 21 hours, discovered a novel CRISPR-like enzyme system it named ART. Citing The New York Times, the article reports that Mario Rodríguez Mestre of the University of Copenhagen says his team found the system about a year earlier after nearly four years of unpublished work, used Claude for code and manuscript drafts, and worries Claude used their data; Anthropic denied training on user transcripts and said it knew of no published data on ART.

refs.title: Clay Mathematics Institute, Navier-Stokes announcement, 11 September 2026
refs.finding: CMI says the Navier-Stokes problem has apparently been settled, and that its rules set out how to evaluate what was achieved and assign credit, in a process that is deliberately unhurried.

refs.title: A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, open letter by 28 Fields Medalists, 11 September 2026
refs.finding: AI-produced solutions are often announced in a rush, leaving no time for a proper writeup or for citing others' prior work, and skipping the long community vetting through talks, discussion and simplification; this raises severe attribution and plagiarism questions that the mathematical community and AI companies must address urgently.

refs.title: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen, Navier-Stokes lost in translation: Why Lean verification of AI autoformalisation does not guarantee correct natural language proofs, arXiv 2610.08144 (October 2026)
refs.finding: The authors argue that OpenAI's Lean formalisation of its Navier-Stokes blowup proof does not correspond to the natural-language proof, so a successful Lean check does not confirm the informal argument.

refs.title: Anthony Ha, OpenAI's 'embarrassing' math, TechCrunch, 19 October 2025
refs.finding: OpenAI VP Kevin Weil posted that GPT-5 found solutions to 10 previously unsolved Erdős problems and later deleted the post after Thomas Bloom, who maintains the Erdős problems site, called it a dramatic misrepresentation: GPT-5 had found references that already solved them.

refs.title: Kaia Glickman, Will AI scoop your science? Some researchers see a gloomy future, Nature, 8 October 2026
refs.finding: Scientists worry that increasingly capable large language models will beat them to discoveries, as AI agents' ability to do science autonomously improves.

nodes.control_note: Labs can publish their prompts, outputs and timelines, credit the work they build on and leave checking and write-up to independent experts, and researchers can keep unpublished work out of tools that train on it. None of this stops a lab from announcing first, and only the lab can show what its model saw.

actions.action: Keep unpublished research out of model training
actions.evidence: OpenAI reserves the right to train its models on Codex interactions but lets users opt out, so researchers who draft unpublished work in these tools have to switch training off themselves.

ref.title: Russell Brandom, OpenAI fought dirty on career-making math problem, says NYU mathematician, TechCrunch, 8 September 2026
ref.finding: OpenAI reserves the right to train models on Codex interactions, and users are able to opt out.

precedents.event: Watson and Crick use King's College data on DNA
precedents.parallel: A rival team used another group's unpublished results, shared informally, to confirm a famous discovery, and the credit took years to set right.
precedents.outcome: Watson and Crick used the King's group's data from an informal MRC report without permission to confirm their double helix, said in their 1953 paper that they were not aware of the details, and only in 1954 wrote that without Franklin's data their structure would have been most unlikely, if not impossible. Cobb and Comfort argue Franklin was an equal contributor, not a victim of theft.

ref.title: Cobb and Comfort, What Rosalind Franklin truly contributed to the discovery of DNA's structure, Nature 616, 657-660 (2023)
ref.finding: Watson and Crick solved the structure by their own trial and error and then used the King's data, from an informal report Max Perutz passed them without consulting the King's group, to confirm it without permission; their 1953 paper said they were not aware of the details of the unpublished results, and their 1954 paper acknowledged that without Franklin's data the formulation of their structure would have been most unlikely, if not impossible. The authors argue Franklin was an equal contributor to the solution, not a wronged heroine whose data was stolen.

nodes.label: Drivers over-trust driver-assist systems and crash
nodes.summary: Systems that steer and brake can lull drivers into looking away. NHTSA found Tesla Autopilot's weak driver engagement system led to foreseeable misuse and avoidable crashes, including at least 13 fatal ones[1]. In small IIHS field studies drivers grew more disengaged or learned to time attention reminders[2][3], and only one of the first 14 systems IIHS rated had acceptable safeguards[8].

refs.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, EA22002 closing resume, Autopilot System Driver Controls, April 2024
refs.finding: ODI analysed 956 crashes reported up to 30 August 2023; in 489 it found insufficient data, another vehicle at fault, Autopilot not in use or the crash otherwise unrelated. It grouped the remaining 467 into frontal crashes with adequate time for an attentive driver to respond (211), roadway departures after Autosteer was inadvertently disengaged by the driver (111) and departures in low traction (145). Tesla's weak driver engagement system was not appropriate for Autopilot's permissive operating capabilities; the mismatch created a critical safety gap that led to foreseeable misuse and avoidable crashes, and ODI identified at least 13 crashes involving one or more fatalities in which foreseeable misuse played an apparent role. Tesla filed recall 23V838 on 12 December 2023 for all vehicles with Autopilot (investigation population 2,031,220), and ODI opened recall query RQ24009 to assess the remedy.

refs.title: IIHS, Drivers let their focus slip as they get used to partial automation, November 2020
refs.finding: In a four-week study by IIHS and MIT AgeLab of 20 Massachusetts volunteers, the ten drivers of a Volvo S90 were, after correction for video coding errors, more than 3 times as likely to show signs of disengagement and 17 times as likely to take both hands off the wheel after a month of Pilot Assist use, compared with the start of the study.

refs.title: IIHS, Drivers quickly learn to skirt limits set by partial automation systems, September 2024
refs.finding: Fourteen drivers of a 2020 Tesla Model 3 logged a little more than 12,000 miles on Autopilot, which issued 3,858 attention warnings; from the first to the fourth week initial reminders per 1,000 miles rose 26% while escalations fell 64%, and drivers grew more likely to take their hands off the wheel, look away and do secondary tasks during alerts.

refs.title: Reuters, Tesla ordered by Florida jury to pay $243 million in fatal Autopilot crash, August 2025
refs.finding: A Miami federal jury awarded $129 million in compensatory and $200 million in punitive damages, with Tesla assigned 33% of compensatory damages ($42.6 million) and the driver 67%; in the 25 April 2019 crash the driver reached down for a dropped phone and drove his Model S through a stop sign and light into a parked Chevrolet Tahoe, killing Naibel Benavides Leon and seriously injuring Dillon Angulo. Plaintiffs argued Tesla designed Autopilot for controlled-access highways but did not stop its use elsewhere; Tesla said the driver was solely at fault and it would appeal.

refs.title: US District Court, Southern District of Florida, Benavides v. Tesla, No. 1:21-cv-21940, Notice of Appeal (Dkt. 616), March 2026
refs.finding: On 16 March 2026 Tesla appealed to the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit from the final judgment entered on 4 August 2025 and from the court's 20 February 2026 order denying its amended renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law or, alternatively, for a new trial or to amend the judgment.

refs.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, PE25012 opening resume, Traffic safety violations while Full Self Driving is engaged, October 2025
refs.finding: Opened 7 October 2025 for an estimated 2,882,566 Tesla vehicles with FSD (Supervised) or FSD (Beta), which Tesla characterises as an SAE Level 2 system requiring a fully attentive driver. ODI counted 58 incidents, including 14 crashes with 23 injuries and no fatalities, in which FSD induced vehicle behaviour that violated traffic safety laws, most often entering intersections against red signals or moving into opposing lanes; six SGO reports describe crashes after a Tesla entered an intersection on red. ODI will assess whether drivers had warning or time to intervene.

refs.title: IIHS, IIHS-HLDI research finds little evidence that partial automation prevents crashes, July 2024
refs.finding: In claims and police-reported crash data for 2017-19 Nissan Rogues with ProPILOT Assist and 2013-17 BMW and Mini models with Driving Assistant Plus, forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking cut crashes and claims, but partial automation showed little evidence of preventing crashes beyond them; ProPILOT Assist's apparent benefits were similar on low-speed roads, suggesting other factors. The vehicles were 5 to 11 years old and the data could not show whether systems were on.

refs.title: IIHS, First partial driving automation safeguard ratings show industry has work to do, March 2024
refs.finding: Of the first 14 partial automation systems tested from nine manufacturers, one (Lexus LS Teammate) was rated acceptable, two marginal and 11 poor, including the Tesla Model 3; IIHS President David Harkey said most lack adequate measures to prevent misuse and there is little evidence partial automation makes driving safer.

nodes.control_note: Driving automation that handles the routine work well is what invites drivers to stop watching, and drivers learn to game the reminders meant to keep them alert. Driver monitoring, limits on where a system will engage and marketing that does not oversell it narrow the gap, but do not close it while a human must take over.

actions.action: Recall systems whose driver controls are too weak
actions.evidence: After NHTSA's investigation, Tesla recalled all vehicles equipped with Autopilot in December 2023 to make driver warnings more effective and reduce mode confusion; NHTSA opened a recall query to assess whether the fix works.
