ref.title: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, EA22002 closing resume, Autopilot System Driver Controls, April 2024
ref.finding: ODI analysed 956 crashes reported up to 30 August 2023; in 489 it found insufficient data, another vehicle at fault, Autopilot not in use or the crash otherwise unrelated. It grouped the remaining 467 into frontal crashes with adequate time for an attentive driver to respond (211), roadway departures after Autosteer was inadvertently disengaged by the driver (111) and departures in low traction (145). Tesla's weak driver engagement system was not appropriate for Autopilot's permissive operating capabilities; the mismatch created a critical safety gap that led to foreseeable misuse and avoidable crashes, and ODI identified at least 13 crashes involving one or more fatalities in which foreseeable misuse played an apparent role. Tesla filed recall 23V838 on 12 December 2023 for all vehicles with Autopilot (investigation population 2,031,220), and ODI opened recall query RQ24009 to assess the remedy.

actions.action: Bar marketing that oversells driver assistance
actions.evidence: California's DMV adopted a judge's finding in December 2025 that Tesla's use of the name Autopilot misled consumers; given 60 days, Tesla stopped using the term in its California marketing and renamed Full Self-Driving to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), avoiding a 30-day licence suspension. The ruling covers marketing in one state, not how the systems behave.

ref.title: California DMV, Tesla Takes Corrective Action to Avoid DMV Suspension, February 2026
ref.finding: In its 16 December 2025 decision the DMV found that Tesla's use of Autopilot for its driver assistance features misled consumers and violated state law; it kept the judge's findings but permanently stayed the manufacturer licence suspension and gave Tesla 60 days to act. Tesla stopped using Autopilot in California marketing and changed Full Self-Driving to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), avoiding a 30-day suspension of its dealer and manufacturer licences.

actions.action: Rate safeguards against driver misuse
actions.evidence: IIHS rates partial automation on driver monitoring, escalating alerts and emergency stops; in its first round only one of 14 systems was acceptable.

ref.title: IIHS, First partial driving automation safeguard ratings show industry has work to do, March 2024
ref.finding: The ratings ask systems to monitor the driver's gaze and hands, start alerts within 10 seconds of inattention and escalate before 20 seconds, begin slowing within 35 seconds, and require the driver to start or confirm lane changes; of 14 systems one was acceptable, two marginal and 11 poor.

precedents.event: Uber self-driving test car kills a pedestrian in Tempe
precedents.parallel: A human was meant to supervise an automated car and stopped watching the road, the same supervision gap that partial automation creates for ordinary drivers.
precedents.outcome: The NTSB found the probable cause was the operator's failure to monitor the road and the automated system because she was visually distracted throughout the trip by her personal phone, with Uber's inadequate safety culture contributing; the system detected the pedestrian 5.6 seconds before impact but never classified her correctly, and the operator looked back at the road about 1 second before impact.

ref.title: NTSB, Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, HWY18MH010, 2019
ref.finding: In the 18 March 2018 crash in Tempe, Arizona, the probable cause was the vehicle operator's failure to monitor the driving environment and the automated driving system because she was visually distracted throughout the trip by her personal cell phone; contributing were Uber ATG's inadequate safety culture, including no adequate mechanisms for operators' automation complacency, and insufficient state oversight. The system detected the pedestrian 5.6 seconds before impact but never accurately classified her as a pedestrian or predicted her path; the operator redirected her gaze to the road about 1 second before impact.

nodes.label: Algorithms set each worker's pay
nodes.summary: In the UK, many platforms now set each job's pay by algorithm, so workers cannot accurately predict earnings, says the Trades Union Congress[3]. One Oxford study of 258 UK Uber drivers found that after dynamic pricing arrived in 2023, inflation-adjusted hourly income before costs fell from over £22 to just over £19[1]. Uber said it did not recognise the figures[4].

refs.title: University of Oxford Department of Computer Science, New Oxford research reveals Uber's algorithmic pricing leaves drivers and passengers worse off, June 2025
refs.finding: Analysing data from 258 UK Uber drivers across more than 1.5 million trips between 2016 and 2024, researchers working with Worker Info Exchange found that after Uber introduced dynamic pricing in 2023 passengers paid more per trip while drivers' inflation-adjusted hourly income before operating costs dropped from over £22 to just over £19, drivers spent more unpaid time waiting, and Uber's commission rose from around 25% to 29%, in some cases over half the fare.

refs.title: Binns, Stein, Datta, Van Kleek and Shadbolt, Not Even Nice Work If You Can Get It; A Longitudinal Study of Uber's Algorithmic Pay and Pricing, FAccT 2025 (arXiv preprint)
refs.finding: A participatory audit of Uber's algorithmic pay and work allocation using 1.5 million trips from 258 UK drivers finds that after dynamic pricing pay fell, Uber's cut rose, job allocation and pay became less predictable, inequality between drivers increased and drivers spent more time waiting for jobs. Published in the Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (doi 10.1145/3715275.3732099).

refs.title: TUC, The human price of dynamic pay, 2026
refs.finding: Says many platform operators in the UK now use algorithms to set an individual price for each job, so different workers may be offered different rates for the same job and can no longer accurately predict what they will earn on a shift; defines dynamic pay as algorithmically determined, variable and potentially personalised pay. Citing the Oxford and Worker Info Exchange study, the median driver retained 71% of the fare, only 46% retained 75% or more, Uber's surplus per hour rose 38%, and 93 of 114 drivers earned less after dynamic pricing while 21 earned more. The TUC calls for ending dynamic pay-setting, employment status reform and collective data rights.

refs.title: TaxiPoint, Uber rejects University of Oxford study that finds drivers see drop in pay under 'Dynamic' pricing, June 2025
refs.finding: Uber said: We do not recognise the figures in this report, adding that UK drivers took home over £1 billion in earnings between January and March 2025, up on the year before, and that all drivers receive a weekly summary breaking down what Uber and the driver received.

refs.title: Dubal and Negrón, How artificial intelligence uncouples hard work from fair wages through 'surveillance pay' practices, and how to fix it, Washington Center for Equitable Growth, August 2025
refs.finding: Describes surveillance pay as digitalised wage-setting using granular worker data, including real-time monitoring. The authors' review of 500 early-stage AI vendors marketing machine-learning products for labour management identified 20 whose products they judged at high risk of producing algorithmic wage discrimination: five in customer service, four in health care, one in last-mile logistics, one in manufacturing and nine cross-sector; 16 of the 20 link directly to payroll or HR systems. The authors argue transparency alone is insufficient and propose banning the use of real-time data to automate pay.

nodes.control_note: Setting each job's price from live data lets a platform match drivers to demand, and the same opacity lets it change workers' share without notice. Bans on pay set from surveillance data, collective data rights and rules on automated decisions can limit it, but Colorado's governor vetoed such a ban in 2026.

actions.action: Require transparency and human oversight of algorithmic management
actions.evidence: The EU platform work directive, published in November 2024, imposes greater transparency on algorithmic management and bans some automated decisions, such as suspending accounts; its rules apply only from 2 December 2026.

ref.title: European Parliament Legislative Train, Initiative to improve the working conditions of people working in the platform economy, 2024
ref.finding: The directive was adopted by the Council on 14 October 2024, signed on 23 October and published in the Official Journal on 11 November 2024, and will apply from 2 December 2026; it imposes greater transparency on algorithmic management and prohibits certain decisions, such as suspending accounts, and the use of algorithms to process emotional or psychological data.

actions.action: Ban pay set from surveillance data
actions.evidence: Colorado's legislature passed a bill in May 2026 that would have barred using surveillance data in price or wage setting algorithms to set individual prices or wages, enforced as a deceptive trade practice; the governor vetoed it on 2 June 2026.

ref.title: Colorado General Assembly, HB26-1210, Prohibit Surveillance Price & Wage Setting, 2026
ref.finding: The bill would bar discrimination against consumers or workers when a price or wage setting algorithm analyses surveillance data about a person's characteristics, online behaviour or biometrics and its output substantially drives individualised prices or wages, enforced under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act. It passed the House 39 to 24 and the Senate 19 to 15, the House concurred on 7 May 2026, and the governor vetoed it on 2 June 2026.

actions.action: Sue under data protection law over automated pay
actions.evidence: Worker Info Exchange International filed a collective claim in the Amsterdam District Court on 2 September 2026 for Uber drivers in seven countries, alleging that automated pay setting and allocation breach the GDPR and that driver data was used for machine learning unlawfully; Uber rejects the claims and no court has ruled.

ref.title: AFP via Noovo, Uber visé par une action collective de chauffeurs à l'échelle européenne, September 2026
ref.finding: WIE International filed a complaint on Wednesday at the Amsterdam district court, where Uber has its European headquarters, for Uber drivers in the UK, Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, France, Poland and Romania, alleging that Uber made pay dynamic from 2020 and breached the GDPR through automated decisions without human involvement on fares and ride assignment and by processing drivers' data for machine learning. Uber told AFP it categorically rejects the claims, says drivers can accept or decline trips with earnings shown, and that its commission rate has stayed stable.

actions.action: Study how platforms set each worker's pay
actions.evidence: In October 2026 the US FTC ordered nine companies, including Uber, Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart, to document the inputs and tools they use to set driver pay and prices, including whether personal data drives individual pay offers; it is a study, not an enforcement action.

ref.title: US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Launches Personalized Pricing and Compensation Inquiry, October 2026
ref.finding: On 28 October 2026 the FTC voted 2 to 0 to issue Section 6(b) orders to Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart; ride-sharing and delivery firms must document the inputs, tools and procedures used to set driver compensation and pricing, including whether shifting pay offers use drivers' personal data. Chairman Ferguson said workers deserve to know if their compensation is affected by how companies use their personal data.

precedents.event: DoorDash used customer tips to cover its own pay to workers
precedents.parallel: An opaque platform pay formula quietly shifted money away from workers, and only an investigation showed how pay was really calculated.
precedents.outcome: The District of Columbia attorney general alleged that from July 2017 to September 2019 DoorDash used consumer tips to cover its own payments to workers; DoorDash paid $2.5 million, including $1.5 million to workers, must pass all tips on without reducing base pay and must give workers an itemised summary of each delivery's pay.

ref.title: Office of the Attorney General for the District of Columbia, AG Racine Reaches $2.5 Million Agreement with DoorDash for Misrepresenting that Consumer Tips Would Go to Food Delivery Drivers, November 2020
ref.finding: Under DoorDash's payment model from July 2017 to September 2019 it used consumer tips to cover its own payments to workers instead of passing them on, so the more consumers tipped the less DoorDash paid; the $2.5 million settlement includes $1.5 million for workers, $750,000 to the District and $250,000 to charities, and DoorDash must keep a pay model that passes all tips to workers without reducing base pay and give workers an itemised summary of base pay, tips and promotions for each delivery.

nodes.label: Experts let AI agents settle their judgment calls
nodes.summary: Experts' judgment calls can quietly go an AI agent's way. In one Anthropic randomised trial, 50 expert analysts went with an agent's coin-flipped lean 86% of the time against about 50% by chance, and experience did not predict who deferred[1]. The effect on final recommendations was weaker, and the study covered one task, one field and one model[1].

refs.title: Herdağdelen, Joren and Tamkin, How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls, Anthropic, 27 October 2026
refs.finding: Of 61 participants, 11 chose not to use the agent; the 50 analysts who used Claude Code matched their agent's coin-flip lean on four analytical choices 86% of the time against about 50% by chance, and experience and expertise did not predict who deferred. In 38 cases where an analyst had already stated a preference, they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed against 6% when it agreed (95% CI for the gap 24 to 82 points). 77% repeated the agent's argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and 15% credited it; 52% of survey respondents rated the recommendation as more their own. 54% recommended rollout when the agent leaned that way against 36% when it leaned the other way. Serious methodological errors: 6 of 11 without the agent against 3 of 50 with it, groups that differed in experience. The leans were deliberately strengthened; one task, field and model; with no lean assigned the model made the same five choices in 112 of 123 runs.

refs.title: Dratsch et al., Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance, Radiology 307(4), 2023
refs.finding: In a prospective experiment, 27 radiologists read mammograms with purported AI BI-RADS suggestions; correct ratings averaged 79.7% with correct suggestions and 19.8% with incorrect ones for inexperienced readers, 81.3% and 24.8% for moderately experienced and 82.3% and 45.5% for very experienced readers.

nodes.control_note: Deferral leaves little trace in the expert's own account, so it is hard to detect. Agents that make the best case for each option or ask for the expert's view first, and organisations that decide which decisions need a person's own informed judgment, could keep the check meaningful, but neither has been tested.

actions.action: Have agents argue each defensible option, not one
actions.evidence: The authors suggest agents could make the best case for each option on a judgment call, or ask experts for their own view before offering one, after analysts in their trial mostly went with whichever side the agent argued.

ref.title: Herdağdelen, Joren and Tamkin, How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls, Anthropic, 27 October 2026
ref.finding: Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one; organisations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person's own informed judgment. In the trial, analysts went with their agent's lean 86% of the time.

precedents.parallel: Professionals given an automated aid used its cues in place of their own checks, as analysts in the agent trial went with the agent's lean.
precedents.outcome: Pilots in flight scenarios made automation-related omission and commission errors; imposed accountability did not help, but pilots who felt accountable for their own performance double-checked the automation more and erred less, and pilots erroneously remembered expected cues being present.

ref.title: Mosier, Skitka, Heers and Burdick, Automation Bias: Decision Making and Performance in High-Tech Cockpits, International Journal of Aviation Psychology 8(1), 1998
ref.finding: Automation bias is omission and commission errors from using automated cues in place of vigilant information seeking; experimentally manipulated accountability did not significantly affect performance, pilots who felt internally accountable checked more and erred less, and pilots erroneously remembered the presence of expected cues.

nodes.label: Deepfakes submitted as evidence in court
nodes.summary: Image, video and voice generators let litigants fabricate evidence that passes a quick look. In September 2025 a California state court found two video exhibits in a civil case were AI deepfakes and threw out the case[1]. Such challenges are still rare in US federal courts: in a March 2026 survey, 15 of 931 responding judges had encountered one[3].

refs.title: Eugene Volokh, Court Throws Out Case After Finding Plaintiffs Submitted Deepfake Videos and Altered Images, The Volokh Conspiracy (Reason), 25 September 2025
refs.finding: Quotes Judge Victoria Kolakowski's 9 September 2025 order in Mendones v. Cushman & Wakefield, Inc. (Superior Court of California, Alameda County): exhibits 6A and 6C are products of GenAI and do not capture the actual speech and image of the witness, who differs in accent, cadence, volume, word choice, pauses, gestures and facial expression from an authentic exhibit; a terminating sanction is appropriate and proportional; referral for criminal prosecution is not appropriate. The plaintiffs were self-represented.

refs.title: NBC News, AI-generated evidence is showing up in court. Judges say they're not ready, by Jared Perlo, 18 November 2025
refs.finding: In a California housing dispute, Judge Kolakowski noticed the witness's voice in exhibit 6C was disjointed and monotone; the video's metadata said it was captured on an iPhone 6, which the plaintiffs' own argument ruled out. She dismissed the case on 9 September and denied reconsideration on 6 November 2025; Judge Erica Yew said AI-faked or altered evidence is likely happening more often than is publicly reported, but no repository tracks it.

refs.title: Reuters, OpenAI, Meta caution US judiciary about risk of 'deepfake' evidence, by Nate Raymond, 15 October 2026
refs.finding: At a Boston meeting of the US Judicial Conference's Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, OpenAI's Shira Anderson said AI images keep improving, she did not think there would be a scientific way to detect them going forward, and because each company has its own watermark system there is no universal way to detect them all; Meta's director of product management Devin Norder said media from leading models is indistinguishable by humans from authentic media and quite trivial in cost and time to create. A March Federal Judicial Center survey found 15 of 931 responding judges had encountered a case where a party challenged evidence as a deepfake, and committee chair Judge Jesse Furman said courts had not yet seen many such cases despite many predictions.

nodes.control_note: The generators that make convincing fake video and voice cheaply are the same tools people use for legitimate editing, so forgeries cannot be stopped at the source, and watermarks differ by company. Duties to verify evidence and early authenticity hearings limit how far a fake gets, but they depend on judges spotting fakes, and judges NBC News spoke to said courts are not ready.

actions.action: Require lawyers to verify evidence and raise suspected AI fakes before trial
actions.evidence: Louisiana's Act 250, in effect since August 2025, requires attorneys to use reasonable diligence to verify evidence before offering it, makes offering evidence they knew or should have known was artificially manipulated without disclosure a violation punishable by contempt, and requires parties to raise suspected AI-generated or altered exhibits at the pretrial conference or a pretrial hearing; it covers civil procedure in one state.

ref.title: Louisiana Code of Civil Procedure Art. 371, as amended by Acts 2025, No. 250 (House Bill 178), Louisiana State Legislature
ref.finding: An attorney shall not knowingly encourage or produce false evidence, including evidence artificially generated or altered, and shall exercise reasonable diligence to verify the authenticity of evidence before offering it; offering evidence the attorney knew or should have known through reasonable diligence was false or artificially manipulated, without disclosure, violates the article, and violators are subject to punishment for contempt of court. The same act amended Art. 1551 (https://legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=122868) so a party that reasonably suspects an opponent's exhibits were falsified, including by AI generation or alteration, must raise it at the pretrial conference or a pretrial hearing. HB 178 was signed on 11 June 2025 and took effect on 1 August 2025.

actions.action: Make a deepfake objection come with evidence before courts examine it
actions.evidence: In May 2026 the US federal evidence rules committee tabled a proposed amendment under which a party challenging evidence as AI-fabricated must first show an inquiry is justified, after which the party offering it must show it is more likely than not authentic; the Justice Department's representative wanted more input on criminal cases, and the committee planned to revisit it at its fall 2026 meeting.

ref.title: Bloomberg Law, Proposed AI Evidentiary Rules Punted Due to Lack of Consensus, by Holly Barker, 7 May 2026
ref.finding: The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules tabled proposed amendments on AI evidence after a couple of hours of debate and will reconsider them at its fall meeting. One would require a challenger to show an inquiry is justified, after which the proponent of evidence challenged as possibly AI-fabricated must prove it is more likely than not authentic. The Justice Department's representative, Elizabeth Shapiro, supported gathering more stakeholder input, particularly on criminal cases.

precedents.event: Forged text-message image in Rossbach v. Montefiore
precedents.parallel: Before generative AI, a litigant built a harassment claim on a fabricated picture of phone messages, and only forensic examination exposed it.
precedents.outcome: A federal district court in New York found by clear and convincing evidence that the plaintiff had fabricated the messages, testified falsely and spoliated evidence, dismissed her claims with prejudice and ordered $157,026.27 in fees; in August 2023 the Second Circuit affirmed against her but vacated the sanction on her lawyers for lack of an explicit bad-faith finding.

ref.title: Rossbach v. Montefiore Medical Center, US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, No. 21-2084, August 2023
ref.finding: The central evidence was an image of three sexually suggestive text messages; a forensic expert found the file lacked the metadata of a photo taken on an iPhone X and that icons, fonts and emoji did not match iPhone messages. The district court dismissed the remaining claims with prejudice and imposed $157,026.27 in fees; the Second Circuit upheld the findings, dismissal and fee calculation and vacated the sanction against counsel.

nodes.label: Students turn away from computer science
nodes.summary: Fewer US students are choosing computer science. Undergraduate enrollment in computer and information science at US four-year colleges fell 8.1% in fall 2025 and graduate enrollment fell 14.0%, while overall postsecondary enrollment grew 1.0%[1]. None of these sources isolates AI as the cause of the decline, and the Clearinghouse says the reasons are not yet clear[2].

refs.title: National Student Clearinghouse, The Changing Landscape of Postsecondary Education, February 2026
refs.finding: In fall 2025, computer and information science enrollment declined across every award level and institution type: undergraduate enrollment at four-year institutions fell 8.1% to about 606,000 and graduate enrollment fell 14.0% to about 190,000, while overall postsecondary enrollment grew 1.0%. Data science and data analytics grew strongly to nearly 80,000 students at the undergraduate and graduate levels.

refs.title: National Student Clearinghouse, Computer Science Enrollment Is Cooling, August 2026
refs.finding: In spring 2026, undergraduate computer and information sciences enrollment fell 8.4% at four-year institutions, 9.3% at primarily associate degree-granting baccalaureate institutions and 11.2% at two-year colleges, declining across every major institutional sector, while overall undergraduate enrollment grew 1.3% and health professions and engineering posted significant increases. The Clearinghouse says the reasons for the declines are not yet clear and does not mention AI.

refs.title: Batten, CRA Update: New CRA Taulbee Survey Findings Show Record Degree Production Alongside a Cooling Enrollment Pipeline, Computing Research News, June 2026
refs.finding: In 2025, across all responding units, new bachelor's computer science majors numbered 33,490, total bachelor's enrollment 169,528 and bachelor's degrees awarded a record 41,858. In the longitudinal cohort of units that reported complete data every year from 2020 to 2025, new majors fell 13%, total enrollment fell 4% and degrees rose 13% from the prior year. The article says the record degree count likely reflects prior surges in enrollment and that the downturns imply degree counts will plateau and decline; it does not attribute the bachelor's trends to AI.

refs.title: George, CERP Pulse Survey: A Snapshot of 2025 Undergraduate Computing Enrollment Patterns, Computing Research News, October 2025
refs.finding: CERP contacted 288 CRA academic member computing units and received responses from 134 leaders (46.5% response rate) at 130 institutions in the US and Canada, fielded 27 August to 17 September 2025. 62% of responding units reported lower undergraduate enrollment for 2025-26 than 2024-25 and 13% reported increases; declines were concentrated in computer science, information systems and software engineering, while computer engineering, data science, cybersecurity and AI programs more often grew. Leaders cited students' concern about hiring and layoffs in tech, fears that AI will eliminate many software engineering jobs, and falling international enrollment, with 54% somewhat or strongly agreeing that international undergraduate computing enrollment is down amid immigration policy changes and visa processing delays; some leaders saw AI as an opportunity.

refs.title: Marken, College Students Weigh AI's Impact on Majors and Careers, Gallup, April 2026
refs.finding: In the Lumina Foundation-Gallup 2026 State of Higher Education Study, web surveys of 6,010 US adults aged 18 to 59 from Dynata's opt-in nonprobability panel, fielded 2 to 31 October 2025 and including 1,433 associate and 2,368 bachelor's students, 16% of currently enrolled students said they had already changed their major or field of study because of AI's potential impact (19% of associate and 13% of bachelor's students; 21% of men and 12% of women), and 42% of bachelor's students said AI had caused them to give at least a fair amount of thought to changing their major.

limiters.limit: Students shift within computing, not out of it
limiters.evidence: Data science and data analytics enrollment grew to nearly 80,000 US students in fall 2025 while computer and information science fell.

ref.title: National Student Clearinghouse, The Changing Landscape of Postsecondary Education, February 2026
ref.finding: In fall 2025, computer and information science enrollment declined across every award level and institution type: undergraduate enrollment at four-year institutions fell 8.1% to about 606,000 and graduate enrollment fell 14.0% to about 190,000, while overall postsecondary enrollment grew 1.0%. Data science and data analytics grew strongly to nearly 80,000 students at the undergraduate and graduate levels.

limiters.limit: Visa limits and the job market blur the AI signal
limiters.evidence: 54% of surveyed computing units somewhat or strongly agreed that international undergraduate computing enrollment is down, with leaders citing immigration policy changes and visa delays alongside job-market and AI fears.

ref.title: George, CERP Pulse Survey: A Snapshot of 2025 Undergraduate Computing Enrollment Patterns, Computing Research News, October 2025
ref.finding: CERP contacted 288 CRA academic member computing units and received responses from 134 leaders (46.5% response rate) at 130 institutions in the US and Canada, fielded 27 August to 17 September 2025. 62% of responding units reported lower undergraduate enrollment for 2025-26 than 2024-25 and 13% reported increases; declines were concentrated in computer science, information systems and software engineering, while computer engineering, data science, cybersecurity and AI programs more often grew. Leaders cited students' concern about hiring and layoffs in tech, fears that AI will eliminate many software engineering jobs, and falling international enrollment, with 54% somewhat or strongly agreeing that international undergraduate computing enrollment is down amid immigration policy changes and visa processing delays; some leaders saw AI as an opportunity.

enablers.action: Hire fewer young workers into AI-exposed jobs
enablers.evidence: In US payroll data through June 2026, employment of 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed occupations was 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mainly through reduced hiring; the authors call this descriptive, not causal.

ref.title: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, revised August 2026
ref.finding: In ADP payroll data on millions of US workers through June 2026, employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, operating primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations; experienced workers show no comparable gap. The authors call these early, descriptive indicators rather than causal estimates.

precedents.event: Computer science enrollment after the dot-com bust
precedents.parallel: Computing degrees fell during the early-2000s downturn and slow job growth, much as enrollment is falling now amid weak entry-level hiring and fears about AI.
precedents.outcome: In CRA's survey of doctorate-granting departments, new computer science majors halved from 15,958 in fall 2000 to 7,915 in fall 2007 and enrollment fell 49% from its 2001-02 peak, before new-major counts levelled off in 2006 and 2007.

ref.title: Vegso, Enrollments and Degree Production at US CS Departments Drop Further in 2006-07, Computing Research News, March 2008
ref.finding: In CRA's Taulbee Survey of doctorate-granting departments, the number of new CS majors in fall 2007 was half of fall 2000 (7,915 versus 15,958), enrollments dropped 49% from their 2001-02 peak, and bachelor's degrees fell 43% between 2003-04 and 2006-07, a decline the article calls foreseeable given the economic downturn and slow job growth of the early 2000s; flat and slightly rising new-major counts in 2006 and 2007 might indicate that interest was stabilizing.

nodes.label: AI text and machine translation degrade Wikipedia
nodes.summary: AI tools and machine translation let people add Wikipedia articles they did not write or cannot read[2][3]. Two detectors flagged 5.36% of 2,909 English articles from August 2024 as significantly AI-generated[1], and volunteers on four African-language editions estimated 40% to 60% of their articles were uncorrected machine translations[2]. One 2025 study puts LLM influence at about 1% in certain categories[4].

refs.title: Brooks, Eggert and Peskoff, The Rise of AI-Generated Content in Wikipedia, Proceedings of the First Workshop on Advancing NLP for Wikipedia (WikiNLP), November 2024
refs.finding: Princeton researchers ran two AI-text detectors, GPTZero and Binoculars, on 2,909 English Wikipedia articles created in August 2024 (pages under 100 words removed), with thresholds set to a 1% false positive rate on articles from before March 2022. They flagged 5.36% of the new articles, a lower bound of 4.36% after subtracting the baseline, and found lower rates for German, French and Italian. Of 45 English articles flagged by both tools, 8 were self-promotional and 8 pushed a viewpoint on polarising topics; some flagged pages had been deleted by moderators. False negatives were not estimated, so the true share could be substantially higher, and the tools are designed mainly for English.

refs.title: Jacob Judah, MIT Technology Review, How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral, September 2025
refs.finding: Volunteers working on four African-language Wikipedias estimated that 40% to 60% of their articles were uncorrected machine translations, and the magazine's own audit of the Inuktitut edition estimated more than two-thirds of pages with more than several sentences contain machine-translated portions. Wikipedia's built-in Content Translate tool relies on external machine translation systems; each community decides whether to allow it, and English Wikipedia has largely banned it, claiming about 95% of articles created with it failed to meet an acceptable standard without substantial work. Wikipedia is sometimes the largest online text source for low-resource languages, so its errors can carry into AI training data. The article says there is no perfect data on the scale of the problem and several figures are volunteers' estimates.

refs.title: Wikimedia Meta-Wiki, Proposals for closing projects/Closure of Greenlandic Wikipedia, December 2024 to December 2025
refs.finding: Kenneth Wehr, the Greenlandic Wikipedia's only active admin, proposed closing it on 25 December 2024: only one or two Greenlandic users had contributed in about 20 years, he had deleted most of the roughly 1,500 articles he inherited, which were mostly a few words long or unintelligible, leaving about 250, a Wikimedia AI translator had produced random letter sequences, and Google Translate's Greenlandic output still makes errors such as translating 'reindeer' as 'parrot'. He argued the project corrupts the Greenlandic language. The Language Committee adopted the closure on 27 September 2025 and decided on 1 December 2025 not to move the remaining content to the Incubator.

refs.title: Huang, Xu, Geng, Wan and Chen, Wikipedia in the Era of LLMs: Evolution and Risks, Transactions on Machine Learning Research (arXiv 2503.02879, March 2025, revised March 2026)
refs.finding: The authors estimate that large language models have influenced Wikipedia content by about 1% in certain categories and conclude that LLMs have not yet fully changed Wikipedia's language and knowledge structures. They warn that if Wikipedia-based machine translation benchmarks absorb LLM-generated text, model scores may be inflated, and that retrieval-augmented generation may suffer if the knowledge base is contaminated.

limiters.limit: Editors delete and ban unreviewed AI text
limiters.evidence: English Wikipedia made unreviewed LLM-generated pages eligible for speedy deletion in August 2025 and in 2026 generally prohibited using AI writing tools to create or rewrite articles, except copyediting and reviewed translation.

ref.title: Wikimedia Meta-Wiki, Artificial intelligence/Policies by project, accessed October 2026
ref.finding: English Wikipedia adopted speedy deletion criterion G15 on 4 August 2025, making pages that show signs of being generated by an LLM with no human review eligible for speedy deletion. Later English rules include a guideline of 10 February 2026 allowing LLM-assisted translation from other Wikipedias if reviewed by a person skilled in both languages, a guideline of 20 March 2026 prohibiting LLM-generated or rewritten article content except copyediting and translation, an editing policy of 11 April 2026 under which using AI writing tools to create or rewrite articles is, save for a few exceptions, generally prohibited, and a guideline of 7 May 2026 permitting presumptive removal of AI-generated content from users with a history of habitual LLM use. Many other language editions list their own AI policies or guidelines.

limiters.evidence: A Wikimedia research review of the main 2024 study says it does not show whether the text readers see is more likely AI-generated, and that the two detectors it used often disagreed across languages.

ref.title: Tilman Bayer, Wikimedia Research Newsletter, October 2024
ref.finding: A review of the Brooks et al. study says it does not report what share of AI-generated articles survived editors' checks and leaves it unclear whether the text readers actually read has become more likely to be AI-generated. It notes that the reliability of AI detection software has been repeatedly questioned, that the two detectors often disagreed, with GPTZero far more aggressive than Binoculars in English, French and German but much less so in Italian, and that assuming pre-GPT-3.5 calibration articles are comparable to August 2024 ones is questionable.

enablers.action: Offer one-click machine translation of articles
enablers.counters: Editors delete and ban unreviewed AI text
enablers.evidence: Wikipedia's built-in Content Translate tool relies on external machine translation systems and each language community decides whether to allow it; English Wikipedia has largely banned it, saying about 95% of articles created with it failed to meet an acceptable standard without substantial work.

ref.title: Jacob Judah, MIT Technology Review, How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral, September 2025
ref.finding: Volunteers working on four African-language Wikipedias estimated that 40% to 60% of their articles were uncorrected machine translations, and the magazine's own audit of the Inuktitut edition estimated more than two-thirds of pages with more than several sentences contain machine-translated portions. Wikipedia's built-in Content Translate tool relies on external machine translation systems; each community decides whether to allow it, and English Wikipedia has largely banned it, claiming about 95% of articles created with it failed to meet an acceptable standard without substantial work. Wikipedia is sometimes the largest online text source for low-resource languages, so its errors can carry into AI training data. The article says there is no perfect data on the scale of the problem and several figures are volunteers' estimates.

precedents.event: Scots Wikipedia written by a non-speaker
precedents.parallel: Text produced by someone who did not know the language filled much of a small-language Wikipedia, and the Signpost warned it had likely poisoned the training data translation algorithms use for that language.
precedents.outcome: Editors proposed a bot mass rollback of the affected articles and recruiting new admins, while the Signpost named the lack of a Scots-speaking editor community as the long-term problem.

ref.title: SnowFire and Nosebagbear, The Wikipedia Signpost, The high road and the low road: Will the Scots language Wikipedia survive?, August 2020
ref.finding: One prolific user, described in a viral Reddit post as an American teenager who could not speak Scots and as the writer of almost every article on the Scots Wikipedia, had edited it for over seven years, keeping English sentence structure and translating words one to one from a dictionary. The Signpost says this had likely poisoned training data sets for Scots used by translation algorithms. Short-term responses were a bot mass rollback of affected articles, enlisting new admins and other bots; the core problem was the absence of a Scots-speaking editor community, since authentic Scots-speaking editors had left by 2012.

nodes.label: Chatbots replace customer-service staff
nodes.summary: Companies are cutting support staff as AI takes over routine contacts, and some walked cuts back. Salesforce's chief executive said he cut support headcount from 9,000 to about 5,000[3], while Klarna piloted freelance human agents and Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversed voice-bot cuts[2][4]. These are company claims, and none isolates AI as the cause of wider job change.

refs.title: Klarna, Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month, February 2024
refs.finding: In its first month of global availability the AI assistant had 2.3 million conversations, two-thirds of Klarna's customer service chats, doing the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents; Klarna said errands were resolved in under 2 minutes against 11 minutes before, customer satisfaction was on par with human agents, and it estimated a $40 million profit improvement in 2024.

refs.title: Fortune, As Klarna flips from AI-first to hiring people again, a new landmark survey reveals most AI projects fail to deliver, May 2025
refs.finding: Chief executive Sebastian Siemiatkowski told Bloomberg that cost had been too predominant an evaluation factor and that the result was lower quality, and that customers must always be able to reach a human if they want; Klarna was piloting freelance human support agents. A spokesperson told Fortune Klarna still does not replace departing employees, apart from freelance agents in its outsourcing division, and is very much still AI-first.

refs.title: Fortune, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says his company has cut 4,000 customer service jobs as AI steps in: 'I need less heads', September 2025
refs.finding: On The Logan Bartlett Show, Benioff said he had reduced support headcount from 9,000 to about 5,000 because he needs fewer people, and that service interactions are now 50% with AI agents and 50% with humans. A Salesforce spokesperson said that after deploying its own AI support site it no longer needs to actively backfill support engineer roles and had redeployed hundreds of employees into professional services, sales and customer success.

refs.title: The Canberra Times, Major bank apologises, reverses AI job replacement plan after 'error', August 2025
refs.finding: Commonwealth Bank had cut 90 jobs, including 45 in direct banking, after introducing a voice bot on its inbound customer enquiries line; on 21 August 2025 it said its initial assessment did not adequately consider all relevant business considerations, that the roles were not redundant, and apologised, and staff could stay in their roles, seek redeployment or leave. The Finance Sector Union called the reversal a massive win and said the bank was caught out trying to dress up job cuts as innovation.

refs.title: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, Customer Service Representatives
refs.finding: US employment of customer service representatives was 2,666,000 in 2025 and is projected to decline 5% (141,800 jobs) from 2025 to 2035, with about 289,500 openings a year from replacement; BLS expects less demand, especially in retail trade, as tasks continue to be automated and self-service systems, social media and mobile apps let customers handle simple tasks. The page does not name AI or chatbots.

refs.title: Fortune, The AI boom hasn't stopped U.S. companies from hiring cheap offshore labor, and overseas call center employment is still skyrocketing, May 2026, updated August 2026
refs.finding: Citing IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines data analysed by Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok, call centre employment in the Philippines rose every year from 2016 through 2025, nearly doubling to 2 million over the decade.

nodes.control_note: Support desks are a large, scripted cost centre, so bots that handle routine contacts are an easy saving to book. Firms still answer for what their bots say, customers want a way to reach a person, and unions can contest cuts, which slows full replacement but does not stop firms leaving departed staff unreplaced.

actions.action: Hold firms liable for what their chatbots tell customers
actions.evidence: A British Columbia tribunal ruled in February 2024 that Air Canada was liable for a bereavement-fare answer its website chatbot got wrong, rejecting the idea that the bot was responsible for itself; the award was about CAD 650.

ref.title: Lifshitz and Hung, BC Tribunal Confirms Companies Remain Liable for Information Provided by AI Chatbot, Business Law Today (American Bar Association), February 2024
ref.finding: In Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149, decided 14 February 2024, the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal found Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation after its website chatbot wrongly told a customer he could claim a bereavement fare within 90 days of ticketing; the chatbot was part of Air Canada's website, so the airline was responsible for its content, and it awarded about CAD 650 plus interest and fees.

actions.action: Require disclosure of AI and a right to a human agent
actions.evidence: A US Senate bill introduced in July 2025 would make businesses that use AI for customer service say so at the start of an interaction and transfer callers on request to a human agent in the United States; on introduction it was referred to committee.

ref.title: S. 2495, Keep Call Centers in America Act of 2025, 119th Congress, introduced text (govinfo)
ref.finding: Introduced on 29 July 2025 by Senator Gallego with Senator Justice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; Section 201 would require a business that uses artificial intelligence for customer service to disclose at the start of a communication that a nonhuman, artificial intelligence or machine is being used, and to transfer the consumer immediately on request to a human customer service agent physically located in the United States. The 50-employee threshold in the bill's employer definition does not apply to Section 201.

actions.action: Contest redundancies blamed on bots
actions.evidence: After a Finance Sector Union challenge, Commonwealth Bank reversed customer service job cuts tied to a voice bot in August 2025 and let staff stay, redeploy or leave.

ref.title: The Canberra Times, Major bank apologises, reverses AI job replacement plan after 'error', August 2025
ref.finding: Commonwealth Bank had cut 90 jobs, including 45 in direct banking, after introducing a voice bot on its inbound customer enquiries line; on 21 August 2025 it said its initial assessment did not adequately consider all relevant business considerations, that the roles were not redundant, and apologised, and staff could stay in their roles, seek redeployment or leave. The Finance Sector Union called the reversal a massive win and said the bank was caught out trying to dress up job cuts as innovation.

precedents.event: Santander UK brings its call centres back from India
precedents.parallel: Moving customer service to a cheaper channel saved money until customers complained, the same pressure that has pushed some firms to put humans back behind their bots.
precedents.outcome: After topping the FSA complaint tables, Santander UK moved all call centre work from Bangalore and Pune back to three UK cities, creating 500 UK-based jobs; its chief executive said customers prefer UK call centres.

ref.title: RTE News, UK bank brings call centres home, July 2011
ref.finding: Santander UK moved all its call centre work from Bangalore and Pune, set up in 2003 when it was Abbey, back to Glasgow, Leicester and Liverpool after customer feedback, hiring 500 more UK staff for about 1.5 million calls a month; the move followed the bank topping the FSA complaint tables, and chief executive Ana Botin said customers prefer call centres in the UK, not offshore.

nodes.label: AI-written books flood online bookstores
nodes.summary: Cheap generative AI is filling online bookstores with books. One working paper, not yet peer reviewed, found 20% of 14,419 self-published genre-fiction e-books on Amazon from January 2023 to March 2026 had substantial AI text, taking 12.1% of sales[1]. Amazon limits self-publishers to three new titles a day and requires them to disclose AI-generated text, images and translations[2][3].

refs.title: Chakrabarty, Liu, Ginsburg and Dhillon, Generative AI floods and dilutes the market for books, arXiv 2607.20349, working paper under review, July 2026
refs.finding: Ran the Pangram v3.3 detector over 14,419 self-published genre-fiction e-books released on Amazon from January 2023 to March 2026, matched to daily sales from a Big Five publisher's panel through June 2026. Books with substantial AI text (over 25% of prose) were 20.0% of books but 12.1% of sales and 11.3% of revenue, and rose from near zero to 31% of new Top 25 entrants. From Q1 2023 to Q1 2026 selling titles grew 19.2-fold and revenue 8.9-fold; revenue per book for no-AI releases fell from the 2023 to the 2025 cohort in seven of eight genre clusters. The authors read the comparisons as observational and specific to one platform.

refs.title: Quach, Amazon 'protects' against junk AI e-books by limiting author-bots to three a day, The Register, September 2023
refs.finding: Amazon told Kindle Direct Publishing users that while it had not seen a spike in publishing numbers, it was lowering the volume limits on new title creations to help protect against abuse, to three a day, with exceptions on request; it already required publishers to disclose AI-generated text, images or translations.

refs.title: Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing, Content Guidelines, Artificial intelligence (AI) content
refs.finding: KDP requires publishers to inform it of AI-generated content (text, images or translations created by an AI-based tool, even if substantially edited afterwards) when publishing or republishing a book, but not of AI-assisted content they created themselves and refined with AI tools.

refs.title: Fortune, Barnes & Noble CEO clarifies the bookseller's stance on AI-written books after refusing to ban them, May 2026
refs.finding: Chief executive James Daunt said Barnes & Noble does not sell AI books as far as it is aware, takes active measures to exclude AI-generated books from its online catalogue and never knowingly orders them for its stores, and demands that publishers label AI-generated books; he would not ban them outright and said it would stock an AI-written book that says so and does not rip off somebody else.

nodes.control_note: Generating a book costs almost nothing, so volume caps and disclosure rules slow the flow rather than stop it, and disclosure depends on sellers telling the truth. Retailers can keep AI books out of their own catalogues and authors can certify human work, but one seller can publish under many pen names.

actions.action: Cap new titles per day and require AI disclosure
actions.evidence: Amazon cut new Kindle Direct Publishing titles to three a day per publisher in September 2023 and requires publishers to declare AI-generated text, images and translations.

ref.title: Quach, Amazon 'protects' against junk AI e-books by limiting author-bots to three a day, The Register, September 2023
ref.finding: Amazon told Kindle Direct Publishing users that while it had not seen a spike in publishing numbers, it was lowering the volume limits on new title creations to help protect against abuse, to three a day, with exceptions on request; it already required publishers to disclose AI-generated text, images or translations.

actions.action: Keep AI-generated books out of the catalogue and demand labels
actions.evidence: Barnes & Noble says it takes active measures to exclude AI-generated books from its online catalogue and demands that publishers label them.

ref.title: Fortune, Barnes & Noble CEO clarifies the bookseller's stance on AI-written books after refusing to ban them, May 2026
ref.finding: Chief executive James Daunt said Barnes & Noble does not sell AI books as far as it is aware, takes active measures to exclude AI-generated books from its online catalogue and never knowingly orders them for its stores, and demands that publishers label AI-generated books; he would not ban them outright and said it would stock an AI-written book that says so and does not rip off somebody else.

actions.action: Certify human-written books
actions.evidence: The Authors Guild launched a Human Authored mark in January 2025, first for members' single-author books, with a public database to check certified titles.

ref.title: Authors Guild, Authors Guild Launches "Human Authored" Certification to Preserve Authenticity in Literature, January 2025
ref.finding: On 29 January 2025 the Authors Guild launched a numbered Human Authored mark for covers and promotion, at first only for members' single-author books, with a public database to verify certified titles; spell-check, grammar tools and AI research or brainstorming are allowed if the text itself is human-written.

precedents.event: Spam e-books clog the Kindle store
precedents.parallel: Cheap repackaged text, before generative AI, already let sellers fill Amazon's self-publishing system with near-identical e-books.
precedents.outcome: Reuters reported thousands of e-books a month going through the system, many built from cheap Private Label Rights content and often priced at 99 cents, and a course claiming to teach publishing 10 to 20 a day without writing a word; Amazon said barely differentiated copies of the same book do not improve the customer experience.

ref.title: Barr, Spam clogging Amazon's Kindle self-publishing, Reuters via NBC News, June 2011
ref.finding: Thousands of e-books a month were being published through Amazon's self-publishing system, many of them built from cheaply bought Private Label Rights content and often listed at 99 cents beside other books; one DVD course claimed to teach publishing 10 to 20 Kindle books a day, and an Amazon spokeswoman said undifferentiated or barely differentiated versions of the same book do not improve the customer experience.

nodes.label: Algorithmic tenant scores shut renters out
nodes.summary: US landlords vet renters with screening software, and when its data are wrong or incomplete, applicants are refused with little chance to appeal. A 2022 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau review of more than 24,000 complaints found over 16,000 about incorrect information in tenant reports[1]. SafeRent settled a class action over its score for $2.275 million without admitting fault[2][3].

refs.title: US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, CFPB Reports Highlight Problems with Tenant Background Checks, November 2022
refs.finding: The CFPB analysed more than 24,000 complaints, over 16,000 about incorrect information in tenant background reports, such as negative data belonging to someone else, outdated entries and inaccurate arrest, criminal or eviction records, and about 4,500 about obstacles to getting errors fixed. It said corporate landlords' automated systems replace a holistic review with a single algorithmic score that can hide data errors and magnify the negative impact of erroneous and outdated information.

refs.title: Bedayn, Suit Claiming Racial, Income Bias in Rental Algorithm Settled for $2.2 Million, Associated Press via Insurance Journal, November 2024
refs.finding: Mary Louis, a Black woman, was denied a Massachusetts apartment in spring 2021 by a third-party service that scored rental applicants; her references showing 16 years of early or on-time rent did not help, and the management company said it did not accept appeals and could not override the outcome of the tenant screening. A federal judge approved a settlement of the class action she led in which SafeRent Solutions agreed to pay over $2.2 million, not to include its score on reports in certain cases including when an applicant uses a housing voucher, and to have any new screening score validated by a third party the plaintiffs agree to; SafeRent admitted no fault and said it believes its scores comply with all applicable laws.

refs.title: Cohen Milstein, Louis, et al. v. SafeRent Solutions, et al., case page
refs.finding: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, No. 1:22-cv-10800 (D. Mass.), alleged that the SafeRent Score has a disparate impact on Black and Hispanic rental applicants who use federally funded housing vouchers, because it relies on credit history including non-tenancy debts and does not account for vouchers, which pay most of the rent directly; a July 26, 2023 ruling let the Fair Housing Act claims proceed, and Judge Angel Kelley granted final approval of a $2.275 million settlement on November 20, 2024.

refs.title: US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, Connecticut Fair Housing Center v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, Nos. 23-1118, 23-1166, opinion, February 2026
refs.finding: Decided 20 February 2026: the court disagreed with the district court that the Fair Housing Act excludes certain types of defendants, but held that CoreLogic, whose CrimSAFE platform reported an applicant's criminal history to the landlord, did not cause the denial of housing, because the landlord set its criteria and decided whether to accept the applicant, so the disparate-impact claim failed; it also held the Connecticut Fair Housing Center lacked standing.

nodes.control_note: Landlords keep the final say, which lets vendors argue a denial is not theirs; one appeals court accepted that in 2026, while a district court let fair-housing claims against a scoring vendor go ahead. Settlements can change how a score treats people, but only for the vendor and the class involved.

actions.action: Apply fair-housing law to the companies that score tenants
actions.evidence: A federal court in Massachusetts let Fair Housing Act disparate-impact claims against SafeRent proceed in July 2023, before the case settled; in February 2026 the Second Circuit held that a vendor that only supplies a report does not cause the landlord's denial.

ref.title: Cohen Milstein, Louis, et al. v. SafeRent Solutions, et al., case page
ref.finding: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, No. 1:22-cv-10800 (D. Mass.), alleged that the SafeRent Score has a disparate impact on Black and Hispanic rental applicants who use federally funded housing vouchers, because it relies on credit history including non-tenancy debts and does not account for vouchers, which pay most of the rent directly; a July 26, 2023 ruling let the Fair Housing Act claims proceed, and Judge Angel Kelley granted final approval of a $2.275 million settlement on November 20, 2024.

actions.action: Keep scores off voucher holders' reports and validate new scores
actions.evidence: Under the November 2024 settlement SafeRent may not include its score on reports for applicants using housing vouchers and must have any new screening score validated by a third party the plaintiffs agree to.

ref.title: Bedayn, Suit Claiming Racial, Income Bias in Rental Algorithm Settled for $2.2 Million, Associated Press via Insurance Journal, November 2024
ref.finding: Mary Louis, a Black woman, was denied a Massachusetts apartment in spring 2021 by a third-party service that scored rental applicants; her references showing 16 years of early or on-time rent did not help, and the management company said it did not accept appeals and could not override the outcome of the tenant screening. A federal judge approved a settlement of the class action she led in which SafeRent Solutions agreed to pay over $2.2 million, not to include its score on reports in certain cases including when an applicant uses a housing voucher, and to have any new screening score validated by a third party the plaintiffs agree to; SafeRent admitted no fault and said it believes its scores comply with all applicable laws.

nodes.label: Less fear of judgment makes people more curious
nodes.summary: Whether chatbots make people more curious is unmeasured, but a machine that does not judge can make questions easier to ask. In one lab experiment, people told a virtual interviewer was automated reported less fear of self-disclosure[1]. Yet in one 286-person experiment, a chatbot drew less fear of judgment than a human but no more intimate disclosure[5].

refs.title: Lucas, Gratch, King and Morency, It's only a computer: Virtual humans increase willingness to disclose, Computers in Human Behavior, 2014
refs.finding: In health-screening interviews with a virtual human, participants who believed it was automated rather than operated by a person reported lower fear of self-disclosure and less impression management, displayed sadness more intensely and were rated by observers as more willing to disclose.

refs.title: de Mello Heredia, Uni students are using AI to 'ask stupid questions' and get feedback on their work, The Conversation, August 2025, reporting Henderson et al., Comparing Generative AI and teacher feedback: student perceptions of usefulness and trustworthiness, Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education 2025
refs.finding: A survey of 6,960 students at four Australian universities, August to October 2024: 49% used AI for feedback on their work; 84% rated AI feedback helpful against 82% for lecturers, but 90% considered teacher feedback trustworthy against 60% for AI. Students described worry about being judged or embarrassed when asking teachers; one said AI 'allows me to ask stupid questions that I'm too ashamed to ask my teacher', another that AI feedback 'feels safer and less judgmental'. The paper's abstract says students valued AI feedback partly because it was perceived as less risky than seeking feedback from teachers.

refs.title: Branley-Bell, Brown, Coventry and Sillence, Chatbots for embarrassing and stigmatizing conditions: could chatbots encourage users to seek medical advice?, Frontiers in Communication, September 2023
refs.finding: In a vignette experiment with 402 UK adults recruited to be nationally representative by age, gender and ethnicity, 65.7% chose a doctor in both scenarios and about 12% a chatbot in both; more participants chose a chatbot for embarrassing sexual symptoms than non-sexual ones, and those preferring a chatbot expected it to get them to seek advice sooner. Choices were hypothetical.

refs.title: Pew Research Center, 34% of U.S. adults have used ChatGPT, about double the share in 2023, June 2025
refs.finding: In a survey of 5,123 US adults from 24 February to 2 March 2025, 26% had used ChatGPT to learn something new, up from 8% in March 2023; among adults under 30 the share was 46%.

refs.title: Croes, Antheunis, van der Lee and de Wit, Digital Confessions: The Willingness to Disclose Intimate Information to a Chatbot and its Impact on Emotional Well-Being, Interacting with Computers, June 2024
refs.finding: In a 2 (human vs chatbot) by 2 (low vs high empathy) experiment with 286 participants, self-reported intimacy of disclosure did not differ between human and chatbot partners; participants felt less fear of judgment with the chatbot and more trust in the human; perceived anonymity was the only variable that directly affected disclosure intimacy.

refs.title: Cheng et al., Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence, Science, March 2026
refs.finding: 11 models affirmed users' actions 49% more often than humans; in three preregistered experiments with 2,405 participants, one interaction with a sycophantic AI reduced willingness to take responsibility for and repair interpersonal conflicts and increased conviction of being right, while participants trusted and preferred the sycophantic models.

ref.finding: Participants judged sycophantic responses as more helpful and trustworthy and became more convinced of their own correctness; the release says sycophancy can 'erode the very social friction through which accountability, perspective-taking, and moral growth ordinarily unfold'.

limiters.evidence: Stack Overflow activity fell 25% within six months of ChatGPT's release relative to comparison forums, which the authors say shrinks the public data future models need.

ref.title: del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs, Large language models reduce public knowledge sharing on online Q&A platforms, PNAS Nexus, September 2024
ref.finding: Within six months of ChatGPT's release, Stack Overflow activity fell 25% relative to its Russian and Chinese counterparts and to mathematics Q&A forums, a lower-bound estimate; peer-rated post quality did not change significantly, and the authors conclude LLM adoption reduces the public data needed to train future models.

enablers.action: Train models to resist users' stated opinions
enablers.evidence: In one 2023 study, a light fine-tuning step on synthetic data teaching robustness to user opinions significantly reduced sycophancy on held-out prompts.

ref.title: Wei, Huang, Lu, Zhou and Le, Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models, arXiv, August 2023
ref.finding: Scaling and instruction tuning increased sycophancy in PaLM models up to 540B parameters; adding synthetic data from public NLP tasks that encourages robustness to user opinions in a lightweight fine-tuning step significantly reduced sycophantic behaviour on held-out prompts.

enablers.action: Teach users to check AI answers
enablers.counters: answers trusted less than a teacher's
enablers.evidence: The EU AI Act, as amended, requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy among their staff and others using AI on their behalf; it does not cover the general public directly.

ref.title: EU AI Act, Article 4: AI literacy, accessed October 2026
ref.finding: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support AI literacy of their staff and others operating or using AI systems on their behalf, without having to guarantee any specific level for an individual; the article applies from 2 February 2025.

precedents.event: Computer-assisted interviews for sensitive survey questions
precedents.parallel: Letting people answer embarrassing questions to a computer rather than on a paper form raised what they admitted, an early sign that a machine can feel safer to confide in.
precedents.outcome: In the 1995 National Survey of Adolescent Males, 1,690 respondents were randomly assigned to audio computer-assisted self-interviewing or a paper questionnaire; reported male-male sex, injection drug use and sexual contact with injection drug users were higher by factors of three or more with the computer. The comparison was with paper, not with a human interviewer.

ref.title: Turner, Ku, Rogers, Lindberg, Pleck and Sonenstein, Adolescent sexual behavior, drug use, and violence: increased reporting with computer survey technology, Science, 1998
ref.finding: 1,690 respondents in the 1995 National Survey of Adolescent Males were randomly assigned to audio-CASI or a traditional self-administered questionnaire; audio-CASI produced prevalence estimates for male-male sex, injection drug use and sexual contact with injection drug users higher by factors of 3 or more, and increased reporting of several other risk behaviours.
